description.value: Brazilian digital account for teenagers and young adults, with Pix, a prepaid Mastercard, savings and an allowance feature in one app.

long_description.value: NG.CASH is a Brazilian digital account built for teenagers and young adults, the people who start their financial life with no bank history. The free account gives a personalised prepaid Mastercard, Pix (including by WhatsApp message), an interest-earning savings pot (Cofrinho), an allowance feature, an app that changes its look with user-chosen skins, and a paid subscription tier priced around R$10 a month. Over time it added consortium financing, insurance, fixed-income investing, an AI assistant and, in 2026, Pix Crédito and a payroll-backed private loan (Crédito CLT). The company earns from payments, the subscription and, increasingly, credit. The story starts with the founders' own YouTube Minecraft channel (Neagle), which two of them created at 15 in 2014: as minors they could not receive their international earnings themselves, a pain they later turned into the Neagle Bank experiment, which opened 70,000 accounts in a day and showed retention among minors at more than twice the market average. The founders, who had also built and sold the banking-as-a-service startup Trampolin to Stone, relaunched it as NG.CASH in August 2021 and reached about 900,000 users in a year, almost all through organic reach and influencer culture rather than paid ads. The Central Bank had published that under 10% of Gen Z had made a Pix, which the founders read as an ignored generation. Traction: more than 2 million users in February 2024, 6 million after absorbing rival Z1's customers in February 2025, more than 7 million in July 2025 and more than 8 million accounts in November 2025, with more than US$2 billion moved. It became a Central Bank-authorised payment institution in 2025 and bought a direct-credit licence from BizCapital. It is backed by a16z, Monashees, NEA, Quantum Light, Endeavor Catalyst, 17Sigma, Daphni and, since September 2026, Blockchain Capital. Next: credit for young adults (the CEO's group targets R$1 billion originated by end of 2027), stablecoin products under a VASP licence, and retaining users as they become adults. Brazil stays the priority; regional expansion is mentioned.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: Brazil's Gen Z was a large group the banks ignored. Minors and 18-to-24-year-olds have no credit history, little income, and until recently few ways to hold money or send a Pix; the founders say the Central Bank found fewer than 10% of Gen Z had made a Pix. Parents or big banks served them badly, and big banks treated them as a rounding error. The logic: the founders came from the audience (a YouTube channel with millions of followers, then Trampolin, a banking-as-a-service startup), so they could acquire users organically, speak the user's language and test product ideas cheaply. Their Neagle Bank experiment showed unusually high retention among minors, and Pix made a fast zero-to-Pix account the core product. Why now: Pix (2020) made instant payments free and universal, the Central Bank has opened licences for payment institutions and credit companies, and a generation raised on mobile games already pays subscriptions. Market: our estimate, not a sourced figure. Brazil has roughly 15 million people aged 20 to 24 (IBGE yearbook table) and a similar number aged 15 to 19, so about 30 million, and the company itself speaks of 50 million young people. If a strong outcome means 20 to 30% of that base as active customers (6 to 15 million, against 8 million accounts today) and revenue of R$100 to R$300 a year per active customer from subscription, card, payments and credit, the revenue pool is about R$0.6 to R$4.5 billion a year in Brazil alone; credit is the upside, and the 2027 target of R$1 billion originated is a first step. Comparables: Nubank, and in the US the teen banks Greenlight and Step, show that a youth-first account can become a lifetime primary bank if it keeps users as they age. What is different: distribution through culture (influencers, trap and rap events) and a product that feels like a game, plus its own payment institution and credit licences, instead of a child's savings account; a16z, Monashees and NEA backing add credibility. Fit with Norte (our reading): obsessed founders who know the audience better than any investor, and a stage where a connector can help (Norte joined the 2022 seed alongside a16z, Monashees and unicorn founders, and its network helps with hiring and funds). Risks: users churn when they turn 18 and large banks and Nubank target the same base; credit to young people with thin files carries default risk and needs capital and regulation compliance; and the newest move into stablecoins distracts from the core.

description.value: Brazilian fintech that sells rental guarantees through real estate agencies, replacing the traditional guarantor (fiador) with a fully digital product.

long_description.value: CredAluga is a Brazilian fintech that replaces the guarantor (fiador) and the cash deposit in rental contracts. It works only through real estate agencies, with no intermediaries: the agency offers the product, CredAluga analyses the tenant's risk with its own credit model, and, if the tenant is approved, charges a monthly fee to act as guarantor. If the tenant stops paying, CredAluga pays the owner and the agency on time and takes over the collection. Contracting is 100% digital, the fee can be split into up to 12 instalments, and coverage can reach 35 to 40 times the rent. The line has three products: CredFiança, the traditional fee-based guarantee, now modular, with monthly rates from 8% for the tenant and a recurring commission for the agency; CredReembolsa, with cashback to the tenant and rates from 6%; and Fundo CredAluga, launched at the end of 2024, in which the tenant puts a deposit that is invested in low-risk fixed income, with no monthly fee. The fund turned out to be an easy way in for agencies that did not use the fiança, and add-ons (painting, debt arrangements) are optional. The company was created in 2022 by Daniel Santos and Guilherme Blumer, who come from the real estate market; it started with money from the founders and their families and began operating in the second quarter of 2023, with a little over 500 agencies by October 2024 and a forecast of R$30 million in revenue for 2024, seven times 2023. By September 2025 it said it had more than 30,000 contracts in three years, 1,300 to 1,500 partner agencies in about 500 cities, 200% revenue growth in twelve months, and R$25 million in the fund, aiming at R$1 billion by 2028. The company's own site now claims more than 2,000 agencies. Backers: Caravela Capital, Honey Island by 4UM, Terracota, FJ Labs and Norte in the 2024 seed (R$22 million), Provence Partners, Caravela, Honey Island and Norte in the R$60 million 2025 Series A, and OLX Group, which put US$5 million in as a minority partner in October 2025 and opened the ZAP, Viva Real and OLX portals as a channel. Plans: grow 10 times by 2030, automate more than half of operations by 2026, launch two new rental products, and be the agency's hub for financial products.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: renting in Brazil still needs a guarantee. The owner wants a fiador, a cash deposit of up to three months or an insurance policy, and most tenants have no guarantor or cannot put down the money. Around 6 million rental contracts are signed a year, and almost 80% still use the old methods, according to InfoMoney (2025-05-07), which slows deals and favours the big digital platforms over independent agencies. The logic: CredAluga turns the guarantee into a financial product priced by risk, sold through the agency (who gets a recurring commission, so it is aligned to push it), and backed by its own credit analysis, anti-fraud technology and a legal structure for collection. The fund product lets it add a second source of funding and a cheaper entry point. Why now: renting is growing (20.9% of households were rented in the 2022 Census, up from 12.3% in 2000), the fiador is disappearing, and the market's biggest portal owner, OLX Group, chose CredAluga after ending its exclusive partnership with Creditas in October 2025, which gives it distribution to 34,000 portal clients. Market: the press quotes a potential of up to R$36 billion a year in guarantee volume (InfoMoney, an estimate repeated from the companies). Our own arithmetic: 6 million new contracts a year, of which about 80% (4.8 million) lack a modern guarantee; at an assumed rent of R$2,000 and a fee of 6 to 8% a month (the site's rates), a guaranteed contract pays R$1,400 to R$1,900 a year; if CredAluga reached 5 to 10% of those contracts (240,000 to 480,000), annual revenue would be about R$0.3 to R$0.9 billion in Brazil alone, and the company's 10x target from the 2025 base would be in that range. Different: it sells only through agencies (a channel conflict-free for them, unlike marketplaces), offers a modular menu of three guarantees, and has the OLX data and portals; competitors are Loft (500,000 contracts under management in fiança), Creditas, insurers' seguro-fiança and the capitalisation bonds that dominate the market. Fit with Norte (our reading): two founders from the real estate trade who bring a clear distribution plan, investors from Norte's circle (Caravela, Honey Island, Provence, FJ Labs) and a stage where connecting funds and OLX-type partners matters; Norte followed in both the seed and the Series A, a pattern consistent with the Manifesto's 'follower and connector'. Risks: default losses are the business, so one bad vintage or a recession could erase the fee income, and the fund product multiplies liability if it grows to R$1 billion; OLX and Creditas could both distribute competing products, and the company depends on agencies' goodwill.

description.value: Software for multichannel commerce brands that connects sales channels, forecasts demand and recommends inventory replenishment, usable in its app, Slack, Google Sheets or through AI tools.

long_description.value: Flieber is a New York-based software company that tells multichannel commerce brands how much inventory to hold, where and when to reorder. Customers are direct-to-consumer brands, wholesalers and the agencies or aggregators that run many brands, selling on Amazon, Shopify, Walmart, TikTok Shop, eBay, Etsy and BigCommerce. A data layer pulls live sales and stock from every channel and warehouse; a planning engine forecasts demand (including for new products, by comparing them with similar ones) and recommends purchase orders, warehouse transfers and promotions; and workflows carry out what the team approves. The newest version is built for AI agents: the same data can be queried from the Flieber app, Slack, Google Sheets, an API, a CLI or an MCP server, so that Claude, ChatGPT or a company's own agents can answer questions such as whether a promotion will cause a stockout. It sells self-serve plans (the Shopify app listing shows a monthly subscription of roughly US$300 to start, with a free trial) and managed services in which Flieber's planners join the customer's team. The idea came from CEO Fabricio Miranda, a Brazilian who had founded and sold a water-treatment company, worked at a hedge fund, then became a top Amazon seller; he found that sellers spend about 80% of their time on operations rather than selling, and built Flieber in 2019 with CTO Jair Vercosa. By September 2021 clients sold in 15 countries, 400,000 products ran on the platform, 20 million sales orders had been processed, and the system made over 500,000 calculations a day; the company says it has served more than 1,000 brands since 2019. It raised US$12 million in a Series A co-led by GGV Capital and Monashees in 2021 (about US$20 million in total at that time), with Monashees joining the board, to hire data scientists and engineers, improve its data and expand its APIs. Next, per its current site: AI-agent workflows and managed planning on top of the data layer.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: online selling has become easy, but everything behind it (how much to make or buy, when to order, where to store it, whether a promotion will empty the shelf) is still run in spreadsheets. A brand selling on several channels is always stuck between stockouts, which lose the best-selling product, and overstock, which ties up cash. Miranda says sellers spend about 80% of their time on operations. The logic: pulling live data from every channel and warehouse into one planning engine, then recommending the next best action, turns inventory into a decision made with cash, margin and stockout days in view. Why now: marketplaces and TikTok Shop have multiplied channels, brands are exposed to tariffs, cash cost and long lead times, and AI agents make it possible to ask the plan a question in plain language, which is what the 2026 product is built around. Market: no independent published figure was found, so this is our bottom-up estimate. The product costs about US$300 a month at the entry tier and more for managed services; if the reachable base is 20,000 to 60,000 multichannel brands and agencies worldwide that outgrow spreadsheets (our assumption, not a sourced count) and each pays an average of US$3,000 to US$8,000 a year, the revenue pool is about US$60 million to US$480 million a year; the company says it has served 1,000 brands since 2019, so it holds well under 5% of the low end. A strong outcome would be a leading mid-market planner for e-commerce brands with US$50 to US$100 million of revenue, which is consistent with the pool. What is different: it plans across marketplaces, direct sites and wholesale in one view, includes cash and promotions in the recommendation, and offers planners as a managed service; competitors include Inventory Planner, Cin7, Netstock and the ERP suites, which are not named in the sources read, so this is our reading. Fit with Norte (our reading): a Brazilian-born founder with prior operating experience building from New York, a global market from day one, and investors that Norte's network overlaps with (Monashees co-led the Series A); but the Manifesto says Norte invests early and is a follower, and no source places Norte in Flieber's 2021 round, so the fit is by profile rather than by a documented investment. Risks: a crowded category in which ERPs and Amazon's own tools bundle forecasting; a small base of publicly known customers and no disclosed revenue since 2021; reliance on third-party channel data and APIs; and the pivot toward AI agents is not yet proven.

milestones.value: Fabricio Miranda and Jair Vercosa start Flieber in New York after Miranda, a former Amazon seller, finds that sellers spend about 80% of their time on operations

description.value: A personal assistant service on WhatsApp where human assistants, helped by AI, pay bills, book appointments, buy tickets and run daily errands for affluent Brazilian families on a monthly subscription.

long_description.value: Tempo sells a personal assistant on WhatsApp to Brazilian families who have no time for the "work after work": paying bills and domestic staff, taxes such as IPVA and IPTU, medical appointments and reimbursements, flights, errands and shopping. The customer writes in WhatsApp; a human assistant employed full time by Tempo does the task, helped by AI that handles a first level of the conversation, suggests answers from each client's context and history, and lets one assistant serve more people (the founder says from 5 to 7 clients per assistant in the traditional model to more than 20 with Tempo, with a goal of 3 to 4 times that). Payments run from a prepaid account that the customer tops up and that the assistant uses to pay; every payment needs the owner's approval on WhatsApp, and the account structure is contracted from Celcoin. Tempo makes money from a monthly subscription. When operations began in June 2024 the price was R$490; by April 2025 the entry plan was R$790 a month for one person and R$1,190 for a family, with an average ticket near R$1,100 (Brazil Journal in February 2025 reported about R$1,000, ranging from R$700 to R$2,500). The target is the high-income segments of the banks, such as Itau Personnalite and Santander Unique, and families spending R$30,000 to R$40,000 a month. The idea came from the experience of co-founder and CEO Eduardo Latache, who as a partner at the venture fund Base Partners hired a personal assistant and called it one of his best decisions; he left the fund in early 2024 to turn that experience into a company with Raul Lima, a former CTO of the banking-as-a-service company Bankly. Tempo worked in stealth mode and launched publicly in February 2025 with about 100 paying clients; by April 2025 it had 150 clients, monthly revenue near R$165,000, growth of 40% in the last month, almost entirely by word of mouth, and a team of a little over 30 people (12 in technology and product, about 20 in service). Beyond direct sales, Tempo sees a B2B channel: it already served a family office that offers the service to its clients, four companies were testing it as an employee benefit in February 2025, and companies can hire it for executives. The founder wants to scale with a human in the loop and turn the service into more product and less manual work, possibly with cheaper packages of fewer services. It targeted 1,000 paying clients by the end of 2025 (about R$1 million a month at the then-current ticket). It is backed by Maya Capital, Norte, Caravela Capital and angels, and cites the American company Duckbill as inspiration.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: affluent Brazilian families and professionals carry a daily load of low-value but unavoidable tasks (bills, taxes, domestic payroll, bookings, reimbursements, errands) that a personal assistant solves well, but a human assistant has historically been affordable only to executives. Latache lived this at Base Partners and says the assistant became his most important service provider. The logic: WhatsApp is the main channel of Brazilians and Pix makes small payments instant, so a conversation can be the whole interface, and the prepaid account lets the assistant pay while the owner approves each payment. Generative AI is what changes the economics: if software drafts answers and handles routine steps, one assistant can serve 20 or more people instead of 5 to 7, and the price can fall from a luxury ticket toward the premium-bank customer. The founder compares the idea to Duckbill, a US company that raised a US$25M Series A in 2023 (Startups.com.br), so the model has a foreign comparable, with the difference that in Brazil Pix and WhatsApp replace the credit card. Market size (our estimate): Brazil Journal quotes the founder saying the Personnalite-type segment alone is more than 2 million people. Assumption: if Tempo reached 1% of that segment (20,000 clients) at an average ticket of R$1,100 a month, revenue would be about R$264 million a year (roughly US$47 million at about R$5.6 per US$); at 5% it would be about five times that. The corporate-benefit and family-office channels could widen it, but these are our assumptions and not company figures. A strong outcome is the leader of a new category, with annual revenue in the low hundreds of millions of reais. What is different: unlike a bank concierge or a chatbot, Tempo owns the whole task (human assistant plus AI plus payment account), so it has the context of the client's transactions that, in the founder's words, the bank often lacks; he frames it as 'principality' in the transactional life, not the financial life. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): two experienced founders, one a venture investor who knows the buyers and one a fintech CTO; an early stage where Norte's Manifesto says it helps by connecting people and bringing top funds and angels onto the cap table, which matches the round, where Maya led, Caravela joined and angels such as founders of Trybe, Mottu and UME came in. Risks: the unit economics depend on AI really raising the clients per assistant while keeping the service personal; the price is still high for a mass market; the service depends on WhatsApp's rules and on a third-party payment partner; and the category is young (the same article says another WhatsApp assistant, Alfredo, announced a strategic pause in 2025). Evidence is thin: only two press articles and a Maya Capital post could be read, and the company's own pages could not.

description.value: An AI-native platform that lets banks, fintechs and online merchants detect and stop fraud and money laundering in real time, while approving more legitimate customers.

long_description.value: GatekeeperX sells software that lets banks, fintechs, payment processors and online merchants decide in real time whether a transaction or a new customer is legitimate, and manage fraud and anti-money-laundering (AML) work on the same platform. Its pitch is to stop the criminals and let the good customers through without friction: a decision engine answers in about 100 milliseconds, using each client's own history compared with millions of similar transactions. The platform brings together four solutions that can be bought separately or integrated: transaction evaluation, monitoring, onboarding and device checks, and disputes. Customers build rules in a visual workflow, test them in simulations before deploying, feed them with native machine-learning models and smart lists that update themselves, and see approval, fraud and anomaly metrics in dashboards with alerts. It also maps fraud rings by linking users, devices and transactions, and uses AI agents that investigate alerts, explain decisions and suggest rule changes around the clock. On 2026-11-11 it launched an MCP connector so that analysts can ask ChatGPT, Claude or Copilot about their real fraud data, simulate rules and manage controls in plain language. The company makes money by selling this software to financial and e-commerce companies, with service levels written into contracts (it cites more than 99.998% of decisions within the expected time). It came from four people, two Argentines and two Colombians, who joined Rappi in the same month about eight years before and built payments and fraud tools there and at Mercado Libre, Stori, Aplazo, Oracle, Idemia and PayU. Carlos Ayalde, who was VP of Payments and Fraud Prevention at Rappi and general manager at Stori, is CEO; the other three leaders on the company page, Renny Hernandez, Martin Moreyra and Diego Nieto, are two engineers and a product leader. They started the company in 2025, and describe it as AI-native from the first day: the team uses AI to prototype and ship and builds agents into the product. Traction: the company announced its arrival in Colombia in January 2026 saying it already processed more than 20 million transactions in more than five countries; by July 2026 it said about 50 million transactions a month; a case on its site says a tier-1 regional acquirer replaced both an external provider and an in-house rules system, gaining 3 points of approval rate and cutting 3-D Secure use by 20% without more chargebacks (company figures). It was named among Forbes Colombia's 100 startups to watch in 2025 and in the Colombia Early Stage 100, has 28 people on LinkedIn, sponsored the Febraban fraud and anti-money-laundering congresses in Sao Paulo in November 2026 as it expands into Brazil, and plans to enter the United States in 2027. Its investors are Monashees, H Twenty Capital, Norte Ventures and, since May 2026, Global Paytech Ventures.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: banks, fintechs and online merchants in Latin America lose large sums to fraud and, at the same time, reject legitimate customers. The company cites more than US$80 billion of yearly regional fraud and financial-crime losses and says over 40% of legitimate transactions are rejected for no good reason (company figures, not independently checked). Fraud and AML teams also work in separate tools, so the same account is investigated twice, at different times. The logic and why now: real-time payments (Pix in Brazil, Bre-B in Colombia) leave no time for a manual review, so decisions must be automatic and cheap; and modern AI lets a vendor propose rules, explain decisions and investigate alerts, which the founders say replaces static rule lists run by large analyst teams. The team built exactly these systems at Rappi, Mercado Libre and Stori, so they know what a buyer needs. Market size: a published estimate from an analyst firm, Fortune Business Insights (quoted by Impactotic), puts the global fraud-detection market at US$67.1 billion in 2026 growing to US$243.7 billion in 2034. For Latin America we have no published figure; our bottom-up assumption is 500 to 1,500 financial institutions, processors and large merchants that could buy a platform at about US$100,000 to US$250,000 a year, which gives roughly US$50 million to US$375 million a year. A strong outcome would be a regional leader holding 10 to 20% of that, plus entry into the US. All of these inputs are our assumptions. What is different: one platform for fraud and AML and for identity, device and transaction signals; simulation before deployment; AI agents and an MCP connector for analysts; and local, hands-on service and real-time data delivery. The CEO says it already competes with vendors that have been in the market for ten years, and a published case says it replaced both an outside provider and an in-house system at a regional acquirer. These are company claims. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): operator-founders with deep domain experience, the kind of 'obsessed founders who know more than we do' that Norte's Manifesto says it backs; and a Brazil expansion where Norte's network of operators can open doors to banks and fintechs. Monashees, H Twenty Capital and later Global Paytech Ventures (a payments-focused fund) are co-investors. Risks: long enterprise sales cycles and trust requirements for a vendor that is two years old; incumbents with large installed bases; concentration in a few big customers; and expansion across several countries and regulators with a team of about 28 people.

milestones.value: Named in Forbes Colombia's list of 100 startups to watch and in the Colombia Early Stage 100 (Colombia Techweek and Numundo Ventures), early recognition for a company founded that year.
Announced its arrival in Colombia as a platform for fraud and AML, already processing more than 20 million transactions in more than five countries.
Added Global Paytech Ventures as a strategic investor to speed up its international expansion and the AI-first evolution of the product.
Reached about 50 million transactions a month with over 99.998% of decisions on time, began expanding to Brazil and set the United States as the next step for 2027.
Launched an MCP connector so fraud teams can query real fraud data, simulate rules and manage controls from ChatGPT, Claude or Copilot.
Sponsored the Febraban anti-money-laundering and fraud congresses in Sao Paulo (17 and 18 November), its first visible push into the Brazilian bank market.

description.value: A telecom technology company that started as a 100% digital mobile operator in Brazil and now sells digital platforms (apps, plans, billing and portability) to mobile and broadband operators.

long_description.value: Nomo began in 2021 as a 100% digital mobile operator for Brazilians, an MVNO (a virtual operator that buys network capacity wholesale and resells it) with a native app, no 0800 line and no queues, plans that could be changed, paused or cancelled at any time, and charges only for what was used. Its infrastructure came from Telecall, which represents Vivo, and its first systems were outsourced; the founders wanted to rebuild the software stack of a telecom company the way fintechs like Nubank and Stone had rebuilt banking and payments. The idea came from Henrique Garrido, who had been at Endeavor, NeoAssist and Stone, and from three long-time colleagues from Stone (Gabriel Lima on product, Marcos Augusto on technology and data, and Pedro Geneze on marketing and growth); he decided in April 2020 to start a company and spent a year looking for backers. In November 2021 Nomo closed a round of about R$14 million led by Iporanga Ventures with Norte Ventures and individual investors such as Elie Horn, Ronaldo Iabrudi, the family office of Jacques Nasser and Guilherme Weege, and started operating with 500 test customers and a waiting list of thousands, first in Sao Paulo and Rio. By February 2023 it had several thousand customers with an NPS near 80, a base growing 30% a month and 35% of sales coming from member-get-member referrals. The consumer business was hard to make profitable, mainly because independent MVNOs have no large sales counter behind them and pay a high cost to win customers, so the founders pivoted to selling their technology to other operators. That B2B business, Wave Tech, offers carriers redesigned apps and plans, digital number portability, billing and CRM systems, and software that connects broadband operators to independent fibre networks. In January 2024 it had about R$3 million of annualised revenue from three customers. In January 2024 the listed telecom-software company Bemobi bought 51% of Wave Tech for R$11.5 million (R$4 million new capital and R$7.5 million paid to Nomo, mostly returning the 2021 investors' money), with put and call options on the remaining 49% exercisable in 2029; the three remaining founders stayed on. Mobile Time reported in April 2025 that Wave, run by Garrido as CEO, had contracts with four operators in Brazil, two in Mexico, one in Colombia and one in Chile, that revenue grew 4.5 times in 2024 with the first profit, that it doubled in the first quarter of 2025, and that about 30% of revenue came from outside Brazil. The consumer MVNO, meanwhile, is now run by the Brazilian group Algar through its innovation hub Brain: it had 5,000 customers in May 2025 and about 9,000 lines in December 2025 in five cities, sells mostly through Meta and TikTok and through an AI seller called Nina, and Algar plans to turn the platform into a service for ISPs and other brands.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: Brazilian mobile telecom is concentrated (98% of 246 million lines were with three operators in 2021) and customers are unhappy: about 130 million lines change operator every year, according to the partner of Iporanga Ventures quoted by Startupi, and the founders said churn was close to 50%. Legacy systems were built to sell expensive voice minutes to few people and are now used to sell cheap data to many. The logic: bring the fintech playbook to telecom, with a native app, self-service and its own software, and use the MVNO model to sell without building towers. Why now: 5G, regulatory openings and a wave of fintech-trained operators. The team (ex-Stone) had taken a company from zero to IPO, which investors cited as decisive. Market size (our estimate, since no independent figure was read): the consumer route is a share of about 246 million lines but, as the Algar executive says in Mobile Time (2025-12), 'in Brazil the MVNO goes sideways, nobody got it right yet'. The B2B route is smaller but sturdier: Bemobi alone serves more than 100 mobile operators in 50 countries and 200 broadband operators (Brazil Journal 2024). Assuming 300 operators that could pay US$100,000 to US$300,000 a year for apps, billing and portability software, the market is about US$30 million to US$90 million a year, and a strong outcome for Wave is a few percent to 10% of that plus platform services. These are our assumptions. What was different: a product-led team that rebuilt systems and the app experience, an NPS around 80 against a telecom average that the CEO put at about 5% in Brazil, and referral-led growth; later, a vendor that avoids lock-in and multi-year contracts, in the CEO's words 'vendor 2.0'. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): founders with Stone's operating experience, in a concentrated market where Norte could join a round led by a specialist fund (Iporanga) and supply other investors, which fits the Manifesto's idea of putting funds and angels on the cap table at an early stage. Risks, which materialised: consumer MVNOs depend on expensive customer acquisition and thin margins, and the 2021 investors only recovered their money in the 2024 sale (Brazil Journal); the B2B business relies on a handful of operators and on Bemobi's option rights.

milestones.value: Launched the Nomo digital mobile operator with 500 test customers and a waiting list of thousands, first in Sao Paulo and Rio, using Telecall (Vivo) for network capacity, and closed its first institutional round.
Pivoted from consumer telecom to B2B, selling its apps, billing, portability and fibre-integration software to operators, after finding the consumer model hard to make profitable.
Reached several thousand customers with an NPS near 80, a base growing 30% a month and 35% of sales from member-get-member referrals.
Revenue grew 4.5 times and the B2B business was profitable for the first time.
Bemobi bought 51% of Wave Tech for R$11.5 million, with call and put options on the rest in 2029, bringing the software to its base of more than 100 mobile and 200 broadband operators.
Wave had contracts with four operators in Brazil, two in Mexico, one in Colombia and one in Chile, with revenue doubling in the first quarter and about 30% from outside Brazil.
The Nomo mobile operator, now run by Algar, had 5,000 customers and plans to become a white-label MVNE for ISPs and to move onto Claro's network by mid-2025.
Nomo by Algar reached about 9,000 lines in five cities, selling mostly through Meta, TikTok and an AI seller called Nina, and preparing a platform to sell the digital MVNO model to other brands.

description.value: A technology and back-office platform for Brazil's private credit market, running fund administration and custody, securitisation and banking services for FIDCs and other structured products.

long_description.value: Kanastra builds the technology and back office for Brazil's private credit market. Companies that lend (fintechs, factoring firms, banks) and the investors that fund them use Kanastra to set up and run structured funds, above all FIDCs (receivables funds), and securitisation products such as CRIs, CRAs, LCAs and LCIs. Before Kanastra, creating a FIDC meant hiring several providers, each doing one part of the process; Kanastra puts fund management, administration and custody, securitisation (issuing, managing and safekeeping the products) and banking services for funds, such as payment accounts, Pix, boletos, CCBs and commercial notes, on one proprietary platform with end-to-end automation and data tools for originators, investors and managers. It earns a commission that Brazil Journal estimates at 0.1% to 0.5% a year on the assets it serves, which at R$35 billion in October 2025 implies roughly R$35 million to R$175 million a year; the company does not disclose revenue. The company was founded in January 2022 by Gustavo Mapeli, who had worked at BNP Paribas in London, BCG and SoftBank, and Manuel Netto, who came from ZX Ventures (AB InBev's innovation arm). The two had already started Kardinal in 2020, a wealth and alternative-assets manager for clients outside the Rio-Sao Paulo axis, and created Kanastra because they originated many structured products and found the back office poorly served. In June 2023, with a US$13 million seed round, it had 35 clients, including Creditas, SolFacil and Patria, and R$2 billion under custody. In 2023 revenue grew 11 times and assets 13 times, to about R$7 billion. In May 2024 it made its first acquisition, Limine DTVM, a fund administration and custody firm, giving the group about 120 vehicles, 100 originators and 300 institutional investors. A R$110 million Series A in June 2024 led by Kaszek was followed in January 2025 by an investment from Itau Unibanco, through Kinea Ventures, together with a commercial partnership in which Intrag DTVM offers fiduciary administration of FIDCs with Kanastra; assets under service then went from R$15 billion to R$35 billion in 2025. In October 2025 a R$170 million Series B led by F-Prime (Fidelity's venture arm), with IFC, financed new products, more automation of liability-side processes such as capital calls, and more clients. At that point Kanastra served nearly 200 clients, including Itau, XP, Banco BV, ABC Brasil, Patria and JGP, with more than 250 operations, and was growing its team by only 35% while assets more than doubled. It has offices in Sao Paulo and Uberlandia, a LinkedIn page with 224 people in November 2026, and its posts show events and product themes such as multi-originator FIDCs and the electronic duplicata, whose testing period runs to January 2027.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: Brazilian private credit has grown fast (a 230% rise in five years, according to F-Prime's partner in the Series B announcement) but its operations still run on fragmented providers, manual processes and legacy systems. Each lender that wants to fund itself through a FIDC or securitisation needs an administrator, a custodian, a bank, an escrow account and data reporting, usually from different firms. The logic: the founders originated structured products themselves and saw that the back office, not the origination, was the bottleneck. A single software-led platform with regulatory licences (DTVM, securitiser, banking-as-a-service) can automate the asset side (policy checks already run automatically) and the liability side, and so serve more funds per employee. Why now: private credit is taking share from bank lending, regulators are moving to electronic duplicatas and standardised structures, and fintechs depend on FIDCs for funding. Market size: Brazil Journal (2023 and 2024) estimates the assets under custody and administration of structured funds and securitised products at about R$1.6 trillion, with the largest providers being BRL Trust (R$400 billion, mostly private equity funds) and Oliveira Trust (R$120 billion). At the 0.1% to 0.5% fee range reported there, the fee pool is roughly R$1.6 billion to R$8 billion a year; at R$35 billion Kanastra holds about 2% of the base. If it reached 10% of today's base, revenue would be about R$160 million to R$800 million a year, before market growth. These figures are the press's estimates and our arithmetic, not company disclosures. What is different: it combines fund services, securitisation and banking in one platform, grows with a small team (assets doubled while headcount rose 35%), and is the technology partner of Itau, XP and BV. Competitors named by Brazil Journal are Oliveira Trust, BRL Trust and Vortx in fund administration and custody, and Opea and Virgo in securitisation. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): operator-founders with deep market knowledge, and a seed round in which Norte joined US and Brazilian specialist funds (Valor Capital and Quona co-led) at the stage the Manifesto describes as bringing 'top funds and angels onto cap tables'; Norte's network of fintech operators can help with the originators who are Kanastra's clients. Risks: regulation and licences (Kanastra is a regulated entity, and the rules for FIDCs and duplicatas are changing); competition from larger incumbents and banks building in-house; credit-cycle exposure through its originator clients; and the challenge the CEO names himself, keeping quality as assets grow from R$7 billion to R$100 billion.

sub_sector.value: Private credit infrastructure and fund administration

milestones.value: Revenue grew 11 times and assets 13 times in the year, reaching about R$7 billion under custody and administration.
Closed a US$13 million seed round with 35 clients, including Creditas, SolFacil and Patria, and R$2 billion in assets under custody.

Kanastra holds CVM licences as manager, administrator and securitiser and a Central Bank licence as a direct credit company, has 70 operations (20 from fintechs) and more than 90 people, and, with Limine DTVM and Trochia, wins the tender to administer the first FIDC structured by a Brazilian state (Cohab Minas).
Made its first acquisition, Limine DTVM, a fund administration and custody firm, giving the group about 120 vehicles, 100 originators and 300 institutional investors and R$7 billion in assets.
Raised a R$110 million Series A led by Kaszek, with more than 130 operations and about 100 people (half in product and technology).
Itau Unibanco, already a client, became a shareholder through Kinea Ventures and started a commercial partnership in which Intrag DTVM offers FIDC administration with Kanastra.
Raised a R$170 million Series B led by F-Prime with IFC, with R$35 billion in assets under service in more than 250 operations after growing 150% in a year, and nearly 200 clients.

description.value: A Brazilian commerce-technology company that started by digitising and restocking small shops and now runs an ecosystem that helps brands and sellers grow on marketplaces, with sales programmes, management software and logistics.

long_description.value: Dolado began in 2020 as a platform to help small shopkeepers in peripheral neighbourhoods and small towns of Brazil go digital and restock. The idea came from Khalil Yassine, an engineer who left Citi's investment banking in November 2019: on weekends he helped his father's small shop in the north of Sao Paulo and saw him leave the store twice a week to buy goods in the centre of the city, paying cash in a informal market with no bargaining power. With Guilherme Freire and Marcelo Loureiro, who had been studying an Indian inventory start-up and were introduced by an iFood co-founder, he planned a marketplace connecting suppliers to small merchants. The pandemic closed the shops in March 2020, so the first product became a free digital catalogue: the founders went door to door teaching merchants to photograph products and share them, the first client was Yassine's father, and the product spread when a merchant posted it in a Facebook group; it reached 5,000 merchants in six months and had more than 3,000 registered companies and 77% monthly growth when the seed round was announced in December 2020. It made money from a network of partners whose services the merchants used, and used local community leaders, trained as business analysts, to guide shopkeepers. In March 2021 it launched the product that became its core, automatic restocking: instead of only a marketplace, Dolado bought goods from suppliers, mainly mobile-phone and computer accessories from Sao Paulo's popular shopping streets, bundled the orders of many merchants and delivered them through third parties, earning the difference in price. By April 2022 more than 20,000 merchants used it, revenue had grown 19 times in a year and the team had grown from 20 to 100 people in 2021, when it raised a R$53 million Series A led by Valor Capital Group. NeoFeed reported in December 2024 that after the B2B marketplace market turned and large players became indebted, Dolado chose to hold on to cash, a decision it presented as the reason it kept going; the same piece describes it as a platform that connects digital sellers to industry. Today its LinkedIn page describes an ecosystem that accelerates the growth of brands and sellers on marketplaces, with sales-acceleration programmes, a management platform integrated with the sales channels in Brazil and logistics solutions; it has 68 people on LinkedIn, and in October 2026 it organised, with Agent.Shop, the first Agentic Commerce Summit in Brazil in Rio de Janeiro (about 400 registered for 150 seats), a sign of its focus on AI agents that buy and sell. The dates of the change from small shopkeepers to marketplace sellers, the business model today and the current traction figures could not be found in readable sources; the company site does not render without JavaScript.

investment_thesis.value: The problem (2020 case): millions of small Brazilian shops outside city centres lose time and margin to buy stock in informal wholesale areas, and have no digital tools; platforms built for larger retailers did not serve them. The founder lived it in his father's shop. The logic: collect many small orders, buy them together from suppliers and deliver, so the merchant saves time and gets better prices and the supplier reaches places it could not; start with a free catalogue to build trust and data, then sell the restocking. Why then: the pandemic pushed small merchants to digitise, WhatsApp was already their sales channel, and venture money was available. Market size (our estimate; no published figure was read): the company had more than 20,000 registered merchants in April 2022 (Startups.com.br). Assumption: if it reached 100,000 merchants and each bought R$5,000 a month through the platform at a gross margin of about 6%, gross profit would be about R$30 million a month, or R$360 million a year. These inputs are our assumptions and the real margin is unknown. What was different: field work with community analysts, a free first product, and an operation that bought and delivered goods instead of only listing them. Comparable companies abroad, as the founders cited, include an Indian inventory start-up for small shops. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): a founder from a merchant family with an investment-banking background, supported by Valor Capital, Global Founders Capital and angels from iFood, Stone and Olist, in an early round where Norte's connection to founders and angels from those companies is the kind of value the Manifesto describes. Risks, partly realised: B2B marketplaces turned out to be capital-hungry with thin margins (NeoFeed, December 2024), and the company has since changed its focus to marketplace sellers; the supply side depended on a few popular-commerce supplier areas; and little public evidence of current revenue exists, so the thesis rests on 2020-2022 sources. Confidence is low.

milestones.value: Launched a free digital catalogue for small shopkeepers in peripheral neighbourhoods and small towns, taught door to door; it reached 5,000 merchants in six months after spreading in a Facebook group.
The team grew from 20 to 100 people during the year.
Launched automatic restocking, buying goods from suppliers for many merchants and delivering them, which turned Dolado from a catalogue into a purchasing and delivery business.
Passed 20,000 merchants impacted and reported 19 times more revenue than the year before.
NeoFeed reported that Dolado had weathered the downturn of B2B marketplaces by preserving cash, and described it as a platform connecting digital sellers to industry.
Organised the first Agentic Commerce Summit in Brazil, in Rio de Janeiro on 8 October with Agent.Shop, drawing about 400 registrations for a 150-seat room.
