description.value: Brazilian credit-infrastructure company that lets retailers and other businesses offer their own consumer credit under their own brand, covering funding, risk models, Pix payments and AI-run collections.

long_description.value: Ume is a Brazilian credit-infrastructure company that lets retailers, marketplaces and service businesses offer their own credit to their customers, under their own brand, and keep the financial profit that normally goes to banks and card issuers. The platform covers the whole credit cycle: the legal and funding structure of each operation (including access to capital-markets funding through FIDC funds), credit policy and risk modelling, a sales and payment layer integrated with Pix, and customer service and collections run largely by AI agents. The site says the proprietary neural-network credit model has run since 2017, that about 95% of customer service is automated, and that the company handles over 270 thousand tickets a month. The company began inside academia: its first idea was a PhD thesis at UFMG, by computer scientists including Marco Cristo, on using a deep neural network to price credit better for one of the largest retailers in northern Brazil. Berthier Ribeiro, a former partner at Méliuz and ex special-situations analyst at BTG, heard about it through his father, the computer scientist Berthier Ribeiro-Neto, and set out to take it to market. From 2019 Ume operated in Manaus as a lender, taking the risk itself: a digital 'crediário' (store instalment credit) for regional retailers with revenue of R$40 million to R$500 million a year, where the consumer downloaded the app, was approved in about five minutes and could split a purchase into up to four instalments, and the retailer was paid in two days for a discount fee, while Ume also earned interest from the consumer. In 2021 it lent R$26 million to 47 thousand people; in 2023 it lent R$220 million through more than 2,000 retailers. Its edge in this period was a lower default rate (30% under the crediário average, its CEO said in 2024) and, from 2024, payment by Pix QR code, which cut transaction costs compared with private-label card competitors such as DMCard. After a seed round in April 2022 it expanded from the North to the Northeast, then to the South and Centre-West, and in 2025 it changed its model from being a lender itself to being the infrastructure that lets other businesses run their own credit. By September 2025 it had about 6,000 partner stores and expected R$1 billion of annualised volume that year. In 2026 its site reports more than 4 million users, over 10 thousand points of sale, R$1.2 billion of credit granted in 2026 and over R$850 million raised from investors in equity and debt, and the company expects R$2 billion of volume in 2026. Backers include NFX, Canary, BigBets, Clocktower Ventures, Norte Ventures, PayPal Ventures, Globo Ventures, FJ Labs, Valor Capital Group and Bewater; loans are funded by FIDCs bought by institutions such as Itaú, Bradesco, XP, Credit Saison, Western Asset, Verde and Milenio. Berthier Ribeiro-Neto joined as CTO in 2024. The Series B was meant to fund proprietary technology, AI infrastructure and commercial scale, and to expand beyond retail and, later, to other countries.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: in Brazil, store credit ('crediário') is a large market, estimated by Ume's co-founder at about R$200 billion a year in 2022, but it was run by a few large retailers; most mid-sized and regional retailers sell on card instalments, so the issuer keeps the credit margin and the retailer carries the cost of the sale. Ume's CEO says 80% of the 300 largest retailers do not offer credit at the point of sale. Logic: a retailer already owns the customer, the sale and the data, so it is the natural originator of credit if it can get what it lacks: a credit model, funding, collections and a payment rail. Ume sells all of that as one service, so it can earn from the credit spread and platform fees without the retailer building a financial arm. Why now: Pix is cheap and instant, FIDCs let institutional money fund consumer receivables, and AI makes customer service and collections far cheaper per account. Market size and share (our estimate): the R$200 billion figure comes from the company's own co-founder (Brazil Journal 2022), so treat it as an upper bound. Ume expects about R$2 billion of volume in 2026, roughly 1% of that figure. If the infrastructure model reaches 5% of a R$200 billion market, that is R$10 billion of annual volume; at an assumed 4 to 8% net revenue on volume (our assumption, from credit spread plus fees), that would be R$400 to 800 million of yearly revenue. These are assumptions, not company guidance. What is different: the team started as a lender, so it has six years of default data and a neural-network credit model built by PhDs (the CEO claims 30% fewer defaults than the crediário average and 30% more approvals at the same risk), and it has already raised R$850 million-plus from equity and debt investors, including large Brazilian institutions. Competitors named: DMCard (private-label cards, the segment leader in 2024), BaaS and credit-as-a-service providers (some are partners, per the CEO), and banks. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): Norte says it invests in obsessed founders and in networks, and brings top funds onto cap tables. Ume's seed in 2022 was co-led by US funds (NFX, Canary) with Norte participating, and later rounds brought PayPal Ventures, Valor and Bewater, the kind of syndicate a connector-style seed investor helps assemble. Risks: credit losses in a downturn or a higher-rate cycle, dependence on FIDC funding appetite, regulation of credit and of Pix instalments, and big banks or card networks entering the same niche. The business also burned cash while growing, so the shift from lender to infrastructure must prove its unit economics.

milestones.value: The seed of Ume is a PhD thesis at UFMG on using a deep neural network to price retail credit; the credit model the company still runs dates from this year.
Ume starts operating in Manaus as a lender, giving digital store credit to customers of regional retailers in the North and building its own loan book.
A US$5.5M seed round lets Ume start a national expansion, beginning with the Northeast, with a target of 450 retailers by year-end; it also took US$4.5M of debt.
Ume lends R$220M through more than 2,000 retailers, over twice the R$100M of the year before, funded by a R$60M FIDC.

Ume uses Pix QR-code payment in its credit product, lowering its cost per transaction against private-label card rivals, and raises a new R$100M FIDC; it now operates in the North, Northeast, South and Centre-West.
Berthier Ribeiro-Neto, who led Google's engineering centre in Brazil, becomes Ume's CTO.
Ume changes from being a lender itself to being infrastructure for other businesses to run their own credit, using the know-how built over six years of lending.
Ume reaches about 6,000 partner stores and positions itself as a platform that gives retailers 'bank power', targeting R$1 billion of annualised volume that year.
Ume structures a R$150M Feeder FIDC, a vehicle that lets it place capital across several retailer-specific credit funds.
Ume raises R$500M through FIDCs, oversubscribed, with Itaú, Bradesco, XP, Milenio, Verde and Credit Saison, and expects R$2 billion of volume in 2026.

description.value: Brazilian fintech whose platform lets investment advisers and family offices create tailor-made investment products from fractions of fixed-income and credit assets, using tokenisation and AI.

long_description.value: Nexa is a São Paulo fintech that builds tailor-made investment products for the clients of financial advisers, family offices and wealth managers. Instead of picking from a shelf of standard products (CDB, COE, LCI, CRA, funds), an adviser describes what a client wants to achieve, such as a monthly income from 2028 or cash for a child's studies abroad in 2027, and Nexa assembles a product from fractions of existing assets chosen for risk, term, liquidity and cash flow. The assets come from institutional originators and include credit-card receivables, trade receivables (duplicatas), consortium quotas, payroll-type loans and loans backed by the FGTS severance fund; the company says it rejects 90% to 98% of the opportunities it reviews. Assets are securitised and tokenised on a blockchain, which lets it split them into very small pieces (down to R$1) and regroup them to match each client. The CEO calls the result a 'mini-ETF'. The company holds licences for asset management, securitisation and distribution, buys assets through an FIDC fund and carries them until they are resold. It earns a margin on each product, which the CEO compares to an investment bank's, with the take rate varying by operation. The founders are Lucas Danicek (CEO, formerly at Nest and Pátria, then at Tera, the family office of Pátria's founders), Eduardo Furuie (fixed income and credit at Pátria and Tera) and Bernardo Mascarenhas (a former M&A and debt-capital-markets banker who founded the credit start-up Noverde, later bought by Dotz, and stayed at Dotz until 2024). The company was set up in early 2024 and ran in beta until mid-2025, when it began to look for its first clients: multi and single family offices and offices of independent advisers. By July 2025 it had three institutional clients and expected to move R$500 million in 2025 and R$1 billion in 2026. In February 2025 it launched tokens that replicate exclusive funds of single family offices and wealth managers. In October 2026 it launched Nexa Genesis, a platform in which an AI turns a plain-language request into a product in about two minutes, so advisers can create products without waiting for Nexa to structure them. The company said it had issued 375 products by the end of August 2026 and 800 by the end of September, that it had grown about 25% a month for two years, and it projects five-fold growth in 2027. Its site says partners hold more than R$200 billion in assets under management. Backers are Norte Ventures (since the pre-seed), MAYA Capital (which led the R$25 million seed in July 2025), Newtopia, Clocktower Ventures, Kiara Capital and Citrino Ventures, and in 2026 Valor Capital Group and Citrino made a further investment of undisclosed size. A new round is planned for 2027. The offer today is fixed income and private credit in reais and dollars, with shares and other assets to be added.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: advisers and family offices in Brazil serve clients with different goals, tax situations and cash-flow needs, but the products they can distribute are standard shelf items made for a mass audience, so each client has to fit the product. Large investors get tailor-made structures from banks; smaller wealthy clients do not. Logic: if assets can be securitised, tokenised and cut into small fractions, a platform can combine them into a product built around one client's goal at low cost, and software (now AI) can do the structuring that used to take a team. Why now: the regulatory and technical base for securitisation and tokenisation in Brazil is maturing, the number of investment advisers has grown from 4,565 in 2016 to about 27,000 and independent offices need ways to stand out, and generative AI lets the structuring be done in minutes. Market size and share (our estimate): the company says its partners hold more than R$200 billion under management (its site). ANCORD counted 26,679 credentialed advisers in September 2026, of whom about 6,300 are not tied to institutions (26,679 minus 20,413). The CEO's own arithmetic (Brazil Journal 2025) is 100 adviser offices with R$2.5 billion each, a 5% share of wallet and a 5% take rate, giving R$500 million of yearly revenue, which that article's reporter calls aggressive. A more careful version: R$250 billion of assets at 100 offices, 5% share = R$12.5 billion a year placed, at a 1% to 2% take rate (our assumption, close to the 1% scenario Brazil Journal used) = R$125 to 250 million of revenue. A strong outcome is therefore a business with revenue in the low hundreds of millions of reais, not a mass-market one, unless it moves into distribution to end clients. What is different: it builds the product from the client's goal and sells to advisers, not to end investors; it controls originating, curating and securitising (licences for management, securitisation and distribution), and its founders come from Pátria and Tera, so they know the buyers and originators. Competitors and comparables: other tokenisation and fixed-income distribution platforms in Brazil, bank-run structured products and the large brokerages' shelves. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): Norte says it backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders and works as a connector, bringing top funds onto cap tables and helping to generate revenue from day zero. Norte was in the pre-seed and followed in the seed, led by MAYA, which fits that follower-and-connector pattern; an experienced founding team with access to originators and family offices is where the network matters. Risks: the model needs funding, distribution and intellectual capital at once, and an industry executive told Brazil Journal that it risks adverse selection if other channels reject its products; take rates are thin and scalability is doubted; tokenisation rules are still evolving; and its volume figures are the company's own and unaudited.

milestones.value: Lucas Danicek and Eduardo Furuie, joined by Bernardo Mascarenhas, start Nexa to build personalised investment products for advisers, after careers at Pátria, Tera and Dotz.
Nexa launches tokens that replicate exclusive funds of single family offices and wealth managers, issued on demand to match a client's risk, return and redemption terms.
After a beta phase, Nexa starts looking for its first clients, family offices and independent adviser offices; by July it has three institutional clients.
A R$25M seed round led by MAYA Capital funds the push to originate and distribute R$500M of assets in 2025 and R$1B in 2026.
Nexa has issued 800 products, against 375 by the end of August, as advisers begin to use its new platform to create them.
Nexa launches Nexa Genesis, an AI platform that turns a plain-language client goal into a custom product in about two minutes, and projects five-fold growth in 2027.

description.value: Brazilian company that offers employers a single platform for flexible employee benefits, HR management and corporate expenses, with a card and app that let workers choose how to spend their benefits budget.

long_description.value: Flash is a São Paulo company that sells companies one platform for employee benefits, people management and corporate expenses. It began as the 'flexible benefits' alternative to the meal and food vouchers of Alelo, Sodexo (now Pluxee), VR and Ticket (Edenred): the employer sets a monthly budget and the worker spends it where they choose, on one pink Mastercard-branded card and an app, instead of several single-purpose cards. Today the product is three connected lines: benefits management (multi-benefit card, transport vouchers, PAT-compliant meal and food benefits, health and well-being partners, a discount club), HR management (admission and dismissal, recruiting with AI, time and attendance) and expense management (corporate card, reimbursements, expense reports). The company says its card has zero fee, and it earns from the benefits and card business and, increasingly, from software subscriptions for HR and finance. The idea came to Pedro Lane while he tried to give meal vouchers to the staff of his own agency and saw that workers accepted losing part of the value (receiving R$400 for each R$500 voucher) to turn the benefit into cash, in a market where a few incumbents held about 95% of it and had little reason to innovate. He built the company with his brother Guilherme Lane, who handled technology, and Ricardo Salem, who became CEO. Work began at the end of 2018 and the product launched in July 2019 with clients from the start, aimed first at small and mid-sized companies that the large incumbents neglected. Seed money came in January 2019 from Kevin Efrusy, Patrick Sigrist and Guilherme Bonifácio (iFood's founders) and Global Founders Capital, and a Series A followed at the end of 2019 led by Monashees; in total the company had received about US$9 million in its first year. In July 2020 it served 60 thousand people at 1,500 companies; the pandemic brought new services such as mental-health support, bill payment and home-office purchases. By mid-2021, after 700 days, it had about 200 thousand users at about 4,000 companies and expected to move R$2 billion that year. A US$22 million Series B led by Tiger Global (June 2021) turned it into an all-in-one HR platform, and a Series C of more than US$100 million led by Battery Ventures and Whale Rock (March 2022) paid for product and hiring; the team then had 300 people. It bought ExpenseOn (July 2022) to enter expense management and FolhaCerta (March 2023) to build its time-tracking module. In August 2024 it had over 30 thousand client companies and 1 million users, and by May 2026 about 60 thousand companies and 1,300 employees, half of them in revenue-generating roles, after growing its operation more than 15 times since the Series C. The company says it has generated cash for almost a year, announced a R$400 million investment plan, and in August 2026 raised a R$150 million Series D led by Battery Ventures and Kevin Efrusy with Endeavor Catalyst joining. Its goal is to lead the benefits market by 2030; it counts on new PAT rules, which cap the fees charged to merchants and shorten payment terms and are meant to open the market to challengers, and plans to use AI to integrate HR and finance tasks and to resume acquisitions. It aims for expense management and HR to make up half of revenue.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil's corporate-benefits market was concentrated in four incumbents (Alelo, Pluxee, VR, Ticket), which Bloomberg Línea says still hold about 80% of the sector, and their model worked against both sides: workers could spend meal vouchers only at accepting merchants and sometimes sold them at a discount for cash, merchants paid high fees, and employers had little choice because competition and innovation were low. HR teams also had to run benefits, time tracking and expense reports in separate tools, often by spreadsheet (80% of reimbursements were still manual, per Flash). Logic: if the employer funds a flexible budget on a card that works everywhere, the worker is happier, the employer keeps the same cost, and the platform earns from card and software revenue; once it holds the relationship with the HR team, it can add adjacent products (time, admissions, expenses) with almost no extra acquisition cost. Why now: the PAT decree of November 2025 and later court decisions cap merchant fees at 3.6% and set a 15-day payment limit, opening the segment to challengers; AI cuts the cost of HR administration; and Flash now generates cash. Market size and share (our estimate): Exame (2021) cited a flexible-benefits market of about R$150 billion a year, which is a company-supplied figure and an old one. Using it as the order of magnitude, Flash's 2021 volume target of R$2 billion was about 1.3% of it. Taking the 60 thousand client companies reported in 2026 and the 15x growth since 2022, Flash's volume is plausibly in the tens of billions of reais today (our inference, not a reported figure). If it reached 10% of a R$150 billion market (R$15 billion) at an assumed net revenue of 2% to 5% (card and platform fees; our assumption), annual revenue would be R$300 to 750 million, with software revenue adding on top. What is different: it built the product for small and mid-sized companies the incumbents ignored, moved up to large clients, and combined benefits, HR and expenses on one platform; it has been backed by well-known investors (Accel's Kevin Efrusy, Monashees, Tiger Global, Tencent, Battery, Whale Rock). Competitors: the four incumbents, and start-up rivals such as Caju. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders and works as a connector that brings top funds onto cap tables and helps hire. Flash's cap table shows the pattern of a founder trio with a strong early syndicate, which a follower-type investor can join; Norte's role in the early rounds is not documented in the sources we read. Risks: incumbents' scale and the lobby against the startups (the benefits association sued, per Startups.com.br 2024), regulation of PAT that can swing either way, credit and payment risk on the card business, and the need to prove that software revenue grows as fast as the card volume.

milestones.value: Seed money (January) and a Series A led by Monashees (end of year) bring about US$9M in the first year.
Flash launches its flexible-benefits card and app, with clients from day one, aiming at small and mid-sized companies the large voucher companies neglected.

During the pandemic Flash adds services such as mental-health support, utility-bill payment and home-office purchases; from 60 thousand users at 1,500 companies in July 2020 it grows to 200 thousand at about 4,000 by mid-2021.
A US$22M Series B led by Tiger Global funds a shift from flexible benefits provider to all-in-one HR platform; Flash expects to move over R$2 billion in 2021.
A Series C of more than US$100M, the second-largest HR-tech round in Brazil at the time, funds technology and hiring beyond the 300-person team.
Flash buys ExpenseOn and creates a corporate-expense business unit, its first acquisition and its entry into a market of about R$80 million a year in revenue.
Flash buys FolhaCerta, a time and attendance software company, which speeds its time-clock module by about two years.
The company has more than 30 thousand client companies and 1 million users, and is repositioned as a work-journey management platform.
A federal decree changes PAT rules, capping merchant fees at 3.6% and limiting payment terms to 15 days, which Flash sees as opening the market to challengers.
Flash announces R$400M of own-cash investment, with about 60 thousand client companies, 1,300 employees and a goal of leading benefits by 2030; it says it has generated cash for almost a year.
A R$150M Series D led by Battery Ventures and Kevin Efrusy adds Endeavor Catalyst and funds product, AI, sales and capital structure; Flash plans to resume acquisitions.

description.value: Mexican business-data platform that gives lenders and fintechs API access, with customer consent, to small businesses' tax, financial and company data, for credit-risk analysis, factoring and KYB/KYC.

long_description.value: Syntage is a business-data platform that lets banks, fintechs and software companies in Latin America connect, with the company's consent, to the public and private data of their small and mid-sized business customers, through APIs and a dashboard. Its core is Mexican: it logs into the SAT (the tax authority) to pull a company's electronic invoices (CFDI), tax returns and compliance status, validates credentials in about three seconds and extracts invoice data in minutes, then adds other public and private sources and builds indicators on top. The site presents three main uses: credit-risk analysis (a personalised report of indicators, with updates and alerts when risk indicators change), factoring (verifying invoices, with notices of cancellations, credit notes and payments, and monitoring financed invoices) and KYB, KYC and anti-money-laundering checks (original documents, blacklists, and links between businesses and their shareholders). It sells to lenders, so its revenue comes from institutional customers integrating the API; the site says more than 400 financial institutions use it and that it holds the ISO 27001:2022 security certificate. The company began in early 2020 as Satws (SAT Web Services), a product focused only on Mexico and SAT data, founded by Matheus Pedroso, a former CTO of the Mexican fintech Credijusto, and Sebastian Carlsson, who had led LenddoEFL in Latin America after a career in corporate investment banking. Pedroso built the technology and Carlsson sold it, based on what they had seen at both companies about gathering business information to onboard customers and assess risk. By mid-2021 a team of five served about 60 institutional customers, with no churn, and was close to break-even. A seed round of US$4.3 million, co-led by Nazca and Costanoa Ventures with QED, RaliCap, Latitud and ten angels, was announced in August 2022, together with the rebrand to Syntage and a plan to add private and public sources and other Latin American countries from the fourth quarter of 2022. Satws then had about 150 institutional customers. Costanoa describes the platform as covering open finance and credit intelligence across Latin America, and a Costanoa-listed client, the corporate-card company Clara, reports faster card approvals (about 24 hours on average) after moving to Syntage from other data providers that could not extract all CFDIs and connected slowly. A directory profile says the company has analysed more than 250,000 businesses; this figure and the count of customers vary between pages (300+ on a directory page, 400+ on the company site).

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Mexican lenders and fintechs that serve small businesses lack reliable financial records for them: many firms are informal or keep thin books, bank statements are partial, and manual document collection slows onboarding and invites fraud. Mexico has one rich, standardised source of truth, the SAT's electronic invoices, which show a firm's real sales, customers and payments, and which firms can authorise a lender to read. Logic: a lender that can read a firm's invoices in minutes can underwrite faster, verify factoring invoices, and monitor risk over time; the same data supports KYB and anti-money-laundering checks. Selling this as an API means each lender does not build and maintain its own SAT connection, which is slow and breaks when the SAT changes. Why now: open-finance and fintech lending have grown in Mexico, factoring and working-capital lenders need invoice data, and a data layer can be extended to other Latin American tax and company registries. Market size and share (our estimate): INEGI's 2024 census counted about 7 million establishments in Mexico; in the private sector there were 5.47 million economic units in 2023, and 64.3% of them were informal, which leaves roughly 1.95 million formal units (5.47 million x 35.7%, our arithmetic). Those are the businesses whose data a lender could pull. On the customer side, Syntage says more than 400 financial institutions use it. If those pay an average of US$20 to 60 thousand a year (our assumption, typical for API data products sold to lenders, not a reported figure), that implies about US$8 to 24 million of annual revenue today; reaching 1,500 institutions across Mexico and a few Latin American markets at similar prices would give US$30 to 90 million. This is the realistic scale of a data-infrastructure business of this kind unless it expands into broader data products or per-query pricing for a much larger number of businesses. What is different: it started narrowly (only SAT data, only Mexico) and went deep, with a fast and complete SAT connection that a client such as Clara preferred over other providers, then widened into a platform with indicators and KYB features; it holds a recognised security certification, important for lenders; and it was backed by specialist early-stage funds (Nazca, Costanoa, QED, Latitud). Competitors and comparables: other Mexican open-finance and tax-data connectors exist (they were not described in the sources we read, so we do not rank them), and large credit bureaus and KYC vendors could add similar features. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders who know more than it does and connects them with funds and people; a two-founder team with credit and technology experience building infrastructure for Latin American lenders fits a follower role beside US and Mexican early-stage leads, but we found no source describing Norte's role. Risks: dependence on one government interface (a change in the SAT's rules or access policy could break the core product), concentration in Mexican fintech lending, which can cool, regulatory limits on data sharing, and the small size of the seed financing relative to the scope of the vision.

sub_sector.value: Business data and open finance infrastructure

milestones.value: Matheus Pedroso and Sebastian Carlsson launch Satws, an API and dashboard that connect Mexican financial institutions and fintechs to the SAT, to speed up credit decisions and onboarding.
A team of five serves about 60 institutional customers with no churn and is close to break-even, which convinces the founders to raise venture capital.
Satws announces a US$4.3M seed round and rebrands as Syntage, a business-data platform for all of Latin America, with Satws about 150 institutional customers and kept as a product.
The company says more than 400 financial institutions use Syntage, and it holds the ISO 27001:2022 security certification.

description.value: Brazilian cybersecurity company with a self-service platform that scans a company's domains, websites, servers and cloud accounts, finds weaknesses and guides their fix, without installing agents.

long_description.value: Unxpose is a São Paulo cybersecurity company that sells a self-service platform to find and fix security weaknesses, aimed especially at companies without a large security team. It needs no agent installation: a customer creates an account, connects its assets (domains, websites, servers, cloud accounts) in minutes, and the platform scans them continuously, lists what is exposed, explains how to fix it, and produces a one-click report that shows its security posture to customers or auditors. It integrates with tools such as Slack, Teams, Jira and Splunk so vulnerabilities can be handled in a company's existing workflow. The product has grown into a set of modules sold as one platform: Attack Surface Management (finding all subdomains, websites, hosts and services of a company that are visible on the internet and their weaknesses), Cloud Security Posture Management (checking cloud accounts against industry frameworks and privacy rules), SaaS Security Posture Management (checking that employee accounts follow good practice and whether company credentials leaked in breaches), Security Questionnaires (AI that proposes answers from past questionnaires, to cut the time spent on customer security reviews) and Third Party Risk Management (sending and tracking questionnaires to suppliers). Pricing in 2021 started at R$2,500 a month, by subscription. The site says hundreds of companies of all sizes around the world use it, and a customer case from CAF (a development bank) praises its visibility and low cost and the ability to check cloud changes in staging. The company was started by Josemando Sobral (CEO), Tiago Assumpção and Patrick Costa. It received a first investment from Canary in March 2021 and used it to develop its new product and grow sales. In September 2021, during a wave of ransomware attacks on Brazilian companies (Lojas Renner, Fleury, JBS), it launched 'Você Protegido', a free online test that gives a company an exposure score from its domain, covering web, DNS and leaked credentials, as a taster of the full product. In October 2025 it was one of 11 start-ups chosen from Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Mexico for the first Google for Startups Accelerator: AI for Cybersecurity in Latin America, an equity-free programme. Public sources give no revenue, customer count or further funding; directory sites list small amounts of total funding (about US$320 to 360 thousand), which we did not rely on.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: most Brazilian companies, especially small and mid-sized ones, do not know everything they expose on the internet (forgotten subdomains, open BI dashboards, leaked credentials, misconfigured cloud accounts) and cannot afford the enterprise security tools and teams that large companies use; at the same time, they face growing pressure from ransomware (Startups.com.br reported a 92% rise in Brazil in the first months of 2021) and from customers asking for security questionnaires and reports. Logic: attack-surface and posture scanning can be automated and sold as subscription software that a non-expert connects in minutes, so it can be priced for the mid-market and sold to many customers with little services work. Why now: cloud and SaaS adoption multiplied the number of places data can leak, regulation of data protection (LGPD) and customers' vendor-risk demands push companies to prove their security, and AI helps with questionnaire answers and fix guidance. Market size and share (our estimate): Brasscom projects R$104.6 billion of cybersecurity investment in Brazil from 2025 to 2028, up 43.8% from the previous three years, or roughly R$26 billion a year (104.6 / 4, our arithmetic). Attack-surface, cloud and SaaS posture tools are a small part of that, which we take as 3% to 8% (our assumption), or about R$0.8 to 2.1 billion a year in Brazil. A strong Brazilian outcome of 3% to 5% of that segment would be R$25 to 100 million of annual revenue; reaching North American mid-market customers (which the company's English site targets) would enlarge this, but we found no evidence of its sales there. What is different: a single, agentless platform that brings attack-surface, cloud, SaaS, questionnaire and third-party modules into one view, designed for companies with small teams, in Portuguese and English, with a price point that a customer cited as unusually low, and a founder-led, product-focused approach; it was selected for Google's first Latin American AI-for-cybersecurity accelerator. Competitors and comparables: global attack-surface and posture vendors, and other Latin American security start-ups in the same Google cohort (such as Damch and others), which the sources do not compare. Fit with Norte (our reading, not a Norte statement): Norte says it focuses on the size of the pie and on obsessed founders, and brings top funds and angels onto cap tables; Unxpose's first backer was Canary, a fund that also co-led Ume's 2022 seed, where Norte took part, so a follower role beside Canary fits, though no source we read describes Norte's role in Unxpose. Risks: very small disclosed funding and no public traction numbers; crowded global competition where large vendors bundle similar features; the need to sell to many small customers at low prices; and possible dependence on Google programme visibility rather than customers.

accelerators.value: Google for Startups Accelerator: AI for Cybersecurity

milestones.value: Canary makes the first investment in Unxpose, which the team uses to develop its new product and increase its sales force.

Unxpose launches 'Você Protegido', a free online test that gives a company an exposure score across web, DNS and leaked credentials, as a taster of its paid monitoring product, during a surge of ransomware attacks in Brazil.
Unxpose is selected for the first Google for Startups Accelerator: AI for Cybersecurity in Latin America, one of 11 start-ups from four countries.

description.value: Brazilian infrastructure company for Open Finance and Pix: it runs the regulatory side of Open Finance for banks and fintechs and lets them initiate Pix payments, including the new Pix modes (biometrics, tap to pay, recurring), earning a fee per successful transaction.

long_description.value: Iniciador is a São Paulo payments-infrastructure company that sits between Brazilian banks, fintechs and platforms and the Central Bank's Open Finance and Pix rails. It holds two Central Bank licences, payment institution and payment initiator (ITP), and its customers use either its licences or their own on top of its technology. The platform has two sides. On the regulatory side it runs, as a managed service, what an institution must operate to take part in Open Finance Brasil (authorization server, consent management, monitoring, certifications, directory registration, ticket handling). On the product side it lets customers initiate Pix payments from the payer's own bank (the 'Pay by Bank' flow) and receive bank data, with newer Pix modes built on top: Pix por Biometria and Pix por Aproximação (tap to pay), Pix Automático (recurring payments such as subscriptions) and Smart Transfers (account sweeping by rule or balance). Revenue is tied to success: a fixed amount, some cents, for each successful transaction on a customer's platform. The company was founded in 2021 by Marcelo Martins, a serial entrepreneur who had already founded and sold a start-up, and Guilherme Decampo, who leads technology; the registry shows the company opened in December 2021. A first round of R$1.2 million, made soon after founding by industry specialists and angels (Edson Santos, former head of Global Payments in Brazil, and Andres Bilbao, co-founder of Rappi), financed the start. The company is a founding member of Open Finance Brasil and sits on its board representing ABFintechs. As the Central Bank released new Pix modes (Pix Inteligente in April 2024, Pix por Biometria in February 2025, Pix Automático in June 2025) Iniciador followed each, and in August 2025 it said it served about 60% of the payment initiators taking part in Pix Automático and more than half of those authorised for Pix por Biometria, with customers including iFood, Stone, Nomad, Núclea, Magie and Jota, and a customer base four times larger than in early 2025. Its 2026 site says one in three Pix initiations in Brazil run on its infrastructure and about 1.4 billion data requests a month, and lists customers such as PagSeguro, CloudWalk and Wise (these figures are the company's own). In August 2025 it raised R$32 million led by Valor Capital, with big_bets, Alter Global, Actyus and Norte Ventures, to invest in technology and scale, to hire, to add the capital the Central Bank requires of licensed institutions and to start targeting large banks. In May 2026 it launched what it calls Brazil's first agentic-payments MCP on Pix, which lets an AI agent propose a payment that the user approves by biometrics, together with an AI toolkit and an embedded-engineers service.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: since the Central Bank opened Open Finance and then Pix by initiation, every bank and fintech that wants to offer 'Pay by Bank', Pix por Biometria or Pix Automático must connect to dozens of institutions' APIs, pass certifications, keep monitoring regulatory metrics and maintain it all every time the rules change. Few have the engineers or the licence to do so, and a failed redirect or consent costs them the sale. Logic: Iniciador sells that burden as a service and earns a few cents on each successful transaction, so its revenue grows with the volume that flows through its customers. Why now: Pix initiation volume jumped from R$3.2 billion in 2024 to R$15.3 billion in 2025 (Banco Central data reported by Finsiders), and the Central Bank keeps adding modes (Pix Automático in 2025, instalment Pix expected next), each of which needs a new integration that Iniciador can ship once for all customers. Market and reachable share: Pix moved R$26.9 trillion in 63.8 billion transactions in 2024 (Febraban and Abecs, quoted by Startupi). Our own estimate: if initiation-based Pix reaches 5% to 10% of that count (3 to 6 billion transactions a year, our assumption) and the infrastructure layer earns R$0.10 to R$0.30 per transaction (our assumption; the company only says 'some cents'), the Brazilian fee pool is about R$0.3 to R$1.9 billion a year (roughly US$55 to US$340 million at the 2025 average rate of 5.59). A player that keeps its claimed one-third of initiations would reach about R$0.1 to R$0.6 billion, or US$19 to US$114 million: a business worth backing but not a giant on its own, with upside from data, regulatory services, agentic payments and other Latin American open-finance systems. Different: in the sources it is the only player that sells both the regulatory operation and the payment products, it has Central Bank licences, it holds a founding-member seat and a board seat at Open Finance Brasil, and it reports approval rates above 95% (company figures). Fit with Norte (our reading of the Manifesto): founders who know the regulatory plumbing better than an investor does, a B2B network business in which introductions to banks, acquirers and funds matter, and a round led by a top fund (Valor Capital) with Norte as one of several funds, in line with Norte's wish to bring the best funds onto cap tables. Risks: dependence on one regulator's rules (a rule change or a bank-built alternative can shrink the layer), customers who internalise the integration once volume is large, thin per-transaction fees, and capital requirements for a licensed payment institution. The sources name no competitor, so differentiation rests on company claims.

milestones.value: Marcelo Martins and Guilherme Decampo start Iniciador to build infrastructure for Brazil's new Open Finance, and a first round of R$1.2 million from industry specialists and angels (Edson Santos and Andres Bilbao among them) finances the first product.
The Central Bank launches Pix Inteligente, the first of the new Pix modes, in which Iniciador acts as payment initiator.
Pix por Biometria goes live, letting buyers pay with Pix at checkout without opening the bank app; Iniciador ends up with more than half of the institutions authorised for it.
Pix Automático, recurring Pix for subscriptions, is launched by the Central Bank; Iniciador says it serves 60% of the payment initiators that offer it.

The company reports a customer base four times larger than at the start of the year, with iFood Pago, Stone, Nomad, Núclea, Magie and Jota among its customers, while announcing its R$32 million round.
The site says one in three Pix initiations in Brazil run on Iniciador and that it handles 1.4 billion data requests a month, a top-two volume in Open Finance (company figures).

Iniciador launches the agentic payments MCP on Pix (said to be Brazil's first), an AI toolkit for customers and an Open Finance Full-Stack service of embedded engineers, and repositions itself as full-stack Open Finance infrastructure with a new site.

description.value: Brazilian developer of forest carbon-credit projects, mainly REDD+ in the Amazon, that sells the credits to companies and individuals and helps companies measure and offset their emissions.

long_description.value: Carbonext is a Brazilian climate company that develops and sells nature-based carbon credits and, since 2025, a wider set of decarbonisation services. Its core is forest conservation (REDD+) in the Amazon: it pays landowners the opportunity cost of not clearing forest they could legally convert to cattle or soy, monitors the area so it stays standing, and sells the resulting Verra-certified credits (one credit equals one tonne of CO2 not emitted) in the voluntary market. It earns fees for designing and managing the projects and from selling the credits. Large clients such as iFood, Cielo and Raízen get tailored contracts, one-off or multi-year; from 2021 individuals and small businesses can neutralise their footprint with a subscription of about R$60 a month. Its areas were about 1 million hectares in the Amazon in 2021, out of 140 to 150 million hectares the company estimates could be protected through direct payments. The company was founded in 2010 by forest engineer Janaína Dallan, a UN expert on carbon projects and president of the Brazilian Alliance for Nature-Based Solutions, with experience at European carbon firms; her brother Luciano Fonseca, a former Pátria Investimentos private-equity executive, structured the operation in its first 12 months and became co-CEO, and he led the first outside rounds. Funding: a seed from angels in 2021, a R$30 million Series A in September 2021 from more than 20 investors including Canary, Alexia Ventures and FitPart, and R$200 million from Shell in 2022. It was one of 10 startups in the first sustainability edition of the Google for Startups Accelerator in 2022. It has four lines: forest conservation, regenerative agriculture (through a stake in NaturAll Carbon, an Anglo-Brazilian carbon-removal company), a reforestation arm still at an early stage, and NetZero Solutions, which began when it bought 40% of Mangue Tech (an AI carbon-inventory software company founded in 2021 by former Linx executives) in August 2025 with money from the Shell round, keeping the acquired companies independent. It sees Brazil's Law 15,042 on a regulated carbon market as a source of demand, especially from small and medium companies that will need to measure, reduce and offset emissions.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: companies that promised to be carbon neutral, and soon those obliged to report under Brazil's regulated-market law, need credible ways to measure, cut and offset emissions, while the world's largest standing forest is under pressure from clearing that landowners can legally do on 20% of their land. The logic: a credit is a payment for the cost of not clearing, so the business works when a trusted party can verify the forest stays and sell the credit at a price above the opportunity cost. Carbonext has done this since 2010 with Verra certification and a founder who sits on UN and Brazilian government advisory bodies, which matters in a market where buyer trust is the scarce asset. Why now: the 2020-21 net-zero pledges lifted demand; Brazil created a regulated carbon market in Law 15.042; and the company is adding measurement software and agriculture-based removals so that it can sell a full package, not just credits. Market: the company estimates that 140 to 150 million hectares of Amazon forest with proven title and clearing risk could be protected through direct payments, and it held about 1 million (under 1%). Our bottom-up illustration, with every input an assumption (we found no read price or yield source): if a strong outcome is 5 to 10 million hectares, with 0.3 to 1.0 tonnes of avoided CO2 sold per hectare a year at US$5 to US$12 a tonne, gross credit sales are about US$7 million to US$120 million a year before the landowner's share, and the other three lines add more, so the pool is mid-size rather than huge. Different: a Brazil-based developer with 15 years of project history, a founder-led credibility, a Shell investor and a plan to own the measure-reduce-offset chain; competitors named in the press are Biofílica (bought by Ambipar) and Sustainable Carbon. Fit with Norte (our reading): founders with deep subject expertise and a finance operator, a network need (international buyers, funds) that a connector can help with, but no source says Norte invested, and the portfolio page lists the company without describing any round; the Manifesto's 'right people at the right time' would fit as a buyer and investor introduction. Risks: voluntary-credit prices and integrity crises (REDD+ credits have been criticised for over-crediting), dependence on a few large buyers, execution across four lines, and the regulated market's rules not yet being clear.

milestones.value: Luciano Fonseca joined as co-CEO and led the company's first investment rounds
Opens a monthly subscription (about R$60) so individuals and small businesses can neutralise their footprint, and reports about 1 million hectares of Amazon forest under protection
Selected for the first sustainability edition of the Google for Startups Accelerator
Bought a stake in NaturAll Carbon, an Anglo-Brazilian regenerative-agriculture company
Bought 40% of Mangue Tech and entered a fourth business line focused on carbon-inventory software and net-zero services

description.value: Brazilian beverage group that holds niche brands (Praya beer, Mamba canned water, Baer-Mate mate soft drinks), now backed by Heineken's production and distribution through Heineken SPIN.

long_description.value: Better Drinks is a São Paulo beverage group that builds a portfolio of niche brands meant not to compete head-on with the big incumbents (Ambev, Coca-Cola) but to ride trends such as sustainability, convenience and lower sugar. It was launched on 1 February 2022 by two former Ambev executives, Felipe Della Negra (CEO, earlier head of Red Bull in Brazil and of Kraft Heinz in Italy) and Felipe Szpigel (Chief Growth Officer, who had left Ambev in 2018 to start the ready-to-drink brand F!VE), by merging five independent brands whose founders became shareholders: Baer-Mate (a mate-based soft drink without added sugar), F!VE (ready-to-drink cocktails), Mamba (canned water), Praya (premium wheat beer created in Rio in 2016 by four surfer friends) and Vivant (canned wine). Together the brands had sold more than R$50 million in 2021, the group started with R$25 million from the founders and angels (among them the Zee.Dog founders, the head of Domino's Pizza in Brazil, executives of Cia. Tradicional de Comércio and Norte Ventures) and set out to reach R$1 billion in revenue by 2026. The group sold through supermarkets, bars and restaurants and online (about a third each in early 2023, in 30,000 points of sale), and added brands such as Vermelhão, an aperitif launched in April 2022 with the singer Gusttavo Lima that became half of its revenue in 2023. It raised about R$65 million in sustainability-linked private debt from W Capital in March 2023, tied to CO2-reduction targets, and estimated an addressable market of R$52 billion. In June 2024 Heineken Brazil became a minority shareholder, without a cash injection, offering its production, purchasing and distribution structure and a path to a larger stake as each brand hit sales and sustainability targets; the group became the 'impact brands' pillar of Heineken SPIN, and its site shows its B Corp certification. Heineken began brewing Praya in 2025 and producing Mamba Water in January 2026, and Mamba's yearly revenue grew from R$10 million in 2024 to about R$100 million in 2026 (NeoFeed). F!VE and Vivant have had no sales since 2024 and are expected to be discontinued. In November 2026 NeoFeed reported that Heineken signed to buy control for R$500 million in cash, all ordinary shares held by 67 shareholders, with Della Negra keeping a non-voting stake, subject to approval by the competition authority Cade, and with plans to take Praya abroad.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil's beverage market is dominated by a few giants that control shelf space, distribution and bars, while small brands with good ideas (a lighter beer, a canned water, a mate soft drink) lack the scale, logistics and purchasing power to grow beyond a niche. Logic: Better Drinks pools such brands under experienced beverage operators, so that they share overheads, buying and sales teams, and pursue consumer trends the incumbents are slow to serve, then hands growth to a partner with a distribution network. Why now: the 2022 start came when younger consumers were moving to lower-alcohol, canned, sustainable and ready-to-drink products and when marketplaces and delivery apps made it easier to reach buyers without the big distributors. Market and share: the company estimated in 2023 an addressable market of R$52 billion, about a third of all beverages in Brazil, growing about 15% a year (Brazil Journal, CEO's figures; not independently checked). Our own check: that is the company's claim, and no independent report was read, so we treat it as an upper bound. Reachable share: the founders' target of R$1 billion in sales by 2026 would be about 2% of R$52 billion; the evidence is that the group reached about R$48 million annualised in 2022 and that Mamba alone reached about R$100 million in 2026, which suggests several hundred million reais is reachable, not R$1 billion for the group as built. The outcome that did arrive, Heineken buying control for R$500 million in cash (about US$90 million at the 2025 rate of 5.59), is a far smaller outcome than the R$1 billion in revenue the group once planned (we do not know Norte's return, since its stake is not disclosed). What is different: a team that had run Red Bull, Ambev and Kraft Heinz operations, brands with strong identity (Mamba is compared by the press to the US canned-water brand Liquid Death, a comparable valued at about US$700 million, according to Startups.com.br), a B Corp certification and sustainability-linked debt, and the structure with Heineken that supplied production and distribution. Fit with Norte (our reading of the Manifesto): experienced operators who know the industry better than an investor, an angel-style cap table around a network (Zee.Dog's founders, restaurant and retail executives), and Norte as one of many names rather than the lead, in line with its 'size of the pie, not the piece' approach. This is also a consumer company in a portfolio otherwise built on software and fintech. Risks: capital-intensive, low-margin physical distribution; heavy concentration in one brand (Vermelhão was half of revenue in 2023, a product tied to a celebrity); dependence on the big players for shelf and production; and brands that stalled (F!VE, Vivant), with the cash needed to rescue them. Confidence is low because market size is a company claim and the competitors come from one article.

milestones.value: Mamba Water, a canned water brand that gives a litre of water to people without access for each can sold, reaches the market in Rio and São Paulo, with surfer Pedro Scooby and skater Letícia Bufoni as partners.

Better Drinks starts operating by merging five independent brands (Baer-Mate, F!VE, Mamba, Praya, Vivant) that sold over R$50 million in 2021, with R$25 million from the founders and angels, aiming at R$1 billion in sales within five years.

description.value: E-commerce logistics company that runs urban warehouses and its own software to store, pack and deliver online brands' orders in Mexico and Brazil, with pick-up points, B2B distribution and cross-border import services.

long_description.value: Cubbo is an e-commerce logistics company that stores, packs and delivers online orders for brands, and sells the software it built to run that work. It started in Mexico City in January 2021, founded by two Colombians, Brian York (CEO) and Josu Gurtubay (COO), who saw that large foreign direct-to-consumer brands wanted to ship to Latin American shoppers without opening local operations. The idea was to fit out urban warehouses close to customers, so that a brand integrates its store (Shopify, VTEX, Mercado Libre and others), sends stock to Cubbo and has each order picked, packed and delivered, including same-day, cross-docking and returns. Over time it added a B2B operation for brands that supply retail chains, an importer and merchant-of-record service for brands that want to sell in a new country without a local entity, a network of pick-up points called Cubbitos, and software it builds in-house (WMS, OMS and TMS), part of which it licenses white-label to carriers in Colombia and Chile. Revenue comes from storage, handling and delivery fees plus software. Cubbo reached Colombia in November 2021 with a US$4 million seed round led by SV LatAm Capital. In March 2022 it bought DedaLog, a profitable São Paulo fulfillment start-up whose CEO, Tiago Pavan, became its country manager in Brazil, and in mid-2022 it closed an undisclosed pre-Series A round with SV LatAm Capital, Gerdau Next Ventures, Gaingels and Community Access Fund, saying it had raised US$8 million before it (the seed is US$4 million, so some other funding, perhaps a bridge, is unreported) and that revenue had grown 274% since the seed. In Brazil it now runs five warehouses (Embu das Artes, Itapeva, Cachoeirinha, Manaus and Extrema, the last two opened in 2026), serves more than 120 customers there (the company names Natura/Avon and L'Oréal among its customers) and says its Brazilian business grew 310% from 2024 to 2025. Across Mexico and Brazil it reports about 300 brands, more than a million orders a month and a projected global revenue of about US$68 million for 2026 (company figures reported by Startups.com.br). In Mexico it opened an 8,850 m² centre in Tultepec in August 2026 (investment of MX$18 million, capacity of 450,000 orders a month) and in September 2026 started a pilot with OXXO to use its convenience stores as Cubbitos pick-up and return points, on top of more than 3,500 active points. Newer products include Cubbo Engage, an AI tool for support, sales and post-purchase, and an MCP for customers to connect their own AI models. The company says it plans more warehouses in Brazil (Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo, Recife and the Centre-West) and a bigger role in B2B.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: online brands in Mexico and Brazil, especially small and mid-sized ones and foreign brands entering Latin America, struggle with logistics. They need local stock for fast delivery, handling at peak events such as Hot Sale and Black Friday, returns, and customs and tax rules, and few can build warehouses and software in each country. Marketplaces solve it but take commissions and the customer relationship. Logic: Cubbo takes the physical work (urban warehouses near shoppers) and the systems (WMS, OMS, TMS, integrations with stores and carriers) and charges per order and storage, so its revenue grows with each brand's sales while cost per order falls with density. Why now: online sales keep growing in both countries and brands want to sell on their own channels as well as marketplaces; Cubbo adds pick-up points (OXXO) and B2B flows that link the same inventory to retailers. Market and share: Mexican retail e-commerce reached MX$941 billion in 2025, up 19.2% (AMVO's Estudio de Venta Online 2026), and Brazilian e-commerce R$235.5 billion in 2025, up 15.3%, with 438.9 million orders (ABIACOM). Our own estimate of the outsourced-fulfillment pool: logistics (storage, handling and last mile) is roughly 10% to 15% of order value and 20% to 40% of it is outsourced to a third party (both our assumptions). Mexico: 941 x 10-15% x 20-40% = MX$19 to MX$56 billion, about US$1.0 to US$3.1 billion at roughly 18 pesos per dollar (our assumption). Brazil: 235.5 x 10-15% x 20-40% = R$4.7 to R$14.1 billion, or US$0.8 to US$2.5 billion at 5.59 (2025 average). Together about US$1.8 to US$5.6 billion; the projected US$68 million of 2026 revenue (company figure) would be 1% to 4% of it, so a leader's share of a few more points is plausible, but the figure is a coarse estimate. What is different: it operates in two of the region's largest markets with its own software and its own warehouses (the Brazilian network is described as run mostly by people, with software for efficiency instead of robots), has customers such as Natura/Avon and L'Oréal, and is building extra layers (Cubbitos, merchant of record, Engage). A competitor named in the press is Melonn (Mexico and Colombia), focused on small businesses; Amazon's logistics and marketplace fulfilment are the obvious alternatives. Fit with Norte (our reading of the Manifesto): operator founders who know the problem better than the investor, a business that depends on introductions to brands, retailers and co-investors in several countries, and a cap table of local and regional funds and angels (SV LatAm Capital, BluStone, Gerdau Next Ventures and founders of Latin American start-ups), consistent with Norte's follower and connector role. Risks: logistics is capital-intensive and low margin, with fixed lease and labour costs before volume arrives; customers can concentrate in a few large brands; Amazon, Mercado Libre and large carriers can undercut it; and the 2022 plan to raise a Series A was not matched by a round we could find, so funding of the growth is not visible. Confidence is low because market size is our estimate and company revenue is a projection.

description.value: Industrial AI company whose sensors and software watch the health of factory machines, diagnosing problems early so plants avoid unplanned downtime.

long_description.value: Tractian is an industrial AI company that protects the machines inside factories from unplanned stops. It puts its own wireless sensors on critical equipment such as compressors, chillers, pumps and palletisers; they collect vibration, ultrasound, temperature, current and voltage, and its AI, trained on a large set of industrial failure data, names the likely root cause and recommends an action. The sensors are lent to customers (comodato) and Tractian earns recurring software revenue. It began with mechanical monitoring, which the CEO calls the 'predictive band-aid', and has expanded into what it calls physical AI, covering mechanical, electrical and operational condition plus computer vision; it also sells maintenance-management software and a product that reads manufacturers' manuals to predict faults, launched in the US with partners such as Siemens and Johnson Controls. The idea came from the three founders: Igor Marinelli, who grew up around his father's maintenance work in a paper mill and was building software at 13, Gabriel Lameirinhas, his classmate at the University of São Paulo, and Leonardo Vieira, a salesman whose brother worked in industrial maintenance and who gave them their first client lead. Founded in 2019, they spent the first year on software only, then talked to more than 80 industrial companies and moved to building their own sensors in 2020. Y Combinator took them in the Winter 2021 batch with about 30 industrial customers. Growth since: an office in Mexico in January 2022, the CEO's move to Atlanta in 2024 as the US became the main market, revenue of about US$40 million in 2024 (up 100%), a first acquisition (a roughly 10-person Atlanta startup, for about US$3 million mostly in shares) to reach equipment makers, and, by October 2026, annualised recurring revenue of almost US$100 million (2.5 times in two years), more than 2,000 factories, more than 700 employees, near-breakeven profitability and clients such as Eli Lilly, McKesson, Whirlpool, Coca-Cola bottlers, Cummins and Embraer, plus three large AI data-centre operators. Mid and large companies are about 80% of revenue. It raised a US$130 million Series D at a US$1.4 billion valuation in October 2026, which made it Latin America's most valuable AI company, and plans to let its models act on machines (not just recommend) next year, monitor robots, expand into data centres and reach about US$500 million of ARR and a US listing in three to five years.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: factories run on machines that wear out and fail, and most maintenance hours still go on reactive fixes. Siemens' True Cost of Downtime (January 2026, as cited in Tractian's Series D post) puts unplanned downtime at about 11% of annual revenue for the world's 500 largest industrial companies, around US$1.4 trillion a year; industrial assets average 24 years of use, and Deloitte projects more than 2.1 million manufacturing jobs may go unfilled by 2030, so the know-how of retiring technicians leaves the plant. The logic: cheap sensors plus a model trained on failures can tell a technician what is wrong and what to do, so the software scales where experts do not; lending the sensors removes the customer's upfront cost and creates subscription revenue, and each installed machine adds data that makes the next diagnosis better. Why now: connected sensors and wireless networks are cheap, AI models can read manuals and sensor data together, and AI data centres and reshoring are driving a build-out of critical physical infrastructure where downtime is not acceptable. Market: the downtime figure shows the size of the problem, not of the software market. Our bottom-up estimate: about 2,000 customers and nearly US$100 million of ARR imply roughly US$50,000 a customer. If 100,000 to 200,000 mid-size and large industrial sites worldwide (our assumption) could pay US$30,000 to US$100,000 a year, the reachable pool is about US$3 billion to US$20 billion; the company's own target of US$500 million of ARR is roughly 2.5 to 17% of that. Different: its own hardware (rather than integrating other vendors' sensors), the multimodal data set, a field sales model with US regional hubs that raised conversion by 45%, and the partnerships with machine makers who might otherwise be rivals. Comparables abroad: Samsara (IoT operations, listed in the US) and Augury (US machine-health company, also raised hundreds of millions), both named from general knowledge, not read here. Fit with Norte (our reading): Norte's own case post describes the three founders' energy ('brio') and shared industrial background, and the Manifesto's focus on obsessed founders who know more than the investor; Norte took part early (2021 pre-seed and seed) and again in the Series D, which fits its follower and connector role with Y Combinator and later funds. Risks: hardware and field-service costs weigh on margins (the company says it is near breakeven, not yet profitable); well-funded rivals and the machine makers themselves can build the same monitoring; revenue is increasingly concentrated in US industrial and AI-infrastructure cycles; and the move to let AI act on machines raises safety and liability stakes.

description.value: Argentine frozen-food company that makes flexitarian ready meals in its own factory and sells them directly to consumers online with home delivery; it has also sold in Brazil, Chile and the United States and now focuses on Argentina.

long_description.value: Frizata is a frozen-food company from Rosario, Argentina, that makes its own ready meals and ingredients and sells them directly to consumers through its online store, with home delivery, instead of through supermarkets. It calls the model a digitally native vertical brand (DNVB): it controls the whole chain, from factory and product design to online sale and delivery, and uses customer data and reviews to change the range quickly, treating each food as a product that gets new versions, like software. The catalogue is aimed at 'flexitarians', people who eat meat but want more vegetables and less impact: vegetables and fruit, appetisers, pizzas, empanadas and meat-free alternatives, with around 50 products in 2021 and almost 80 by 2022. The site today sells ready meals, packs and discounts in Rosario, Buenos Aires and Córdoba. It was founded in 2019 (Forbes Brasil says 2018) by Adolfo Rouillon (CEO) and José Robledo, friends since university in Rosario and serial entrepreneurs who had already founded and sold other companies (Congelados del Sur and Amtec.net, according to Forbes Argentina). In its first twelve months it reached 30,000 customers, revenue was about US$10 million in 2020 with a US$15 million run rate in mid-2021. In July 2021 it announced a Series A of R$25 million (about US$4.65 million) led by SP Ventures with Marcos Galperin of Mercado Libre, Jaime Soler Bottinelli (former global CEO of Cencosud), Gonzalo Ramírez Martiarena (former global CEO of Louis Dreyfus), Glocal AgriFood Tech and Norte Ventures, to expand abroad. It had entered Chile earlier in 2021, began selling in Greater São Paulo in July 2021 (importing from its Argentine factory) and planned a first online store in San Francisco in September 2021. The international plan then slowed: in 2022 it put Chile and the United States on hold because of freight costs and currency problems, and in October 2023 it said it would focus on São Paulo for three to five years, with revenue of about R$100 million (over US$20 million), 90% from Argentina, Chile and the United States and 10% from Brazil, and 70% of products made at its own factory. In June 2026 Descubre.vc reported, from Argentine press, that it had paused its global expansion (Brazil, Chile and the United States) because of higher logistics costs and would concentrate on Argentina, keeping its direct-to-consumer model, serving Buenos Aires, Córdoba and Rosario and investing 900 million pesos to optimise its plant with artificial intelligence.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: frozen food is a large category in which supply has hardly changed in years. A long chain of producers, distributors and supermarkets limits which products reach shelves, so new, healthier, vegetable-based or more convenient dishes struggle to get listed, and producers learn little about who buys what. Logic: Frizata sells direct, so it can launch and test products fast, use customer data to improve them, capture the retailer's margin and offer lower prices, and use its own factory to control cost and quality. Why now: the pandemic pushed households to buy food online and to keep stock at home, and interest in vegetable-based eating was growing; in 2021 the company was already making about US$10 million a year and growing in several cities. Market and share: the only market figure we read is a paid-report summary from IMARC, which puts Brazil's frozen-food market at US$5.9 billion in 2025, growing about 3.2% a year to 2034; we treat it as a rough order of magnitude, since the method is not visible. No comparable Argentine figure was found. Our own estimate for direct-to-consumer: if online brands take 1% to 3% of Brazilian frozen sales (our assumption), the pool is about US$60 to US$180 million a year in Brazil alone; the company's reported Brazilian sales were 10% of about US$20 million, or about US$2 million in 2023 (AgFeed), so the Brazilian opportunity was far from captured, and a strong outcome would be a few tens of millions of dollars of Brazilian revenue plus the Argentine business, not a regional giant. What is different: a factory of its own with direct delivery and a wide range of vegetable-based products, plus founders who had built and sold two companies. A natural comparison is the plant-based and flexitarian food brands abroad, but we found no sourced comparable outcome. Fit with Norte (our reading of the Manifesto): experienced founders who know the industry better than the investor, a cross-border expansion in which Norte's network in Brazil could help hiring, partners and co-investors, and a Brazilian lead investor (SP Ventures) with Norte as one of several funds, in line with its follower role. Risks, which later events confirm: perishable cold-chain logistics are expensive, imported products from Argentina suffer from freight costs and currency swings, and the company paused the expansion into Brazil, Chile and the United States in 2022 and again in 2026; the 2026 refocus on Argentina means the Brazilian thesis behind the 2021 round has not materialised. Confidence is low because market size comes from a paid-report summary and the company's recent figures are missing.

description.value: Brazilian maker of open-source financial infrastructure: Midaz, a ledger for core banking, plus modules for onboarding, risk, reporting and reconciliation, sold to fintechs and financial institutions, earning from hosting, features and services.

long_description.value: Lerian is a São Paulo company that builds modular financial infrastructure for fintechs, payment institutions, credit operations and banks, with an open-source core at its centre. Its first product, Midaz, is a ledger, the database where a financial institution records, reconciles and audits every transaction, and the heart of a core banking system. Because the code is open, a customer can audit and customise it and avoids vendor lock-in, and Lerian charges not for the software itself but for hosting it, for added functions, and for implementation, support and consulting. Around the ledger it has added tools for onboarding and compliance orchestration (Flowker), real-time transaction risk (Tracer), regulatory reporting (Reporter) and transaction reconciliation (Matcher). Its site now groups the offer as core banking (accounts, balances, fees, Pix, boleto, TED, bill payment, regulatory reports), credit (product design to payment, with automatic accounting), multi-source reconciliation, and its own messaging connections to the Central Bank, Nuclea, Dataprev and the courts, plus professional services to design, migrate and run the architecture; it also offers a path for companies leaving banking-as-a-service to operate under their own licence. It was started by Fred Amaral, a co-founder of the payments company Dock, with two former Dock colleagues, Jefferson Rodrigues (CTO) and José Zapata (named as co-founder in 2024 coverage; the 2026 coverage lists Maísa Amaral, HR director, as the third partner). Coverage disagrees on the start (2023 in Startups.com.br and Finsiders; January 2024 in Brazil Journal and Baguete); the company began as a product-technology consultancy, which in eight months served six clients and found they all lacked control over their transactional database, which led to Midaz. Midaz was launched in July 2024 as, in the company's words, the first open-source ledger for core banking in the world, and the company says it offers 32 modules that can be contracted separately. In November 2024 it raised R$18 million, one of the largest seed rounds of the year in Brazil, led by MAYA Capital with Quartz, Supera Capital, Norte Ventures, Crivo Ventures and angels, enough for about two and a half years, to hire engineers. In January 2026 it raised a further R$30 million (US$5.5 million per Finsiders) in an oversubscribed seed, again led by MAYA with Norte Ventures, Supera Capital, Crivo Ventures, BluStone and Kevin Efrusy, a partner at Accel, to apply AI to the platform, build sales and customer success and start positioning abroad. Within 24 to 36 months the company plans to enter other Latin American markets and the United States.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: small and mid-sized banks, payment institutions and fintechs in Brazil depend on third-party core banking platforms, which are closed, are priced per account and per transaction (a poor fit when the regulator or competition stops them charging customers for Pix, for example), and offer little flexibility, while the largest players (Nubank, Inter and the incumbents) build their cores in house. Many fintechs also outgrow banking-as-a-service and must take their own licence and operate their own connections to the Central Bank. Logic: Lerian offers a modular, open-source ledger plus the connections and tools around it, and earns on hosting, features and services, so the customer controls the code and Lerian's revenue grows with the platform's use instead of with a licence fee. Why now: more fintechs are moving from banking-as-a-service to their own licence, the Central Bank keeps adding rules and rails that need maintenance, and cloud-native, AI-assisted development lowers the cost of building such software. Market and share: one market-research summary (Market Research Future, which sells the report) puts Brazil's core banking solutions market at US$640 million in 2025 and US$2.17 billion by 2035, a 13% yearly growth; other editions of the same report and other research firms give very different numbers, so we treat it as a rough order of magnitude and not as fact. A comparable outcome abroad: Visa agreed in 2023 to buy Pismo, a Brazilian cloud-native core banking and issuer-processing platform, for US$1 billion in cash (Visa press release), which shows that a strategic buyer values the category. Our own estimate: if Lerian reached 5% to 15% of the Brazilian market by 2035 (our assumption), that is US$110 to US$325 million a year of revenue at that report's figure; Latin American and US expansion would add to it. What is different: a team with experience in Dock's infrastructure and in the design of Brazil's instant-payment systems (its site says its founding team helped design the architecture of Latin America's largest payments platform and Brazil's instant payments), an open-source model that reverses the usual pricing, and its own messaging layer for Central Bank connections. Named competitors are Pismo (Visa), which Lerian says it wants to beat, and the established core banking vendors in the report above. Fit with Norte (our reading of the Manifesto): serial founders with deep domain knowledge, who know the problem better than an investor; a network business in which introductions to banks, fintechs and funds count; a Norte partner quoted by Startups.com.br says Lerian is 'exactly the type of start-up we look for: serial entrepreneurs, passionate about solving acute pains' and that Brazil has a clear 'right to win' in global financial infrastructure, and Norte joined both rounds led by MAYA, which fits its role of one of several funds on the cap table. Risks: long and trust-heavy sales cycles to regulated institutions; competing with Pismo, which now has Visa's distribution; an open-source model that makes it easy to copy or to use without paying (the licence terms were not checked); and a small team with a product line growing quickly. Confidence is low because the company is two years old, with no published revenue or customer count, and market size comes from a vendor-sold report.
