description.value: Crown issues BRLV, a Brazilian real stablecoin fully backed by federal government bonds and held in a bankruptcy-remote structure, and sells institutions FX, savings and settlement services built on it.

long_description.value: Crown is a São Paulo fintech that issues BRLV, a stablecoin pegged one to one to the Brazilian real and backed fully by Brazilian federal government bonds, mainly Tesouro Selic. Its customers are institutions, not consumers: fintechs, exchanges, tokenisation platforms, asset managers, treasuries and companies that move money across borders. What sets BRLV apart, in Crown's telling, is its legal structure: the reserves sit in a bankruptcy-remote vehicle and are pledged to an independent security agent, so that if Crown itself failed, holders could claim reais from the reserves directly. Reserve and issuance figures are published daily on a transparency page, with attestations from independent auditors. The yield on the bonds is not kept by the issuer: it funds a rewards programme, so that holders who meet conditions (such as holding a position and making certain transactions) earn roughly 93.5% of the CDI rate, less a management fee. Around the token Crown sells four things: value-accrual savings products that other companies can offer their clients through an API, foreign exchange and payments (conversion between BRLV, reais, dollars and dollar stablecoins, with instant settlement), on-chain treasury, and settlement infrastructure for tokenised products. The company was founded in 2024 by John Delaney, an American lawyer who has worked in crypto since 2013, when he started with bitcoin arbitrage, and who noticed that the high Selic rate usually paid more than dollar assets even after the real's falls, while foreign investors found it hard to reach Brazilian fixed income. Stablecoins were the way round that barrier. He founded Crown with Vinicius Correa (a former Nubank developer and co-founder of Pipo Saúde) and Alex Gorra (a former partner at Brainvest), and Bruno Passos, formerly of Hashdex, is COO. Edward Wible, a Nubank co-founder, is on the board, and the economist André Lara Resende, one of the designers of the Plano Real, advises on strategy. Crown launched BRLV in October 2025 with more than R$200 million already subscribed and a US$8.1 million seed round led by Framework Ventures, with Norte Ventures among the investors. In December 2025 a US$13.5 million Series A led by Paradigm, its first investment in Brazil, valued Crown at about US$90 million. By then BRLV had passed R$360 million in subscriptions and the team had seven people. In June 2026 Crown added a foreign exchange desk that converts reais, dollars and BRLV with instant settlement up to US$100,000 per operation, and in August 2026 it agreed with Nexa Finance to offer BRLV in Nexa's investment infrastructure, which serves advisers and family offices managing about R$170 billion; the two estimate about R$200 million of new allocations in twelve months. About R$374 million of BRLV was in issue in August 2026. Crown says it is applying to the Central Bank to be authorised as a virtual asset service provider and meanwhile operates under the Bank's temporary authorisation regime. Its stated ambition is that around 8% of Brazil's monetary base, about R$1 trillion by its own estimate, will move onto blockchains within a decade.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilian fixed income pays some of the highest real rates in the world (Selic 15% in late 2025), but foreign investors and many Brazilian fintechs find it hard to hold it: capital controls, tax rules, local custody and currency conversion get in the way, and moving reais across borders is slow and gated by banking hours. Dollar stablecoins already solve the speed problem for dollars, and Brazil is among the largest crypto markets in Latin America (Chainalysis counted about US$319 billion in crypto received between July 2024 and June 2025, with stablecoins above 90% of volume), so the demand for a native real stablecoin is real. Logic: Crown issues a token that is always backed one to one by government bonds, passes most of the bond yield on to holders through a rewards programme, and sells institutions the plumbing (API-based savings products, FX, treasury, settlement). The legal structure, with reserves in a bankruptcy-remote vehicle held by a security agent, is meant to answer the issuer-failure risk that keeps banks and asset managers away from stablecoins; the Central Bank's new framework for virtual asset providers (Law 14,478/2022) makes licensed issuers a scarce asset. Why now: Brazilian regulation has just been defined, Pix has taught the market instant settlement, and stablecoins have become mainstream finance infrastructure. Market size (our estimate, rough order of magnitude): the Central Bank reports M3 of R$13.8 trillion and M1 of R$656 billion (May 2026), and a restricted monetary base of only R$427.8 billion. Crown's own goal of 8% of the monetary base equal to R$1 trillion matches 8% of a broad aggregate such as M3 (about R$1.1 trillion), not of the restricted base (which would be about R$34 billion), so we read it as a company aspiration, not a market figure. A more cautious bottom-up view: BRLV in issue was about R$374 million (about US$70 million) after ten months; if the token reached 1% of M3 it would be about R$138 billion (about US$25 billion), and 0.1% about R$14 billion. Revenue is the spread between bond yield and what is paid out plus fees (Valor implies about 93.5% of CDI is paid to holders, so the retained spread would be a few percent of balances before costs), so at R$14 billion of float a margin of 1 to 2% would be about R$140 to 280 million a year; these margin figures are our assumption. Different: Crown is the only issuer we found that sells a real stablecoin with enforceable rights over the reserves and a yield pass-through to institutions; the competitors that exist are dollar stablecoins (Tether, Circle) and other local real tokens, which we did not research in depth, so this comparison needs checking. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): the founding team combines a US lawyer who has worked in crypto since 2013 with Nubank and Hashdex alumni, which matches the Manifesto's focus on obsessed, highly intelligent founders; Norte's network of operators and its habit of bringing top funds onto the cap table fits a company whose seed already carried Framework, Valor, Coinbase Ventures and Paxos and whose Series A brought Paradigm. Risks: regulation (Crown still operates under the Central Bank's temporary authorisation, and the Bank has voiced concern about stablecoins); concentration (issuance depends on a few institutional holders such as asset managers and family offices); competition from bank-issued tokens and from Pix itself, which the Central Bank's governor says already solves most payment problems; and a thin revenue model if yields fall with the Selic.

milestones.value: American lawyer John Delaney, in crypto since 2013, founds Crown to give foreign investors access to Brazilian fixed income through a stablecoin backed by government bonds.

Crown launches BRLV, a real stablecoin fully backed by federal bonds, with more than R$200 million already subscribed; Nubank co-founder Edward Wible joins the board and economist André Lara Resende advises on strategy.
BRLV passes R$360 million in subscriptions, which Crown presents as the largest emerging-market stablecoin; the team has seven people.
Crown opens an FX desk that converts reais, dollars and BRLV with instant settlement up to US$100,000 per operation, taking it beyond issuing the token; BRLV in issue is R$373 million.

Crown and Nexa Finance agree to offer BRLV on Nexa's investment infrastructure, which serves advisers and family offices with about R$170 billion; the partners expect about R$200 million of allocations in 12 months.

description.value: Newtail was a Rio de Janeiro retail media platform that let e-commerce retailers sell ad space (sponsored products, banners, video) to brands; VTEX bought it in January 2025.

long_description.value: Newtail was a retail media company from Rio de Janeiro: it built the software with which an online retailer sells advertising space on its own site, until VTEX bought it in January 2025 and made it part of VTEX Ads. Retail media is advertising shown where people are already shopping, so that brands pay a retailer for sponsored products, banners and video on its pages. Newtail offered retailers a self-service platform to sell those formats (sponsored products, display banners, sponsored brand and video ads), plus a way to earn money from the retailer's audience outside its own site, through partners such as Google and Meta, and it had also begun to put ad screens inside physical stores. Its customers were e-commerce retailers such as Casas Bahia, Panvel, KaBuM! and Leroy Merlin, and on the other side more than 400 advertising brands (Baguete counted over 3,000 advertisers on the platform). VTEX's general manager for ads said Casas Bahia, the largest client, did not run its e-commerce on VTEX, so Newtail brought retailers outside VTEX's base. The company was started in 2020 or 2021 (sources differ) by Gabriel Monteiro, Rafael Amorim and Diego Bona, who had already sold earlier businesses to B2W (today Americanas): Monteiro founded the fashion marketplace Shopgram, bought by B2W in 2015, and then ran the Submarino operation. Newtail's first idea was different: in 2021 Startupi described it as a platform to digitise supermarkets using WhatsApp, and the founders took part in the Latitud fellowship, which gave them their first money. By August 2023 the company presented itself as a retail media specialist, with Monteiro writing about the 'third wave' of digital marketing. VTEX, which had launched its own Ad Network in April 2024, bought 100% of Newtail on 2025-01-10, announcing it at the NRF show; the price was not disclosed, but VTEX's ads head told Brazil Journal it was between US$1 million and US$10 million. The three founders stayed to work with VTEX's retail media lead, João Werner. VTEX said retail media was a bet for its expansion: it served 50 retail media clients such as Fast Shop, Drogaria São Paulo and Pague Menos, and Werner argued that capturing 2% of the retailer-side GMV, as Mercado Livre does with its ads, would equal almost VTEX's annual revenue. The newtail.com.br site now leads to VTEX Ads.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilian retailers have a large online audience but earn money mostly on product margin, while brands want to advertise where the purchase happens and today pay Google, Meta and Amazon-style marketplaces for it. A mid-size e-commerce site had no easy way to sell its own banners and sponsored products, measure results for the advertiser, and bring in brands and agencies. Logic: Newtail sold retailers a self-service ad stack and the demand side (brands and agencies) at once, so a retailer could turn audience into a new, high-margin revenue line; the retailer keeps most of the ad money, Newtail takes a commission. Why now: retail media is called the third wave of digital advertising, Omdia expects it to reach about US$293 billion worldwide by 2029 (Startupi), and Brazilian retail media was new enough in 2025 that Brazil Journal listed only three main players (VTEX, Newtail and Topsort) besides marketplaces' own platforms. Market size (rough order of magnitude, our reading): the global figure above is Omdia's, relayed by Startupi, a forecast we did not verify at source. For Brazil there is no figure we read, so we estimate bottom-up from VTEX's own statement: VTEX processes US$18.2 billion of GMV, about half of it from retailers; Mercado Livre earns around 2% of GMV from ads, and VTEX says that rate on its retail base would nearly equal its annual revenue (about US$220 million, from the US$56 million quarterly revenue Baguete reports). That points to a few hundred million dollars of ad revenue on one platform's retailers, and a Brazilian market of perhaps US$1 to 3 billion if 1 to 2% of an assumed US$100 to 150 billion of online retail GMV were captured; the GMV total and the percentage are our assumptions. A small specialist could realistically keep a low single-digit share of that, consistent with the US$1 to 10 million price VTEX paid, which implies a modest outcome rather than a venture-scale one. Different: Newtail's pitch was self-service for mid-market retailers outside any single commerce platform (Casas Bahia did not use VTEX), with offsite monetisation and in-store screens, against VTEX's own tool and the US specialist Topsort. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): serial founders with two earlier exits to B2W who came through Latitud, backed early in a niche that a larger platform could absorb; the Manifesto's focus on obsessed operators and on connecting them to the right funds and customers fits, and the exit confirms the pie-not-piece logic without being a large return. Risks: dependence on a few big retailers (the largest client was Casas Bahia), the lock-in of retail media to platforms such as VTEX and Mercado Livre that own the audience, and a thin price: the acquisition was disclosed only as US$1 to 10 million.

milestones.value: Newtail, still presented as a platform to digitise supermarkets through WhatsApp, enters the Latitud fellowship and receives its first investment from the Latitud fund.

The company is positioned as a retail media specialist; CEO Gabriel Monteiro writes that retail media is the third wave of digital marketing and lets retailers monetise audience through personalisation and tracking.
VTEX launches its Ad Network, creating the competitor-turned-acquirer that would buy Newtail nine months later.
VTEX buys 100% of Newtail, announced at NRF in New York, adding retailers outside VTEX such as Casas Bahia, more than 400 advertisers and in-store screens to VTEX Ads; the three founders stay on.

description.value: Pier is a São Paulo digital insurer selling cell-phone and car insurance online, with AI-driven underwriting and instant claims payouts; in 2025 it had revenue above R$250 million.

long_description.value: Pier is a São Paulo digital insurer that sells cell-phone insurance and car insurance entirely online and through an app, and presents itself as the first digital insurer in Brazil. Its phone policy covers simple theft, qualified theft and robbery with no waiting period and no deductible, including phones without a receipt, and is charged monthly. The car policy covers theft, total loss, partial damage and third-party damage, can be customised, and, according to the founder in 2021, was priced on average about 30% below competitors because Pier's selling and administrative costs were roughly half those of an incumbent and it has no distribution cost. The company says its edge is in technology: it built everything in house, scores each customer from hundreds of behavioural signals instead of the few questions traditional insurers ask, and uses its own AI agents for underwriting, pricing, fraud prevention, claims and service. Its claims promise is speed: it reports a payout in one second, and its site says it has paid out R$211 million to more than 31,000 people. Brokers became a sales channel from 2022. Pier was founded in 2018 by Igor Mascarenhas, Lucas Prado and Rafael Oliveira, starting with phone insurance only and adding cars in 2020. In October 2020 it became the first insurtech authorised to operate in the regulator Susep's sandbox, a simplified regime with limits on vehicle value and cover, and raised a US$14.5 million Series A led by Monashees. In September 2021 a US$20 million (R$108 million) Series B led by the family office Raiz Investimentos aimed to give it the capital to ask for a full licence; at that time it had 50,000 customers, 120 staff and R$3 million of monthly revenue, with 2020 revenue at R$11 to 17 million depending on the source. The International Finance Corporation approved a US$5 million loan in December 2021. By 2025 revenue exceeded R$250 million; Camila Kataguiri, who joined as COO in early 2022 and became co-CEO in 2023, took over as CEO from Mascarenhas in January 2026. In May 2026 Pier launched an app inside ChatGPT, in June 2026 Forbes and Statista ranked it Brazil's best auto insurer, and by August 2026 it reported R$200 million of revenue for the year, 200,000 active customers across the two lines, 500,000 members assisted and break-even with positive cash generation. It plans a Series C of up to US$50 million within 12 months to fund products and possible acquisitions, and aims for 100,000 auto members by the end of 2026. The registry shows Pier Seguradora S.A. (CNPJ 39.380.513/0001-00) opened in October 2020, matching the sandbox licence.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: most Brazilians with a phone, car or home are uninsured or under-insured (Pier's CEO said in 2020 that only about 30% of the population had car insurance, 10% home and 2% life), because traditional insurance is expensive, slow to sell and slow to pay. Logic: a digital insurer that sells without brokers or branches, prices from behavioural data and pays instantly can undercut incumbents on cost and win customers who had no cover (Pier said in 2021 that 75% of its customers had no insurance before). Starting with cell-phone theft, where the loss is small and frequent, gave it data and a brand before it moved to cars. Why now: Susep's sandbox (2020) let a startup become an insurer, mobile penetration is universal, and AI lowers underwriting and claims costs. Market size (rough order of magnitude): Susep reported R$28.9 billion of auto premiums in the first half of 2025, 41.4% of the property and casualty segment, so roughly R$58 billion a year, and total market collections of R$206 billion in the half (including life and pension products). Pier's 2025 revenue of more than R$250 million is therefore only about 0.4% of annualised auto premium, but its revenue also includes phone insurance and is gross of reinsurance (we do not know how it is measured). If a strong outcome were 2 to 4% of auto premiums, that would be about R$1.2 to 2.3 billion of premium a year; the share is our assumption. Different: native digital onboarding and claims, sandbox heritage, in-house technology and a phone-theft product that incumbents did not offer (simple theft, no receipt). Comparables abroad: Lemonade (the US digital insurer Pier compared its payout speed with). Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): three founders and a tech-heavy team in a regulated sector where a connector with funds and operators helps; the sandbox first-mover advantage and leading funds (Monashees, Canary, Mercado Livre, BTG, Raiz) fit the Manifesto's logic of bringing top funds to the cap table. We found no source naming Norte in any Pier round, so the fit is inferred from the portfolio listing only. Risks: capital and solvency needs in insurance (the sandbox and then licence rules demand technical reserves of 30 to 45% of premiums), claims ratio on auto (about 60% in 2021 per the founder), competition from Porto Seguro's Blue brand and other incumbents, and leadership change after the founder stepped down in 2026.

milestones.value: Pier starts selling cell-phone insurance, covering simple theft and robbery with no waiting period, which few insurers offered.
Pier adds car insurance, an easy-to-buy basic policy for cars up to R$70,000 covering theft, total loss and technical assistance.
Pier becomes the first insurtech authorised to operate in Susep's regulatory sandbox, allowing it to underwrite its own policies, and raises its US$14.5 million Series A.
A US$20 million Series B led by Raiz Investimentos funds the capital needed to apply for a full Susep licence; Pier has 50,000 customers, 120 staff and R$3 million of monthly revenue.
The IFC board approves a US$5 million loan to Pier Seguradora to support growth and regulatory capital.
Camila Kataguiri, who joined as COO in early 2022 and led the entry into the broker channel, becomes co-CEO next to founder Igor Mascarenhas.
Camila Kataguiri becomes CEO, succeeding founder Igor Mascarenhas, as the company that reached R$250 million in revenue in 2025 aims for 50% growth in 2026.
Pier launches an app inside ChatGPT, presenting itself as the first Brazilian insurer integrated into the ecosystem, to test AI platforms as an insurance distribution channel.
Pier reports R$200 million of revenue for the year, 200,000 active customers, 500,000 assisted members and break-even with positive cash generation.

description.value: IORQ is a São Paulo credit platform that originates and funds corporate credit through its own managed funds and gives companies white-label tools to run credit and embedded finance, founded by iFood and Nomad co-founder Patrick Sigrist.

long_description.value: IORQ (Investimentos Orquestrados) is a São Paulo credit platform that wants to change how companies in Brazil get and give credit. It sits between borrowers and investors: it raises money from investors into funds it manages (mostly FIDCs, the receivables-backed funds that finance companies directly) and lends or buys receivables from companies, while giving other companies the technology to run credit as part of their own business. The site presents three products: direct credit for upper-mid-market and corporate companies, embedded finance (credit inside a company's own ecosystem, under its brand and control, white label and via API), and structured operations that securitise receivables originated by third parties. The technology, proprietary, structures and monitors each loan in real time and controls the collateral, with AI automating the credit pipeline, so that, in the words of its COO Bernardo Mergár, the technological difference is less in granting the loan than in everything that comes after it. The pitch to borrowers is autonomy and data granularity; to investors, more return and scale without intermediaries. The company was created by Patrick Sigrist, co-founder of iFood and of the global account Nomad, who says that after fifteen years at iFood and six at Nomad he needed something new and that the idea came from Nomad, where building a credit area meant either outsourcing everything or finding someone to help. Bloomberg Línea says building IORQ took 18 months. The company has been a business from day one because it was formed around an acquisition: Quatá Investimentos, a São Paulo credit manager founded in 2008 with more than 15 years of track record and more than R$15 billion of corporate credit originated, which also served as the cradle of QI Tech, was bought for an undisclosed price, paid in shares. Quatá's founder Beatriz Degani became IORQ's CEO, Sigrist is executive chairman and Mergár is COO and partner. The structure brought R$2.5 billion under management on day one. In August 2025 IORQ announced R$35 million in what Sigrist called a 'compact Series A' led by Monashees and Upload Ventures, with ONE.VC and Norte Ventures, to strengthen its technology infrastructure; the goal was to raise credit origination by 50% by the end of the year. In late 2026 its site claims more than R$15 billion originated, R$3.5 billion under management, default below 0.7% and more than ten dedicated funds structured, among them the Alume FIDC for embedded finance, the Quatá FGTS payroll-credit funds, the Prass direct-lending funds and a multisector FIDC.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: credit in Brazil is concentrated (the central bank's data, relayed by Bloomberg Línea, says banks gave 85% of credit in 2024 and the four largest institutions 58% of operations), so companies outside the biggest banks' reach pay high spreads, and many companies and startups that want to offer credit to their own customers, suppliers or employees face a choice between outsourcing to a third party and building a credit desk themselves. Investors, for their part, lack direct, transparent access to corporate credit. Logic: IORQ combines an experienced credit manager (Quatá) with a technology layer, so it can originate credit itself and also lend its structure to others (embedded finance, white label), and it earns fees on assets it manages and on the services around them; funds give it scalable, recurring funding. Why now: Brazil's regulators have encouraged FIDCs and receivables markets, high interest rates make private credit attractive to investors, and the founders' own experience at Nomad showed demand for credit as a feature. Market size (rough order of magnitude): the Central Bank's statistics (June 2026 bulletin, May 2026 data) show a financial-system credit stock of R$7.3 trillion, of which R$2.7 trillion to companies, and broader corporate credit including debt securities of R$7.2 trillion. IORQ says it manages R$3.5 billion, so it holds roughly 0.1% of corporate bank credit; reaching 1% of the R$2.7 trillion would be about R$27 billion under management. At an assumed 1 to 2% management and structuring revenue on assets (our assumption), that would be R$270 to 540 million a year. Different: unlike a pure fund manager, it also sells the platform to companies that want their own credit operation; Bloomberg Línea names QI Tech (a unicorn for lending and banking as a service, born from Quatá) as the relevant comparable, and other credit-as-a-service players exist that we did not research. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): a serial founder with two proven companies, an operating CEO with 15 years of credit execution, and a Series A led by top funds where Norte joined as a follower, the pattern the Manifesto describes (networks and connecting the right funds to the cap table). Risks: credit risk and default cycles on funds that carry the company's name, regulatory changes on FIDCs, dependence on funding appetite when interest rates fall, and unclear differentiation among credit platforms; the 2026 performance figures are not audited by any source we read.

milestones.value: Patrick Sigrist, after iFood and Nomad, starts building IORQ; the structure takes 18 months to design, around the idea of letting companies run their own credit operations.
IORQ launches with R$2.5 billion under management after absorbing the credit manager Quatá Investimentos (founded 2008) in a share swap; Quatá founder Beatriz Degani becomes CEO.
IORQ announces R$35 million from Monashees, Upload Ventures, ONE.VC and Norte to expand its technology infrastructure, and aims to raise origination by 50% before year end.

The company reports more than R$15 billion originated, R$3.5 billion under management, default below 0.7% and more than ten dedicated funds, including an embedded-finance FIDC (Alume) and consigned-FGTS funds.

description.value: The Coffee is a Curitiba-born chain of tiny, minimalist, cashless coffee shops inspired by Japan, sold mostly through franchises in Brazil and abroad.

long_description.value: The Coffee is a Brazilian coffee chain, born in Curitiba, that sells espresso drinks to take away in very small, minimalist shops inspired by Japanese mini cafés. The shop is often under 10 square metres with one barista; the customer orders and pays on a tablet or in the app, there is no cash, and the chain's own software runs the store. Beans are selected and roasted by the company itself in Curitiba, with a roasting centre in Europe too, and the brand also sells beans, mugs and bags online and in its shops. The business is almost entirely franchising: franchisees and master franchisees are more than 95% of the network, and the company earns royalties and a franchise fee (about R$50,000 in Brazil and €15,000 in Europe, with an average initial investment of R$300,000 in Brazil and €75,000 in Europe) plus income from selling ingredients and its own software, which, according to a co-founder in 2022, leaves the franchisor with 40 to 50% of total shop revenue. About 15% of sales are food and the rest drinks. The format comes in several sizes, from the 12 m² street shop to malls and a modular container, and menus are part global and part local. The Fertonani brothers (Carlos, the CEO; Alexandre, a former commercial director at Latam Airlines, in charge of expansion; and Luis, a designer who built the brand identity) planned the company at family Sunday lunches in late 2017 and opened the first store in Curitiba in 2018 on the Alameda Prudente de Moraes. In 2019 Monashees put in R$500,000 and in December 2020 a R$28 million (US$5 million) Series A led by Monashees, with Norte Ventures and Shift Capital following as existing shareholders, financed the push from 30 stores to a plan of 100, with the first stores in Lisbon, Madrid and Barcelona opening in 2021. In December 2022 a US$7.5 million Series B led by Monashees and CapSur Capital valued the company at US$45 million; by then it had 195 stores, 11 of them in Europe, and was in talks for Mexico and Peru. The chain reached 350 shops (175 in Brazil, 175 abroad) in 2026 with its first store in Morocco, so it operates on five continents; it entered the US with a shop in Miami's Wynwood, run by a franchisee from Mexico City, and had opened in 70 new places abroad in 2025. The company projects 480 shops and about US$78 million (R$392 million) of revenue in 2026, with sales split roughly evenly among Brazil, Europe and other master franchisees. Carlos Fertonani now lives in Portugal and expects Europe to grow 70% and Brazil 20% this year.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: coffee shops in Brazil and abroad are costly to open (large rents, staff, cash handling), so premium-quality coffee reaches few places, and the dominant chains compete on the experience of sitting rather than on speed and quality to take away. Logic: a very small shop with one worker, self-service ordering and cashless payment lowers the cost of opening and operating (Brazil Journal: franchisee investment about R$100,000 in 2020, R$300,000 on average in 2026), and a franchisor that also sells ingredients and software earns on every cup. A format that shrinks to a few square metres fits busy pedestrian sites and malls, which are scarce but valuable. Why now: specialty coffee is growing as consumers trade up (the 'third wave'), tablets and apps replace the till, and master franchising lets a Brazilian brand reach 24 countries with little capital. Market size (rough order of magnitude, our reading): Starbucks alone had 35,700 stores and US$32.25 billion revenue in fiscal 2022 (Bloomberg Línea), which shows how large a branded coffee chain can become; The Coffee has 350 stores (about 1% of that store count). If the chain reached 2,000 to 3,000 units at the roughly US$160,000 of annual sales per store implied by its own projection (US$78 million on 480 stores), network sales would be US$320 to 480 million, and, with the franchisor keeping 40 to 50% of shop revenue as the co-founder said, franchisor revenue of about US$130 to 240 million; the store counts are our assumptions. That is about 5 to 10 times today's scale but still below one tenth of Starbucks, so we call it a credible, not an aggressive, strong outcome. Different: the format is the smallest and cheapest in the market, with its own software and a master-franchise model, and Japanese minimalism as a differentiating identity; competitors named in the press are Starbucks, and other Brazilian and regional chains we did not research (Juan Valdez, Cafe Martinez and others). Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): a family founding team that builds slowly with operating discipline and international ambition fits the Manifesto's preference for obsessed founders and a follower role next to Monashees, which led the Series A and B; a company that went from 30 to 350 stores, mostly via franchisees' capital, fits its stress on the size of the pie. Risks: franchisee economics (a store sells about R$33,000 a month by our arithmetic from the Brazil Journal numbers and depends on foot traffic), brand quality across 24 countries and master franchisees, coffee bean price swings, and the fact that the revenue figures come from the company itself.

milestones.value: The Coffee opens its first shop, under nine square metres in downtown Curitiba, designed after Japanese mini cafés with tablet ordering and no cash; a second shop follows a year later.
Monashees makes the first investment, R$500,000, a US$500,000 seed according to Bloomberg Línea.
A R$28 million (US$5 million) Series A led by Monashees finances growth from 30 stores toward 100 in 2021 and the first European shops in Lisbon, Madrid and Barcelona.
The first European stores open in Portugal, Spain and France, run by a team sent from Brazil, with a roasting centre built in Europe.
A US$7.5 million Series B led by Monashees and CapSur Capital values the company at US$45 million; it has 195 stores, 11 in Europe, and is in talks for Mexico and Peru.
The first shop in the United States opens in Miami, run by a Mexico City franchisee; the chain closed 2025 with 70 new units abroad and is present in 24 countries.
With 350 shops (175 in Brazil, 175 abroad) and Morocco added, the chain operates on five continents and targets 480 shops and about US$78 million of revenue for 2026.

description.value: BHub is a São Paulo back-office-as-a-service company that offers accounting, tax and financial management by subscription and grows by buying accounting firms.

long_description.value: BHub is a São Paulo company that acts as the outsourced back office of other companies: accounting, tax, payroll, accounts payable and receivable, reconciliations, corporate and legal services, sold as a monthly subscription (plans started at R$1,799 in 2021) through a platform with a dashboard and chat. It was born as a technology-led replacement for the finance department of startups and small and mid-sized companies, with a team of engineers, accountants and lawyers; the pitch at launch was a cost 14 times lower than hiring in-house, saving about R$20,000 a month per client. Today its main business is accounting, and it targets companies one step above the smallest: those under the Presumed or Real Profit tax regimes, with more complex accounting than the small-business Simples regime served by rivals such as Contabilizei. Customers include startups such as Kovi and Pipo Saúde, NGOs such as Gerando Falcões and TETO, and asset managers such as Pátria and Tarpon. The site claims more than 51 million invoices booked a year, R$44 billion reconciled a year and 119,000 lives on its payroll platform. From November 2024 the company grew through acquisitions of accounting firms: it describes itself as a group of specialists, among them Agrocontar, with 26 years in agribusiness accounting and about R$40 million of revenue, and Quality Associados, with more than 25 years in the non-profit sector. Jorge Vargas Neto, a former Pinheiro Neto lawyer, started BHub in June 2021 with Fernando Ricco (a former Adyen investor-relations head), Vanessa Muglia and Marcelio Leal. It is his third company, after the peer-to-peer lender Biva (bought by PagSeguro in 2017) and the credit-as-a-service Zen Finance (bought by Rappi in 2021): he says that a capital-gains tax surprise caused by a missed accounting entry during the rushed Zen Finance sale gave him the idea. Funding came fast: R$23 million pre-seed, then a Series A of about R$116 million in December 2021 led by Monashees and Valor Capital Group, an extension of R$40 million in September 2022 led by Moore Capital (with Norte among the participants), R$74 million led by the IFC in September 2024, and a US$10 million round in November 2025 led by Next Billion Capital Partners, described as a pre-Series B. In 2022 it had 150 employees and 400 clients; in September 2024 it had 4,000 clients and said it had grown 400% since early 2024; in November 2025 it had 8,500 clients, an expected R$150 million of revenue in 2025 (up 160%) and an annualised run rate of R$168 million, and said it expects to pass R$300 million in 2026 and raise a Series B to fund more acquisitions. It says it has become profitable and has made 10 acquisitions (Startups.com.br counts 20 companies bought since 2021). The founder says the Tax Reform will force consolidation among accounting firms and that BHub wants to lead it with artificial intelligence.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: small and mid-sized Brazilian companies face one of the world's most complex tax and accounting systems, often relying on small local accounting offices that are slow, manual and error-prone, and startups find that accounting mistakes can become expensive surprises (the founder's own experience at Zen Finance). Logic: BHub bundles accounting, finance and legal back-office into a subscription run on its own platform, automates the repetitive work, and uses its capital to buy local firms, which brings clients, specialists and cash flow, and then runs them on shared technology. Why now: the Tax Reform will require companies to operate under two tax regimes for a transition period, which raises compliance costs and favours scale; AI can automate bookkeeping tasks; and an ageing, fragmented accounting market is ready to consolidate. Market size (our estimate, rough order of magnitude): we found no independent market figure. Bottom-up with our assumptions: if about one million Brazilian companies fall in BHub's target (above the small-business Simples regime, with enough complexity to pay for outsourced accounting and finance) and each spends R$20,000 to R$40,000 a year, the addressable spend is about R$20 to 40 billion a year. BHub's expected R$150 million of revenue in 2025 is therefore around 0.5%, and the R$300 million it aims for in 2026 about 1%. A strong outcome of 3 to 5% would mean R$600 million to R$2 billion of annual revenue. The number of target companies and the spend per client are assumptions, not sources. Different: BHub is the only one we found combining a roll-up of specialist accounting firms with a proprietary platform and focusing on mid-market companies; Contabilizei (backed by Warburg Pincus) serves the smallest firms, and the Big Four sit above it. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): a serial founder (Biva, Zen Finance) whose earlier companies were sold, with a team that raised large rounds led by Monashees, Valor and IFC; Norte joined as a follower in the extension, which matches the Manifesto's logic of bringing top funds and angels onto the cap table and focusing on the size of the pie. Risks: roll-ups depend on integration and on debt and equity to pay for acquisitions (the founder says a first instalment is typically 60% equity and 40% debt), the quality of earnings may differ between acquired firms and the platform, growth figures are the company's, the Tax Reform timeline may change, and AI could reduce barriers for new competitors.

milestones.value: Jorge Vargas Neto, who sold Biva to PagSeguro and Zen Finance to Rappi, starts BHub with Fernando Ricco, Vanessa Muglia and Marcelio Leal to be the outsourced finance and accounting department of startups.
Monashees and Valor Capital Group lead a R$115 million Series A in a company created only months earlier, with plans to grow from about a hundred to thousands of clients and to hire 100 people.

A R$40 million extension led by Moore Capital closes the Series A at R$156 million; BHub has 150 employees and has served more than 400 companies, and launches a free dashboard, the Hub do Empreendedor.
The IFC leads a R$74 million round, bringing total funding to about R$250 million, as BHub serves more than 4,000 clients after growing 400% since early 2024.
BHub starts buying accounting firms, a consolidation strategy financed by equity, debt and the cash flow of the acquired businesses.

BHub buys Agrocontar, Brazil's largest agribusiness accounting firm (about R$40 million revenue), alongside a US$10 million pre-Series B round led by Next Billion Capital Partners; it has 8,500 clients and expects R$150 million of revenue in 2025.

co_investors: iFood, Rappi, Olist and VTEX founders

description.value: Stark Bank is a São Paulo payment institution and bank-like platform for mid-sized and large companies, offering accounts, Pix, cards, collections, credit and digital fixed income through its own infrastructure and APIs.

long_description.value: Stark Bank is a São Paulo financial institution for mid-sized and large companies that combines banking with its own software. It is licensed by the Central Bank as a payment institution and as a direct credit company, and it built its banking infrastructure from scratch rather than renting it, which its founder says gives it control over the product. Customers use a business account and cash management (paying and receiving through Pix, boletos and transfers via an API or the web, with reconciliation by cost centre and approval flows), card acquiring (online card payments and the bank domicile for card-machine receivables), Pix subscriptions for recurring charges, a corporate card with unlimited virtual cards and 1.5% cashback, invoicing and receivables management, payroll and supplier payments, a credit limit it says is 10 to 20 times larger than what banks offer, digital fixed income paying 100% of the CDI with daily liquidity, and crypto trading. Revenue comes from the take rate on payments, card interchange, receivables and credit. Rafael Stark founded it in 2018, first as a bank for startups driven by an API that replaced the old remittance files, a product comparable to Stripe, with early clients such as Rappi, Buser, Ingresse and Kovi; he first compared it with the US company Brex. Along the way the plan changed and it aimed at large companies, and the founder now compares the ambition to Apple's control of its stack. It raised an undisclosed round led by Iporanga Ventures in February 2020, a US$13 million Series A in December 2021 led by the solo investor Lachy Groom (with K5 Global, Iporanga, Norte and founders of Coinbase, Dropbox, Flexport, Figma, Slack, Rappi and dLocal), and a US$45 million Series B in April 2022 led by Ribbit Capital with Jeff Bezos's Bezos Expeditions, which valued it at more than US$250 million; the Series A article said it had been profitable since June 2021, moved more than R$1 billion a month and grew volume 33% a month. In 2023 it started credit on the corporate card with R$300 million planned for the first half, backed by a fixed-income token as collateral. By November 2026 it reported US$61.1 million raised in five rounds and total payment volume above R$670 billion in the previous year. At the end of 2025 it created Stark Digital Assets, which began operating in January 2026 with a multi-currency account for Bitcoin and stablecoins, applied to the Central Bank for virtual-asset-provider authorisation, and plans to use stablecoins for Brazil-US payments, with expansion expected in 2027. In 2026 it was also named, according to Times Brasil, as the private partner running the Goiás state government's financial platform Pequi Bank.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: mid-sized and large Brazilian companies run payments and receivables through legacy bank processes (remittance files, boletos, separate systems for cards and cash), with little transparency over cash flow and limited credit; banks give them poor APIs and slow service. Logic: Stark Bank builds a modern banking stack and gives companies one place for accounts, Pix, collections, cards and credit, with APIs and automated reconciliation, making money on every flow and later on credit secured by its own fixed-income product. Because it built its own infrastructure, it can iterate faster than banks and cut third-party costs. Why now: Pix and the Central Bank's open regulation of payment institutions have lowered barriers; the largest incumbents are slow at software; and companies want finance operations automated. Market size (rough order of magnitude, our reading): Stark Bank says it processed more than R$670 billion in the last year (Let's Money, company figure). If its net revenue were 0.05 to 0.1% of volume (our assumption, covering fees, float, card revenue and credit margin), that would be R$335 to 670 million a year. A strong outcome of several times today's volume (for instance R$2 to 3 trillion, which is 3 to 4 times today's) would give R$1 to 3 billion of revenue at the same take rates. We found no independent market-size figure for corporate banking, so these are assumptions. Comparable: Brex, founded by two Brazilians and valued at US$12.3 billion at its October 2021 round (NeoFeed), which targets companies' spending and cards in the US. Different: focus on mid and large companies rather than small ones, a self-built stack, software-style API integration, and early profitability (the Series A article said profitable since June 2021, a company statement). Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): a technical founder building a product-led infrastructure company in a regulated field, with a Series A led by a solo investor who had worked at Stripe and with founders of Coinbase and other fintechs on the cap table, where Norte (called Norte Capital in press) joined as a follower; this matches the Manifesto's focus on obsessed, highly capable founders and on bringing the right funds and angels to the cap table. Risks: regulation and reputation (Central Bank tightening of the use of 'bank' in names, an exposure to the betting market that led to two Senate committees calling the company, and a Goiás state contract that the state prosecutors are examining, according to Times Brasil, which we could not verify), concentration in a few large customers and payment flows, dependence on Pix margins that are regulated, and a crowded field of banks and fintechs for business clients.

milestones.value: Rafael Stark founds Stark Bank to give startups a bank whose API replaces the old remittance files for payments and collections.
The company receives its Central Bank licence, and by late 2020 it announces a corporate credit card, widening its model to earn on card transactions.

Stark Bank raises its first announced round, led by Iporanga Ventures, with clients and founders such as Rappi's former CEO in Brazil, Buser and Ingresse taking part; it says it grew 81% a month in revenue in 2019.
A US$13 million Series A led by solo investor Lachy Groom; the company says it has been profitable since June 2021 and moves more than R$1 billion a month.
A US$45 million Series B led by Ribbit Capital and Bezos Expeditions (the first Brazilian startup in Bezos's fund) values it at more than US$250 million, four months after the Series A.
Stark Bank starts offering credit on its corporate card, with about R$300 million of credit lines planned for the first half and a fixed-income token as collateral.
Stark Digital Assets starts operating, with a multi-currency account for Bitcoin and stablecoins; it later applies to the Central Bank to act as a virtual asset service provider.
Goiás launches Pequi Bank, a state financial platform managed with Stark Bank as the private partner chosen by public call, reported by Times Brasil to be under review by the state prosecutors.

co_investors: founders of Coinbase, Dropbox, Flexport, Figma, Slack, Rappi, dLocal and Wildlife

description.value: AI financial assistant for small businesses and self-employed people that runs inside WhatsApp and its own app, handling payments, charges and money management by text, voice or photo.

long_description.value: Jota is a Brazilian fintech that gives micro-entrepreneurs and small businesses a digital account run through an AI assistant, in WhatsApp or in its own conversational app (launched in February 2026). The owner opens an account in a few minutes by starting a chat, then pays suppliers by text, voice note or a photo of a bill, charges customers with a Pix QR code, boleto or card (up to 12 instalments), records who owes money, and asks the assistant for revenue reports, calculations and tips; the name plays on 'PJ' (pessoa jurídica). Extra agents handle calendar reminders, scheduled payments and receipts, and overdraft alerts through Open Finance. Most features are free; the main income today comes from FalaTap, a function that turns a phone into a card machine, launched in 2026 (Brazil Journal says about a month before June 2026, Startups.com.br says the first quarter), plus receivables advance; credit tied to the overdraft alert is planned, and a 'reverse trial' subscription (full product free up to a daily limit, then paid) comes with Jota 3.0. The assistant runs on Meta's WhatsApp APIs and OpenAI models, with Jota training its own finance model on top. Founder Davi Holanda, from Ceará, spent six years at PagBank leading more than 15 products (including its card-machine and prepaid and credit card lines), left right after its 2018 IPO, and helped found Bankly, a banking-as-a-service company bought by Méliuz and later sold to Banco BV; he created Jota in July 2024 with Marcelo Leite. It launched publicly on 24 January 2025 after a beta with friends and family, with a US$8.9 million seed led by Maya Capital (HOF Capital, BigBets, Alter Global, Bogari, Norte Ventures and angels), which the press also puts at R$60 million. By June 2026 it had about 300,000 clients, mostly small businesses and freelancers, and R$3.5 billion of annualised payment volume; it aimed at R$50 million of annualised revenue by December, 1 million clients and more than R$10 billion of volume in 2026. In June 2026 it raised a US$30 million (R$150 million) Series A led by Haun Ventures, its first Brazilian investment, at a US$185 million post-money valuation, with HOF, Alter Global and Greyhound Capital. The money goes to Jota 2.0, a proactive agent that sorts expenses and acts without being asked (about five times more engagement in early tests), to credit, and to hires: in November 2026 it named a CTO, CFO and its first head of HR.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: Brazil's micro-entrepreneurs run their business from the phone and a notebook. They charge by Pix over WhatsApp, track debts on paper, and use banks whose apps were built for individuals, while big banks treat them as a low-priority segment. The Maya Capital partner called the segment very under-served and not a priority for large banks. The logic: if the interface is the chat the customer already uses all day, onboarding takes minutes, the assistant does tasks (pay, charge, record, remind) instead of showing menus, and the account becomes the source of data for credit and acquiring offers; the founder's thesis is that after branches, internet banking and apps, the next interface is an AI agent that works continuously for the client. Why now: Pix made instant payments free and universal, WhatsApp's business APIs and language models make a reliable conversational agent possible and cheap to build, and Open Finance opens the data for overdraft and credit. Market: the Receita Federal's government panel (as reported by Brasil 61 in June 2025) shows 23.5 million active companies in Brazil and 12.7 million of them MEIs, half of all firms; many more are micro and small businesses and freelancers. Our estimate of the revenue pool: if a strong outcome is 2 to 3 million active clients (about 15 to 25% of MEIs, our assumption, against about 300,000 today) each yielding R$200 to R$600 a year from acquiring, receivables advance, credit and subscription (our assumption; the company's own R$50M target on 300,000 to 1 million clients implies about R$50 to R$170 a client in 2026), the pool is about R$0.4 to R$1.8 billion a year, with credit as the upside. What is different: a conversational-first account with a product leader from PagBank's growth era, a free entry that spreads quickly (about 300,000 clients in 17 months), and tier-one backers new to Brazil (Haun, HOF). Competitors: PagBank, Stone, Mercado Pago, Nubank PJ and CloudWalk's InfinitePay, named as card-machine rivals in the press, are far larger and chase the same segment. Fit with Norte (our reading): a repeat founder with an operating record and a clear view that the interface is changing, an early stage where Norte joined the seed beside Maya, and a network need around funds and hiring that suits its connector role. Risks: the free product has to be monetised, and most revenue so far comes from a card-machine product that competes with giants on price; dependence on WhatsApp and one AI vendor; credit to micro-businesses has losses; and a young company (2 years old) is growing fast with new executives.

milestones.value: Company created by Davi Holanda
Official launch of the WhatsApp financial assistant after a beta with friends and family
Launches FalaTap, a function that turns a phone into a card machine (up to 12 instalments), which becomes its main revenue source
Launches its own conversational app alongside the WhatsApp assistant
Reaches about 300,000 clients and R$3.5 billion of annualised payment volume, and starts 'Jota 2.0', a proactive agent that sorts spending without being asked
Hires a CTO (Arosti Nahas), a CFO (Mateus Furini) and its first head of HR (Ana Flávia Justino) to prepare for regulatory demands and AI platform growth

description.value: Nomad is a São Paulo fintech that gives Brazilians a US-dollar or euro account, an international card, a Brazilian credit card and a global investing platform.

long_description.value: Nomad is a São Paulo fintech that gives Brazilians a global financial life: a US-dollar or euro account (the dollar account sits at a US bank, with FDIC cover up to US$250,000), an international debit card accepted at more than 35 million places, a Brazilian credit card (Nomad Explorer), instalment purchase of foreign currency, an international SIM card, travel insurance and bookings, international payments and a way to receive payments from abroad. On the investment side it offers a platform with more than 2,000 international options (US stocks, bond and other ETFs, REITs and selected funds by risk profile) and a wealth advisory service called Nomad Wealth, and it has opened physical lounges and a benefits programme. It makes money from foreign-exchange spreads and fees, card interchange, and investment and advice fees, and in 2025 it launched a service so that Brazilian startups can bring home money raised abroad at competitive rates with 24/7 support. The company went live in November 2020 (the second half of 2020 per Bloomberg Línea), founded by Patrick Sigrist, co-founder of iFood, with Marcos Nader and Eduardo Haber, and run by Lucas Vargas, a former head of the Zap Viva Real group who is CEO and also counted as co-founder. The founders started with their own capital, raised about US$7.5 million in two early rounds from angels and funds, and in July 2021 closed a US$20 million Series A co-led by Monashees and Spark Capital, when it had 50,000 accounts after nine months, 75 staff and R$140 million raised. It reached 100,000 accounts by its first anniversary, 300,000 by April 2022 and 1 million by August 2023. A US$32 million round led by Stripes (valuation US$200 million) came in May 2022, and a US$61 million Series B led by Tiger Global in August 2023 valued it at R$1.8 billion. At the end of 2022 it bought Husky, a start-up for international transfers to people in Brazil working for foreign employers. In November 2026 a R$172 million Series C led by Tether Capital, with Endeavor joining, valued it at R$4 billion; the company says it reached EBITDA break-even in 2025, has annualised revenue above R$880 million, gross margin above 70%, 5 million customers (four times the Series B base) and more than R$10 billion under custody. The funds go to AI, fixed-income and Nomad Wealth, and new payment rails with Tether, which Nomad says will enable faster and cheaper international transfers.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilians who travel, study, work or invest abroad, or who want part of their wealth in dollars, face expensive and slow routes: traditional banks charge high spreads and IOF tax on foreign-currency operations, opening a US account is cumbersome, and Brazilian investors have few ways to buy US assets. Logic: Nomad offers a fully digital US account and card, a Brazilian credit card, and an international investing platform in Portuguese, built for Brazilians by Brazilians, and monetises FX, interchange and advice; once the account is the customer's global wallet, investments and credit follow. Why now: Brazilians are increasingly diversifying into hard currency (Nomad's own cofounder says the habit is changing), international travel and remote work abroad have grown, and stablecoin rails promise cheaper cross-border transfers (the new partner Tether). Market size (rough order of magnitude, our reading): no independent market study was read. From the company's own figures, annualised revenue of more than R$880 million on 5 million customers is about R$176 a year per customer; if the market were 20 to 30 million Brazilians with international spending or dollar savings (our assumption) and each generated R$150 to 300 a year, the addressable revenue would be R$3 to 9 billion a year, and the 5 million customers would be 15 to 25% penetration, so the growth case depends on raising revenue per customer through investments, credit and payments. R$10 billion of assets under custody is small next to the R$13.8 trillion M3 reported by the Central Bank in May 2026 (about 0.07%), so even a modest rise in the share of wealth held abroad would be large. Comparables: Wise and Revolut abroad, and Brazilian rivals such as Wise-like fintechs and large banks; none was researched here. Different: Nomad built around the Brazilian customer's needs (instalments, Portuguese support, wealth advice, a physical lounge) and reached break-even while growing. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): a serial founder (iFood co-founder Sigrist) with a strong operator CEO and an investor group of top funds (Monashees, Spark, Stripes, Tiger, Tether, Endeavor), where a connector with the founders' network adds value early; the Manifesto's emphasis on obsessed operators and top funds on the cap table matches. Risks: regulation of foreign-exchange operations and taxes (IOF), competition from banks and global fintechs (the cost of acquiring customers), dependence on FX spreads that tend to shrink, partnership risk with Tether and the US account bank, and the fact that profitability and revenue figures are the company's own.

sub_sector.value: Global accounts and investing for Brazilians

milestones.value: Nomad launches a digital US-dollar account for Brazilians, started by iFood co-founder Patrick Sigrist with Lucas Vargas, Eduardo Haber and Marcos Nader.
A US$20 million Series A co-led by Monashees and Spark Capital funds growth from 75 to 150 staff; the company already has 50,000 accounts after nine months.
Nomad passes 100,000 accounts at the end of its first year of operation.
A US$32 million round led by Stripes values Nomad at about US$200 million; accounts reach 300,000 by April 2022.
Nomad buys Husky, an international transfer startup that helps Brazilians paid by foreign employers receive money in Brazil, using Series A money.
A US$61 million Series B led by Tiger Global values the company at R$1.8 billion and funds credit products; Nomad passes 1 million accounts.
Nomad launches an FX service for Brazilian startups that receive money from foreign investors, with competitive rates and 24/7 support in Portuguese.
A R$172 million Series C led by Tether Capital values Nomad at R$4 billion; the company reports EBITDA break-even in 2025, R$880 million of annualised revenue and 5 million customers.

description.value: Kovi rents cars to ride-hailing drivers in Brazil and Mexico, with taxes, maintenance, protection and assistance included and no credit check; Moove bought it in 2025.

long_description.value: Kovi is a São Paulo car-rental company built for people who drive for ride-hailing apps such as Uber and 99. Instead of selling or financing a car, it rents one with the costs of owning it bundled in: taxes (IPVA), maintenance, a protection package, 24-hour assistance and a replacement car. It does not ask for a credit check or a credit-card limit, which was the point from the start: its first customers were drivers with a credit profile that banks and traditional rental firms would not serve. Today the plans are an annual rental of new cars with an option to buy from the 13th month, with the deposit counted towards the price, and a flexible plan with a minimum stay of eight weeks, plus used cars and a "Kovi Próprio" plan of up to 48 months with a purchase option. Kovi makes money from the weekly rent (from R$299 a week in 2021) and, in its cofounder's words, behaves like a fintech that delivers the car while using other companies' balance sheets (carmakers, rental firms and lessors) to fund the fleet. This asset-light model differs from Localiza, Unidas and Movida, which buy cars in volume and resell them. The company was founded in August 2018 by Adhemar Milani Neto, a former Bain consultant who ran the taxi unit of the 99 app, and João Costa, 99's product director, who is CTO. It went through Y Combinator (Winter 2019), raised a US$10.5 million seed round led by Monashees in May 2019, then a US$30 million round led by Global Founders Capital in November 2019, and began renting in São Paulo and Porto Alegre, with Mexico planned for the end of 2019. The pandemic cut demand from app drivers, so Kovi leaned into car subscription, grew 70% in 2020 and said it had become the largest subscription company in Mexico within eight months there. In August 2021 it raised about US$100 million (R$500 million) in a Series B led by Valor Capital and Prosus Ventures, with Norte among the investors, to take the fleet to about 20,000 cars and its team to about 900, and to enter more Latin American countries. That expansion did not happen: by October 2022 the company said it had not opened new cities in a year and was recalibrating towards longer contracts and customers of social classes C and D. In January 2025 Moove, a Nigerian fintech that finances vehicles for ride-hailing drivers and is backed by Uber, acquired Kovi in a share deal of undisclosed value, using it as its entry to Latin America. Startups.com.br reports that Kovi had considered an IPO but chose M&A when funding and listing windows closed, and that its investors became shareholders of Moove. The Kovi site (2026) says it has more than 1,400 employees and operates in 12 Brazilian cities and in Mexico.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: in Brazil about a million cars worked for ride-hailing apps in 2019, and 20% to 30% of them were rented from traditional firms; a driver without a clean credit record or a card limit could not rent or finance a car, yet the car is the tool of their income. Logic: Kovi rents the car on weekly terms with taxes, maintenance and protection bundled in and no credit check, and prices the risk with its own telematics (the company says it collects about 40 million km of driving data a month) instead of a credit score. It funds the fleet with carmakers' and lessors' balance sheets rather than its own, so growth needed less equity per car than at Localiza, Unidas or Movida. Why now: ride-hailing created millions of self-employed drivers, car prices and interest rates rose, and carmakers wanted to move volume through rental. Market: the cofounder cited a Goldman Sachs projection of 7 to 8 million subscription cars in the next decade, but that is a claim, not a source we read. Our estimate for the app-driver niche: about 1 million app cars (Brazil Journal, 2019) times about 25% rented times about R$15,500 a year (R$299 a week, Startups.com.br 2021, times 52) is roughly R$3.9 billion, or US$0.7 billion a year; a range of US$0.5 to 1.5 billion allows for fleet growth and price changes. A strong outcome is a 10% to 20% share, so US$70 to 200 million of yearly rent. What is different: no credit check, a weekly contract with a minimum of eight weeks, an asset-light fleet and a platform view of driver behaviour; competitors are the big rental firms, the carmakers' own subscription plans and bank car loans (the cofounder named banks as the real competitor). Comparable: Moove, the Uber-backed fintech that bought Kovi, had raised more than US$500 million for the same kind of customer in other countries. Fit with Norte (our reading): founders from the 99 operating team who know the driver, the app and the carmaker, at the stage when a connector who helps bring funds such as Valor and Prosus onto the cap table adds most; Norte is named in the Series B. Risks: the model depends on the willingness of lessors and carmakers to supply cars, a funding squeeze in 2022 stopped the Latin American expansion, drivers depend on the apps' take rate, and the exit to Moove was in shares at an undisclosed price, so the outcome for early investors is unknown.

sub_sector.value: Car rental and subscription for app drivers

milestones.value: Adhemar Milani Neto and João Costa, both from the 99 ride-hailing app, start Kovi to supply and manage cars for app drivers, using cars leased from carmakers and lessors instead of buying a fleet.
Kovi goes through Y Combinator (Winter 2019), which brought it US investors such as Accel's Kevin Efrusy and YC itself onto its cap table.
Kovi says it will start operating in Mexico by the end of 2019, in addition to São Paulo and Porto Alegre, with a large Mexican group among its new investors.
Facing a collapse in demand from app drivers during the pandemic, Kovi starts offering car subscriptions to a wider public and grows 70% over the year.
Kovi launches, with an insurer, an insurance product that people who do not rent a car from it can buy, to draw drivers into its plans.

After eight months in Mexico it calls itself the largest car-subscription company there, has supply contracts with Volkswagen, Renault-Nissan and Toyota, and plans a fleet of 20,000 cars and 900 employees.
Kovi recalibrates after a year without new cities: it tests "Kovi Próprio", a plan of up to 48 months with a purchase option after 24, aimed at customers beyond app drivers.
Moove, a fintech backed by Uber, buys Kovi to enter Latin America, taking its fleet to more than 36,000 vehicles in 19 cities; Kovi keeps operating under its brand and CEO.
Kovi reports more than 1,400 employees and rental points in 12 Brazilian cities plus operations in Mexico, selling new and used cars on weekly and annual plans.

description.value: Nekt is a Brazilian data platform that connects a company's data sources, organises them in its own cloud and serves them to analysts, BI tools and AI agents, aimed at growing mid-sized companies.

long_description.value: Nekt is a Brazilian data platform company that began as a "Brazilian Databricks" for growing small and mid-sized businesses and now describes itself as a context platform for AI agents. The product connects a company's data sources (more than 300 connectors for SaaS tools, databases and files), stores them in the customer's own cloud, lets teams clean and transform them with SQL, Python or PySpark in scheduled, versioned pipelines, and then serves the result to BI tools, assistants and agents. Its newest layer is a "context graph", where a company writes down once what its terms mean (what an active customer is, how MRR is counted), so that an agent such as Claude, ChatGPT or Codex that queries the data through Nekt's governed MCP server answers with the company's own definitions instead of guessing. Pricing is on the site and the product can be started for free. It was founded in 2024 by Antonio Duarte (CEO), Vinícius Justo, Pedro Ceriotti and Andrio Frizon, who met studying control and automation engineering at UFSC in Florianópolis. In 2018 they had started Jungle Devs, later Olby, a software agency serving US and Australian clients that Trybe, a coding school, acquired in 2021; they ran it until 2023 and then left to start Nekt. Duarte says the idea came in 2023 during 50 days beside his premature son in an ICU, watching doctors decide from live dashboards. The team began operating in January 2024 and, because their agency's network was in the US and Australia, the first customers were in the United States, Australia and Brazil. In June 2025 Nekt raised R$5 million in a round led by Alexia Ventures, with angels linked to Trybe, Hapana, RD Station and Luxor Group, and had eight people and more than 40 customers. Norte Ventures had been a customer since the start of 2025 and its venture-capital side was the first of that kind; in October 2025 it put in R$1.3 million as a partner, to take the product into Norte's more than 100 portfolio companies and 400 LPs. At that point Nekt had 60 customers, 140% growth in 2025 and a goal of 100 customers by the end of the year and 400 in 2026. By November 2026 the company reports 320 customers, among them Tractian, Adapta, Lastlink, Softplan, Lastro, Seazone, Hapana, BT Créditos and OneBlinc, with about 15% of revenue from abroad (mostly the United States, plus Canada, Australia and Europe), and says it already competes with Databricks in the Brazilian middle market. Duarte is moving to Mountain View while the development team stays in Brazil, and the company is considering a seed round with US funds. Its targets are 400 customers by the end of 2026 and 700 to 800 in 2027.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: growing companies hold their data in a dozen tools (CRM, ads, billing, product) and cannot answer simple questions consistently; they cannot afford a data team or enterprise platforms such as Databricks, and the rise of AI assistants makes the gap worse, because an agent that reads raw tables guesses what "active customer" or "MRR" means. Logic: Nekt sells one pragmatic platform (connectors, cloud storage in the customer's account, transformation, a catalogue and a context layer) with a services layer to get customers started, so the buyer needs no data engineers. Why now: AI agents and the MCP standard turn "clean, defined data" from a back-office project into a condition for using AI at all, and the shift makes the context layer, which Nekt is already building, a natural wedge. Market: we found no readable independent market-size report (MarketsandMarkets' Latin America data-integration page returned 403 and so is not used). Our bottom-up estimate: Brazil has hundreds of thousands of companies that are big enough to need a data stack, but only the digitally mature ones buy; if we assume (our assumption, unsourced) about 30,000 Brazilian growth-stage companies are reachable and the average contract is about US$6,000 a year, the Brazilian segment is roughly US$150 to 250 million a year, and a global, English-speaking segment is many times larger. At 320 customers today, the company would reach about US$2 million of revenue at that price; 800 customers in 2027 would be about US$5 million. A strong result is a few percent of the reachable Brazilian segment plus a foreign base, i.e. tens of millions of dollars of revenue. What is different: it targets mid-sized companies instead of enterprises, keeps data in the customer's cloud, and bundles engineering, analysis and activation with onboarding help; competitors named in the press are Databricks at the top and, by our own knowledge (not read here), tools such as Fivetran and dbt on the pieces. Growth so far is fast (40 customers in mid-2025, 320 in November 2026) but from a small base, and the figure is the company's. Fit with Norte (our reading): obsessed technical founders with a prior exit to Trybe, a product Norte itself used before investing, and a role for the network (Norte's portfolio of 100+ companies is both customer base and referral channel), which matches Norte's own stated way of creating value through connections and revenue from day zero. Risks: the market is crowded and the large platforms are moving down-market with AI features; the context layer may be copied by AI labs and BI vendors; and the Norte relationship gives early customers who are also investors, so early traction may overstate organic demand.

sub_sector.value: Data and context platform for AI agents

milestones.value: Duarte, Justo, Ceriotti and Frizon, friends from the UFSC engineering course, start the software agency Jungle Devs (later Olby), which serves US and Australian clients; Trybe buys it in 2021.
Nekt starts operating as a data and AI platform for growing companies, with its first customers in the United States, Australia and Brazil taken from the founders' old agency network.
Norte Ventures becomes a Nekt customer, the platform's first venture-capital client, and later spreads it to other portfolio companies.
With R$5 million raised the team grows to eight people and the platform has more than 40 customers, among them Seazone, Hapana, BT Créditos and OneBlinc.
Nekt reports 60 customers and 140% growth in 2025, with first customers in Europe, and sets a goal of 100 customers by the end of the year.
The product is repositioned around agents: a governed MCP server and a "context graph" let Claude, ChatGPT or Codex query company data with the company's own definitions.
Nekt has 320 customers (Tractian, Adapta and Lastlink among them) and about 15% of revenue from abroad; the CEO announces a move to Mountain View to lead international expansion.

description.value: Liti is a Brazilian online clinic that follows overweight and obese patients with doctors, dietitians and an app, including prescription of GLP-1 weight-loss medication.

long_description.value: Liti is a Brazilian online weight-management clinic: a subscription in which a doctor, a dietitian and a behavioural scientist follow a patient through an app, mainly for people with overweight or obesity. A patient is matched with a doctor for their profile, gets a meal plan built on their tests and routine, and shares data with the team through the app and, in the first versions, a Liti-designed bioimpedance scale and a food scale sent in a kit; the team reaches out when the data change, even if the patient has not asked. Patient groups, a 24-hour assistant called Lito and a WhatsApp line complete the service. The company says the plan is a medical programme rather than a diet: the doctor prescribes and adjusts weight-loss medication when it makes sense, and the site (2026) is built around the new GLP-1 injectables, with discounts on Wegovy, Ozempic, Mounjaro and Rybelsus through pharmacy and manufacturer programmes, medication not included in the fee. It says most patients stay 12 to 18 months and that 9 in 10 clients lose weight (a company claim). Revenue comes from the subscription; in 2022 the price was R$700 a month for the first five months and R$150 afterwards, and in 2023 independent coverage listed a R$350 plan and a R$700 "Liti Max" plan. Liti also sells to employers that want to cut health-plan claims and improve performance, and has a section for health professionals. It was started in 2022 by Eduardo Rauen, a nutrologist and sports physician from the clinical staff of Hospital Israelita Albert Einstein and a daily commentator on CBN radio, and Fernando Vilela, an economist who had been a partner and CMO of Rappi in Brazil. Vilela was Rauen's patient, lost 25 kg and the two began the clinic as a side business before making it a start-up. In November 2022 it announced a R$21 million seed round (about US$4 million) led by Canary, with Monashees, Grão, Norte, Eclipseon, Newtopia, The Fund, Latitud and Rappi, Inventa, Loopi, Yuno and JHSF founders as angels, after an earlier round led by Monashees. At that time it had nine months of operation, 41 health and technology professionals, 20% monthly growth and a goal of reaching 100 million people. In 2023 it formed a medical board, planned to publish studies of the method, and said one in three patients opened the app daily. We found no later funding or customer numbers.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: two thirds of adults are overweight or obese by the founders' count, yet the health system deals with it episodically; people try diets, then give up, and the new GLP-1 drugs require medical follow-up, dosing and a plan to avoid regaining weight. Logic: Liti combines a doctor-led programme, nutrition and behaviour support and data from the patient in a subscription whose revenue recurs for 12 to 18 months and, per the company, beyond; the medication is outside the fee but a source of clinical engagement. Why now: GLP-1 pens have made medical treatment of obesity mainstream in Brazil and are about to become cheaper as semaglutide generics and the first Brazilian-made products arrive. Market: L.E.K. estimates the Brazilian anti-obesity market at R$10 to 11 billion in 2025 and expects the addressable market to multiply by four with a 60% to 70% price drop; Forbes reports R$4 billion of GLP-1 sales in the large pharmacy chains between May and July 2026 alone (about R$16 billion annualised, our extrapolation), and L.E.K.'s survey finds about 44% of recent weight-loss patients have used a pen. Medication, however, is bought at pharmacies, not by Liti; the clinic's own slice is the follow-up service. Our estimate, labelled assumption: if 1 million Brazilians on GLP-1s paid R$300 to R$700 a month for medical and nutritional follow-up, that service pool would be R$3.6 to R$8.4 billion a year (US$0.6 to 1.5 billion); a leading online clinic holding 5% of it would have R$180 to R$420 million of revenue. What is different: a doctor and a dietitian assigned to the patient who proactively act on data, a recognised physician-founder with media reach, and a founder who is a former customer and a consumer-marketing operator from Rappi. Competitors are the large players and telehealth clinics offering pens, the drug makers' own programmes, and pharmacies; US comparables named by Bloomberg Línea are Noom and Forward, both once valued above US$1 billion. Fit with Norte (our reading): founders who combine product-market insight and distribution, a seed that attracted funds and Latin American angel founders where a connector adds value, and a theme (consumer health) that grows through the network of operators. Risks: the pens commoditise the problem and move price pressure to the clinic; drug makers and pharmacies can bundle follow-up; regulation of prescriptions and advertising of GLP-1 products is tightening (Anvisa suspended batches in 2026); and public information after 2023 is thin, so we cannot confirm traction.

milestones.value: Fernando Vilela, a patient of the physician Eduardo Rauen who lost 25 kg with his follow-up, and Rauen start Liti as an online weight-loss clinic with its own bioimpedance scale.

Liti announces a R$21 million seed round led by Canary; after nine months of operation it has 41 professionals and 20% monthly growth, and wants to use the money to lower prices and reach more than the high-income segment.

Liti forms a medical advisory board and plans to publish studies of its method; it serves consumers and also employers that want to reduce health-plan claims, and says one in three patients opens the app every day.
Independent coverage lists two plans: Liti at R$350 a month with the Litibox kit and a physician visit every four months, and Liti Max at R$700 a month.

Liti repositions its programme around GLP-1 medication: the doctor prescribes and adjusts the dose in the app, patients get discounts on Wegovy, Ozempic, Mounjaro and Rybelsus, and an AI assistant called Lito answers questions 24 hours a day.
