description.value: Alchemy sells an AI-native ERP for accounting and finance to fast-growing technology and service companies, in which agents capture, classify, post and reconcile documents and executives can operate it from Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini.

long_description.value: Alchemy is a São Paulo company that sells an "AI-native" ERP: an accounting and finance system for fast-growing technology and service companies, typically with R$20 million to R$500 million of revenue, which today run on spreadsheets or an ERP that has not kept up. Its argument is that AI is in the engine rather than bolted on: agents fetch the invoices and payment slips issued against the customer (from e-mail, the national invoice portal and the DDA direct-debit feed), read documents, classify entries, apply the company's own deterministic accounting rules, calculate taxes, post to the ledger, reconcile bank statements, schedule billing, flag errors and keep budget and forecast current. It says more than 90% of reconciliations happen without human intervention, close is continuous (hours, not weeks), and every posted entry is immutable and traceable back to the supplier e-mail that started it. The product has eight modules on one ledger: cash, receivables, payables, purchasing, people (CLT and contractor payroll, ISS withholding, tax credits), FP&A and the accounting core. It supports multi-entity, multi-currency consolidation under Brazilian CPC/IFRS, US GAAP and Mexican NIF, connects to more than 130 financial institutions through Open Finance, bank files, cards and Pix, and works with Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini through MCP, so a CEO can ask an assistant for margin by customer and get the number straight from the ERP under the same permissions. Implementation is promised in a week with no setup fee; pricing is an annual subscription with no per-user charge. Co-founder and CEO Fernando Ribeiro was CFO of the insurtech Pitzi and worked at the hedge fund Bridgewater; co-founder and CTO Willian Menegali leads technology. In Brazil Journal's sponsored launch piece (about September 2026) Ribeiro frames the pain as ERP implementations that take nine months on average (Panorama Consulting) and as customers feeling like hostages, and says the goal is for clients to grow from R$20 million to over R$500 million of revenue with the same three-person finance team. The company says its base already includes customers with operations in Brazil, Mexico and the United States, many migrated from spreadsheets, Omie and TOTVS, and it presents the Brazilian tax reform (two parallel tax regimes until 2032) as the reason to switch now. It compares itself to Rillet, a US AI-native ERP the article says is valued at US$1 billion. It targets CFOs, controllers and heads of finance in technology and services firms and says it is not suited to retail, manufacturing, construction, agriculture or logistics where inventory and fixed assets are central. The careers site says customers run in four countries and that the company is backed by global funds; the founding date, funding rounds and customer names are not public on the pages we read.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: growing service and technology companies outgrow spreadsheets and entry-level accounting software, but ERPs take nine months to implement on average (Panorama Consulting, quoted in Brazil Journal), turn the CFO into a project manager, and still leave more than half of mid-sized and large firms feeding the ERP manually, with 40% relying only on spreadsheets to consolidate results (survey figures quoted in the same article). Logic: Alchemy rebuilds the ledger around agents that capture, classify, reconcile and post under deterministic rules, so the team reviews exceptions; exposing it to an AI assistant over MCP makes finance queryable by executives. Why now: language models can read invoices and e-mails reliably enough to do clerical work; Brazil's tax reform forces companies to compute taxes in two regimes until 2032, which prompts system reviews; and Open Finance and the national invoice portal give machine-readable data. Market: we found no readable independent market-size report. Our bottom-up estimate, labelled assumption: between 10,000 and 30,000 Brazilian technology and services companies fall in the R$20 million to R$500 million revenue band; at R$120,000 to R$400,000 a year of subscription (our guess, since pricing is not published) that is R$1.2 to R$12 billion, roughly US$0.2 to 2 billion a year, with Mexico and the United States adding more. A strong outcome is 3% to 5% of the Brazilian pool: US$10 to 100 million of revenue. Comparable: Rillet in the United States, which Brazil Journal says is valued at US$1 billion with Sequoia and a16z as investors (a claim in a sponsored piece). What is different: continuous close with immutability and a full audit trail, an assistant interface via MCP, multi-country entities in one ledger, and the no-implementation-fee promise that attacks the main cost of incumbents. Customers have migrated from Omie and TOTVS, which are also the incumbents; Sankhya and Senior are adding AI agents too (named in search results, not read). Fit with Norte (our reading): the first customers are the finance teams of fast-growing start-ups like those in Norte's network, and the CEO's profile (startup CFO plus Bridgewater) is the operator-founder type the Manifesto describes; we could not confirm Norte's participation or funding. Risks: incumbents are shipping similar agents and have distribution; ERP replacement is a slow, high-trust sale; AI accounting errors are costly; and almost nothing is public on revenue, funding or customer names, so this thesis rests on company statements.

sub_sector.value: AI-native ERP for finance and accounting

milestones.value: Alchemy says its customers already include companies operating in Brazil, Mexico and the United States, migrated from spreadsheets, Omie and TOTVS, and that the platform connects to more than 130 financial institutions.

Alchemy launches what it calls the first AI-native ERP in Brazil for technology and services companies, with agents that do capture, classification, reconciliation and billing, operation through Claude or ChatGPT, and implementation in a week at no setup cost.

description.value: nullplatform is an internal developer platform for large companies that lets developers and AI agents deploy through self-service while platform, security and finance teams enforce governance.

long_description.value: nullplatform is an internal developer platform that lets large engineering organisations give developers, AI agents and business users a self-service way to ship software while platform, security and finance teams keep control. Developers create environments, databases and queues and deploy at any time without tickets; the platform team sets policies, approval flows and compliance guardrails once, and they apply across clouds and accounts to every deploy, whether made by a person or an AI agent; managers get visibility of delivery, cost and incidents. Its 2026 pitch is that it is the governed harness for AI-generated code: an agent can build and ship an app from a prompt inside nullplatform, with test gates, approvals and an audit trail, and AI assistants and "AI Ops" agents trace the root cause of an incident or detect cost, security and performance drift, with a human approving production changes. It claims to be vendor-independent, running on top of existing clouds, on-premise systems, Terraform and Ansible, and is SOC 2 Type II compliant. The founders are four engineers who ran Mercado Libre's engineering platform as it grew from a team of 20 to about 10,000 engineers: Darío Simonassi (CEO), Julián Klas (CPO), Gabriel Eisbruch (CTO) and Pablo Vilas (VP Engineering). After more than 15 years together they founded nullplatform in 2022, and in a 2024 interview said the company already served Falabella and Ualá and that clients had saved about 30% while keeping the same impact. Argentine tech press (September 2024) reported that it had gone in a few months from working with start-ups to serving large companies such as Falabella Financiero, Ualá and Ueno Bank, and planned expansion across Latin America, the United States and Canada. The site (2026) says it powers more than 10,000 engineers and lists customers including a Big 4 audit firm in 150 countries, Falabella Group in four countries, FEMSA Group's fintech in Mexico (12 million users), and Banco Galicia in Argentina, plus insurance, energy, agtech, travel and music clients.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: as companies grow, developers wait for infrastructure tickets, platform teams build brittle internal portals, and security and finance cannot see what was shipped or who paid for it; AI coding agents now multiply the volume of code and the risk. Logic: nullplatform provides the platform as a product, extensible to a mature organisation's own rules, so large companies avoid the cost of building and maintaining an internal platform and get a control point for human and AI-generated code. Its sales argument is a measurable saving (clients report about 30% lower infrastructure and operating cost, a company claim) and speed. Why now: AI agents make governed deployment a board-level topic, cloud costs are under scrutiny, and the founders' team has built such a platform at scale. Market: we found no readable independent market-size report. Our bottom-up estimate, labelled assumption: 500 to 1,500 large and mid-sized enterprises in Latin America and the Spanish-speaking market have 300 or more engineers and a platform-engineering need; at US$150,000 to US$500,000 of annual contract value that is roughly US$75 million to US$750 million a year in the region, with a much larger United States market; the company claims 10,000 engineers served, which at an assumed US$300 per engineer per month would be about US$36 million of annual value, so we regard it as a small share of the regional pool. What is different: leadership that built Mercado Libre's platform, a vendor-independent model that extends to legacy and on-premise systems, and an explicit governance layer for AI agents. Competitors named in the press we read: none; from our own knowledge, commercial and open-source internal developer platforms (Backstage-based portals, Humanitec, Port, Cycloid), cloud-provider tools and in-house platforms. Fit with Norte (our reading): exceptional operator-founders who 'know more than Norte does', a product sold to Latin American banks and retailers where a network of operators opens enterprise doors, and a stage at which funds from the region can join. Risks: long enterprise sales cycles, concentration in a few large Latin American customers, strong global competitors and open-source alternatives, and no funding or revenue disclosure we could read.

sub_sector.value: Internal developer platform and AI governance

milestones.value: Four leaders of Mercado Libre's engineering platform (Darío Simonassi, Julián Klas, Gabriel Eisbruch and Pablo Vilas) found nullplatform to sell the kind of platform they built there as a product.
Within months nullplatform moves from start-up customers to large companies such as Falabella Financiero, Ualá and Ueno Bank, and prepares expansion to Latin America, the United States and Canada.
The founders report client savings of about 30% with the same impact, with Falabella and Ualá as named customers.
Google joins nullplatform's partner network; the platform is used daily by more than 3,000 engineers at companies such as Falabella, Uala, Ueno Bank, Tiendamia and Nowports, in six countries.

nullplatform repositions itself as the governed platform for AI agents and human developers, with prompt-to-production, AI Ops and AI Insights, SOC 2 Type II compliance and more than 10,000 engineers on the platform.

description.value: Comunica.In sells large companies a platform, and now an AI agent, to plan, send and measure internal communication to all employees.

long_description.value: Comunica.In is a Curitiba software company that helps large employers talk to their staff. Its platform lets an internal-communications team write announcements and surveys from templates in the company's own visual identity, send them in bulk to segmented lists across e-mail, WhatsApp, Teams and other channels, build automated employee journeys (a welcome message on the first day, a check-in survey a week later), collect quick feedback by emoji or text, and read reports on who actually received and opened each message. The company says it counts eight years and 350 million sends of experience. Its newest product, shown on the site in 2026, is an AI agent for internal communication that works as the team's creative staff, adviser and data analyst: it learns the company, audience and history, proposes the plan from a conversation, creates the concept and the visual identity, adapts it into every format (banner, poster, story, TV), assembles the message for each channel, suggests the audience and the best send time, and writes the report for leadership. Its own example cuts a typical campaign from about 21.5 working days to under six hours. Customers quoted on the site include Arcos Dorados, Alura and Sankhya. The founder and CEO, Felipe Hotz, is an advertising professional who worked in corporate communications and saw that large companies spent far more on external than on internal communication and had no tool to make sure every employee, not just office staff, got the same message, and no data on whether it landed. He built an e-mail analytics tool first and then widened the product. The company dates itself from 2018, and the public registry shows the legal entity opened in February 2017. Traction: revenue grew six times in 2020 to about R$1 million, and the company then served customers such as Volvo, Bayer, Leroy Merlin, Burger King and Electrolux, reaching more than 300,000 employees in 10 countries. In December 2021 it announced a R$10 million seed round led by Valor Capital Group with Norte and Honey Island Capital, to grow in Brazil and the rest of Latin America. By early 2023 it had 35 people and nearly 100 customers (including Deloitte, Assaí, Tigre and Alpargatas), launched a 21-day free trial in Portuguese, English and Spanish, and made internationalisation a goal for the year. We found no later funding round.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: in large companies, internal communication is run by small teams that cannot reach all staff (many without e-mail), cannot prove who read what, and spend most of their week on operations (briefs, formats, sends, reports) rather than strategy. Logic: Comunica.In started as a measurement and delivery layer, sold to enterprises that need uniform, auditable reach, and now adds an agent that does the production work, which turns a seat-based software line into a labour-replacement one. Why now: remote and frontline work made reaching everyone a board-level topic after 2020, and generative AI made creative and analytical work cheap. Market: we found no readable independent market-size figure. A Bloomberg Línea piece cites a data point that companies invested more than R$148 billion in employee-facing solutions in 2020 (source not named), which is far too broad for this niche. Our bottom-up estimate, labelled as assumption: perhaps 3,000 to 5,000 Brazilian and Latin American employers have 1,000 or more staff and a dedicated internal-communications team; at US$15,000 to US$40,000 a year per customer, the reachable market is roughly US$50 to 200 million a year; reaching 5% to 10% of it would mean US$3 to 20 million of revenue. At the 2023 figure of nearly 100 customers the company was at roughly the low end. What is different: eight years of delivery data on large Brazilian employers, multi-channel sending that includes WhatsApp, and an agent trained on each company's own tone and templates. Competitors named in our own knowledge, not in the press we read, are global employee-communication tools such as Staffbase, Poppulo and Simpplr, and the broad suites (Microsoft Viva, Workplace-style intranets). Fit with Norte (our reading): a single operator-founder from the customer side of the problem, a seed-stage check where a connector can open doors to enterprise buyers across Norte's network, and a lead from Valor Capital that brought a top fund onto the cap table, which matches the Manifesto's way of working. Risks: a narrow buyer (internal-communications teams are small and budgets are sensitive to headcount cuts), large suites bundling similar features, a long enterprise sales cycle, and no public funding or traction update since 2023 suggests slow growth.

sub_sector.value: Internal communications platform and AI agent

milestones.value: Felipe Hotz, who worked in corporate communications, starts Comunica.In to give large companies a way to reach every employee equally and to measure it.
Revenue grows six times to about R$1 million as the pandemic makes internal communication a priority for employers.

A R$10 million seed round led by Valor Capital Group, with Norte and Honey Island Capital, funds growth in Brazil and Latin America; customers by then include Volvo, Bayer, Deloitte and Electrolux in 10 countries.
With 35 staff and nearly 100 customers, Comunica.In opens a 21-day free trial of its platform in Portuguese, English and Spanish as part of an internationalisation push.

The company launches an AI agent for internal communication that drafts the plan, creates the visual identity, builds each channel's message and writes the leadership report, cutting a campaign from about 21 days to under six hours in its own example.

description.value: Kamino is a Brazilian financial-management platform for mid-sized companies, combining payments, collection, automatic bank reconciliation, reporting, a business account and cards, with an AI financial agent.

long_description.value: Kamino is a São Paulo financial-management platform for mid-sized Brazilian companies, mostly service businesses with yearly revenue between R$5 million and R$300 million. In one system the finance team pays suppliers in batches of Pix and TED with approval limits, issues invoices and collection notices on a schedule, reconciles bank statements automatically from more than 50 banks and platforms, and reads cash flow and the income statement without building spreadsheets. It also offers its own business account and corporate cards, and credit, but works with whatever bank the company already uses; it connects to the company's ERP through an open API, leaving tax and accounting to the ERP. Roughly 80% of its revenue is software subscription, and the rest comes from cards and the account. It was founded in 2021 by Benjamin Gleason (founder of GuiaBolso, sold to PicPay in 2021), Gonzalo Parejo (CEO, founder of the European logistics start-up Ontruck), Guto Fragoso (ex-Amazon, McKinsey and Groupon) and Rodrigo Perenha (ex-CTO of Mercado Pago); Juliana Strohl, former head of legal and compliance at GuiaBolso, joined later and the site counts her among five founders. The first product, announced in March 2022 after a US$6.1 million pre-seed, was infrastructure for early-stage startups: opening the Brazilian company, building the Cayman and Delaware structure that global funds require, and a digital account and card, with law and accounting firms as partners. Within a year the team saw that the real gap was in mid-sized companies still running finance on Excel and generic ERPs, bought the start-up Nimbly in March 2023 for R$4 million to own its card and account stack, and turned the product into a platform. Revenue grew seven times from 2023 to 2024 and more than tripled from 2024 to 2025. In September 2025 it raised R$54 million (about US$10 million) co-led by Flourish Ventures and Quona Capital, with Endeavor Catalyst joining, at which point it served more than 2,000 clients and had moved over R$15 billion; the company's total funding is above R$108 million. It targets R$60 million of annual recurring revenue in 2026, has no plans to leave Brazil, and says about one million mid-sized companies could use it. In 2026 it announced more than R$40 million of investment in its own AI infrastructure and launched a Financial Agent that answers CFO questions over the customer's structured data through an MCP layer, with the plan to move gradually to autonomous classification, reconciliation and payments under human supervision. By late 2026 it reports more than 5,000 company registrations (CNPJs) and over R$25 billion managed, and plans a Series B in 2027.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: mid-sized Brazilian companies are too complex for a bank app and too small for an enterprise ERP or treasury suite; their finance teams reconcile statements and chase payments by hand, spending, by the company's estimate, about 70% of their time on repetitive tasks and up to 15 days to produce a report. Logic: Kamino sells a software-first product (about 80% of revenue from subscription) that sits across banks, so the buyer keeps their bank and ERP, and then monetises the account and cards that fit naturally inside the workflow. Why now: open finance and Pix made bank data and payments programmable, and AI turns the structured data it holds into agents that answer and eventually execute, which raises the value of the data layer. Market: the company claims a US$14 billion opportunity for financial-management solutions in mid-sized Brazilian companies (Bloomberg Línea, 2025, the company's own figure), and the CEO estimates about one million mid-sized firms. Our check, labelled assumption: if 300,000 of those are reachable and a company pays about R$24,000 a year for software plus cards (R$2,000 a month; the average actual price is not published), the market is about R$7 billion, or roughly US$1.3 billion a year, well below the company's own figure; reaching 3% to 5% of it would mean US$40 to 65 million of revenue, which is in line with its target of R$60 million of ARR in 2026. What is different: it is bank-agnostic and built for the mid-market, with its own account and cards in the same system, and its founders have already built and sold a fintech, a logistics scale-up and Mercado Pago's technology organisation. Comparable US companies named in the press are Bill.com and Ramp; local rivals include Omie and bank-led offers (Omie is shown against Kamino on CB Insights, an aggregator). Fit with Norte (our reading): repeat founders with distribution into the start-up community, a pre-seed where a connector can bring top global funds (Inspired, GFC, QED's Fontes, Flourish and others joined) at the earliest stage, and a product that Norte's own portfolio can use. Risks: crowded category (ERPs adding payments, banks and cards-first fintechs), reliance on banks' integrations and on card economics, and a pivot from start-ups to the mid-market in 2023 that makes the customer count (2,000 clients, 5,000 CNPJs) depend on how a client is counted.

sub_sector.value: Financial management software for mid-sized companies

milestones.value: Benjamin Gleason, Gonzalo Parejo, Guto Fragoso and Rodrigo Perenha, alumni of GuiaBolso, Ontruck, Amazon and Mercado Pago, start Kamino.
Kamino launches infrastructure for early-stage startups (company opening, Cayman and Delaware structures, digital account and card) with a US$6.1 million pre-seed led by Inspired Capital.
With a mature platform, Kamino's revenue "explodes": it grows seven times from 2023 to 2024 and more than triples in 2025.
Kamino buys the start-up Nimbly for R$4 million to own its card and account technology and turns the product into a financial-management platform for small and mid-sized companies.

A R$54 million round co-led by Flourish Ventures and Quona Capital, with Endeavor Catalyst, funds a push into mid-sized companies and a product for CFOs; the company has more than 2,000 clients and R$15 billion moved.

Kamino announces more than R$40 million of investment in AI and presents its Financial Agent, built on an MCP layer over the customer's own financial data; it reports more than 5,000 CNPJs and R$25 billion managed.

description.value: Ximple is a Mexican digital lender that gives direct and catalogue sellers working-capital loans and a payout card, and lets them distribute credit to their customers.

long_description.value: Ximple is a Mexican digital lender that gives working-capital credit and consumer credit to direct and catalogue sellers, whom it calls Aliadas, and through them to their customers. An Aliada applies in about ten minutes with her voter ID, receives a loan of MXN 1,000 to MXN 10,000 to buy merchandise ("buy now, pay later"), repays in fixed weekly instalments over 4 to 12 weeks at a rate that improves with her payment history, and can also lend to her own end customers and earn a commission on the loans she distributes. Funds are paid out in cash at a network of partner locations (more than 15,000) or on a Ximple prepaid card, launched in early 2025 with Dock and Mastercard, which widens payout points to more than 75,000 and lets the credit be used at 6 million card terminals; there is also a mobile top-up and a referral programme. Its own site shows an average annual cost (CAT) of 223% in September 2024 and 387% in February 2025, before VAT. The operating entity, Finanzas Embebidas Ximple, S.A. de C.V., SOFOM ENR, is an unregulated multiple-purpose financial company supervised by Mexico's banking commission for limited purposes. The company says about 90% of its customers are women and it has customers in every Mexican state with a fully digital relationship. It was founded in early 2024 by Daniel Sujo (CEO), Rodrigo Aparicio (CFO), Juan Pablo Salem and João Ramos, and in June 2024 announced a US$2.7 million pre-seed round with BoostCapital Partners, Clocktower Technology Ventures, Graph Ventures, 99 Startups and Lotux.VC to launch and scale in Mexico, aiming ultimately at the roughly 300 million Latin Americans without credit access. In 2025 it added the card product. A commercial-data aggregator lists a further seed round in December 2025, which we could not confirm in a readable source.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: direct sellers (Avon, Natura and catalogue resellers) in Mexico run a small business with no access to formal working capital, because they have little credit history and sell to neighbours on credit themselves; informal lenders and store credit are expensive. Logic: Ximple lends against a seller's repayment behaviour and her role in a social network, with short weekly instalments that match her cash cycle, and uses her as a distribution channel for loans to her customers, which lowers customer acquisition cost. Why now: cheap digital onboarding, partner payout networks and prepaid card issuing made it possible to launch in months, and catalogue selling is moving online. Market: Mexico had about 3.1 million people working in catalogue sales (Rest of World, 2024) and direct selling generated US$6.8 billion in 2024 (Milenio quoting a trade-body executive). Our estimate, labelled assumption: if 10% of them (310,000) borrow four times a year MXN 5,000 each, origination is MXN 6.2 billion (about US$330 million at MXN 19 per dollar), and at a gross revenue yield of 30% to 60% of originated volume the revenue pool is about US$100 to 200 million a year; a 5% share would be US$5 to 10 million of revenue, plus more from the customers' loans. The yield figure is our guess from the company's disclosed CAT of 223% to 387%, which is annualised and not a yield on volume. What is different: a distribution-led model through sellers, a card payout, a focus on women entrepreneurs, and a team of founders with prior fintech experience in the region (their backgrounds are not given in the sources we read). Comparables in Mexico and Latin America are microcredit and BNPL lenders; the specific competitors are not named in the sources we read. Fit with Norte (our reading): early, hands-on founders in a market (Mexico) where Norte's network of Latin American operators and funds adds the most, at a pre-seed stage where connecting follow-on investors is valuable. Risks: high-cost, high-default unsecured lending to a thin-file segment, regulatory scrutiny of consumer-credit pricing in Mexico, dependence on funding lines (a seed and debt facilities are reported only by aggregators), and little public information beyond the 2024 announcement.

milestones.value: Daniel Sujo, Rodrigo Aparicio, Juan Pablo Salem and João Ramos start Ximple to give direct and catalogue sellers credit, using the seller as a distribution channel for loans to her customers.
Ximple announces a US$2.7 million pre-seed round from BoostCapital Partners, Clocktower, Graph Ventures, 99 Startups and Lotux.VC to launch its platform in Mexico.
Ximple says it has customers in every Mexican state, that 90% of them are women, and that the relationship is fully digital.
Ximple launches a credit card, with Dock and Mastercard, as a way to disburse loans, expanding payout points from more than 15,000 to more than 75,000 and access to 6 million card terminals.

description.value: ZAX is a São Paulo marketplace where small shop owners and resellers buy clothing and accessories at wholesale prices straight from suppliers in the Brás, Bom Retiro and other fashion districts, with freight and payment handled on the platform.

long_description.value: ZAX is an online wholesale marketplace for fashion in Brazil. It connects small and mid-sized retailers (clothing shops, resellers, independent sellers) with factories and wholesalers in São Paulo's traditional wholesale districts, the Brás, Bom Retiro and 25 de Março, and, more recently, Fortaleza. The buyer browses a catalogue, compares prices from many suppliers, picks a freight option (or collects at the supplier) and pays in a way that fits their cash flow: up to six card instalments, Pix, bank slip or a boleto with a payment term. The site stresses that there is no minimum order and that more than a thousand suppliers are listed. Before ZAX, shop owners from the interior often took long bus trips to the Brás to restock, ordered on paper or WhatsApp and had little working capital; the founders say wholesale had about 1% e-commerce penetration against about 7% in retail. ZAX started in 2019 as a clothing marketplace for the state of São Paulo and, from 2020, added shoes, electronics, toys, accessories and beauty. It earns from the transactions on the platform and from services around them: in April 2021 it added 30-day working-capital credit and a point-of-sale payment solution through partners, and planned a digital wallet and buy-now-pay-later pilots. It was founded by Bruno Ballardie, who had built and sold the eyewear e-commerce eÓtica, and Fernando Zanatta, a former CTO of Dafiti and technology director at Netshoes, both second-time founders with consumer e-commerce backgrounds who chose to digitise B2B trade. Growth came during the pandemic: suppliers rose from about 100 to about 700 and revenue grew ten times from March 2020; by October 2021 it listed more than 900 sellers, 70,000 items and 50,000 registered shops, with a team of 40 to 65 people. In 2021 it raised R$32 million led by Atlantico to hire, add categories and open other wholesale hubs (Maringá, Brusque, Goiânia, Fortaleza and Santa Cruz do Capibaribe were being studied). The app today also invites consumers to buy at retail or wholesale with factory prices, which suggests the company has widened its audience beyond resellers; no article after 2021 explains how the business has evolved, so its current size is unknown.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil has roughly 1.5 million fashion shops (Exame, 2021, citing R$229 billion a year in sales) and many more independent resellers. They restock in person in a few districts (Brás, Bom Retiro, 25 de Março), travelling for hours, ordering by WhatsApp or paper, paying cash or on short terms and having no way to compare suppliers. Suppliers, for their part, reach only the buyers who show up. Logic: a marketplace that puts hundreds of factories on one catalogue, solves freight and payment, and adds credit works because the supply side is concentrated (a few thousand suppliers in a few streets, so onboarding is tractable) and the demand side is large and fragmented; the 2020 to 2021 pandemic forced shops to buy online and ZAX reported revenue growing ten times and suppliers going from about 100 to 700. Market size: the company's own figure is a B2B market of R$2.4 trillion in 2019 with about 1% online (E-Consulting via Startupi; a company claim and a very broad number, not a market for this product). Our bottom-up estimate, with labelled assumptions: 1.5 million fashion shops with R$229 billion of sales; if goods bought from wholesalers are about half of that (assumption: cost of goods around 50% of sales) the wholesale purchases are about R$115 billion a year; if the online share reached 5% to 10% (assumption; today about 1%) that is R$6 billion to R$11 billion a year; if ZAX held 10% to 20% of that online volume it would move R$0.6 billion to R$2 billion a year, which at an 8% to 15% take rate (assumption) is about R$50 million to R$300 million in revenue, plus credit and payments income. That is a good venture outcome in Brazil, and the model can be copied in other districts and Latin American countries, as Atlantico's partner said. What is different: a team of second-time founders from large consumer e-commerce (Dafiti, Netshoes, Buscapé, eÓtica), a focus on the Brás wholesale culture instead of a generic B2B catalogue, and payment terms and credit built around the shop owner's cash flow. We read no page on rivals or comparables, so none is assessed here. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does, and helps by connecting people and bringing top funds onto the cap table; ZAX's founders match the operator profile, and a follower role at an early stage (the 2019 and 2020 rounds were led by GFC and Canary) fits that approach. This is our reading, not a Norte statement. Risks: marketplaces leak, since a supplier and buyer who have met can trade off the platform; general marketplaces and WhatsApp commerce can compete for the same shop owners (our assumption, no page read); credit adds default risk; and we found no news after 2021, no later round and no revenue figure, so traction after the pandemic is unproven.

milestones.value: Bruno Ballardie, who had sold the eyewear e-commerce eÓtica, and Fernando Zanatta, ex-CTO of Dafiti, start ZAX to bring wholesale fashion trade in the Brás district of São Paulo online, a market that still ran on bus trips, paper and WhatsApp.
ZAX widens the catalogue beyond clothing to shoes, electronics, toys, accessories and beauty, to give shop owners one place for more of their restocking.
The pandemic closes the physical wholesale streets and shop owners start buying online; from March 2020 revenue grows ten times and suppliers go from about 100 to about 700.
Through partners, ZAX starts offering buyers 30-day working capital and a point-of-sale payment solution, the first step from marketplace into financial services.

With more than 900 sellers, 70,000 items and 50,000 registered shops, ZAX announces a R$32 million round to hire, add a digital wallet and open new wholesale hubs; Maringá, Brusque, Goiânia, Fortaleza and Santa Cruz do Capibaribe are the targets studied.

ZAX lists more than 1,000 suppliers from the Brás, Bom Retiro, 25 de Março and Fortaleza with no minimum order, payment in up to six instalments or boleto with a term, and an app that also targets retail buyers.

description.value: Yuno is a payments orchestration platform: one API that lets large merchants, banks and wallets accept payments, payouts, fraud checks and stablecoins across more than 1,000 payment methods in 190+ countries, with smart routing and AI agents to raise approval rates.

long_description.value: Yuno is a global payments orchestration company founded by two former Rappi executives. Large online merchants usually work with half a dozen payment providers, acquirers and fraud tools, each with its own integration, local methods and failure modes. Yuno puts them behind one API and one dashboard: it routes each transaction to the provider most likely to approve it at the lowest cost, retries failures, offers one-click checkout, handles pay-ins, payouts, subscriptions, reconciliation, fraud prevention, KYC and KYB, and stablecoins, and now sells itself as an AI-native system whose specialised agents recover failed payments and tune routing. It says it connects to more than 1,000 payment methods and 460 integrations in 190+ countries, and that in a year it recovered over US$5 billion of failed volume, lifted authorisation rates by about 5 percent and saved merchants more than US$500 million in processing cost. Its revenue comes from the payment volume that merchants run through it, plus white-label deals with banks and processors such as dLocal and Mexico's Prosa. The idea came from Juan Pablo Ortega, who helped start Rappi and built its payments and fraud teams and RappiBank, and Julián Núñez, who created Rappi's one-click checkout and led its e-commerce unit; they teamed up in 2021 and formally founded Yuno in January 2022. After a first cheque from Andreessen Horowitz it closed a US$10 million seed in March 2022, co-led by Kaszek and Monashees, with 40 employees and Rappi as first customer; the product launched in October 2022 focused on Mexico, Brazil and Colombia. In March 2024 it raised a US$25 million Series A at a reported US$150 million valuation with DST Global Partners, a16z, Tiger Global, Kaszek and Monashees, then had enterprise customers such as McDonald's, Avianca and inDrive in 50 countries and set out to expand to Europe, Asia and Africa. It opened offices on five continents (16 listed on its site), a Gulf regional hub in Doha, and in April 2026 its Saudi unit received a Payment Technical Service Provider licence from the Saudi Central Bank. In August 2026 it raised a US$45 million Series B led by Global PayTech Ventures to reach profitability, add in-person payments and agentic commerce and grow in the United States; it says it is on track to process US$100 billion in annual volume within 12 months, for customers that now include McDonald's, NetEase Games, GoFundMe, inDrive, Rappi and Uber. Where it stands today (LinkedIn posts, November 2026): Yuno is selling local payment methods through one integration, with a direct Nequi connection in Colombia, while it hires for partnerships in LATAM, Brazil, North America and Mexico, and for engineering, incident and risk leadership, including remote roles in Europe.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: a global merchant (an airline, a food chain, a game publisher) must accept payments in many countries through many acquirers, wallets, bank-transfer schemes and cash vouchers, each with its own integration, approval rates, fees and fraud rules; in Latin America, where cards are a minority of payments and local methods such as Pix, OXXO and PSE matter, the fragmentation is worst. Logic: an orchestration layer lets the merchant add a market or a provider in days, route to the best acquirer per transaction, retry failures and consolidate reporting; every point of approval rate is revenue the merchant already earned, so the value is easy to measure (Yuno claims US$5 billion of recovered volume and US$500 million of cost saved in a year), and the volume is recurring. Why now: cross-border and local-method commerce keeps growing, merchants had already built the multi-provider mess, and enterprise buyers began issuing RFPs just for orchestration (TechCrunch, 2024). Market size: published research puts the software market for payment orchestration platforms at about US$2.7 billion in 2025 growing to about US$7.3 billion in 2031 (Mordor Intelligence; other firms range from US$1.9 billion to US$9 billion, so this is a rough order of magnitude), and TechCrunch cited about US$7 billion by 2032. A bottom-up view is better suited to a volume business: Yuno says it is on track to process US$100 billion a year; at an assumed net take rate of 0.1% to 0.2% of volume (our assumption, between a pure software fee and a processor's margin) that is US$100 million to US$200 million of revenue a year, and the share of the orchestration market that implies is large, which suggests either that the research figures understate volume-based pricing or that the take rate is lower. A strong outcome is a leading enterprise orchestrator in emerging markets, comparable to dLocal (a listed cross-border processor and a Yuno partner, per the Series B release). What is different: enterprise focus when many rivals (Gr4vy, Plug, Revio) serve SMBs; over 460 integrations built in emerging markets; founders who ran the problem at Rappi across nine countries; and an AI-agent layer on top of the routing data. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does and that it brings top funds and angels onto the cap table; Yuno's seed was co-led by Kaszek and Monashees with a16z, so a Norte role would be as a follower or angel-type connector; Norte's participation is not stated in any source we read. This is our reading, not Norte's. Risks: TechCrunch names Gr4vy, Plug, Revio and Simetrik as rivals and large payment processors may add orchestration features (our assumption), and orchestration can be commoditised, enterprise sales cycles are long, and take rate and gross margin are undisclosed.

milestones.value: Juan Pablo Ortega and Julián Núñez, who ran payments and fraud at Rappi while it expanded to nine countries, team up to build a single layer that lets a merchant accept payments through many providers; the idea had occurred to Ortega as early as 2015.
Yuno is formally founded; after a conversation with Andreessen Horowitz it gets a first cheque from the fund's fintech-founders programme and, weeks later, closes a US$10 million seed.

Yuno presents itself with 40 employees from Rappi, Ingenico, Worldpay, McKinsey and Mastercard, with Rappi as a first customer and a focus on Mexico, Brazil and Colombia, planning 100 employees by April.
Yuno launches its product, with more than 300 payment methods, fraud detection, one-click checkout and smart routing.
Yuno opens a regional headquarters in Doha to cover APAC, Europe, the Middle East and Africa and is named among top fintech companies by CNBC, Statista and CB Insights.

With US$25 million from DST Global Partners, a16z, Tiger Global, Kaszek and Monashees at a reported US$150 million valuation, Yuno serves McDonald's, Avianca, inDrive and Rappi in 50 countries and plans to expand to Europe, Asia and Africa.

Yuno builds out its partnerships team to cover LATAM (acquirers, alternative payment methods, banks, fraud providers), Brazil, and North America and Mexico, which signals commercial expansion beyond its Latin American base.

Yuno Payments Arabia receives a Payment Technical Service Provider certification from the Saudi Central Bank, followed by partnerships with Tap Payments (Mada, KNET, NAPS across the six GCC countries) and Tabby (buy now, pay later).

Yuno recruits a Staff Incident Manager and Staff Engineers for its global domains, describing the product as an "autonomous operating system for global commerce" built on versioned APIs and event-driven architecture; in October it also hires an Engineering Manager for its Money & Risk teams (fraud, chargebacks, reconciliations), remote from Europe.

Yuno raises a US$45 million Series B to reach profitability, add in-person payments and agentic commerce and grow in the United States, reporting white-label partnerships with dLocal and Prosa and a path to US$100 billion of annual volume.

Yuno promotes its direct connection to Nequi, Colombia's largest digital neobank (more than 29 million users), through a single integration for pay-ins and payouts; it says the two have worked together for more than three years.

description.value: Baze offers the "Linha Baze", a revolving credit line in Brazil secured by the customer's property or vehicle: opened once, reused as it is repaid, at rates from CDI plus 0.7% a month, entirely through an app.

long_description.value: Baze is a São Paulo fintech that sells what it calls the first "Linha Patrimonial" in Brazil: a revolving credit line backed by a property or vehicle that the customer already owns, fully paid or with a low balance. The pitch is that wealth tied up in a house or a car should work as financial infrastructure, as home-equity credit does in the United States (the site cites about US$350 billion outstanding there against less than 1% of Brazilian families with a paid-off property having anything similar). Unlike a personal loan (which the site prices at 5% to 15% a month) or a traditional home-equity loan (1.5% to 3% a month, weeks to release, a new contract for each use), the Linha Baze is opened once, with no end date: the customer signs in the app, connects Open Finance data, receives a "Carta Baze" stating limit, rate and terms, and Baze handles the registry, notary and formalisation. Each withdrawal is repaid in instalments the customer chooses, and the limit regenerates as it is paid down, which the company describes as an "adaptive intelligence" that adjusts the line to the customer's income and cash flow. Pricing is post-fixed, from CDI plus 0.7% a month. Typical uses on the site are renovations, working capital for a small business, replacing expensive card or overdraft debt, buying a second property, medical bills, education and divorce settlements. Baze also builds a channel of 30 hand-picked "founding partners" (wealth advisers, accountants and lawyers, family offices, real-estate agents and architects, and credit correspondents), who earn a commission on every withdrawal their client makes. The company was registered in December 2024 and a US limited liability company joined as a partner in October 2025; a Baze FIDC (a receivables fund) is registered with the CVM, administered by Vórtx and managed by Harbour Capital, and still pre-operational in the regulator's data, which suggests the credit is meant to be funded through a fund structure. The site mentions "investors, technology partners and custody regulated by the Central Bank" but names none. We found no press coverage, no named founders in public text and no round, so the company is very young and its size is unknown.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilian families and small-business owners with a paid-off property or car sit on assets but borrow with personal loans, overdrafts and cards at 5% a month or more because home-equity loans are slow, notary-heavy and re-done for each use. Logic: since 1 July 2025 the "Marco das Garantias" lets the same property back several credit operations, which is what makes a reusable line over one collateral possible, and Open Finance data lets a lender size the limit and the risk without paper; a revolving product over secured collateral can charge much less than unsecured credit and still earn a spread over the CDI. Market size: Abecip data cited by Portas show home-equity originations of R$3.17 billion in the first quarter of 2026, up 25.8% on a year earlier and the highest first quarter since the series began in 2018; annualised that is about R$12 billion to R$13 billion, tiny compared with the stock of residential property. If the segment kept growing 25% a year for four years it would reach about R$31 billion a year by 2030 (our extrapolation); a company that took 3% to 5% of that would originate about R$0.9 billion to R$1.6 billion a year. Because a revolving line is reused, balances and revenue per client could exceed a one-shot loan, though credit risk and funding cost decide the economics. What is different: the product framing (a permanent, regenerating line instead of a loan), app-only onboarding with Open Finance, a curated advisory channel paid per withdrawal, and a planned fund structure for funding. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does, and brings top funds and angels onto cap tables and generates revenue from day zero; a secured-credit fintech needs funding partners and distribution, which is where a network helps. This is our reading, not a Norte statement, and we do not know the founders' backgrounds. Risks: credit and collateral risk if the cycle turns, dependence on a funding vehicle that is still pre-operational, a regulated activity (the company is a financial-institution correspondent per its registry), incumbent banks and home-equity lenders with cheaper funding, and no public traction data. Evidence is thin: one company site, a registry, a fund page and a market article.

milestones.value: Baze offers the Linha Baze, a revolving line secured by a property or vehicle priced from CDI plus 0.7% a month, opens a "Time Parceiro" of 30 hand-picked founding partners (advisers, accountants, lawyers, family offices, agents) paid a commission on every withdrawal, and hires a product engineer.

description.value: Pomelo is an Argentine payments-infrastructure company that lets banks, fintechs and large companies issue and process prepaid, debit and credit cards across Latin America through one API, including its own network licences (BIN sponsorship).

long_description.value: Pomelo is a Buenos Aires company that sells the plumbing behind card programmes in Latin America. A fintech, bank or global company that wants to launch prepaid, debit, credit or corporate cards (physical, virtual or digital) would normally spend 12 to 18 months and repeat the process in each country; Pomelo offers a modular, API-first platform that handles issuing, tokenisation, printing and logistics, real-time transaction processing, a credit core, wallet migration and fraud prevention, and can act as the "BIN sponsor" so that smaller clients launch under Pomelo's Visa and Mastercard licences without building the regulatory and compliance layer themselves. Its use cases range from replacing a traditional processor and corporate cards to crypto wallets, remittances, instant funding, stablecoin payments and single-use cards for travel agencies and agentic payments. It earns from processing and issuing fees on the volume that runs through the platform. The company was started in early 2021 by three executives: Gastón Irigoyen, a third-time founder with two exits (one to TripAdvisor), early Google Latin America employee and former CEO of Naranja X, Argentina's largest neobank; Juan Fantoni, former fintech director at Mastercard; and Hernán Corral, former product chief of Naranja X and head of digital accounts and cards at Mercado Pago. It raised a US$9 million seed in May 2021 when it was three months old and had no product, a US$35 million Series A led by Tiger Global in October 2021 (when it had 100 employees), a US$15 million extension in August 2022 that added Bill Maris's Section 32 and took it to Colombia and Peru, a US$40 million Series B led by Kaszek in January 2024 and a US$55 million Series C co-led by Kaszek and Insight Partners in January 2026. Its first customer went live in January 2022 with prepaid cards in Argentina; by 2024 it served more than 100 corporate clients (Rappi, Bitso, Stori, Nomad, PayJoy, Ripio, AstroPay) in Argentina, Mexico, Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Peru, revenue had tripled in 2023, payments volume had grown seven times and it could process 55 million transactions a day. By January 2026 it had over 150 clients including BBVA, Santander and Bancolombia, Binance and Western Union, with Mexico and Brazil as its largest markets; the Series C funds a global stablecoin-denominated credit card (initially on Circle's USDC), real-time and agentic payments, and expansion beyond Latin America. Where it stands today (LinkedIn posts, November 2026): after the US$55 million Series C, Pomelo has hired a new CFO and is pushing a global card-issuing offer and cross-border payments, including stablecoins and other digital assets, while adding fintech partners such as Racional in Chile.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: in Latin America issuing cards is slow and fragmented: each country needs its own processor, network licences and compliance, so a fintech or a bank takes 12 to 18 months to launch a card (company, 2021) and must repeat it for each market. Logic: cards are still the dominant digital payment in the region, and every new fintech, neobank, remittance app or loyalty programme needs an issuer-processor; a single modern, API-first processor with network licences lets clients launch in weeks and expand country by country, and processing revenue grows with client volume without the platform's cost growing at the same rate. Why now: the neobank and embedded-finance wave, the move of traditional banks (BBVA, Santander, Bancolombia are now customers per Bloomberg Línea) away from legacy processors, and new demand for stablecoin cards and agentic payments. Market size: the company said in 2021 that cards in the region carry about US$900 billion of payments a year, 95% processed by local incumbents (company claim, via TechCrunch). Our estimate of the processing and issuing pool: if issuer-processing and BIN-sponsorship take 0.05% to 0.2% of volume (our assumption), the pool is about US$0.45 billion to US$1.8 billion a year at 2021 volumes, and larger as card volume grows; a leader that held 10% to 20% would earn about US$45 million to US$360 million a year, with more from the credit core and the global stablecoin card. Reported traction is consistent: revenue tripled in 2023 and was expected to double again in 2024, and 150+ clients by 2026. What is different: it was built cloud-native after the incumbents, pursues both fintechs and banks, offers BIN sponsorship that lowers the barrier for small clients, and covers six countries on one platform. Comparables the company itself cites are Galileo, Marqeta and Stripe in the United States. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does; Pomelo's founders (ex-Naranja X, Mastercard, Mercado Pago) and its round leaders (Index, monashees, Tiger, Kaszek) suggest Norte would have been a small follower connecting the company with operators and funds; no source we read names Norte. This is our reading. Risks: incumbent processors and other fintech infrastructure (the company names Galileo and Marqeta as models, not rivals) can compete on price; revenue concentrates in a few large clients; client fintechs are exposed to credit and rate cycles; Argentina's macroeconomic and currency risk affects the home base; and the stablecoin card faces regulatory uncertainty.

milestones.value: Gastón Irigoyen, Juan Fantoni and Hernán Corral, executives from Naranja X, Mastercard and Mercado Pago, start Pomelo to give Latin American fintechs a single card-issuing and payments platform instead of 12 to 18 months of work per country.
With US$35 million and about 100 employees, Pomelo says it will expand its card-processing business in Mexico and Brazil.
Pomelo goes live with its first customer, supporting only prepaid cards in Argentina.
A US$15 million extension to the Series A funds expansion into Colombia and Peru and new products in Brazil, Argentina and Mexico; Pomelo then had about 60 client brands including Rappi and Bitso.

Revenue triples, payments volume grows seven times and processing capacity reaches 55 million transactions a day, as the company widens from prepaid to debit and credit cards and from fintechs to banks and multinationals.
Pomelo has more than 100 corporate clients (Rappi, Bitso, Stori, Nomad, PayJoy, Ripio, AstroPay) and operates in Argentina, Mexico, Brazil, Chile, Colombia and Peru when it closes its Series B.

With more than 150 clients, now including BBVA, Santander, Bancolombia, Binance and Western Union, Pomelo announces a US$55 million Series C to build a global stablecoin-denominated credit card and real-time and agentic payments, with Mexico and Brazil as its largest markets.

Chilean investing app Racional launches payment accounts and prepaid cards on Pomelo's infrastructure, with Pomelo acting as the authorised non-bank issuer, an example of its issuer-as-a-service model.
Pomelo names Martín Zanella, a former dLocal and Naranja X executive, as Chief Financial Officer as it pursues its goal of becoming a global company from Latin America.

Pomelo markets a single integration that lets banks and fintechs issue cards in more than 150 countries, led by a General Manager of Global Card, and says it expects digital-asset cross-border payments to grow in 2027 (stated at a São Paulo payments forum).

co_investors: founders of Marqeta, Rappi, Auth0, Kavak, Loft, RecargaPay

description.value: Lemon connects clean-energy plants (mostly solar) to small businesses, condominiums and households in Brazil: customers receive energy credits on their grid bill, save on electricity and need no installation or upfront cost.

long_description.value: Lemon Energia is a Brazilian energy-tech company that sells distributed-generation solar energy as a subscription. Remote plants, owned by third-party generators, feed energy into the local distribution network; this produces credits that are discounted from the electricity bill of Lemon's customers, who pay Lemon instead (and a residual conventional charge to the utility) and usually save 10% to 20%. Customers need no panels, works or upfront payment, sign up online and manage billing in an app with Pix or boleto payment; they can cancel at any time. On the other side, generators that would otherwise sell wholesale reach the retail market and, per Kaszek, can nearly double their earnings, while Lemon takes over billing, collection and energy management. It earns a fee charged to the generators. The target started as small and mid-sized businesses (bars, restaurants, groceries, supermarkets, laundries spending R$500 to R$8,000 a month on power), and the site now also addresses homes, companies and condominiums. The founders are Rafael Vignoli (CEO), Luciano Pereira (CTO) and Rafael Mezzomo, with Ariel Amar (CFO) named as a co-founder in 2020 and 2022 coverage. It started in 2019 with early customers such as the Oyo hotel chain; when the pandemic hit that concentration, it pivoted to bars and restaurants, piloted with 200 establishments with the utility Cemig in Minas Gerais and in October 2020 took an investment from Ambev's corporate venture arm Z-Tech, which led to a role in Ambev's and Budweiser's "Energy Collective" to bring clean energy to up to 250,000 bars by 2025. After a R$60 million Series A in June 2022 led by Kaszek (with Lowercarbon Capital, its first investment in Brazil), it grew from 3,000 clients and 6 states to about 10,000 clients in 2024 and, by July 2026, 40,000 clients, more than 250 connected plants (against fewer than 50 in 2022), over ten states and more than 15 utilities. A recent growth channel is taking over the customer portfolios of generators that no longer want to run retail, and it is considering acquisitions to consolidate the sector. Next it plans a residential product and entry into Brazil's "free market" for energy, which opens to low-voltage commercial users in November 2027 and to households in November 2028 and would let it serve large cities such as São Paulo and Rio, where distributed generation is limited by the rule that plant and consumer must be in the same utility area. Lemon won gold at the 2026 Energy Summit Awards in sustainability. Where it stands today (LinkedIn posts, 2026): the founder Rafael Vignoli still leads the company, and in March 2026 it was picked for KPMG's Emerging Giants list of scale-ups, with Norte confirming it as a portfolio company.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil has more than 80 million electricity consumer units (Lemon's CEO, 2022) that are bill payers, not customers: they pay high tariffs, have no choice of supplier and, for small businesses and renters, cannot install solar because of upfront cost, space or ownership. Hydro supplies about two thirds of power and Kaszek notes that droughts push prices up and solar is under 2% of the mix. Logic: distributed generation rules let a consumer receive credits from a plant in the same utility area, so a software company that signs up many small consumers, matches them to plants and handles billing creates savings for the customer and better prices for the generator, with a low acquisition cost through partners; Lemon says its unit economics are good and growth came at low acquisition cost. Why now: new distributed-generation regulation, the ESG push, and the planned opening of the free energy market (November 2027 for low-voltage commercial users, November 2028 for households), which would let Lemon serve São Paulo and Rio. Market size: no independent figure was read, so we estimate bottom-up with labelled assumptions: 80 million consumer units x an assumed average bill of R$1,800 a year (R$150 a month) is about R$144 billion a year of retail electricity bills; if 3% to 5% were served through subscription-type clean energy that is R$4 billion to R$7 billion a year billed, and at an assumed 10% to 15% gross take on billings Lemon's pool is R$0.4 billion to R$1 billion in revenue, of which a leader could hold a large share. Traction fits: 40,000 clients and 250 plants in 2026, up from 10,000 in 2022. What is different: a technology and customer-experience focus in a market of analog utilities and small generators (CTO's own words in 2022), customer acquisition through partners (such as Ambev), and a portfolio-takeover channel that consolidates distressed generators. Competitors named in the press: Sunne (similar model) and, with a financing model, Meu Financiamento Solar, Solfácil and Nextron. Fit with Norte: a 2022 Startups.com.br article lists Norte among Lemon's investors before the Series A; the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does and generates revenue from day zero by connecting people, which fits an Ambev distribution partnership; this is our reading. Risks: regulation (the distributed-generation framework, utility and tariff rules) changes the economics; generator and customer credit risk; thin take rates; the free market opening also invites bigger energy traders; and the company said in 2023 it did not expect break-even soon.

milestones.value: Rafael Vignoli, Luciano Pereira, Rafael Mezzomo and Ariel Amar start Lemon to sell solar energy credits to small businesses without installing panels; its first customers include the Oyo hotel chain.
The pandemic dries up demand from Lemon's main customer, the Oyo hotel chain, and the company pivots to bars and restaurants, running a pilot with 200 of them with the utility Cemig in Minas Gerais.

Ambev's corporate venture arm Z-Tech invests, opening the way to Ambev's network of more than 700,000 bars, restaurants and supermarkets; Lemon has 23 employees and 300 MW of clean capacity at that time.

Lemon is chosen to lead Ambev's and Budweiser's "Energy Collective" in Brazil, which aims to bring clean energy to 250,000 bars, restaurants and stadiums by 2025; it already serves 2,700 establishments in four states.
A R$60 million Series A led by Kaszek gives Lemon capital to grow from 3,000 clients and six states to more than ten states and to hire about 40 people; the plan is 250,000 clients by 2025.
Lemon opens in Mato Grosso do Sul, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo and Goiás plus the Federal District, has about 5,000 clients and doubles its team to 120 employees in a year.
With more than 10,000 clients in six regions, Lemon hires a former Buser public-policy head and a former Nubank engineering executive to lead regulatory affairs and engineering.

Lemon Energia is among the 16 startups chosen for KPMG's Emerging Giants 2026 programme, which picks Brazilian scale-ups with global ambition; Norte Ventures announced it as one of four of its portfolio companies in the list.

Lemon reports 40,000 clients, more than 250 connected plants, over ten states and more than 15 utilities; it grows by taking over client portfolios of generators and plans a residential product and entry into the free energy market.

Founder Rafael Vignoli appears on the Founder Hacks podcast and says companies founded more than two years ago must rebuild their premises for AI; Conta Simples' CEO adds that Lemon was its first customer.

description.value: Morado is a Colombian fintech that sells beauty products and credit to hair salons, barbershops and nail studios, financing their supplier purchases at 30, 60 or 90 days through an app and WhatsApp.

long_description.value: Morado is a Bogotá-based company that started in 2022 as an online "everything store" for beauty businesses and has become a credit provider for them. Its founder, Ángela Acosta, spent about eight years at Rappi, from intern to vice president, working on grocery and on the fintech side (Rappi Pay and RappiBank), and in 2021 resigned to build something for the beauty industry; she even took a manicurist course to talk with women who ran salons and heard that the lack of capital was their main obstacle. The first version was a vertical marketplace and logistics business: more than 6,500 products at launch (20,000 by early 2023), no minimum order, same-day or next-day delivery from warehouses in Barranquilla and Bogotá, national coverage in Colombia within 30 days and more than 60 employees, most of them women. She described 700,000 beauty salons in Latin America whose supply chain had not changed in 40 years, 85% of them without any digital tool. The business then moved toward finance: salons order supplies and Morado funds the purchase for 30, 60 or 90 days, assessing risk with traditional data plus non-financial signals such as headcount, location, inventory and client appointments, starting with small loans (about US$820 on average) and raising limits as clients repay. According to Morado, over 72% of its borrowers had their first credit with it and more than half had no bank account. The company site says 28,000 women-led businesses have grown with it, US$12 million in sales and that 64% of the businesses it finances never had credit; it is an award winner of the IDB Lab WeXchange programme and of Forbes Colombia's "30 promesas" of 2023, and its 2024 impact report is published. Morado raised a US$5 million pre-seed in April 2022 led by Tiger Global and H20 Capital with a16z (where it joined the START programme), QED, Latitud, Village Global and Rappi founders as angels. The site later announces a new round of equity and debt without giving date or size. The stated plans were to expand to Mexico, which we found no evidence of, and to grow from 30,000 to a million businesses.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Latin America has about 700,000 beauty salons (the founder's figure, 2022), mostly micro-businesses run by women, whose supply chain is fragmented (up to seven channels to buy inputs per salon, Forbes), almost 85% without digital tools, and who lack bank credit: over half of Morado's clients have no bank account and 72% got their first credit from it. Logic: the supplier purchase is a natural place to lend, because the loan is tied to inventory the salon turns over daily, Morado sees the order, the delivery and the repayment behaviour, and alternative data (headcount, location, inventory, appointments) can replace credit scores; starting at about US$820 and raising limits builds a repayment history. Why now: WhatsApp-based commerce and data that lets a lender assess businesses without a credit history. Market size: no independent figure was read. Our estimate: 700,000 salons x an assumed US$6,000 to US$10,000 a year of purchased supplies per salon (our assumption; Forbes says about 20% of a salon's revenue comes from product sales and salons average eight workers) is US$4 billion to US$7 billion of annual supply purchases; if a lender-distributor served 5% to 10% of them at an assumed 10% to 15% gross margin including financing, revenue would be about US$20 million to US$100 million. Morado's own US$12 million of cumulative sales and 28,000 businesses show it is still early. What is different: a Rappi-alumni team with fintech experience applying lending to a niche vertical, a first-credit focus on informal businesses and an inventory-linked loan. Rivals named in the press are SuperBeauty in Colombia and Círculo de Belleza in Mexico (marketplaces). Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does; a Rappi-network founder at pre-seed fits Norte's network-led approach, but no source names Norte in Morado's round; this is our reading. Risks: credit losses on informal micro-businesses and funding cost (the new round includes debt), thin margins in distribution, competition from beauty brands and marketplaces, one-country concentration, and little public data beyond company statements.

sub_sector.value: Credit and supply for beauty micro-businesses

milestones.value: Ángela Acosta, who spent eight years at Rappi, starts Morado to give beauty salons one place to buy hair, nail and cleaning supplies with next-day delivery; she left Rappi after CEO Simón Borrero asked her to stay until February.

Morado starts with national delivery coverage in Colombia in its first 30 days, more than 60 employees (72% women), a catalogue of 6,500 products and warehouses in Barranquilla and Bogotá, with Medellín and Mexico City next.

Ten months in, Morado has shipped more than 25,000 orders, lists more than 20,000 products and keeps 90% of its technology team in Buenos Aires; Forbes Colombia names it one of its 30 business promises of 2023.

Morado now describes itself as a fintech for beauty businesses: it finances supplier orders for 30, 60 or 90 days, starts with loans of about US$820 and reports over 72% of borrowers on their first credit; it is named a winner of the IDB Lab WeXchange Women STEMpreneurs 2024 competition.

The company reports 28,000 women-led businesses served, US$12 million in sales and 64% of financed businesses without prior credit access, publishes a 2024 impact report and announces a new round of equity and debt.

description.value: Brazilian fintech that offers companies private pension plans and other financial-wellbeing benefits for their employees, with onboarding and plan management done through WhatsApp.

long_description.value: Stay is a Brazilian fintech that lets employers offer corporate private pension plans (previdência) as a benefit, in the way Vestwell and Human Interest do in the United States. It works as the connecting layer between companies of any size and the leading insurers: the employer picks a plan, the employee enrols and manages the plan, balance, contributions, withdrawals and life-insurance cover through WhatsApp, and the HR team gets data about its people. Products today: private pension plans, group life insurance, a financial-health programme (check-up, data for HR and compliance with the NR-1 workplace-risk rule), and long-term incentive plans (ILP) and executive pay design, used to retain talent; the site says a pension strategy can save the company about 40% against paying the same amount in salary, through tax efficiency. It earns fees on the plans and services sold to companies, and the plans are issued through an insurer partnership with Zurich Seguros that began in 2024. It was started in 2023 by a team of tech and finance executives: CEO Tsai Chi-Yu (formerly Morgan Stanley, Uber and the defunct Hash), Nicolas Frajhof (operations), Pedro Iglesias (business development) and Caio Elias, who appears as a founder in 2024 coverage and as CTO in 2026. The pitch rests on a gap: fewer than 3% of Brazilian workers have corporate pension, against 70% to 90% in comparable economies, and the CEO ties the product to record household indebtedness. In October 2024, a little over a year in, it had about 10 people, dozens of clients (a law firm, an operator and a hospital-products multinational) and raised a R$15 million seed led by MAYA Capital and Better Tomorrow Ventures, with 17Sigma, Grão, Ralicap, Sequoia's scout fund and the founders of Vestwell and Human Interest; it planned to double the team and grow clients tenfold. In September 2026 it raised R$30 million in a round led by Citrino (a multi-family office linked to leading business families), with Norte, 17Sigma and BTV, and reported assets under management up 31 times since its start (the site says R$48 million for 127 companies and 12,400 employees), clients such as iFood, Claro, Milky Moo and the Araújo Jorge cancer hospital, and a goal of more than 100 corporate clients by the end of 2026. It will use the money to move beyond traditional pensions into financial-health tools and ILP.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: almost no Brazilian worker saves for retirement through the employer. The CEO says fewer than 3% of workers have corporate pension, against 70% to 90% in comparable economies, while household debt is at record levels; employers compete for talent with salary alone and lose people. The logic: private pension is tax-advantaged for the employer and the employee, so paying part of the package that way can cost the company less than the same amount in salary (Stay claims about 40% saving), and it also works as a retention tool, especially through long-term incentive plans. The hard parts are the paperwork, the insurer's systems and getting employees to enrol, which Stay solves with a digital platform and a WhatsApp interface on top of insurers' plans; it keeps the trust-heavy part (the plan and the insurer) with established partners such as Zurich, and sells the experience and the advice. Why now: record household debt, a tight market for talent, higher interest rates that make fixed-income savings visible, and WhatsApp as the default service channel. Market: IBGE (via Correio, 2026-10-30) counts 39.4 million private-sector employees with a formal contract, a record. If 25 to 30% of them (about 10 to 12 million, our assumption) work for employers large or mid-sized enough to offer a plan, contribute an average R$300 to R$500 a month (our assumption), and Stay captures a distribution and platform fee of 0.5% to 1% of assets a year, then a fully penetrated plan base would carry about R$36 to R$72 billion of new contributions a year and, after several years of accumulation, hundreds of billions in assets; at a 10% share of that pool, Stay's fee revenue would be of the order of R$0.2 to R$1 billion a year. Today it has about R$48 million of assets for 127 companies (about R$3,900 an employee, per the company), so the opportunity is mostly ahead. What is different: it is employer-first and digital, packages pension with life insurance, financial health and ILP, runs on WhatsApp, and is backed by operators of the same model in the US (Vestwell and Human Interest founders are investors) and by Citrino's family-office network, which matters in a trust business. Fit with Norte (our reading): founders with a finance and tech record who found a clear structural gap, and a stage where a connector can bring funds and business families to the cap table, as the Citrino-led round shows; Norte took part in the 2026 round. Risks: revenue is tied to assets and takes years to build; Stay depends on insurers such as Zurich for the product and its economics; sales cycles with HR and finance are long; and incumbents such as banks' own pension arms and benefit platforms could sell the same package.

milestones.value: Started a partnership with Zurich Seguros

With a little over a year in the market and about 10 people, serves dozens of clients (a law firm, a health operator and a hospital-products multinational) and aims to grow clients tenfold by year-end

Reports assets under management up 31 times since its start, clients including iFood, Claro, Milky Moo and the Araújo Jorge cancer hospital, a goal of over 100 corporate clients by year-end, and a widening of its range to financial-health tools and long-term incentive plans

description.value: Skelt is a Curitiba cosmetics group, known for Brazil's leading self-tanning brand Skelt and for the affordable dermocosmetics brand Creamy, sold online, in its own stores and through pharmacies.

long_description.value: Skelt Beauty Brands is a Brazilian beauty group based in Curitiba. It began in 2017, when Gabriel Beleze, then 23 and a long-time fan of self-tanners that were expensive and left skin orange, launched Skelt, a self-tanning product whose formula was developed with a Brazilian pharmaceutical lab and whose first months were financed by his parents. The brand became the reference in autobronzeadores, appeared at the top of independent rankings and was used by celebrities, and it widened into body splash, body makeup, moisturisers and bath products, now with fragrance notes as part of the pitch. In 2019 Beleze and the Curitiba dermatologist Luiz Romancini started Creamy, a dermocosmetics brand with high concentrations of recognised actives at roughly a third of competitors' prices (a 0.3% retinol for R$79 against about R$300 for a multinational brand, said the founder in 2022), made possible by a direct-to-consumer model and lean formulas without fragrance; it launched in November 2019 with R$5 million invested and, by June 2021, had a waiting list of 100,000 people. The business sells online, through its own stores (a target of 55 own stores by the end of 2025) and in pharmacies and cosmetics chains; by March 2022 Skelt was in more than 4,000 points of sale including Raia Drogasil, Drogaria São Paulo and Época Cosméticos, with physical stores making 70% of sales, and Creamy, then sold only digitally, produced almost half of the company's R$56 million revenue in 2021, with a goal of over R$100 million for 2022. Its first outside capital was a R$30 million round from Shift Capital in March 2022 to diversify the portfolio and speed up its skincare pipeline; it also has a third brand, The Joy Lab. In September 2025 it opened its first own factory, in Vinhedo (São Paulo state), which also makes Skelt and The Joy Lab, aiming at 15,000 points of sale by the end of 2025; the same month the group hired Itaú BBA to run the sale of a stake, which the company did not comment on. In November 2025 it reorganised its leadership: Henrique Beleze, who had been COO for five years, became co-CEO alongside Gabriel Beleze. We found no report of a completed sale; Norte lists it as an exit. Where it stands today (LinkedIn posts, 2026): the group presents itself as Skelt Beauty Brands with several brands, is hiring for CRM, marketing and own retail stores, and runs B2B and B2C fulfilment on a DHL network.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: in Brazil the self-tanning and skincare categories were small and expensive (Beleze, 2022): products that left skin orange or cost R$300 for a retinol that could be sold for about R$79, and prescription formulas that patients did not keep buying because of cost.
