Logic: a digital-first brand that controls formulas (lean, fragrance-free, high-concentration actives) and sells direct can offer a third of the price with healthy margin, build a customer base and community online, and then add pharmacy and own-store distribution; the pandemic accelerated skincare (ABIHPEC reported skincare up 21.9% in 2020, via Forbes). Market size: Brazil's personal care, perfumery and cosmetics market was R$175 billion in 2025, up 6.8% (ABIHPEC with Euromonitor data, O Hoje, 10 Aug 2026), the third largest consumer market of beauty in the world. A skincare and body-care niche share is our estimate: if skincare and body care are about 10% to 15% of the total (our assumption, no page read) the pool is R$17 billion to R$26 billion, and a leading affordable brand at 3% to 5% of it would sell R$0.5 billion to R$1.3 billion a year, compared with Skelt's R$56 million in 2021 and goal of R$100 million for 2022 (the group's growth after 2022 is not documented). What is different: a founder-brand with two distinct hits (the self-tanner category leader and a dermocosmetic price disruptor), a doctor co-founder for credibility, a D2C base with a shift to pharmacy distribution and own stores, and its own factory since 2025. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does; a young consumer-brand founder with proven product-market fit and a follow-on from a specialised growth fund (Shift Capital) matches a connector role; we found no source naming Norte's participation, which our reading cannot assume. Risks: brand-led categories are copied and subject to fashion cycles, retailer and influencer dependence, regulatory and Anvisa risk for dermocosmetics, margin pressure as the mix shifts to pharmacy, and the 2025 sale process suggests the owners were looking for liquidity or a partner.

milestones.value: At 23, Gabriel Beleze launches Skelt, a self-tanning product made with a Brazilian pharmaceutical lab and funded at first by his parents, in a Brazilian market that offered expensive products that left the skin orange.
Beleze and dermatologist Luiz Romancini launch Creamy, an accessible dermocosmetics brand sold only online, with R$5 million invested.
Creamy has a waiting list of 100,000 people, helped by the pandemic boom in skincare, and Beleze is on the Forbes Under 30 list (2019 edition).

Skelt has more than 4,000 points of sale including Raia Drogasil, Drogaria São Paulo and Época Cosméticos, R$56 million of revenue in 2021 (almost half from Creamy) and a goal of more than R$100 million; it announces R$30 million from Shift Capital.
Creamy opens its first own factory, in Vinhedo (São Paulo), which also produces Skelt and The Joy Lab, as part of a plan for 55 own stores and 15,000 points of sale by the end of 2025.
The group is reported to have hired Itaú BBA to sell a stake in the company, a secondary sale of existing shares (the buyer is not disclosed); it declines to comment on market rumours.
Skelt Beauty Brands (Creamy, Skelt and The Joy Lab) reorganises its leadership: Henrique Beleze, COO for five years, becomes co-CEO with Gabriel Beleze.

Skelt Beauty Brands recruits for CRM, marketing, own-store business partner and store managers, including stores at Shopping Center Norte in São Paulo and Shopping Parque Dom Pedro in Campinas, which shows its own-store retail and direct channels growing.
DHL Supply Chain publishes a case saying Skelt Beauty Brands, with several brands and fast growth, unified its B2B and B2C fulfilment on a DHL network of hubs.

description.value: Loopi is a São Paulo fintech that gives medium-sized companies their own platform to offer early payment of supplier invoices (receivables anticipation), with invoice validation, digital assignment and accounting handled by Loopi; it began as a social-commerce app and a crypto on-ramp.

long_description.value: Loopi is a company that has changed its business twice. It was founded in April 2021 in São Paulo by Ricardo Bechara, who had brought Rappi to Brazil in 2017, with Felipe Brasileiro and Cesario Martins, and launched as a "social commerce" app: an endless feed of videos in which content creators show products from partner brands, with a button to buy in a few clicks and delivery; it opened with more than 5,000 products in fashion, beauty and home decoration, and announced a US$5 million first round in June 2021 led by Monashees. In 2022 the team launched LoopiPay, a bridge between Brazil's bank network and decentralised finance: the user pays by Pix and receives crypto tokens straight in a self-custodied wallet such as MetaMask (and can sell the same way), the company charged a fee of 0.9% to 3% plus network gas and, in August 2022, said it offered 1,960 tokens, more than any exchange tracked by CoinMarketCap. By late 2023 it had moved again: Loopi Securitizadora S.A. was incorporated in November 2023 with Bechara as president and Brasileiro as director, and the company, now Loopi Finance, describes itself as an embedded-finance platform for medium-sized companies that want to finance their supply chain. A buyer company gets its own branded platform where its suppliers upload invoices (notas fiscais), the buyer sets the rates, and suppliers anticipate payment in minutes at any time; Loopi provides invoice validation, registration of duplicatas, payment reconciliation, digital signature of the assignment documents, KYC and KYB, and the accounting formalisation. The buyer earns a financial return on a programme it already runs, and the suppliers get better rates and terms than the market. The company calls itself a collective-investment platform and receivables securitiser. We found no press that dates the pivot, names customers or gives traction, and the old crypto site could not be reached.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: medium-sized companies pay suppliers in 30 to 90 days; their small suppliers need cash earlier and pay high rates to banks and factoring houses, while the buyer has no way to share its better credit with them or to earn from the programme. Logic: a white-label supplier-finance platform lets the buyer offer anticipation at attractive rates funded by investors or funds, with invoice validation and duplicata registration reducing fraud and double-pledging, and the securitiser structure and software make each programme repeatable; the new electronic duplicata (duplicata escritural) regime and registry that the central bank is bringing online make receivables safer to finance. Market size: the Brazilian electronic-duplicata market is estimated to be able to move up to R$12 trillion a year (Capital Aberto, May 2025, citing market estimates); how much is anticipated is not clear from the pages we read. Our estimate for the slice Loopi targets (supplier programmes of medium-sized buyers): if 20,000 medium companies (our assumption) ran programmes anticipating an average of R$20 million of invoices a year (our assumption) that is R$400 billion of volume; at a net fee to the platform of 0.1% to 0.3% of volume (our assumption) it is R$0.4 billion to R$1.2 billion a year, and a company with 1% to 3% of that would earn R$4 million to R$36 million; the figures are illustrative and carry low confidence. What is different: a team that already built consumer products at Rappi scale and pivoted quickly, an embedded-finance model that makes the buyer the distributor, and a securitiser licence structure in house. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does and that it brings top funds onto the cap table; Loopi's founders raised US$5 million from Monashees, Canary, OneVC and GFC at first, and a later pivot is the kind of case where a network can help find buyers and funding; this is our reading, not Norte's statement. Risks: two pivots in three years show the original theses did not work, the new model competes with banks, factoring fintechs and the registries' own platforms, credit and fraud losses fall on the investors and the brand, there is no public traction data, and fund-raising from investors for receivables depends on rates and regulatory approval.

milestones.value: Ricardo Bechara, who brought Rappi to Brazil, starts Loopi with Felipe Brasileiro and Cesario Martins to build a social-commerce app where content creators sell products from partner brands in a video feed.
Loopi announces a US$5 million first round led by Monashees and presents an app with more than 5,000 products in fashion, beauty and decoration and a goal of hiring in product and technology.
The company launches LoopiPay, a way to buy and sell crypto tokens by Pix directly into the user's own wallet, turning away from social commerce.
LoopiPay says it offers 1,960 tokens, more than any platform in the CoinMarketCap ranking, using decentralised liquidity instead of an order book and charging between 0.9% and 3%.

Now called Loopi Finance, the company offers medium-sized companies a white-label platform for supplier invoice anticipation, with the securitiser Loopi Securitizadora S.A. incorporated in November 2023.

description.value: Elven (Elvenworks) is a Brazilian reliability company that sells an observability and incident-management platform, plus SRE, DevOps and FinOps consulting and a 24x7 operations centre, billed in reais with data kept in Brazil.

long_description.value: Elven, legally ElvenWorks Soluções em Tecnologia Ltda., is a Brazilian company built around the idea of reliability for digital products. It started as a consultancy in Cloud, DevOps and SRE (site reliability engineering) and, as companies kept asking it to recommend engineers, created in November 2021 a training programme in SRE for firms and for people changing careers (basic, standard and advanced tracks). Its three founders, Bruno Almeida, Bruno Pereira and Fabrício Lopes, had wide experience in digital products and, seeing few Brazilian firms able to do this work, built the Elven Platform, a B2B SaaS product that watches applications and services actively and manages incidents, including those raised by third-party APMs and open-source tools, in one place. Today the offer has four parts: Elven Observability (metrics, logs and traces, real-time monitors, web monitors and synthetic tests, on an open OpenTelemetry-based stack), Elven Incidentes (alerting, escalation and a mobile app), Elven NOC / Command Center (a 24x7 operations team with an incident commander process) and professional services to implement and tune observability and cloud cost (FinOps). The commercial pitch is explicitly against global tools such as Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace and PagerDuty: billing in reais by use instead of in dollars per host, metric or gigabyte, customer data hosted in Brazil or in the customer's own environment (the company argues for data sovereignty under Brazil's LGPD), support in Portuguese and, it says, costs about 50% lower on average. Named customers include the electronics retailer KaBuM!, the bus-ticket platform Buson, the credit cooperative Unicred (where it replaced weekly crisis rooms with observability by product and a 24x7 command centre), and the AI firm Technium (30% lower cloud cost). In December 2025 Magalu Cloud reported that Elven, which it describes as about six years old and focused on FinOps, SRE, DevOps and observability, had moved the Observability product, its core product and the engine of its growth, from an international cloud to Magalu Cloud after instability and a bill near R$100,000 a month, cutting cost by about 30% and by 40% to 50% on storage, with an environment of more than 30 TB (peaks above 100 TB) and plans to double the infrastructure and grow the customer base by 50% to 70% by year end. The company has added AI agents to its pitch. We found no funding round, investor or revenue figure. Where it stands today (LinkedIn posts, 2026): CEO Bruno Pereira fronts the company at developer events, it ran its own Observability Day in September 2026, and it is still hiring operations leaders, SREs and NOC analysts.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilian companies running critical digital operations pay global observability vendors in dollars, by host, metric or gigabyte, with data hosted abroad and support in English, and many lack the SRE skills to use the tools well (the company's own comparison; the market for SRE, DevOps and Cloud talent is tight, which is why Elven began training engineers). Logic: observability and incident management are mission-critical and recurring, spend grows with cloud usage, and a local vendor that bundles software with an operations team can sell on cost, currency, data residency and responsibility for results; costs of the stack fall when metrics, logs and traces are stored as Parquet in cheap object storage, as Elven did on Magalu Cloud (storage costs 40% to 50% lower than attached disks). Why now: cloud cost pressure (FinOps), the shift to open standards (OpenTelemetry) that reduces lock-in, and AI agents that can act on incidents. Market size: published figures vary widely by scope (search results ranged over an order of magnitude, none of which we could open), and we read only that Brazil held 22.8% of the Latin America, Middle East and Africa IT observability platform market in 2025 (KBV Research), so no dependable Brazilian dollar figure is available. Our bottom-up estimate with labelled assumptions: about 5,000 Brazilian mid-sized and large companies with serious cloud operations, spending R$200,000 to R$500,000 a year on observability, incident and NOC services, is R$1 billion to R$2.5 billion a year; a local leader with 5% to 10% would have R$50 million to R$250 million of revenue, with no public data that Elven is near the lower end. What is different: a combined software-plus-NOC model, pricing in reais, local data, and a team that already trains the market's SRE talent. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does and does not meddle with operations; a technical founder team selling to Brazilian CTOs is consistent with a connector role; no source we read names Norte or any investor in Elven, so this is purely our reading. Risks: global vendors can add a Brazilian region and cut price, observability is a crowded and fast-moving category, the business mixes services and software (lower margins), customer concentration, and there is no public information about funding, revenue or customer count.

milestones.value: Bruno Almeida, Bruno Pereira and Fabrício Lopes found Elven to bring SRE-grade reliability practices to Brazilian companies, starting with consulting and a platform to monitor applications and manage incidents.
Elven launches its SRE training programme (basic, standard and advanced tracks) after companies keep asking it to recommend Cloud, DevOps and SRE specialists.

Elven moves its Observability product to Magalu Cloud after instability and a bill near R$100,000 a month; costs fall about 30% (40% to 50% on storage), the environment holds more than 30 TB, and it plans to double infrastructure and grow its customer base 50% to 70% by year end.

Elven takes part in The Developer's Conference Floripa 2026, where CEO Bruno Pereira speaks on SRE with AI Ops and the company pitches "sovereign observability, made in Brazil"; in May it also held an AI engineering meetup in Rio de Janeiro.

Elven holds Observability Day 2026 in São Paulo, a free one-day event with sixteen speakers from Sicredi, PicPay, Mottu, Grupo Kontik and Elven and panels on AI Ops and observability of AI applications, sponsored by Magalu Cloud, Vertigo and Azion.

Elven positions its platform against Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace and PagerDuty with billing in reais, data in Brazil, a 24x7 NOC and AI agents, and shows customers such as KaBuM!, Buson, Unicred and Technium.

Elven opens a role for an Operations Leader to run its SRE, observability, FinOps and helpdesk teams across multicloud environments, and describes itself as a reference in incident management, monitoring and observability.

description.value: Dr. Jones is a Brazilian men's grooming brand (razors by subscription, shampoo, shaving foam, face scrub and body gels), sold online and, since 2023, through retailers; Grupo Boticário bought it in 2022.

long_description.value: Dr. Jones is a men's grooming and personal-care brand that Guilherme Campos and André Popoutchi founded in 2013, a former banker and a former treasury trader at Itaú BBA, inspired by Dollar Shave Club (sold to Unilever for US$1 billion in 2016) and Harry's. It began inside Beauty Box and sold B2B and through physical retail and marketplaces. In early 2019 it bought the Home Shave Club, a razor-blade subscription club, and at the end of 2019 it made a radical change: it pulled its products from stores and marketplaces and went fully direct-to-consumer, with its own e-commerce and subscriptions. The timing helped, because the pandemic pushed sales online: from March 2020 it grew about 30% a month, cut prices by 15% to 20% in April by passing on the margin saved from retail, and in September 2020 had a run rate of R$7 million and 2,500 subscribers (20% of revenue). Revenue nearly tripled in 2020 to R$3.3 million, reached R$7.3 million in 2021 and the brand closed 2021 with a run rate of R$10 million; the portfolio grew from 11 products in 2020 to 20 products in 2022 (shampoo, face scrub, shaving foam, soaps, an after-shave cream and Abdoburn, an abdominal-fat gel), supported by humorous advertising inspired by Dollar Shave Club that reached almost 5 million views. It had more than 150,000 registered customers and 80,000 active ones in 2022. Funding came from Astella Investimentos, IgniteXL, Igah Ventures and Norte Ventures, plus two founders of Trybe as individuals, and in 2021 and 2022 it tried a bridge round that included an equity crowdfunding offer on Kria (the first for a VC-backed Brazilian startup), which hit its R$3.5 million target with almost 200 backers but was not concluded because of defaults. In October 2022 Grupo Boticário bought 100% in cash for an undisclosed price after a year of talks, giving exit to all the funds, and the founders stayed as executives. Under Boticário, Dr. Jones entered B2B in October 2023 and by July 2024 was in more than 14,000 points of sale, with revenue up 130% in 2023; in 2026 it is listed among the group's brands.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: male grooming in Brazil was concentrated in three product types (razors, deodorants, fragrances) held by a few large brands that struggled to innovate (Igah's partner, 2020); razors in particular were sold in stores at high prices and bought in a hurry. Logic: a direct-to-consumer brand with a humorous voice and a subscription for blades (the Dollar Shave Club and Harry's playbook, which ended in a US$1 billion sale to Unilever in 2016) can win customers online, own the relationship and data, and expand into hair, skin and body care with a retention base; in Brazil the pandemic accelerated online buying, and D2C saved the retail margin to cut prices 15% to 20%. Why now (2019 to 2020): digital advertising costs were still low, the founders had already bought a subscription club, and the retail channel was not working for a young brand. Market size: Brazil's men's beauty and personal-care market was about R$22 billion a year in 2020 (Brazil Journal, citing the Igah investor) and about US$5.4 billion in 2022, growing 14.5% a year (Euromonitor, via a Grupo Boticário release); these use different scopes. A bottom-up view of the brand's reachable share: a 1% to 3% share of R$22 billion is R$220 million to R$660 million a year, against the R$10 million run rate at the 2022 exit, so the upside was far above the realised outcome; the founders had also projected R$20 million for 2022 and R$50 million for 2023. What was different: a brand and marketing-led D2C model in a category dominated by established brands; a founder pair from finance (an ex-banker and an ex-trader at Itaú BBA) running a lean operation; subscription revenue (20% of revenue in 2020); and distribution later extended by a strategic buyer. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than it does and brings top funds to cap tables; Norte took part in the 2020 round led by Igah and, per Startups.com.br, suggested crowdfunding for the bridge, and the company was bought by a strategic buyer in 2022 (our reading, not a statement of Norte's reasons). Risks that materialised or remained: small scale at exit, customer-acquisition cost inflation in D2C, the bridge round and crowdfunding that did not close, and dependence on one category (razors) and on marketing spending.

milestones.value: Guilherme Campos and André Popoutchi found Dr. Jones, a men's beauty brand that starts inside Beauty Box and sells B2B and in physical retail, inspired by Dollar Shave Club.
Dr. Jones buys Home Shave Club, a razor-blade subscription club, giving it its first base of subscribers.
The founders pull the products out of physical stores and marketplaces and put everything into direct-to-consumer sales through their own e-commerce, with single purchases and subscriptions.
As the pandemic speeds up online buying, Dr. Jones lowers prices 15% to 20%, passing on the margin saved from retail; sales grow about 30% a month and the run rate reaches R$7 million by September.

Dr. Jones opens an equity crowdfunding offer on the Kria platform, the first by a VC-backed Brazilian startup, to turn customers into shareholders; it reaches its R$3.5 million target with almost 200 backers but is not concluded because of defaults.
Grupo Boticário buys 100% of Dr. Jones in cash, giving full exit to Astella, Igah, Norte Ventures and IgniteXL; the founders stay as executives.
Under Boticário, Dr. Jones enters B2B, selling to supermarkets, drugstores and specialised stores.
Dr. Jones reaches more than 14,000 points of sale and a 130% revenue increase in 2023 after its B2B strategy.

description.value: AI data company that designs expert-written training tasks, feedback loops and benchmarks for frontier AI labs, using a paid network of remote specialists. It began as the Brazilian student-careers platform Start Carreiras.

long_description.value: Vetto builds data and evaluation systems that help frontier AI labs train and test their models, and it pays experts (doctors, lawyers, engineers, researchers) to create and review the tasks. It does not sell fixed datasets: its pitch is that data is an interface, so it designs learning tasks, expert feedback loops, adaptive benchmarks and evaluation cycles that follow real use. It sells to AI labs (the customer side is a 'get data' enterprise contact, with a product called Atlas) and recruits remote experts through a talent pool at work.vetto.ai, who are paid per task (the expert page shows clinical scenarios at US$50-200 an hour as an example). The company started in 2022 as Start Carreiras, an HR-tech from São José dos Campos founded by three friends from the ITA engineering school, José André Nunes (CEO), Alexandre Bernat and Gabriel Albuquerque, after they found internship hunting poor. It began as software for colleges to onboard students, then became a student-first platform that connects students, companies and universities: by August 2024 it claimed 120,000 students, 500 recruiting companies and 600 institutions, and it shared revenue with universities that distributed its white-label software. In April 2025 it had 700,000 registered students, was adding AI matching and AI interviews (more than 50 hires in the first month of the AI launch) and expected revenue to grow from R$4 million in 2024 to R$25 million in 2025. By January 2026 the company was operating as Vetto, an AI data company: the former Start Carreiras base of students and experts became the supply side, and the business turned to frontier AI labs. In January 2026 Rodrigo Schmidt, an engineering executive with about 15 years at Facebook/Meta, joined as co-founder and CTO, and Lucas Smaira, a former DeepMind researcher, became Head of Research. Its site now publishes research and open benchmarks (Terminal Tasks Open, Vetto Science Bench, Plot Twist Bench, SlopCode Vetted) as proof of its pipelines. Backers named in the press are Maya Capital, Graphene Ventures, Reach Capital and Norte Ventures (seed of R$13 million in April 2025). The public sources do not give Vetto's current revenue, customers or round size after the pivot.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: frontier AI labs are limited by the quality, not the volume, of their training and evaluation data. Easy web data is largely used up, and improving reasoning, coding and domain skills needs expert-written tasks, careful human feedback and benchmarks that models cannot simply memorise. Labs buy this from a few vendors and are short of skilled people to do the work. Logic and why now: buyers' budgets are large and growing (Sacra estimates Scale AI made about US$2 billion of revenue in 2025, up from US$870 million in 2024, and Meta paid US$14.3 billion for 49% of it), and Meta's stake reportedly pushed other labs, Google among them, to cut ties with Scale and look for neutral suppliers. Vetto's team already had a supply asset: a base of hundreds of thousands of Brazilian students and a way to recruit and pay people at scale. Brazil and Latin America have many qualified professionals (doctors, lawyers, engineers) at lower hourly cost than the US, and Portuguese and Spanish capacity that English-first vendors lack. Market size, a rough order of magnitude: from the vendors we could read, Scale alone was near US$2 billion in 2025, and search summaries of Sacra pages put Surge and Mercor above US$1 billion each, so the expert-data market for labs is plausibly US$5-10 billion a year in 2025-26 (our assumption). If Vetto reached 1% to 3% of it in a good outcome, revenue would be US$50-300 million. What is different: it pairs a research team (ex-DeepMind and ex-Meta leaders) that publishes open benchmarks with a Brazilian expert supply that already runs at scale, and it frames its work as designing the learning experience, not selling labelled rows. Fit with Norte (our reading): the founders are young, obsessed operators who already shipped one product to 700,000 users and then reinvented the company; Norte joined after Maya and Graphene, which matches its follower and connector style, and it can help by introducing US labs and senior hires. Risks: customer concentration in a handful of labs that can change vendors quickly; rivals with far more capital (Scale, Surge, Mercor, Turing); a recent pivot with no public customers or revenue; and the chance that synthetic data reduces demand for human experts.

sub_sector.value: AI training data and model evaluation

milestones.value: Start Carreiras is founded by three ITA friends, José André Nunes, Alexandre Bernat and Gabriel Albuquerque, after poor experiences hunting internships; it starts as software for colleges to onboard students.

The company rebrands around three pillars (students, companies, universities), reporting 120,000 students, 500 recruiting companies and 600 institutions, and launches a white-label revenue-share model with universities.

With 700,000 registered students, Start Carreiras adds AI matching and AI-run interviews (over 50 hires in the first month) and sets a goal of R$25 million in revenue for 2025, up from R$4 million in 2024.
Now operating as Vetto, an AI data company for frontier labs, it names Rodrigo Schmidt, ex-Facebook/Meta engineering executive, co-founder and CTO, to lead research, engineering and product.
Lucas Smaira, a former DeepMind researcher, joins as Head of Research to strengthen work with frontier labs.

Vetto publishes Terminal Tasks Open, an open-source benchmark of 30 terminal tasks, extending a research line (Science Bench, Plot Twist Bench, SlopCode Vetted) that shows its evaluation pipelines to labs.

description.value: Digital prescription-drug benefit for companies: employees buy medicines at any pharmacy in Brazil through an app, with AI prescription checks and Pix payment, and employers get a health-management dashboard.

long_description.value: Omni Saúde sells companies a prescription-drug benefit for their employees, the same way an employer buys a meal voucher or a health plan. The employer picks a plan and a monthly balance per person (plans start at about R$50 a month and can exceed R$1,000, with generic-only and any-drug tiers); the employee sends the doctor's prescription in the app, an AI checks it, and the purchase is paid by Pix at any pharmacy in Brazil, with no accredited network (more than 95,000 pharmacies, physical or online). The fiscal receipt is then checked by AI against the prescription. Omni does not earn from selling drugs or from pharmacy commissions: it earns the monthly fee per covered life and makes its margin by managing risk, controlling the claims ratio and preventing fraud, a model Brazil Journal compares with US pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs). A dashboard (Omni Care) shows each employer the use of the benefit, and the company now sells the same infrastructure to insurers and digital health platforms (partnerships with Seguros Unimed and Care Plus). The company was founded in May 2023 by Fernando Domingues, a serial health entrepreneur who co-founded the telemedicine company Conexa Saúde and the medical-cannabis marketplace Cannect Life, and Leopoldo Veras, with more than 25 years in health management. Domingues says the idea follows his telemedicine bet: Brazil's drug coverage inside health plans is small compared with the US. It started with a R$5 million seed in June 2023, had sold more than 15,000 plans by August 2024 (target 50,000 lives and about R$10 million of annual revenue), closed 2024 with R$5 million of revenue, reached about 30,000 lives in May 2025 and, by November 2026, had more than 70 clients, 350,000 paid lives and annualized revenue of R$26 million, aiming at R$30 million by December and R$50 million by the end of 2027. Clients named include Azul, Light, MetLife and Spoleto. Investors named in the press are VEC Investments, Greenrock (the family office of the owners of the Salomão Zoppi laboratory), Norte Ventures, Enseada (the Larragoiti family office, owner of SulAmérica), Wayra (Vivo) and, in the latest round, the venture manager ACNext, plus angels from Neoway, Dr. Consulta and Unimed Nacional. It was picked for KPMG's Emerging Giants programme in 2026, and says AI will be used to predict treatment drop-out and clinical risks.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: private health plans in Brazil rarely cover outpatient drugs (the Startups.com.br and Saúde Business pieces point to chronic patients left without cover), so patients and families pay for them from their own pockets. Employers see the cost in absenteeism and in sick leave, and insurers see it in hospital bills when a patient stops treatment. Logic and why now: a drug benefit managed like a voucher (a balance, an app, Pix) is cheap to launch for HR, needs no deals with pharmacy chains, and gives the employer a data dashboard. AI makes the hard part, validating prescriptions and receipts at scale, cheap, and Pix removes card networks. Domingues' own comparison is the US PBM market, which is worth trillions of dollars; Brazil's equivalent is small and still organising. Market size: Brazilian pharmacy retail reached R$241 billion in the twelve months to October 2025 (IQVIA, via Central do Varejo, page read). Prescription drugs for chronic use are a large share of it (our assumption: 40-60%, not sourced). If employers and insurers paid for even 5% of retail drug spend through a benefit like this, that is R$12 billion of annual premiums; at the 5-10% administration and risk margin we assume, revenue would be R$0.6-1.2 billion for the whole category, and a leader holding a third would reach R$200-400 million. Bottom-up check: the company reports R$26 million of annualized revenue from 350,000 lives, or about R$75 a life a year, so each additional million lives is about R$75 million of revenue, a figure we derived from the company's own numbers. What is different: it is a benefit sold to employers and insurers, not a discount card or a pharmacy network; it works at any pharmacy; it earns from risk and fraud control, and its growth is real (revenue from R$5 million in 2024 to a R$26 million run rate in about two years, on the company's own figures). Fit with Norte (our reading): a founder on his third health company, known by Norte's partner Pedro Teo from Conexa and Cannect, where a connector that brings co-investors and enterprise clients helps; Norte entered as a co-investor alongside Greenrock, the follower role its Manifesto describes. Risks: the claims ratio (a bad year of claims or fraud hurts margin), concentration in a few large clients, a possible regulatory reaction from ANS or the drug-price board (CMED) if the product looks like insurance, and large pharmacy chains or health insurers building their own benefit.

milestones.value: Omni Saúde is founded by Fernando Domingues (co-founder of Conexa Saúde and Cannect Life) and Leopoldo Veras to sell a prescription-drug benefit to employers.
It launches with a R$5 million seed and a product that works as a balance for buying prescription drugs at any pharmacy, paid by Pix in the app with face recognition and AI.
Having sold over 15,000 plans and growing threefold in the first quarter of 2024 against 2023, it reaches R$16 million raised and plans to double its covered lives to 50,000 by the end of 2024.
Closes 2024 with R$5 million of revenue.
Reaches about 30,000 lives and about 40 client companies, and sets a goal of 70,000 lives and four times the revenue by the end of 2025, as Wayra (Vivo) joins the investors.
Brings AI to the centre of operations (prescription validation, anti-fraud audit and adherence analytics), signs partnerships with Seguros Unimed and Care Plus and is chosen for KPMG Emerging Giants.

Counts over 70 clients (among them Azul, Light, MetLife and Spoleto), 350,000 paid lives and R$26 million of annualized revenue, and raises a round led by ACNext to double its lives by the end of 2027.

description.value: Operates online stores and apps for retailers using senior engineers, AI agents and its own software, charging for the results it delivers. Started as the deco.cx website builder for developers.

long_description.value: deco operates online stores for retailers and brands and charges for the results it produces. Its pitch today is that senior engineers, AI agents and its own software run a company's digital experience (site, app, storefront), from audits ranked by revenue to headless storefronts built in weeks, native commerce apps, an AI sales assistant, A/B tests in production, SEO and visibility in AI answers, monitoring around the clock, and integrations with ERP, order management, CRM and payments. Two products sit under that service: the Storefront, with blocks, a site editor and templates, and the Studio, where a company connects its context and builds its own apps and agents. At VTEX Day 2026 (April) deco showed a new CMS that puts the live site next to an AI chat so marketing and design staff can describe a bug or feature and an agent implements it in a preview, a super agent that audits any site across seven dimensions in 10 to 15 minutes, and agents for content and for journey optimisation. It was founded in Rio de Janeiro in 2022 as deco.cx by Guilherme Rodrigues (CEO), Luciano Júnior (CTO) and Rafael Crespo (CMO), three ex-VTEX people (two programmers since their teens and a designer from VTEX's talent team). The first product was a website builder for developers, pitched as an alternative to Wix and WordPress: pick a template, get the code in two minutes, with an own lightweight analytics, A/B testing and hosting, and a marketplace where agencies and freelancers sell programming services. It sold through agencies (36 partner agencies and a Discord with almost 2,500 developers in January 2024). In January 2024 it had 65 signed contracts and 35 sites live, with clients such as Zee.Dog, Embelleze, Osklen and Baw, and aimed at US$1-2.5 million of revenue in the year, with a US self-service launch. Later it moved from selling a tool to operating stores with agents: the company's own pages list case studies (Oficina, New Balance's migration to FastStore in three days) and a May 2026 report says the logistics platform SuperFrete uses deco's AI agents in fraud prevention and customer service. Money raised: about US$600,000 from angels in late 2022, including VTEX founders Geraldo Thomaz and Mariano Gomide, and a US$2.2 million seed in January 2024 led by Maya Capital with FJ Labs, Lanx and Crivo Ventures. Norte's part is not stated in the sources read.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: large and mid-sized Brazilian retailers run their sites on platforms such as VTEX through agencies. A small fix can wait a week in an agency backlog, and sites decay silently (speed, search visibility, broken funnels). Developers cost a lot and are scarce, and each store needs continuous operation, not a one-time build. Logic and why now: coding agents can now implement a described change inside a preview, and AI answers (search assistants) are a new channel to be visible in. deco came from the platform's inside (its founders worked at VTEX), builds on open-source blocks, and ties its price to results, which lowers the barrier for retailers to try. As agents do more of the engineering, the margin moves from selling developer hours to selling operated outcomes. Market size: ABComm counted R$204.3 billion of e-commerce revenue in Brazil in 2024 and projected R$234.9 billion for 2025 (Mercado&Consumo, read). Our assumption: retailers spend 3-6% of online revenue on technology, agencies and site operation, which would make a R$7-14 billion addressable pool in Brazil in 2025 (R$235B x 3-6%). If deco reached 2-4% of that in a good outcome, revenue would be R$140-560 million; expansion to Latin America and the US (it entered the US in 2024) would multiply it. What is different: it sells operated results rather than seats; it is built by ex-VTEX engineers who know the stack, is open-source at its core, and now ships agents that fix and audit stores. Comparables are the headless CMS and agency model (VTEX FastStore, Shopify partners, Vercel-style platforms), and AI-first agencies. Fit with Norte (our reading): obsessed, technical founders on a second product cycle, backed by Maya and angels from VTEX's founding team; Norte's network of operators from VTEX-like companies and its connector role can bring large retail clients and later-stage funds. Risks: the move from a tool to a service lowers software margins and ties growth to engineers; AI coding assistants may let retailers do this themselves; dependence on the VTEX ecosystem; and few public numbers on revenue after 2024.

milestones.value: deco.cx is founded in Rio de Janeiro by three ex-VTEX colleagues, Guilherme Rodrigues, Luciano Júnior and Rafael Crespo, to build a developer-friendly alternative to Wix and WordPress.

With 65 signed contracts, 35 sites in production, 36 partner agencies and a Discord of almost 2,500 developers, deco.cx announces its first institutional round and a launch of its self-service product in the US.
At VTEX Day, deco presents a new CMS with an AI chat beside the live site, a super agent that audits any site on seven dimensions and agents for content and journey optimisation.
The logistics platform SuperFrete adopts deco AI agents for fraud prevention and customer service, showing the move from selling software to operating work with agents.

description.value: Brazilian app for intercity bus travel: it pools travellers to charter executive buses, resells tickets from over 150 bus companies and now owns regulated bus lines.

long_description.value: Buser is a Brazilian app for intercity bus travel that has grown from a group-charter platform into a mix of three businesses: collaborative charter (fretamento colaborativo), regulated bus lines it now owns, and a marketplace that resells tickets from more than 150 bus companies. In the original model, travellers going to the same destination are pooled so that they split the cost of chartering an executive bus from a licensed charter company; Buser sells the seats, runs customer service, pricing, network planning and marketing, and does not own buses or employ drivers (the company's own pitch, and Valor Capital's description), taking a commission from the bus company (reported in 2019 at up to 35%, 20-25% on average). Trips can cost up to about 60% less than a bus-station ticket. Buses carry fatigue cameras and telemetry, and companies and drivers are certified by the transport regulator ANTT. It began when co-founder Marcelo Abritta, from Belo Horizonte, found it cheaper to charter a 48-seat bus for 30 relatives to his wedding in Bahia than to buy 30 tickets (November 2016). With his friend Marcelo Vasconcellos he launched a Facebook page on 2 June 2017, which had 10,000 followers in under 30 days; the first trip, planned for 7 July 2017, was blocked by a court order from incumbents, the passengers were refunded and the press coverage helped. The two founders then raised a seed from Canary, Yellow Ventures and Fundação Estudar Alumni Partners (early 2018), a Series A from Valor Capital, Monashees and Canary (end of 2018) and a Series B led by SoftBank's Latin America fund with Monashees, Valor, Canary and Grupo Globo (October 2019), which carried a plan to spend R$300 million in 12 months. After the pandemic it added a ticket marketplace (end of 2020), parcel delivery inside buses for companies (Buser Encomendas, May 2021), bus financing and urban transport plans, backed by a R$700 million Series C in June 2021 led by LGT Lightrock. It then built a WhatsApp sales channel (expected to reach 35% of revenue in 2022), relaunched its brand in 2024 and, per the press, passed US$100 million of annual revenue in 2024, with 20% growth in operating profit. In 2025 it raised R$30 million in media-for-equity from 4Equity Media Ventures to pay for marketing. In March 2026 it bought two regulated bus companies, Expresso JK and Transportes Santa Maria, its first acquisitions, and in November 2026 co-founder Marcelo Vasconcellos took over as CEO, with Abritta staying on. It reports gross revenue of R$580 million in 2025, expects R$700 million in 2026 and aims for R$1 billion by 2027 through acquisitions of traditional bus companies, AI and the marketplace; it has 14 million registered customers, carries about 5 million passengers a year and wants 6 million in 2027. The company still fights lawsuits from traditional operators and a federal prosecutor over whether its model needs ANTT authorisation, though a Federal Court in Espírito Santo declared the model legal in November 2024.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil moves people by road. Valor Capital counted 4,600 destinations served by buses against 530 by air, and over 300 million bus tickets sold in 2019, twice as many as airline tickets. Yet most routes were run by one company under per-route government authorisations (about 65% of routes with a single operator in 2019), so prices were high and options poor, and many people turned to clandestine transport. Logic and why now: shared chartering lets an asset-light platform pool demand digitally and rent seats on buses that already exist, so a bus fills and costs fall. The model copies the logic of ride-hailing and of Flixbus in Germany, which grew an open market after deregulation (Valor's explanation). Minas Gerais authorising independent charter operators in 2021 and a favourable federal ruling in 2024 moved the regulatory risk in its favour, and Buser now buys licensed bus companies to put its pricing and data into them. Market size: NeoFeed (read, November 2026) cites the regulated road passenger market at R$15-20 billion a year and over 100 million passengers, 60% of which still happens offline. Buser itself reported R$580 million of gross revenue in 2025, so it is already about 3-4% of that market; a strong outcome could be 10-15% (R$2-3 billion), mostly through acquisition and marketplace. The sum is our own: R$15-20B x 10-15% = R$1.5-3B. What is different: it has the brand and the app that millions of Brazilians know, a regulatory track record, and technology (pricing, network planning, fatigue cameras) it can apply to acquired operators; competitors are traditional operators, ClickBus-style marketplaces and BlaBlaCar. Fit with Norte (our reading): this is a Fund I company (Norte's portfolio page), with founders who kept going through years of court battles; as a connector, Norte's role would be introducing top funds (the cap table shows SoftBank, Lightrock, Monashees, Valor) and operators. No source we read says when or in which round Norte invested. Risks: regulation and litigation (ANTT and prosecutors), bus safety incidents and legal responsibility for delays, margin pressure from owning operations, and execution of acquisitions. Travel demand is cyclical, as the pandemic showed.

milestones.value: The idea appears when Marcelo Abritta finds it cheaper to charter a bus for 30 relatives to his wedding in Bahia than to buy their tickets, and with Marcelo Vasconcellos he budgets charters showing savings of up to 60%.

Buser is launched on 2 June 2017 as a Facebook page and reaches 10,000 followers in under 30 days; the first trip is blocked by a court on 7 July 2017, and the founders refund passengers, turning the dispute into press attention.
Buser raises its first seed from Canary, Yellow Ventures and Fundação Estudar Alumni Partners and hires regulatory-law specialists to defend the charter model.

With 250,000 passengers carried in 50 cities, 40 partner bus companies and 15 times year-on-year growth, Buser raises a Series B led by SoftBank's Latin America fund and plans to spend R$300 million in 12 months, including sponsoring the Flamengo football club.
Adds a ticket marketplace (Buser Passagens), selling bus tickets from regular operators; within six months it reaches 3,000 passengers a week with 40 partner companies.
Starts Buser Encomendas, a B2B parcel service using the luggage space of buses, for e-commerce, logistics firms and small carriers.
Raises a R$700 million Series C led by LGT Lightrock, with a R$1 billion two-year plan to diversify into marketplace, parcels, bus financing and urban transport, after almost 4 million customers.

Marketplace already represents 15% of revenue and is the second source after collective charter; Buser reports 2 million new customers in recent months and 1 million passengers in December 2021, and builds boarding points, starting in Rio de Janeiro with R$50 million.
A Federal Court in Espírito Santo declares the legality of Buser's travel model, adding to a series of court wins; the company relaunches its brand the same year.
Closes R$30 million media-for-equity with 4Equity Media Ventures to fund marketing, after annual revenue above US$100 million in 2024.
Buys Expresso JK and Transportes Santa Maria, its first two acquisitions, entering the regulated bus market.
Marcelo Vasconcellos becomes CEO, with Marcelo Abritta staying on; Buser reports R$580 million gross revenue in 2025, 14 million customers and a goal of R$1 billion by 2027.

description.value: Colombian electricity retailer for businesses that installs a smart meter and gives customers consumption analytics, a single invoice for all their sites and clean-energy options; it is also building distributed solar generation and an energy-software spin-off, Olibia.

long_description.value: Bia sells electricity to businesses in Colombia and wraps it in technology. It buys power in the wholesale market and resells it to companies, installing a smart meter (replacing the traditional one and handling the change of supplier) so the customer can see consumption by site and by hour, get alerts and forecasts, detect reactive-power problems, ask an AI assistant why consumption rose, centralise invoices for many sites in one payment, and see how much of its energy is clean (renewable-energy certificates are available at extra cost). Bia says its tariffs beat the grid operators' average for the same voltage level, and the pitch is that energy should be understood and chosen, not only paid. It was founded in 2022 in Bogotá by two ex-Rappi people, Juan Sebastián Ruales (CEO) and Guillermo Plaza, together with energy-sector executive Leonardo Velásquez. It launched with a US$6 million pre-seed in July 2022 led by Canary, with angels such as the Rappi founders and the founders of NotCo and Frubana. By October 2023, with a Series A of US$16.5 million led by Kaszek, it had more than 1,500 business clients; in November 2024, with a US$8.5 million bridge ahead of a Series B led by RA Capital's Planetary Health fund and IDB Lab, it reported more than 3,000 businesses (Coca-Cola Femsa and Falabella among them), 140 employees and more than US$8 million of monthly revenue, and said it had used up to US$20 million of debt facilities. In August 2026 it raised US$18.5 million led by Kaszek, with Endeavor Catalyst, RA Capital and the IDB, bringing total capital to about US$40 million, and reorganised as a group with three units: energy retail (more than 4,000 companies, including Coca-Cola, Falabella, Ikea and Parmalat, about 50 GWh a month, or roughly 0.7% of the national market), distributed generation (small hydro plants and 'remote panel' solar communities of 1 MW, aiming for at least 15 communities in 2026) and Olibia, a software spin-off of the operating system Bia built for its own acquisition, billing, collections and trading, in talks with customers in five countries and aimed at gas, water and telecoms as well as power. The CEO says the business will grow 60-70% in 2026 with 92% retention in the first cohort and an NPS of 83, and that it will open a free market-intelligence platform to the whole industry. Backers named in the press include Kaszek, Canary, Nazca, 8VC, Global Founders Capital, EWA Capital, WildSur, RA Capital, IDB Lab and Endeavor Catalyst; Norte Ventures appears in aggregator investor lists and in a 2026 LinkedIn event post that tags it, but no round article names it.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Colombian businesses buy electricity without seeing what they use until the bill arrives, with limited choice of supplier, and tariffs rose 15.3% a year between 2021 and 2024 (Corficolombiana, cited by Forbes Colombia), the sharpest rise in 23 years after a drought. A regulated or contract customer with several sites has no clean data, no forecast and no single invoice. Logic and why now: the market for larger customers is open to competition, so a retailer that buys well in the wholesale market (using hydrology and weather models) and installs its own smart meter can give a lower price and data at the same time. The meter and billing data are also a software asset, which Bia now spins off as Olibia. Rising prices and El Niño make customers receptive. Market size: Bia says 50 GWh a month is about 0.7% of the Colombian market (Ecosistema Startup, read), implying about 7,100 GWh a month or about 86 TWh a year nationally (our arithmetic: 50 / 0.007). At an assumed average of US$0.10-0.15 per kWh, that is about US$8-13 billion a year of electricity sales in Colombia; the part open to Bia's customers (businesses above the regulated threshold) is only a share of it (our assumption: 20-30%, so US$2-4 billion). Bia's own revenue run-rate of more than US$8 million a month (about US$100 million a year) is therefore roughly 2.5-5% of that addressable part, and a leader at 15-20% would be US$300-800 million, before Latin American expansion and software. What is different: the company combines a retail licence with its own meter, billing and trading software and reports 92% retention and an NPS of 83, which is uncommon for an energy supplier. A comparable the company itself names is Kraken Technologies, spun out of Octopus Energy, which in September 2025 reported US$500 million of contracted annualised revenue and more than 70 million accounts (Ecosistema Startup) - Bia's software unit is much earlier, with no licence revenue reported yet. Fit with Norte (our reading): ex-Rappi founders, a network of Latin American operators, and a cap table with Kaszek, Canary and Nazca fits Norte's co-investor role; the Manifesto says it brings top funds and operators into cap tables. No article says what Norte put in or when. Risks: wholesale-price exposure in a drought year (the CEO says demand is matched with contracts), regulatory change in Colombia's electricity market, financing needs for the energy contracts and solar communities (debt, guarantees), and the distraction of three business lines.

sub_sector.value: Business electricity retail and smart metering

milestones.value: Bia launches in Bogotá with a US$6 million pre-seed led by Canary, offering businesses smart meters and a consumption-analytics app, backed by angels from Rappi, NotCo and Frubana.
With more than 1,500 business customers in retail, services and manufacturing, Bia raises a US$16.5 million Series A led by Kaszek to expand in Latin America and add features.

Reports more than 3,000 business customers (Coca-Cola Femsa, Falabella), 140 employees and over US$8 million of monthly revenue, with US$31 million raised in equity and up to US$20 million in debt lines.
Adds climate-specialised investors RA Capital Planetary Health and IDB Lab in an US$8.5 million bridge ahead of a Series B.

Reorganises as a group of three units (energy retail, distributed generation and the Olibia software spin-off) after an US$18.5 million round led by Kaszek, with over 4,000 business customers and about 50 GWh a month.

Plans to open a free market-intelligence platform (hydrology, spot prices, costs, news) to the whole industry at the Andesco congress, and to lead a working group with the Colombian government on innovation.

description.value: Brazilian fintech that gives manufacturers a co-branded Pix virtual card and an AI credit assistant so their small retail customers can buy in instalments while the manufacturer is paid upfront and Robbin carries the risk.

long_description.value: Robbin is a Brazilian fintech that lets manufacturers and distributors sell on credit to their small retail customers without carrying the credit risk. A large industry offers its retailers a co-branded virtual card (it sits in a digital wallet app and runs on Pix instead of the Visa or Mastercard networks); the retailer buys in instalments from the industry's suppliers and earns points (convertible into discounts on future purchases or Livelo points), and the industry receives the money upfront while Robbin takes over the collection. Robbin builds and runs the whole credit journey: customer onboarding with automatic validation and fraud detection, credit intelligence and limits, risk management and capital. Its AI sales assistant, Robbinson, runs on WhatsApp, the channel the sales team already uses, and approves credit in real time during the sales conversation (the site claims decisions in 30 seconds instead of two weeks, and that a network buys 73% more; these are company claims). It sells to textile, construction materials, electronics, auto parts, food, pharma, household goods, telecom and marketplace players, and also offers its AI agents (KYC and anti-money-laundering checks in about 20 seconds, credit, monitoring and collection) to banks, insurers and asset managers. It was founded in 2023 (about two and a half years before May 2026) by Leonardo Moura (CEO; about 15 years at XP, where he built the international debt-capital-markets franchise, and at Itaú BBA in London and New York), Henrique Meyer (COO; Itaú BBA, Citi and HSBC debt markets) and Tomás Corrêa (CTO; co-founder and CTO of OpenCo, the digital lender formed by the merger of Geru and Rebel with SoftBank backing, where he led technology for almost ten years). The founders' thesis is that retailers got modern card and instalment experiences while the link between industry and retail was left with short, rigid terms and badly calibrated limits. In May 2026 it announced its first institutional round, a US$8 million seed co-led by Canary, Atlântico and Caravela, with AB Seed, Norte Ventures, Clocktower and Tomorrow Capital, plus a US$100 million receivables fund (FIDC) structured with Augme, the XP manager, to fund the credit it extends (it plans to deploy all of it by the end of 2027). Until then its funding was bilateral lines from banks, which had financed about R$200 million of credit since inception. It had eight partner industries (Cantu Pneus, Chilli Beans, Baterias Moura, Malwee, Brinox, Votorantim, Tigre and Gerdau's Juntos Somos Mais marketplace among them), a potential base of more than 300,000 small and mid-sized businesses linked to them, a target of 50 industries by the end of 2026, and a default rate it says is below the 5.5% Brazilian-central-bank SME average. It targets industries with annual revenue above R$500 million.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: a manufacturer selling to thousands of small retailers has to decide, for each one, whether to give credit, how much and for how long. Short, rigid terms and badly calibrated limits cap its sales, and the retailer has no access to the instalment and benefits experience a consumer gets. Banks serve these small companies badly, and the industry carries the credit risk and the collection effort on its balance sheet. Logic and why now: Pix gives a cheap real-time payment rail, so a card-like product does not need card networks; AI agents make onboarding, fraud checks, limit setting and collection cheap enough for small tickets; and a receivables fund (FIDC) lets the company fund credit without using its own equity. The industry gets cash upfront, the retailer gets terms, and Robbin earns on the transaction and the credit spread. Market size: no published figure for B2B trade credit in Brazil was found (search results gave only default statistics). Our bottom-up estimate: the company says its eight partner industries give access to more than 300,000 small and mid-sized businesses. If each bought R$50-150 thousand a year on instalment terms (our assumption), that is R$15-45 billion of annual purchases from only the current partners; at an assumed 2-4% revenue per real financed (fees and credit spread), the revenue pool is R$0.3-1.8 billion a year from them alone. With 50 industries (the company's end-2026 goal) the pool could be several times that. A strong outcome of, say, 10-20% of such a pool would be several hundred million reais of revenue. What is different: it combines a co-branded Pix card owned by each industry, AI agents in WhatsApp and a fund that carries the risk, run by founders from debt capital markets and from a digital lender. Comparables (SME trade-credit fintechs and card issuers) were not researched. Fit with Norte (our reading): obsessed, experienced founders at the earliest institutional stage, with credit and technology experience, which matches a follower role in a seed led by Canary, Atlântico and Caravela; Norte's network of operators and industry executives can open doors to large manufacturers, the customers the model depends on. Risks: credit losses and funding cost if the portfolio grows faster than risk models learn (a thin loss history, a young company); dependence on a few large industries; competition from banks and trade-credit fintechs; and the need for repeated FIDC capacity.

sub_sector.value: B2B trade credit for industry and retail

milestones.value: Robbin is founded in São Paulo by Leonardo Moura, Henrique Meyer and Tomás Corrêa to modernise credit between manufacturers and their retail customers.
Launches Robbinson, an AI assistant for industry sales teams that approves credit in real time on WhatsApp.
Announces its first institutional round, a US$8 million seed, and a US$100 million FIDC with Augme (XP), eight partner industries and a goal of 50 by year-end.

description.value: Brazilian technology-skills school that began as an income-share developer bootcamp and now sells AI courses, workshops and corporate training, including a programme for lawyers with OAB state sections.

long_description.value: Trybe is a Brazilian school for technology skills that began by training software developers and is now centred on teaching artificial intelligence at work. In its first form, a developer course of about 12 months (later also mobile, data science, cybersecurity and data engineering) could be paid only after the graduate got a job above a salary floor: the student paid up to 17% of the salary, over up to five years, for a total of R$36,000 (the company calls it the shared-success model, MSC; the press calls it an income share agreement, ISA). Trybe made money from those instalments and from deals with employers who hired graduates; 94% of graduates were working within 30 days of graduating (company claim, 2021). It built a financing arm, Trybe SCD, authorised by the Central Bank as a direct credit company in May 2021, and raised a R$50 million receivables fund (FIDC) in March 2021 to fund the ISA. It was founded in August 2019 by five partners who earlier built AppProva, an education-data startup with 5 million students that was sold to Somos Educação: Matheus Goyas (CEO), Cláudio Lensing, João Daniel Duarte, Marcos Moura and Rafael Torres. Six months after opening it raised a R$42 million Series A led by Atlantico (about US$10 million), with Norte among the investors, then a US$6 million extension led by Base Partners in January 2021, the acquisition of the Santa Catarina software house Jungle Devs in June 2021 and a R$145 million (US$27 million) Series B in October 2021 led by Base Partners and Untitled, at a valuation of about R$1.3 billion. By then it had 2,200 students, 130 partner companies (CI&T, Ford, Localiza, Méliuz, Thoughtworks, XP), more than 190,000 applications and students in eight countries besides Brazil. When tech hiring turned in 2022, Trybe cut 47 people (about 10% of nearly 500) in August 2022 and 128 people (about 35% of staff) in June 2023, saying it aimed at breakeven within 180 days; it launched an intensive live course (FIT) and a free JavaScript course for 2,000 people to bring in students. Its public site today sells AI courses, workshops and training for companies and for lawyers: it says more than 1,000 companies have developed their teams with it, that it is the AI-training partner of 16 OAB state sections, and that its AI-literacy programme for law, run with the OAB sections, Jusbrasil and ITS Rio, has had more than 100,000 professionals. The date of the move to AI training is not given in the sources read; no round after 2021 was found.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil's tech sector cannot find enough trained people: Brasscom projected demand of 797,000 professionals from 2021 to 2025 against 53,000 graduates a year in technology courses, a gap of 106,000 a year (Convergência Digital, December 2021). Many candidates cannot pay for a bootcamp up front. Now a second gap has opened, in using AI at work: employees and professional groups such as lawyers need practical training at speed, because the tools change weekly. Logic and why now: the income-share model aligns the school with the student's job outcome and made it attractive to investors in 2020-21, when hiring was strong; the 2022-23 downturn showed its weakness (graduates take longer to place, financing needs are large). The new AI-training line moves to a lighter model (subscriptions, workshops, corporate training) that sells to employers and professional associations with a distribution channel, the OAB, and does not carry student credit. Market size: we found no published figure for the market of corporate AI training in Brazil. Our bottom-up estimate for lawyers: Brazil has on the order of one million registered lawyers (our assumption, not read), so an annual subscription of R$1,000-2,000 (assumption) would give a pool of R$1-2 billion; a 5-10% share is R$50-200 million. For company training, the company says it has served over 1,000 companies; at R$30,000-100,000 per contract (assumption) and 300-500 contracts a year, revenue would be R$10-50 million. These are our assumptions only. What is different: it has a large Brazilian base of developers' alumni and employer relationships, a brand known by 190,000 applicants, and an association channel (OAB) that lowers the cost of acquiring customers; it also has experience of running credit for students. Fit with Norte (our reading): Norte invested at the Series A when the founders were second-time entrepreneurs with a sold company (AppProva) and a clear talent-supply problem; Norte's network of operators who hire developers fits the early distribution need. Risks: the 2023 layoffs show a dependence on tech hiring; the AI-training market is crowded (universities, platforms, vendors) and low-priced; the pivot is recent and little is published on its revenue; the finance arm's loan book from 2020-22 may still weigh on results.

sub_sector.value: Tech and AI skills training (income share)

milestones.value: Trybe opens in Belo Horizonte as a school for full-stack developers where students pay only after getting a job, founded by five partners who built AppProva, an education-data startup sold to Somos Educação.
Raises a R$42 million Series A led by Atlantico six months after launch, planning nine more classes and 3,000 students within a year.
Closes a R$50 million receivables fund (FIDC) to finance student instalments, and in May gets Central Bank authorisation to operate as a direct credit company (Trybe SCD).
Buys 100% of the software house Jungle Devs (Santa Catarina, 80 staff, 75% international clients) to give graduates a first job and connect with investors.
Raises a R$145 million Series B at about R$1.3 billion valuation, with 2,200 students, 130 partner companies and 190,000 applications, and plans courses in mobile, data science and cybersecurity.
Cuts 47 people (about 10% of nearly 500) as the tech hiring market cools.
Cuts 128 people (about 35% of staff), its second layoff in under a year, and says it aims at breakeven within 180 days.
Offers AI courses and workshops, with a training programme for lawyers as partner of 16 OAB state sections and more than 1,000 company clients.

description.value: Brazilian payment orchestrator for physical stores: one integration connects a shop's point-of-sale software to every acquirer and Pix provider and routes each transaction by lowest cost.

long_description.value: Destaxa is a Brazilian payments company that sits between a shop's point-of-sale (PDV) software and the card machines and payment processors, so one integration lets a retailer use any acquirer or Pix provider and route each transaction through the cheapest option. It describes itself as the first payment orchestrator for physical (offline) merchants and says it will never be a payment processor, only infrastructure, which keeps it neutral between acquirers. Its customers are the software houses and commercial-automation vendors that build PDV systems (it was connected to about 130 of them in 2024, with nearly 150,000 PDV clients, of which fewer than 5,000 were Destaxa's), and through them the merchants, with monthly revenue of R$100,000 to R$1 million. Products on its site: a TEF (card-payment integration) and an advanced version, the DTX+ web platform to set parameters for every client in real time, a card-and-Pix integration for Android smart terminals (it bets on the 'androidisation' of the PDV market, where each acquirer's Android machine forces vendors to maintain a separate integration), an 'Oferta Inteligente' programme that lets automation vendors earn a share of their clients' card transactions, receivables advance (the cheapest working capital a merchant has) and a partnership to sell energy directly from the producer with savings of up to 30%. Earlier it sold a merchant-side dashboard with reconciliation of cards and banks, fee audits and cash-flow automation. It was founded in 2021 by Felipe Ayres, a third-time entrepreneur (he earlier created the asset manager F3 Capital and the sub-acquirer Nexu), together with businessman Sigvard Von Baranow Neto. Ayres got the idea of orchestration after a trip to India to study UPI, where he met a former sub-acquirer who had moved to orchestration. Growth in new clients per month went from 5-20 in 2022 to 50-100 in 2023 and 300-500 in 2024, with a target of 5,000 a month by mid-2025. Processing reached more than R$2 billion a year at the end of 2023 and about R$4 billion a year in mid-2024; in June 2024 it was testing its platform as infrastructure for acquirers (one in test, one in talks). Backers named in the press are Quona Capital (lead of the 2022 seed), Caravela, Norte Ventures, the angels Tiago Dalvi (Olist) and Alessio Alionço (Pipefy), and, in the November 2023 R$30 million round, Astella (lead), Supera, Quona, Caravela and Endeavor ScaleUp Ventures. The CEO said in June 2024 that a Series A was planned for early 2025; the sources read do not show that it happened, and no later news was found.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: a small merchant sells with many card machines and contracts, does not know which acquirer is cheapest for each transaction, and cannot easily renegotiate. The software house that makes its point-of-sale system must build and maintain a separate integration for each acquirer, a growing burden as Android terminals multiply. Logic and why now: Pix and the open card market gave merchants choice, and Android machines made it possible to run one payment app on any acquirer's terminal. An orchestrator that is neutral and cheap to integrate can give the software house new revenue (a share of each transaction) and the merchant the lowest-cost route per transaction. Market size: Abecs reports R$4.5 trillion of card volume in Brazil in 2025 (Finsiders, read), with online purchases above R$1 trillion, leaving roughly R$3.4 trillion in physical stores (our subtraction: 4.5 - 1.0 and a little). Destaxa processes about R$4 billion a year (2024, company), about 0.1% of the in-store volume. If it reached 5% of in-store volume (about R$170 billion) and kept a net take of 0.05-0.15% of volume (our assumption: a fraction of the spread it helps save, shared with the PDV vendor), revenue would be R$85-255 million. A strong outcome is therefore in the low hundreds of millions of reais of revenue. What is different: neutrality (never a processor), integration with about 130 PDV vendors (distribution, not direct sales), and a revenue share for the vendor. Online orchestrators (Yuno, Malga, PoolPay) and the offline player Shipay are named as comparables by Finsiders. Fit with Norte (our reading): a serial founder with a payments background and an infrastructure-style product, at the seed stage with Quona and Caravela leading; Norte joined as follower in 2022 and can help with introductions to PDV vendors, acquirers and later funds. Risks: acquirers may cut costs for vendors directly or build their own multi-acquirer terminals; low take rate per transaction; concentration in the PDV vendors' channel; and no published sign of growth or a Series A since mid-2024.

milestones.value: Destaxa is founded in São Paulo by Felipe Ayres, a third-time entrepreneur, to give small retailers a single platform that connects their point of sale to any card acquirer.
Raises a seed led by Quona Capital, with Caravela, Norte Ventures and angels from Olist and Pipefy; it adds 5-20 clients a month.

Raises R$30 million led by Astella to build machine-learning routing and support Android terminals, after reaching more than R$2 billion a year processed, 130 PDV integrations and about 3,500 merchants.
Reaches about R$4 billion a year processed, adds 300-500 clients a month and starts testing its platform as infrastructure for acquirers, with a second acquirer in talks.

description.value: AI sales agents on WhatsApp that answer, qualify and book the leads generated by a company's ads, tie each sale back to the ad that started it and charge per qualified meeting.

long_description.value: Patagon AI sells AI agents that talk to the people who answer a company's ads. A lead who clicks an ad on Meta or another channel lands in a WhatsApp conversation instead of a web form; the agent replies in under a minute, at any hour, holds an open conversation (the buyer can ask anything or send audio, unlike a chatbot built as a decision tree), qualifies the lead by the client's own rules, books the meeting or showroom visit with a human seller and keeps following up until the person answers or opts out. The second layer is attribution: it captures the ad click and campaign data at first touch, ties it to every conversation and sends the outcome (qualified, booked, sold) back to the ad platforms and the CRM as an offline conversion, so the client sees which ad brought which buyer and campaigns optimise for buyers instead of clicks. Its site now also offers to run the ads themselves, as an end-to-end marketing service for sectors such as automotive, education, finance, real estate, insurance, retail, health, telecoms and travel, and integrates with Salesforce, Meta and Microsoft tools. It makes money on results rather than seats: the client pays a fixed fee when a conversation ends in a meeting with a human seller (about R$50 in Brazil as of November 2025), on top of a setup fee of about R$10,000 and a minimum monthly fee that suited large companies but kept small ones out. The company promises about 30% more qualified leads. A Mitsubishi operation in Ecuador is the showcase: 35% more sales with a 20% smaller marketing budget, as told by the company. The company was founded in 2023 in Argentina by four people, two Ecuadorians and two Argentines: David Grandes (CEO), Mariano Rey (CMO), Cristian Adamo (CTO) and Roberto Guerrero (CRO). Grandes had co-founded ZAK, a Brazilian restaurant-software startup backed by Tiger Global and Monashees that was later shut down, and had worked at OLX and Restorando; Rey says the product is what he needed as head of marketing at Botmaker and head of growth at NaranjaX. Traction: a US$1.1 million pre-seed in late 2024 (OneVC and 17Sigma) paid for the Colombian launch; the company aimed at US$130,000 of annual recurring revenue at the end of 2024 and reported US$1 million in October 2025. It entered Brazil in April 2025, which became its second market by revenue after Ecuador; by November 2025 it had more than 100 clients in 12 to 15 countries (30 in Brazil, among them Pluxee, with banks and tech unicorns in implementation, a process of three to six months) and a team of about 25 in Argentina and Brazil. In November 2025 it raised R$15 million (about US$2.7 million) led by Kfund, with all earlier investors including Norte Ventures following, to build a self-onboarding product that lets small companies start without a sales process. Its target for 2025 was about US$2 million in revenue.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: companies that buy ads to generate leads lose most of the value between the click and the sale. A form is answered hours later by an overloaded team, nobody can tell good leads from noise, and the ad budget cannot be tied to sales. In Latin America the natural channel is WhatsApp, and the usual answer, a chatbot built as a decision tree, is rigid. Logic and why now: language models make an open conversation possible at a cost that lets the company charge per qualified meeting instead of per seat, and WhatsApp is the default channel for consumer-to-business talk in the region (Kfund cites hundreds of millions of users). Linking each conversation to the ad click and sending the result back to the ad platform closes the loop that marketing teams lack, so the product sells ROI, not software. Market: no published market size for AI sales agents on WhatsApp in Latin America was found. A bottom-up estimate: Brazil Journal gives a price of about R$50 per qualified conversation. If 5,000 mid-sized and large advertisers in the region (our assumption) each generated 2,000 qualified conversations a year (assumption), the revenue pool is about R$500 million (US$90 million) a year; at 20,000 advertisers and 3,000 conversations it is about R$3 billion. A realistic strong outcome is a 5-10% share, or tens of millions of dollars of revenue, far above the US$1 million ARR of October 2025. What is different: pay-for-outcome pricing, attribution built into the agent, and a regional focus (bilingual agents, local messaging habits, teams in Argentina and Brazil). Competitors named in the press are chatbot vendors such as Blip, which is adding AI layers; global conversation platforms were not researched. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): obsessed, experienced founders, one of them a repeat founder with Brazilian experience; Norte joined as a follower in a round led by a European fund, and its network of Brazilian operators can open large Brazilian accounts, where the company has 30 clients and its largest implementation backlog. Risks: low switching costs and fast-moving model vendors; dependence on Meta's WhatsApp policies and prices; a pay-per-meeting model that exposes the company to the client's lead quality; and revenue concentration in Ecuador and a few big clients.

milestones.value: Patagon AI is founded in Argentina by two Ecuadorians and two Argentines to sell AI agents that turn marketing leads into sales conversations.
Closes a US$1.1 million pre-seed led by OneVC and 17Sigma and opens operations in Colombia with a local team, with a roadshow planned for Ecuador, Mexico, Brazil and Argentina.
Starts selling in Brazil, which becomes its second market by revenue within seven months and reaches about 30 clients, with banks and tech unicorns in a three-to-six-month implementation.
Reaches about US$1 million in annualised recurring revenue, against a year-end 2024 target of US$130,000.
Announces a self-onboarding product, to be shown on 12 November at a summit in Mexico City, so small companies can build WhatsApp agent flows in minutes without the setup fee and monthly minimum.
Passes 100 clients in 12 to 15 countries, among them Pluxee in Chile and Brazil and Mitsubishi in Ecuador, with a team of about 25 in Argentina and Brazil.
Adds an Attribution product, which shows which channel and ad drive qualified chats, and widens its offer to running the client's ads end to end.

description.value: Brazilian private B2B marketplace where large brands sell surplus inventory to vetted small and mid-sized retailers, with AI matching and pricing and a 12% take rate.

long_description.value: BackChannel is a private B2B marketplace in Brazil where large brands sell their excess inventory to vetted small and mid-sized retailers. A brand lists a lot, sets the rules for who may buy it (for example, only offline stores far from big cities, so the cheap stock does not undercut its own online collection), and the platform matches the lot with buyers that fit, using AI for matching and dynamic pricing. The buyer sees a chat-style interface in which they describe their business and receive recommended lots.
