BackChannel does not hold or manage the goods; it earns a take rate of about 10% to 12% of each transaction (12% in March 2026), with an average ticket of about R$50,000, plus a logistics fee paid by the buyer in the first model. It was started by two Argentines, Guillermo Freire (CEO) and Guillermo Arslanian, who had founded Trocafone ten years earlier, a used-phone e-commerce that reached about R$400 million of yearly revenue in Brazil. Working with Apple, Samsung and Motorola, they saw how every new model left old stock in the channel, creating channel conflict and cash tied up in inventory; they found no Brazilian solution but found Ghost, a US private marketplace for brand overstock, and adapted the model to Latin America. They left the day-to-day of Trocafone (where they remain partners) in 2024 to start it. The founders say the company was built with AI from the start: the platform was built in two months, and by March 2026 it had a team of about 40 and eight AI agents handling prospecting, emails and onboarding. Traction: a R$17 million pre-seed in October 2024, led by Cathay Latam (an investor in Ghost), financed the first product. By June 2025 it had 30 brand sellers, more than 1.5 million items listed and 50 vetted buyers. It closed 2025, its first full year, with about R$25 million of gross merchandise value (GMV), growing about 30% a month according to the company; by March 2026 it reported about 100 large brands and 18,000 retailer buyers (a smaller figure of over 1,000 active buyers appears in the funding release). Fashion and footwear came first, because the ten largest fashion brands hold most of the market and R$30 to 40 million each in idle stock; cosmetics followed. In March 2026 it raised a R$25 million seed led by Sunna Ventures with nine other funds including Norte Ventures. The plan is to speed up the onboarding of sellers and buyers with agents, add categories such as beauty, personal care, electronics and food, import surplus from China, the US and Europe, and launch embedded finance (buy-now-pay-later and payment terms) for retailers. The company aims at R$150 million of GMV in 2026 and R$1 billion within three years.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: brands that launch new collections or models are left with millions of reais of unsold stock. It ties up cash, loses value each month and, if sold in the usual way, leaks into the brand's own online channel or ends up in informal markets such as Brás with no control over where it goes. Small retailers, on the other side, cannot buy branded goods at good prices and often lack credit to do so. Logic and why now: a private marketplace lets the brand set who can buy and where, which protects its prices, while AI handles matching, pricing and the prospecting that once needed a large sales team (the founders say the platform was built in two months, against six months and twice the staff at Trocafone). The same founders already ran a large two-sided marketplace in Brazil, so they know how to find liquidity on both sides. Market: Freire puts the addressable market at US$9 billion in Brazil (company claim, Brazil Journal) and US$8-9 billion in the first verticals (Startups.com.br); an independent figure is Abrappe's survey of retail losses, R$35 billion in 2023 and a forecast R$36.5 billion in 2025, quoted in a Startups.com.br opinion article (read; not all of it is overstock). Our own check: if 100 brands each place R$30 million of stock a year through the platform (assumption), GMV is R$3 billion and a 12% take rate yields about R$360 million of revenue; the company's own goal of R$1 billion of GMV would give about R$120 million. What is different: it is the first, as far as the founders found, to bring the Ghost model to Brazil, it controls the channel through rules set by the seller, and it plans to add credit for the small buyer, which would raise the take per transaction. Ghost (about US$100 million raised, Startups.com.br) is a foreign comparable, not a competitor in Brazil. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): repeat founders who already built a marketplace and have the network that Norte values; Norte entered at the pre-seed and followed in the seed, a follower role next to funds such as Cathay Latam and Sunna. Risks: liquidity on both sides of a marketplace, brands going direct or to rival liquidators, a lumpy GMV that depends on a few large sellers, the credit product exposing the company to default, and results that are the company's own figures from a business only a year and a half old.

milestones.value: Guillermo Freire and Guillermo Arslanian, who built Trocafone into Brazil's largest used-phone e-commerce, leave its day-to-day to start BackChannel, a private marketplace for brand overstock based on the US company Ghost.
Completes its first full year of operation with about R$25 million in GMV, focused on fashion and cosmetics, with growth of about 30% a month.
Has 30 large brands listed as sellers, more than 1.5 million products and 50 retailers admitted after screening, earning a 10% to 12% take rate on each sale.

Reports about 100 large brands selling and 18,000 retailer buyers, more than 2 million items listed (about R$200 million of stock), a team of 40 and eight AI agents that handle prospecting, emails and onboarding.

Plans to move beyond fashion into beauty, personal care, electronics and food, import surplus from China, the US and Europe, and add buy-now-pay-later credit for retailers, with a GMV target of R$150 million in 2026.

description.value: Curitiba legal-tech company that sells software and AI to digital labor-law firms, to manage case flow, generate client demand and settle cases faster.

long_description.value: Igual is a legal-technology company from Curitiba that builds software for digital law firms working on labor law (trabalhista) that aims to bring labor law to the people who need it most. Its site says it uses technology and AI so that lawyers can serve more people better, and describes three layers: legal software that runs a firm's case flow end to end, AI applied across the legal journey to automate repetitive tasks and speed up decisions while keeping a human lawyer in the loop, and tools that let a firm generate qualified demand, offer end-to-end service and use a settlement (conciliation) framework meant to shorten the life cycle of a case. Stanford's CodeX TechIndex classifies it as matter-management software for litigation, sold to law firms on a subscription, and says small operational teams can coordinate large volumes of lawsuits with it. The company was founded in 2024 and is based in Curitiba; its job posts as of November 2026 (a commercial analyst, a systems analyst working with Python and Odoo, an infrastructure analyst) show a team that is still building its commercial and internal systems. Investor directories list Norte Ventures in a 2024 pre-seed and a later seed of about US$2 million with BFF Ventures, Honey Island Capital, 1616 Ventures and 4UM Investments, but no article or company page that was readable states these rounds, so none is recorded. The founders are three people from Curitiba's technology scene (their LinkedIn profiles, read through Linked API in November 2026): André Boaventura, co-founder and CEO, who was EBANX's chief marketing officer until 2022; Ariel Patschiki, co-founder and CTO, who was EBANX's chief product officer until 2023 after a decade in its product teams; and the lawyer Jacqueline Jianoti, co-founder, who came from the legal and institutional-relations side of the accounting platform Contabilizei and still runs her own law practice. Their profiles date their work at Igual from January to March 2024. No customers, revenue or volume figures were found in readable public sources, so this profile stays short.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: workers with modest incomes often have valid labor claims but are not served by traditional firms, which find small cases unprofitable; digital labor-law firms try to serve them at volume but are short of tools to manage thousands of cases, to find clients and to settle quickly. Logic: software that handles case flow, AI that drafts and triages, and a conciliation framework that shortens the cycle can lower the cost per case so that a small team can handle large volumes. Market: no published figure for the market of software for labor-law firms was found. Our rough bound: Brazilian labor courts receive on the order of millions of new cases a year (not verified here, a figure to check against the TST's statistics); if even 5,000 firms paid R$2,000 a month (assumption) the software pool would be about R$120 million a year, and revenue shared on settlements could be larger. The company's own numbers are not public. What is different: it targets the digital, volume-based firm and not the traditional office, and it joins software with demand generation and settlement. Competitors in legal software (EasyJur, Jusfy, Leggal and others appeared in searches) were not compared. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): the founders are two former EBANX executives (a chief marketing officer and a chief product officer) and a lawyer from Contabilizei, so the team combines product, go-to-market and legal expertise in the exact sector; the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed, high-quality founders and brings the right people and funds at the right time, which is how we read the fit, while no readable source says why Norte invested or in which round. Risks: thin public evidence on customers and traction, dependence on a single legal area, regulatory and bar-association limits on how lawyers may advertise and be organised, and the competition of general legal-management software.

milestones.value: Igual is founded in Curitiba to build technology for digital labor-law firms.

description.value: Brazilian insurer (Susep-authorised) that designs and underwrites embedded insurance for fintechs, lenders, retailers and platforms, connected by one API.

long_description.value: 180° Insurance (180 Seguros) is a Brazilian insurance company, authorised by Susep, that builds and underwrites insurance products for other companies to sell inside their own customer journeys. A fintech, digital bank, lender, retailer, real-estate platform or cooperative connects through a single API, and 180 designs the product with it (white label or co-branded), runs issuance, claims and commission splits automatically, and gives the partner a hub with metrics, quotes, policies and claims. The partner earns a commission and a recurring revenue line, 180 earns a fee on each policy sold (its early description was a success fee) and, as it became a carrier, the underwriting result. Its largest product today is credit-life (prestamista) insurance sold with loans, followed by life, Pix and extended-warranty cover, home, business and personal-accident policies; a phone-insurance product was next in 2025. Partners named in the press include Loft, Caju, Buser, Zul+, Mottu, iClinic, Pipo Saúde, DMCard, CredPago, Solfácil and QI Tech. It was founded in October 2020 in São Paulo by two Nubank alumni, Mauro Levi D'Ancona (CEO, who ran fundraising and investor relations at Nubank) and Franco Lamping (a software engineer, later CTO), with Alex Körner, an insurance executive from Mapfre and Santander, who has since left to found Dobbra.ai. They saw that Brazilian insurance was little digital and little penetrated, that Susep had opened a regulatory innovation agenda, and that insurance could be sold at the moment of purchase. It reached the market in April 2021 with a R$44 million seed, the largest for insurance in Latin America at the time and the first seed in Brazil for Dragoneer and Rainfall. Traction: at the end of 2021 it had eight clients; in February 2022, nine products across eight channels and 50 employees, including an hourly R$0.49 cover for items left in cars sold with the Zul+ blue-zone parking app, called the first intermittent insurance in Latin America. The R$177 million Series A of February 2022 financed hiring (to about 110) and joint ventures with large partners. Growth later was fast: annualised revenue of about R$100 million in December 2024, R$384 million in May 2025 and a run rate of R$348 million to R$500 million expected at the end of 2025, with growth of about 500% in 2025, according to the company. More than 80% of claims are analysed and settled by its own models. In September 2025 it raised R$50 million in a pre-Series B (R$35 million of equity and R$15 million of subordinated debt that counts toward Susep's regulatory capital) at a valuation of R$1.35 billion, and in October 2025 Vivo Ventures added US$2.5 million to build insurance products for Vivo's customers. Next, the company is building an AI vertical: a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server through which partners' AI agents quote, sell and service policies with no custom integration (it announced a partnership with Klubi's agent). The CEO said he wanted a Series B of at least US$50 million in the first half of 2026; none was found by November 2026.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilian insurance has low penetration and sells through brokers and branches. Banks, fintechs, retailers and platforms that own the customer relationship and the purchase moment do not have insurance products designed for their journey, nor the licence, the actuarial and claims machinery and the integrations with insurers. Logic and why now: embedded insurance sold at checkout converts better and costs less to acquire, Pix and open-finance rails put more digital credit and payments in the hands of platforms, and Susep's regulatory sandbox and innovation agenda let a technology company become a carrier. 180 sells to partners that already have the customers, shares commission with them and, as it grew, took the risk itself. Market: the company says Brazilian insurance premiums were R$303 billion in 2021 (Bloomberg Línea, citing 180) and the CEO said the market should be twice its size (NeoFeed, 2022). The segment it addresses, mass-market insurance sold with loans, cards and purchases, is a part of that figure. A realistic share: with a revenue run rate around R$350 to 500 million in 2025, 1% of a premium pool of R$300 billion would already be R$3 billion; our assumption is that a leading embedded carrier could reach 1-2% of premiums in the long run, which means R$3-6 billion, an order of magnitude above today's size. What is different: it is a carrier plus a technology platform, with product design per partner; the CEO says no other startup competes in the mass segment, with Pier, Justo and Darwin focused on auto through brokers (Brazil Journal, 2025); incumbents such as Mapfre, Zurich and Tokio Marine are the real competitors. Comparables abroad (Cover Genius, Bolttech) were not researched. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): Norte took part in the seed and the Series A, behind funds such as Canary, Dragoneer, Rainfall and 8VC; the founders are alumni of the Nubank network, and their ability to bring top funds to the cap table is the kind of connection Norte describes. Risks: it now holds underwriting and regulatory capital risk, with a steep growth curve that needs more capital (the planned Series B had not been found); concentration in credit-linked life insurance and a few large partners; loss ratios on fast-growing books; and regulatory change on credit-linked insurance.

milestones.value: Mauro Levi D'Ancona and Franco Lamping, from Nubank, and Alex Körner, from Mapfre and Santander, found 180° Seguros in São Paulo to sell embedded insurance integrated into the purchase journey of other companies.
Closes its first year with eight active clients, among them Caju, Loft and Zul+, and launches products in several channels.
Reaches the market with 17 insurers behind it and 20 projects with real-estate, finance and retail companies, funded by a R$44 million seed announced in May.

Has nine products in eight channels, 27 insurers, 50 employees and clients such as Loft, Caju, Buser and Mottu, including the R$0.49 hourly cover for car belongings sold with Zul+, which it calls the first intermittent insurance in Latin America.

Reaches about R$100 million of annualised revenue, which rises to R$384 million by May 2025 as credit-life, life, Pix and warranty products grow with partners such as DMCard, CredPago, Solfácil and QI Tech.

Announces a pre-Series B at a R$1.35 billion valuation, with R$15 million of subordinated debt to build Susep regulatory capital and an AI vertical, as more than 80% of claims are already analysed by its own models.

Vivo Ventures invests US$2.5 million so that Vivo and 180 build insurance products together, and the company develops an MCP server so partners' AI agents can quote and sell policies without custom integrations.

description.value: Online school for tech and AI careers across Latin America that began with no-upfront-cost bootcamps (pay after getting a job) and now also sells AI talent and training to companies.

long_description.value: Henry (HENRY, short for "high earner, not rich yet") is an online school that trains Latin Americans to work in technology and connects them with employers. Its original offer, launched in March 2020, was a full-time bootcamp of about four months (or eight months part time) in full-stack development and data science, with no upfront cost: the student paid only after getting a job, through an income-share agreement of 15% of salary for two years capped at US$4,000. The company says most graduates find a tech job within six months and multiply their previous pay several times. Today the site sells AI-focused careers (Full Stack + AI, AI engineering, AI automation, data science and a new part-time Forward Deployed Engineer programme) with payment plans, and a business side: AI Talent (hiring graduates with no intermediary fees), AI Training for company teams, Henry Projects (graduates work on a client's backlog at no cost), live sessions and Henry Data, an educational analytics offer. The idea came to Martín Borchardt, an Argentine serial entrepreneur, after he saw half of his developers at the payments startup Nubi resign for dollar-paying jobs in 2018, when the peso collapsed. After a first attempt at student loans for existing academies failed with devaluation, he designed a school that trains people from zero and shares the risk. He founded Henry with his sister Luz Borchardt (acquisition) and with Leonardo Maglia, Federico Hernández and Manuel Barna, started in the Summer 2020 batch of Y Combinator (after being turned down in 2018), and has run the company as a remote-first team with no offices. Traction: 800 students by December 2020, with 200 graduates and 600 students in Colombia, Chile, Uruguay and Argentina by the end of that year, and about 30% of students in Colombia in January 2021. A US$1.5 million seed (December 2020) was followed by a US$10 million Series A in May 2022 led by Kayyak Ventures and Seaya Cathay Latam. By then it had 2,500 graduates, 5,000 students in training, 25,000 applications a month, 1,500 employers, about 105 staff and a target of 100,000 trained developers and breakeven in 2023. The YC page lists a team of about 100. Students come from Argentina (50%), Colombia (25%) and Mexico (15%), with Mexico and Colombia the priority markets. The 2025 target of 100,000 graduates was not reported as met, and no revenue figures after 2022 were found.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Latin American companies, and the remote employers who hire there, cannot find enough software and AI talent, while millions of people who could do those jobs cannot pay for training or lack a route to a first job; traditional universities teach slowly and bootcamps charged upfront fees that excluded most. Accion's 2020 release said, from Henry's own estimate, more than a million engineering vacancies in the region against fewer than 100,000 trained professionals. Logic and why now: an income-share model aligns the school with the outcome (it only earns if the graduate gets paid), remote work and the dollar-paying demand of foreign employers created high wages for graduates, and online cohorts have almost no marginal cost. The AI wave moved the offer to AI engineering and a business side that sells talent and training to companies. Market: no independent market size for LatAm tech bootcamps was read. Bottom-up: the company's goal was 100,000 graduates; at a maximum of US$4,000 each that is up to US$400 million of lifetime revenue over several years, and at a realistic 20,000 paying graduates a year and an average of US$2,500 collected (assumptions) the annual pool is about US$50 million; corporate training and hiring fees could add a similar order. A strong outcome would be a leading regional position with tens of millions of dollars of annual revenue. What is different: zero upfront cost and a graduate-pays-later model with no debt, remote cohorts with a career coach and employer network, and a quick pivot to AI careers. Competitors named in the press: Microverse (also YC, ISAs), Platzi, Acamica, Crehana and Protalento (Forbes Colombia). Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): a repeat founder from the Nubi exit with a strong team and a mission of upward mobility; value that a network of operators gives is access to employers and later-stage funds. The sources do not show Norte in any round, so its exact role is not recorded. Risks: income-share economics depend on graduates getting hired and paying, which weakens when tech hiring falls and AI tools lower entry-level demand; ISA financing needs capital; the 2025 goal was missed or not reported; and the company's later revenue and financing were not found.

sub_sector.value: Tech and AI skills training (income share)

milestones.value: Joins the Summer 2020 batch of Y Combinator, after being rejected in 2018, and receives early money from YC, Tim Draper and Mike Santos.
Launches its first bootcamp, a remote course with no upfront cost in which graduates pay 15% of salary for two years up to US$4,000.
Has 200 graduates and 600 students in Colombia, Chile, Uruguay and Argentina and plans to expand to Mexico and teach in Portuguese.
Has 105 graduates working for companies in the US, Mexico, Colombia and Chile and about 5,000 monthly applicants with a 3% acceptance rate, with 30% of students in Colombia.
Reports 2,500 graduates, 5,000 students in training, 25,000 applications a month, 1,500 employers and about 105 staff, and sets a goal of 100,000 trained developers by 2025.
Re-focuses its offer on AI: Full Stack + AI, AI engineering and a Forward Deployed Engineer programme, with AI Talent, AI Training, Henry Projects and Henry Data sold to companies.

description.value: Brazilian HR-tech that digitises occupational health and safety: online booking and tracking of exams, reports and legal programmes, with eSocial filing; acquired by Senior Sistemas in 2026.

long_description.value: Salú is a Brazilian HR-tech company that digitises occupational health and safety, the legal chain of exams and paperwork that every employer must run for its workers. In the traditional process a new hire had to find a clinic, book by phone or email, take the exam in person and bring the result to the employer, while HR acted as go-between and then typed the data into the government system (eSocial). Salú's SaaS platform lets the employee book exams online, tracks the whole life cycle (admission, periodic and dismissal exams, reports, ASOs, risk and medical-control programmes, certificates, leaves, absenteeism, protective equipment) and sends the obligations to eSocial, backed by an operations team and an accredited network of clinics; companies can also hire an on-site doctor or run a corporate clinic managed by Salú. It charges a monthly fee per covered life that varies with the modules used. It was founded in 2020 in São Paulo by René Neme (CEO), André Boff and Ricardo Silveira, with the physician Irineu Massaia. The founders' view in 2022 was that occupational health is a captive, provider-centred market, protected by law, and that Salú had to invert the logic and serve HR; the cheap entry point of exams was meant to become a "one-stop shop" for company health, with a chronic-care tool and a health-plan history viewer already added. Traction: about 100 to 108 clients and more than 30,000 lives by early 2022 (C6, Olist, Loft, Viveo, GetNinjas, RD Station, Warren), a target of 120,000 lives by the end of that year, and a team of about 50. In March 2022 it raised R$12 million, its first and only disclosed round, led by SoftBank's Latin America fund, and in September hired Sergio Cagno as chief medical officer. By 2025 it reported net revenue of R$76.8 million, annual recurring revenue of R$97.2 million, an adjusted EBITDA margin of 20.2%, more than 800 clients in every state (Nubank, XP, QuintoAndar, GPA, C6 Bank, Afya, Ipiranga), more than a million appointments, about 300,000 hours given back to HR teams and about 250 employees; revenue grew 115.5% a year from 2023 to 2025. On 10 June 2026 Senior Sistemas, a Brazilian HR and ERP software group, agreed to buy 100% of Salú for R$318.7 million (about 3.5 times last-12-month revenue of about R$100 million), its largest purchase and its first in health, to add occupational health to its human-capital suite just as the NR-1 rule on workplace risk management comes into force. The deal required approval by the competition authority Cade, and René Neme stays at the helm. The company registry shows Senior's executives as administrators from September 2026, which suggests the deal closed by then.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: every Brazilian employer is legally obliged to run occupational health and safety programmes and exams for each worker, but the market is fragmented, manual and provider-centred: clinics set the rules, HR chases paper and employees lose days. Compliance errors expose companies to fines and lawsuits. Logic and why now: a software layer that books, tracks and files each obligation lowers the cost of compliance, and the rule is mandatory, so demand does not depend on a discretionary budget. Digital eSocial reporting and the arrival of the NR-1 risk-management rule (Senior calls it the trigger) make a unified data trail more valuable. Market: no published market size for Brazilian occupational health was read. Bottom-up, with assumptions: about 45 million formal employees (assumption, to be checked against IBGE) each needing about one exam or programme service a year at an average of R$100-200 (assumption) is a pool of R$4.5-9 billion a year, of which the software and operations margin could be a fraction. The best evidence of value is the market's own: a strategic buyer paid R$318.7 million, about 3.5 times revenue, for a company with R$76.8 million of 2025 revenue and 20% EBITDA margin; the Senior platforms alone manage more than 11 million workers. What is different: it combines software with a service operation, uses occupational health as a low-cost way into the HR budget, and grew above 100% a year while profitable. Competitors in occupational-health software and clinic networks were not researched. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): founders who focused on a mandatory process with a clear buyer and brought SoftBank, Aggir, Tau and health-sector angels to the cap table in the first institutional round, with Norte as a follower; the outcome shows that the follower role can still return capital in a few years. Norte's return on its stake is not public. Risks: price pressure from clinics and large insurers, regulatory change, dependence on the clinic network's quality, and integration under a new owner.

milestones.value: Salú is founded in São Paulo by René Neme, André Boff and Ricardo Silveira, with the physician Irineu Massaia, to digitise the paperwork and exams of occupational health.
Ends its first full year with about 100 clients, more than 30,000 lives in its platform and 50 staff, among them C6 Bank, Olist, Loft, GetNinjas and RD Station.
Hires Sergio Cagno, a doctor with 40 years in occupational health and founder of Bioqualynet (sold to Porto Seguro), as chief medical officer after the first round.
Reports net revenue of R$76.8 million (up 115.5% a year on average over two years), ARR of R$97.2 million and an adjusted EBITDA margin of 20.2%, with more than 800 clients and about 250 employees.

Senior Sistemas agrees to buy Salú for R$318.7 million, about 3.5 times revenue, its largest acquisition and first in health, to add occupational health to its HR suite as the NR-1 rule takes effect; the founders join Senior as executives.

description.value: Software that digitises the operations of private credit in Latin America: asset onboarding, collateral verification, servicing and reporting for lenders and borrowers of asset-backed debt.

long_description.value: Vaas builds the operating software of private credit in Latin America: the back office that lenders, fintech borrowers and servicers use to onboard assets, verify collateral and run a debt facility day to day. A fintech that borrows against a portfolio of loans, devices or receivables normally reports to its lenders in spreadsheets and email, and every facility goes through a queue of manual checks. Vaas replaces that with one platform: a loan-tape mapper that turns a borrower's data into the lender's format, daily document verification with an OCR and AI engine, digital signature, ownership and payment tracking, waiver portals and reporting for originators, lenders, servicers and securitisation vehicles. The company says it began as a direct servicing tool and has become an embedded infrastructure platform, and that it now grows by servicing the assets directly and by tokenising assets. It sells to companies on both sides of the loan, with pricing that the sources do not give. It was founded in 2022 by Valentina Valencia, from Cali, Colombia, who started at PayJoy in 2016 and then worked at Architect Capital, one of the first debt funds to structure credit facilities for Latin American startups, so she saw both borrowers and lenders struggle with structured debt. She raised a US$5 million seed, led by a16z, in February 2023 when the team had 32 people (many from Globant, Mercado Libre and Rappi) and two clients, and says she landed a16z before having a product. Traction as the company tells it: first clients Addi and PayJoy; Goldman Sachs and Architect adopted it as lenders and later named it a verification agent; a first Mexican deal with Clara and Goldman Sachs; digital signature adopted by Bancolombia and Actinver; a waiver portal for CIM; and daily document verification for all clients. It operates in Colombia, Mexico and Chile; its CEO told La República in 2026 that it has 40 clients, works with about 100 institutions, monitors about US$3 billion of assets and earns about 70% of its revenue in Colombia. It won the Latin American final of She Loves Tech in September 2023, and Valencia made Forbes' 30 Under 30 list in 2025. 30N Ventures published why it invested in Vaas, describing it as the operating backbone of asset-backed lending; the size and date of that investment were not found.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: private credit is among the fastest-growing asset classes, yet asset-backed lending in Latin America still runs on spreadsheets, e-mail, notaries (a podcast cites US$500 stamp fees in Mexico) and manual document checks. Fintechs find it hard to borrow debt, lenders cannot see their collateral, and every facility needs bespoke reporting. Logic and why now: as fintechs and non-bank lenders move from equity to debt funding, and global lenders such as Goldman Sachs enter the region, each facility needs a neutral layer that verifies assets, reconciles cash and gives the lender daily visibility. A software layer that sits between borrower and lender is paid per facility or per asset, and gets stickier once it is embedded in the legal process (verification agent, waivers, digital signature). Market: no published market size was read. Bottom-up, with assumptions: if US$20-60 billion of asset-backed and private credit facilities are outstanding in Latin America (assumption) and a platform earns 0.1-0.3% a year on the balances it verifies and services, the revenue pool is about US$20-180 million a year, with more if Mexico and other markets grow. What is different: it was built by a founder who worked on both sides of the facility and was adopted early by a global lender as verification agent, which gives it distribution that purely local competitors lack; Kanastra (Brazil, also in Norte's portfolio) is the closest regional comparable and appeared in the same searches, but the two were not compared. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): a young founder with unusually strong technical depth in the product she sells, which is the kind of founder profile the Manifesto describes. The sources do not place Norte in the seed (the company's own post lists every investor) or in any later round found, so how and when Norte took part is unknown. Risks: a small market in the near term, concentration in a few fintech borrowers and lenders, long enterprise sales and legal cycles, the entry of larger servicers and Brazilian players, and a business model whose pricing and revenue are not public.

milestones.value: Valentina Valencia founds Vaas after working at PayJoy and at Architect Capital, to automate the management of structured debt for fintech borrowers and lenders.
Announces a US$5 million seed led by a16z with a team of 32 and two clients using the product.
Wins the Latin American final of She Loves Tech at the Capital Summit in Cali, earning a place in the global final in Singapore in October.
Valentina Valencia is named to the Forbes 30 Under 30 list.

In an interview the CEO says Vaas has 40 clients, works with about 100 institutions and monitors about US$3 billion of assets in Mexico, Colombia and Chile, with about 70% of revenue from Colombia, and plans to enter the United States and El Salvador.

description.value: US startup whose AI career agent, Lia, matches tech candidates with jobs and makes warm introductions to hiring managers; candidates pay 20% of their first month's salary only if hired and employers use it free.

long_description.value: Refer is a US startup, a public benefit corporation based in Palo Alto, that gives each job seeker an AI career agent called Lia. The candidate tells Lia what they are good at, what they want next, their salary range, location, company size and visa status; Lia then searches a base of about 7,000 open jobs at about 2,000 employers and, only when the candidate and the hiring manager both show interest, sends a warm email introduction instead of an application into a queue. It is free for the candidate until they are hired, and then the candidate pays 20% of the first month's salary; companies use it for free and can pay a priority tier of 20% of first-year salary to be shown first. The founder's argument is that job boards earn when vacancies stay open and recruiters are paid by employers, whereas Refer's client is the candidate. It was started in 2024 by Andre Hamra, a Brazilian entrepreneur and Stanford alumnus, who put up flyers at Stanford offering to help people find jobs. The service began with Stanford software-engineering alumni and moved to all tech workers across the US, and its program was being extended to about 20 more universities in 2026. Traction: by July 2026 it had set up nearly 6,000 interviews at more than 2,000 companies, with more than half of users getting an interview within 24 hours of an introduction, according to the company. In July 2026 it disclosed a previously unannounced US$7.5 million seed round led by Canary, bringing total funding to about US$10 million (after an earlier US$2.5 million round); the money is meant to add candidates and employers. The candidate-pays model is unusual and draws a regulatory question, as the International Labour Organization's Convention 181 bars worker fees in the countries that ratified it (not the US).

investment_thesis.value: Problem: job seekers, above all in tech, send many applications that go unanswered, and recruiters and job boards work for the employer or profit when vacancies remain open. Employers receive floods of low-fit applications. Logic and why now: a language-model agent can read a profile and a job base, filter for mutual fit and write a credible introduction at near-zero marginal cost, so a placement fee that was once paid for human recruiters can be charged to the candidate for a larger share of wins and still be small against a tech salary (20% of one month's pay is about 1.7% of annual pay). Market: no market size was read. Bottom-up with assumptions: if the platform places 20,000 people a year at an average first-month salary of US$10,000 (assumption), a 20% fee is US$2,000 each and revenue is US$40 million; 100,000 placements would be US$200 million. US tech and professional hiring runs in the millions of hires a year (assumption, not sourced), so this is a small share of it. What is different: the candidate is the client, introductions are bilateral and warm, and employers pay nothing, so supply of jobs grows faster than in a model that charges them; established AI-recruiting vendors named in the press (Paradox, HireVue, Eightfold AI, Findem) sell to employers. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): a Brazilian founder building in Silicon Valley with a distribution trick (campus alumni networks), the sort of founder-led, network-driven start that Norte describes; the single source that lists Norte (a Spanish blog) calls it a follow-on investor, which would fit Norte's follower role after earlier support. Risks: the legality and acceptance of charging candidates (ILO and industry codes oppose it, and US states may regulate), collection risk once a candidate has the job, a crowded market of AI recruiting tools and large job platforms, and the dependence on a small team and one lead investor's round.

milestones.value: Andre Hamra starts helping Stanford alumni find jobs, putting up flyers on campus, and builds Lia, an AI agent that sends warm introductions between candidates and hiring managers.
Has set up nearly 6,000 interviews at more than 2,000 companies, has opened from Stanford alumni to all US tech workers and plans to take its programme to about 20 more universities.
Discloses a previously unannounced US$7.5 million seed round led by Canary, bringing total funding to about US$10 million, and a 20% priority tier for employers.

description.value: Malga is a Brazilian payments infrastructure company that lets digital businesses connect to many acquirers, anti-fraud tools, wallets and banks through one API, route each payment to the best option, and increasingly build their own payment products on top.

long_description.value: Malga (called Plug until early 2023) sells payments infrastructure to Brazilian digital businesses. A company that sells online normally has to integrate with each payment provider separately, a job that takes developers months, and it loses sales whenever its one provider declines a card or goes down. Malga gives it one API in front of more than 30 connections (acquirers, anti-fraud tools, digital wallets, banks and reconciliation providers, per its site; 20-plus processors in 2025 press). The customer builds a payment flow and chooses which provider handles each method; if the first provider declines, the payment is retried on the second and the third. Malga says its customers cut Pix costs by up to 90%, boleto costs by 50% and credit-card costs by up to 40%, and reduced declined transactions by 20%, recovering about R$170 million in lost sales by the end of 2024. The product has three layers, all on its site: orchestration (routing, split, recurrence, tokenization, anti-fraud); a white-label infrastructure (dashboard, payment links, checkout and SDKs under the client's own brand); and a payment processor, a sub-acquiring service of its own, so a platform can earn revenue on each transaction it processes, with settlement, split, reconciliation and receivables advance included. Its customers have included Petlove, Privalia, JCA and Ingresse; since about 2025 it has aimed mainly at B2B platforms (SaaS companies, ERPs, fintechs and digital banks) that want to turn payments into a product and a source of revenue. Malga earns from the volume it processes and from platform fees (the sources do not give the pricing). It was started in 2020, as Plug, by Alex Vilhena (CEO, formerly at Chute and PayPal's Braintree), Thiago Garuti (COO, formerly at Medicinae Solutions) and Marcel Nicolay (CTO, formerly at Zoop and Gympass), after Vilhena saw companies integrating many providers just to have a fallback. Plug went through Y Combinator in 2021 (which took about 7%), was then based in Rio de Janeiro, and raised a US$2.7 million seed in November 2021 led by Costanoa with QED, Verve Capital, Latitud and Norte Ventures; Costanoa led an extension in 2022. In February 2023 it rebranded as Malga (from amalgam), with 36 clients and a first client in Chile. Traction: revenue grew five times in 2022 according to the company, and Brazil Journal reports it five-folded in 2023 and tripled in 2024, when volume reached R$4 billion (R$5 billion annualized). In December 2024 it made its first acquisition, Drip, a Pix-instalment (buy now, pay later) start-up with about 30,000 users, to start offering consumer and merchant credit. In February 2025 it raised a R$32 million Series A led by iDEXO (TOTVS's venture arm) and Costanoa, with Ignia and Gaingels joining and QED, Norte and Y Combinator following on; the CEO said it was close to breakeven. Malga expected about R$15 billion in volume in 2025, three times 2024, and plans to double volume and revenue in 2026, focusing on Brazil, the evolution of Pix and ways to earn more from volume.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: an online business in Brazil depends on payment providers it does not control. Each integration costs months of developer time, any provider outage or card decline loses a sale, and Malga's CEO cites one in four e-commerce purchases denied in Brazil against under 5% in developed markets (Brazil Journal, 2025). Logic: a single API in front of 20-plus processors that retries a declined payment on the next one turns payments from a cost into a growth lever, and the vendor is paid on volume that grows with its customers. Why now: Pix and instalment Pix, new anti-fraud and wallet providers, and platforms (SaaS, ERPs) that want to embed payments to earn revenue, as Mercado Pago does for Mercado Libre (the CEO's own example). Market (our estimate): Abecs reports R$4.5 trillion in card payments in 2025 (R$3.1 trillion credit). Pix, boleto and other methods add to the volume Malga orchestrates, but no read source gives total online payment volume, so we do not size the whole. Malga processed about R$5 billion in 2024 and projected R$15 billion for 2025, about 0.3% of card volume alone. Bottom-up, if it reached 3% to 5% of today's card volume (R$135 to R$225 billion) and kept 0.1% to 0.3% of it (our assumption, since pricing is not public), revenue would be roughly R$135 million to R$675 million a year: a rough order of magnitude, not a forecast. Latin America beyond Brazil is upside, not in the estimate. What is different: Malga is both an orchestrator and a processor with a white-label stack, so platforms can launch a payments product without becoming acquirers, and it owns a small credit line from Drip. Payment orchestrators elsewhere (Yuno, another Norte portfolio company, and Spreedly abroad; our naming, not read) suggest the model is real, and the CEO names merchants' inertia, not a competitor, as the main rival. Fit with Norte: Norte followed on in the seed and the Series A, which fits its connector role at a stage where founders need funds and a network (our reading of the Manifesto, not Norte's statement); the founders have payments experience (Braintree, Zoop, Gympass). Risks: the take rate falls as volume grows and large customers negotiate; value depends on a few big acquirers and wallets; the credit business adds risk; and the target market has moved more than once (Plug, Malga, B2B platforms).

milestones.value: Alex Vilhena, Thiago Garuti and Marcel Nicolay start Plug, a layer where merchants choose and swap payment providers, after Vilhena saw companies building many integrations just to have a fallback.
Plug goes through Y Combinator and sells about 7% to it, which gives the young company its first US network.
Plug announces a US$2.7 million seed and a product that lets a merchant reach up to 11 payment connections through one API, cutting integration time from months to days.
Plug becomes Malga after six months of work on the brand, with 36 clients, a first client in Chile and a plan to grow beyond Brazil; revenue had grown five times in 2022.

Malga buys Drip, a Pix-instalment start-up, for cash and shares, its first acquisition, to add consumer credit and receivables products; it reports R$4 billion in volume and R$170 million in recovered sales that year.

Malga narrows to B2B platforms (SaaS, ERPs, fintechs, digital banks) and offers white-label infrastructure and its own processor, expecting R$15 billion in volume for the year against R$5 billion in 2024.
Malga raises a R$32 million Series A led by iDEXO and Costanoa, with revenue having tripled in 2024 and breakeven expected within months; it plans its own payment systems and digital accounts.
Malga says it will double volume and revenue, focusing on Brazil, new Pix features and ways to earn more per payment.

description.value: Payments network for Latin America that lets banks, fintechs and large platforms offer bill payments, cash in and out, mobile top-ups and gift cards through a single integration.

long_description.value: tapi is a payments-infrastructure company that lets banks, fintechs and large platforms offer bill payments, mobile top-ups, digital gift cards and cash-in and cash-out through a single API, across Argentina, Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Peru. Behind that one connection it holds the links to thousands of service companies (utilities, telecoms), physical networks (OXXO, Walmart, 7-Eleven and Tiendas 3B in Mexico) and banks, so a customer such as Nubank, Mercado Pago, Santander, Banamex or HSBC does not have to integrate each one. It also sells tapipay, a collections platform for small and mid-size companies, financiers and insurers that charge on a recurring basis, which automates billing and connects to the banking system and every payment method. It earns from the volume it routes (our reading; the sources do not state its fees). The company began in August 2019 when Tomás Mindlin, a returning Londoner inspired by Revolut, and his childhood friend Kevin Litvin, then in Madrid, met in Buenos Aires to build a consumer wallet called Tap; Nicolás Andriano, a classmate of Mindlin from ITBA, joined months later to lead technology and product. The wallet reached 700,000 users in about a year and a half, but the team found that the payment providers' systems were built for shops with a few hundred transactions a day, not for fintechs, and they had to rebuild their suppliers' technology. They pivoted from consumers to B2B and spent their first operating year building coverage in five countries before signing a first client, on the bet that the large fintechs (Mercado Libre, Nubank, Ualá) needed regional payment rails. A US$9 million seed led by Andreessen Horowitz in 2022 and a US$22 million Series A led by Kaszek in mid-2024 followed; in July 2025 it bought two business units of Arcus, a Mastercard company, in Mexico (bill payments, top-ups, gift cards and cash services), its first acquisition; and in February 2026 it raised a US$27 million Series B led by Kaszek with Endeavor Catalyst and Latitud, bringing the total above US$60 million. Mexico is now its main market, where it says 85% of payments are still in cash and the market is three times Argentina's. It reports more than 250 million transactions and over US$6 billion of volume a year, 20,000 service companies and 70,000 physical points, ten times growth in billing and volume in under 18 months, and profitability. More than 70% of staff are in technology. The funds go to new products, scaling tapipay and the Mexican network.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: Latin American payment systems are fragmented. Each country has its own utilities, bill-payment rails, cash networks and top-up providers, and a bank or fintech that wants to let customers pay a bill or deposit cash in a shop has to integrate dozens of them, each with old technology that was not built for digital scale. In Mexico, the founders say, 85% of payments are still in cash. The logic: be the single connection. Once tapi has built the network (it began in five countries before it had a client), every new client's volume uses the same rails, so the cost per transaction falls and the network becomes hard to copy; owning the infrastructure (and buying Arcus' Mexican units) lets it keep the margin instead of reselling someone else's. Why now: fintechs and neobanks are scaling across the region and need cash and bill-payment features to serve the unbanked, and Mastercard sold off regional units, leaving room for a local specialist. Market: no independent market-size figure was read. Our estimate is from the company's volume: more than US$6 billion across 250 million transactions is about US$24 per transaction; with a revenue take of 0.3% to 0.8% of volume (our assumption) that is roughly US$18 million to US$48 million a year now. The company grew ten times in under 18 months; if volume reaches US$30 to US$60 billion a year (5 to 10 times today, our scenario, which would still be a small slice of Mexico's cash payments) the revenue pool would be about US$90 million to US$480 million a year. What is different: an own, regional network built before demand, direct links to the physical networks and utilities, and a collections product for businesses; the competitors are local aggregators and bill-payment providers (such as Arcus before the sale, Pagos Inteligentes and others), named from general knowledge, not from the sources read. Reported profitability is unusual for a venture-backed payments company and shows discipline. Fit with Norte (our reading): founders who pivoted early on what customers taught them, a stage and region where a connector can bring Latin American funds and clients (Kaszek, Endeavor Catalyst and Latitud are in the network), and an infrastructure business that grows with the fintechs Norte also backs. No source says Norte invested in tapi, so we do not claim a role. Risks: thin margins and customer concentration (a few large fintechs and banks), integration and regulatory complexity in five countries, the Mexican strategy depends on integrating the Arcus units, and the cash-to-digital shift (Pix-like instant payment systems, such as Mexico's CoDi and SPEI) could shrink the cash and bill-payment volume over time.

milestones.value: Founders Mindlin and Litvin start developing the idea, first as a consumer wallet called Tap
Relaunched as tapi, a B2B payments network, and built coverage in five countries before signing its first client
Reached profitability
Bought two business units of Arcus (a Mastercard company) in Mexico, its first acquisition

Closes a US$27 million Series B and reports more than 250 million transactions and over US$6 billion in volume a year, 10 times growth in billing and volume in under 18 months, profitability, while putting its collections platform for businesses (tapipay) at the centre of its plans

description.value: Brazilian B2B marketplace where restaurants, bars, hotels and small food businesses buy supplies from many pre-qualified suppliers, with next-day delivery and pay-later credit.

long_description.value: Cayena is a business-to-business marketplace where restaurants, bars, bakeries, hotels, dark kitchens, schools, caterers and small markets buy their groceries and supplies from many suppliers in one place. Before platforms like it, an owner either spent hours in wholesale stores comparing prices and queuing, or negotiated one by one with distributors over WhatsApp, with no guarantee of the best price (Norte's case post found a 60% price gap for the same bag of rice across 15 suppliers on one day). Cayena pre-qualifies the suppliers (the company said in 2021 that only about 30% of candidates are accepted), shows a real-time catalogue (more than 100 suppliers and 50,000 items by 2024), recommends the best mix of suppliers for each basket on price and convenience, and offers next-day delivery, free freight and a dedicated account consultant. It makes money mainly as a commission paid by the suppliers on the demand it brings them, and, through Cayena Pay, from a credit layer: launched in early 2022 as buy-now-pay-later, it lets the restaurant pay the supplier on term while the supplier is paid promptly, so the financing arm both helps the buyer's working capital and keeps default away from the suppliers. By 2024 the company said more than R$2 billion in credit had been made available in three years, with an approval rate 50% above the industry average, backed by relationships with Itaú, Safra, Santander and Allianz. Cayena is asset-light: it handles neither inventory nor logistics, which separates it from Colombia's Frubana and Brazil's Pantore, which buy and deliver the goods (Brazil Journal, 2022). The three founders met at Insper in 2011: Gabriel Sendacz (private equity at NEO Investimentos), Pedro Carvalho (investment banking at Merrill Lynch) and Raymond Shayo (investment banking at JP Morgan). In 2018 they left finance to start a company and chose the sector with a checklist (a B2B, recurring, offline, large and fragmented market, with a win-win model) after looking at cemeteries and healthcare; Carvalho's family runs a Japanese food delivery kitchen in Salvador, which tested the first tool, with a reported 20% drop in the cost of goods sold. The MVP went live in September 2019 in São Paulo. Funding and traction: a R$2.5 million seed led by Canary with Norte in 2020; a US$3.5 million Series A led by Picus Capital in September 2021 (about 2,000 establishments then); a R$100 million round led by Vine Ventures in March 2022, when it had passed 30,000 SKUs and R$100 million in transactions; and a R$300 million (about US$55 million) Series B led by Bicycle Capital in September 2024, when it said it moved about R$1 billion a year (US$200 million of sales by the end of 2024). The money is meant to take Cayena from about 100 to more than 500 Brazilian municipalities over two years, and the company has talked of monetising B2B commerce data and, later, reaching Latin America, a wholesale market it puts at US$200 billion a year. InvestNews reported in 2024 that it had not yet reached breakeven (a search summary; page not read).

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil has about 1.1 million food service outlets that spend over US$35 billion a year on supplies (Norte case post), most of them small and family-run. They buy by phone, WhatsApp, or by visiting wholesalers, with no price transparency (a 60% spread on one bag of rice across 15 suppliers) and stock-outs of up to 10%; suppliers, for their part, fear unpaid invoices. Logic: a marketplace that pre-qualifies suppliers, optimises the basket and guarantees payment to suppliers (through Cayena Pay) removes the buyer's search cost and the supplier's credit risk, and takes a commission on recurring purchases (clients bought five to seven times a month in 2021 to 2022). Asset-light operation lets growth use little cash. Market: the Norte post puts Brazil's food service procurement at over US$35 billion a year, and Cayena's CEO and Norte put Latin America at about US$200 billion (company and investor figure; not an independent source). Cayena moved about R$1 billion a year in 2024, roughly 0.5% of Brazil's US$35 billion (R$190 billion at about R$5.4 per US dollar, our conversion), so even a 5% share would mean US$1.75 billion of purchases a year; at a 3% to 5% commission-plus-credit revenue (our assumption, not sourced) that is about US$50 to US$90 million of revenue, a rough order of magnitude for Brazil alone. What is different: it is asset-light (no inventory or trucks) while Frubana and Pantore buy and deliver (Brazil Journal, 2022), which keeps capital needs low; it owns the credit and payment layer, which is the real trust problem between small buyers and suppliers; and its team is from finance, which suits that layer. Fit with Norte: Norte backed it at the seed (2020), followed on in the Series A and the Series B, and wrote a case post on it, consistent with its pattern of following strong founders with a network of funds (our reading of the Manifesto). Risks: credit losses in a sector with thin margins; bigger rivals with logistics scale, such as Frubana or distributors with their own apps; and the 2024 plan to expand to 500 cities needs a heavy sales force. Evidence is thin on profits (breakeven not confirmed).

milestones.value: Cayena puts its first product (MVP) online in São Paulo, a marketplace where restaurants order from several wholesale suppliers instead of calling each one.
With R$2.5 million from Canary and Norte, Cayena gets through the first months of the pandemic, when restaurants closed and its buyers shrank.
A US$3.5 million Series A led by Picus Capital funds growth beyond the first 2,000 establishments and more than 20,000 products.
Cayena launches Cayena Pay, a buy-now-pay-later product that lets restaurants pay suppliers on term, and passes 30,000 SKUs and R$100 million of purchases through the platform.
Cayena says it has made more than R$2 billion of credit available over three years and moves about R$1 billion a year of supplies; it works with more than 100 suppliers and 50,000 items.
A R$300 million Series B, one of the biggest rounds of the year, is meant to take Cayena from about 100 to more than 500 municipalities in two years.

description.value: Platform that lets employers pay frontline workers instantly for shifts, tips, commissions and bonuses, linked to attendance and performance, to cut absenteeism and turnover.

long_description.value: Quansa lets employers pay frontline workers the moment they earn the money, instead of at the end of the month, and ties that pay to attendance and performance. An employer connects Quansa to its time-clock and payroll systems; when an employee finishes a shift, sells, receives a tip or reaches a target, the amount becomes available in an app straight away, and the employer still pays once a month (the company fronts the advance and the employer settles with Quansa at month end). Quansa says this is not a loan, and the employee's own earned wages are what is advanced. Its pitch is operational: less absenteeism, less turnover, a more stable operation, with no extra work for HR or finance and no change to payroll. Customers have reported up to 50% fewer absences and up to 30% lower turnover (company claims). The Brazilian site lists several products: on-demand pay, instant tips, instant commissions, incentive campaigns, and management and payment of intermittent workers and freelancers (Quansa Extras). Its customers include a McDonald's franchisee with more than 500 employees, Grupo Fit (more than 10 brands, airport operations), Grupo Alife Nino and, in Chile, LimChile, Derco and Ultramar. It shows ISO 27001, LGPD and SOC 1 compliance, and its product was designed with labor-law lawyers. At the start the company sold financial health as an employee benefit, like a Gympass for finances, with financial coaching and salary advances, and said it earned only a per-employee fee from the employer, never interest or lending margin (Startups.com.br, 2021); by 2026 its Brazilian pitch had moved to frontline retention, in a context where, it says, the updated NR-1 workplace rule makes financial stress an employer responsibility. It was founded in the second half of 2020 in Chile by Gonzalo Blanco (Uruguayan, CEO, ex-McKinsey and Stanford GSB, who had always been the family's financial adviser) and Mafalda Barros (Portuguese, COO, also ex-McKinsey and Stanford GSB, in Latin America since 2013). Pear VC, the first investor, backed them at Stanford. Quansa launched in Chile in late 2020 and began operating in Brazil in June 2021; in July 2021 it announced a US$3.6 million seed led by Valor Capital Group with Pear VC, Canary, Norte, Magma, Sequoia Scouts and angels (Ariel Lambrecht of 99, Gupy's Mariana Dias and Bruna Guimarães, Volanty's Maurício Feldman, Branch's Mada Seghete). The team then had 10 people; the money was for technology and doubling the team. Brazil is now its main market, with a Brazilian company opened in March 2021 and based in São Paulo, and Chile remains a market; no later round was found.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: frontline workers in retail and food service live on monthly paychecks, so a bill that cannot wait pushes them toward payday loans or toward skipping a shift to do gig work, which employers see as absenteeism and turnover. Brazil had 57.1 million formal jobs at the end of 2024 (RAIS), and the Quansa site says 82% of retailers report rising turnover. Logic: if pay arrives the same day, workers keep their main job; the employer pays Quansa once a month and gains attendance and retention, so the employer is the buyer and the bill is a fee per employee, not interest on loans. Why now: platform work (delivery, ride-hailing) set an expectation of instant pay; Pix makes small instant transfers cheap; and the employer-side pain of turnover is rising. Market (our estimate): of RAIS's 57.1 million formal jobs, we assume 8 to 12 million are frontline positions in retail, foodservice, facilities and logistics that fit the model (our assumption; the RAIS summary lists commerce at about 10 million in a page we did not read). If an employer pays Quansa R$10 to R$20 per employee per month (our assumption; pricing is not public), full penetration would be R$1 billion to R$3 billion a year, and 3% to 5% of that, a realistic target for a Brazilian leader, is R$30 to R$150 million of revenue: a rough order of magnitude. Chile and other markets add a smaller upside. What is different: Quansa links pay to attendance and incentive rules (so it is a retention tool, not just a wage advance), integrates with time clocks and payroll, advances the money itself and bills the employer, and says it does not earn from credit interest. Competition in on-demand pay is dense (benefit apps, payroll fintechs and banks; our knowledge, not read), so the differentiation is retention results and integration. Fit with Norte: it is a follower in the seed, next to Valor, Canary and Pear, which matches its pattern of joining at the seed with strong funds (our reading of the Manifesto); founders are McKinsey and Stanford operators with a clear problem, though the story moved from a financial-health benefit to frontline retention. Risks: rising cost of capital for advancing wages; regulation of wage advance; customer concentration in a few chains; and no financing round found since 2021, so growth may have been funded from revenue (unknown).

milestones.value: Gonzalo Blanco and Mafalda Barros, who met at McKinsey and studied at Stanford GSB, start Quansa in Chile to make financial health a benefit that employers offer.
Quansa launches in Chile with on-demand pay and financial coaching sold to employers; some customers have been with it since 2020.
Quansa starts operating in Brazil, its largest market, a month before announcing its seed.
A US$3.6 million seed led by Valor Capital Group, with Sequoia Scouts taking part, pays for technology and for doubling a 10-person team.

Quansa has a new administrator in its Brazilian company and by 2026 sells on-demand pay, instant tips and commissions, incentive campaigns and payment of freelancers (Quansa Extras) to foodservice and retail chains.

description.value: Brazilian home-care company that selects, trains and places caregivers, nursing technicians and physiotherapists with older people at home, using AI to match them to families.

long_description.value: Sanii organises home care for older people in Brazil. Families that need a caregiver, nursing technician or physiotherapist for a parent or grandparent come to Sanii, which selects, trains and places professionals with them, assures the payment and the replacement of the professional, and keeps monitoring the older person's condition with a team of gerontologists and nurses, available 24 hours a day by its own account. The founders call it a closed marketplace: thousands apply each month and only about 3% are approved, after screening, experience checks, background checks and interviews, and nearly 30 factors (distance, skills, availability) are crossed to match a caregiver with a family. Most permanent-shift clients stay one to two years, usually until the patient dies, and Sanii reallocates the caregiver to another family, which gives caregivers more stable work in a sector that is otherwise informal and fragmented. Revenue comes from what the families pay for care, with the professionals' pay deducted (the sources do not give prices or margins). Technology is used behind the care: a system called Care IA, built on Google's Gemini, refines the match between caregivers and patients; AI agents interview candidates and collect new clients' needs; and an AI assistant on WhatsApp helps caregivers during the shift, writing handover reports and reminding them of medication times. Sanii also trains caregivers (for example in palliative care and handling devices), and sells courses. The long-term plan, according to InfoMoney, adds medicine and vaccine delivery, dental care and smart sensors and cameras. Its history has two parts. The company was started by Renato Tilkian (a health executive with more than 20 years' experience, who led Amil's roll-up and consolidated Lavebras and Vitus), Michael Kapps (Canadian founder of mental-health start-up Vitalk, bought by Gympass/Wellhub in 2022) and Angelina Clarke (ex-McKinsey, founder of the recruiting start-up AssuredLabor, former head of strategy at Descomplica). In October 2023 it announced a R$8 million pre-seed led by Valor Capital Group, with 15 other investors including GreenRock and Norte Ventures, then a prevention service: weekly home visits of up to 90 minutes to stimulate memory, body and social life of people over 60, in 28 São Paulo neighbourhoods, with a physical space planned in Higienópolis, a team of 12, and a target of 30 clients by the end of the year. The founders later bought Senior Services, a traditional home-care company founded by gerontologist Margherita Mizan (about 14 years old), and merged it into Sanii, which is why the site says it has more than 14 years in elder care. Traction: the company says its monthly recurring revenue grew six-fold in 18 months, that it had delivered half a million hours of care by December 2025, and that it expected to grow 300% in 2025. In late 2025 it closed a R$5 million follow-on round led by Sororitê Ventures (total raised R$13 million), used for expansion to the interior and coast of São Paulo and for technology. In mid-2026 it opened an office in Campinas and said it will enter eight more cities, by organic growth and acquisitions (the ABC region, Alphaville, Brasília, Recife, Salvador, Goiânia and Porto Alegre are mapped), aiming to be the largest home-care company in Latin America.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil is ageing fast; in 2023 IBGE counted for the first time more older people than young, and the share aged 60 or over rose from 8.7% in 2000 to 15.6% in 2023 (InfoMoney). Families that want an older relative to stay at home (aging in place) have to find caregivers in an informal, fragmented market, with no guarantee of quality or replacement, while caregivers face irregular income and unpaid work. A study of Unifesp reports 1.76 million Brazilians over 60 with dementia, a number expected to triple by 2050 (Startupi, quoting Unifesp and the Ministry of Health). Logic: a company that selects strictly (about 3% accepted), trains, guarantees payment and replacement, and matches with data can charge a premium and keep caregivers loyal; AI in the back office (matching, recruiting, handover reports) lowers cost per hour and error. Why now: demographic change, a family structure with fewer relatives available, and cheap AI for operations. Market (our estimate): 15.6% of Brazil's population of about 203 million (IBGE 2022 Census, our recollection; not read) is about 32 million people aged 60 or over. If 2% to 3% of them (0.6 to 1 million, our assumption) pay for home care at R$3,000 to R$6,000 a month (our assumption), spending is roughly R$20 billion to R$70 billion a year; it is a rough order of magnitude for professional home care in Brazil. If Sanii reached 1% to 2% of that spending, revenue would be R$200 million to R$1.4 billion. Latin America is upside. What is different: it operates the care (clinical team, replacement guarantee), not a classified-ads marketplace; the founders pair a health-sector operator (Tilkian), a startup operator who sold a company to Gympass (Kapps) and a McKinsey-trained operator (Clarke); and it owns a heritage brand (Senior Services). Fit with Norte: Norte joined the pre-seed with Valor, an early-round pattern that suits connecting a new team to funds and talent (our reading of the Manifesto, not Norte's statement). Risks: it is a service business with labour-intensive margins and caregiver supply as the bottleneck; unit economics are not public; roll-ups outside São Paulo are hard to integrate; competition from established home-care firms and health plans; and the change of strategy from prevention to caregivers within two years.

milestones.value: Sanii announces itself with a prevention service for people over 60: weekly home visits of up to 90 minutes to exercise the brain and body and reduce isolation, in 28 São Paulo neighbourhoods, plus a planned physical space in Higienópolis.
A R$8 million pre-seed led by Valor Capital Group, with 15 other investors including Norte Ventures, funds a 12-person team and its first sales push.
Sanii builds Care IA on Google Gemini for caregiver-patient matching, and uses AI agents in recruiting and in client intake, with a WhatsApp assistant for caregivers on shift.
A R$5 million follow-on led by Sororitê Ventures takes total funding to R$13 million; the company reports half a million hours of care delivered and expects 300% growth in 2025.
Sanii opens an office in Campinas, its first outside the capital, and plans eight more cities through organic growth and acquisitions, after multiplying monthly recurring revenue by six in 18 months.

description.value: Brazilian marketplace where individual resellers buy beauty products from popular brands, pay in instalments without a credit card and sell to their own networks and on social media.

long_description.value: Vendah is a Brazilian reselling marketplace for people who sell products to their own contacts and over social media, usually women looking for extra or main income. A reseller signs up for free (adult with a bank account in her own name), picks products on the Vendah app, shares photos with her network, and orders what she sold; Vendah ships to her, with free freight on larger orders, and she keeps the margin between her price and the price of the kit. The product line has changed. When it raised its seed in 2023, Vendah sold more than 700 low-ticket items for home, kitchen, decor and babies, bought from importers and distributors and stored in its own distribution centre; the reseller needed no minimum purchase or demo kit and earned a 15% to 20% commission paid within two business days. Today its site is organised around beauty: it sells the internet's favourite beauty brands to resellers, with instalments at no interest and without a credit card, and with support from specialists on WhatsApp. The Y Combinator profile describes this as a marketplace connecting digital-first beauty brands to a network of individual sellers, powered by embedded microcredit and a proprietary credit engine, and says that after the pivot to marketplace plus credit, GMV was growing about 30% a month, with close to 1,000 active sellers and positive, improving risk-adjusted margins. The company makes money on the margin of the goods it sells to resellers and, in the credit model, on the financing that lets a reseller pay in instalments without a card (the sources do not give the numbers). It is a cousin of the traditional direct-selling industry: the ABEVD reported R$45 billion in direct sales in Brazil in 2022 (Startups.com.br), and Startupi counts more than 5 million women in the channel. It was started in 2021 by Luis Felipe Franco (CEO; created Endeavor Brazil's Scale-up Endeavor programme and led growth at the beauty brand Sallve), Marcelo Canovas (an administrator since the company's registration in May 2021; the COO's Y Combinator biography says he co-founded Liv Up and a software house) and, according to a single directory, Pedro Pedruzzi as CTO. Before it had operations it raised an R$8.5 million pre-seed in 2021 led by Maya Capital, with Norte Ventures, Village Global and angels from 99, Creditas, MadeiraMadeira and Sallve. It went through Y Combinator in the Winter 2023 batch and in August 2023 announced an R$12 million (about US$2.4 million) seed, with YC, Goodwater and Domo Invest and angels in the US, India and China; the CEO said the money gave it the option to reach breakeven before a Series A and that it expected to grow five times in 2023 and to expand from São Paulo and the coast to Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte in 2024. At that time it had served more than 30,000 informal resellers. No later round was found.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: millions of Brazilians, mostly women, earn extra income by reselling products, but the traditional direct-selling model asks them to buy kits upfront, hold stock and carry catalogues, and many have no card or credit history. The ABEVD counted R$45 billion of direct sales in Brazil in 2022 and Startupi counts more than 5 million women in the channel. Logic: an app that gives resellers a catalogue of products people already want, ships to them, pays commission or margin quickly and lets them buy on instalments without a card lowers the barrier to starting, while Vendah's data on seller behaviour lets it price credit. Why now: social media made every reseller a store, Pix and cheap fulfilment lowered logistics costs, and traditional direct sellers are losing consultants. Market (our estimate): R$45 billion of direct sales in Brazil in 2022 (ABEVD, via Startups.com.br; Startupi quotes US$8 billion). If Vendah reached 1% to 2% of that, GMV would be R$450 to R$900 million; at a gross margin of 20% to 30% (our assumption; unit economics are not public), gross profit would be R$90 to R$270 million. The YC profile quotes a beauty market of about US$30 billion in Brazil (company claim, not independent), so the reachable area is large. Latin America (50 million-plus potential sellers, per YC) is upside. What is different: it targets people with no capital and no card, offers credit built on its own seller data, and has moved to branded beauty products from online brands with their own demand (which sell by themselves, as a seller says on the site), instead of a catalogue of generic goods. Competitors: Natura, Avon and O Boticário in direct selling, plus new reseller platforms (our knowledge, not read). Fit with Norte: Norte backed the pre-seed alongside Maya Capital and Village Global, before operations, which matches its early, founder-first pattern; the founders have e-commerce and growth credentials (Endeavor, Sallve, Liv Up) (our reading of the Manifesto and of the YC profile). Risks: the product line changed once already (home goods to beauty and credit), no round since 2023 was found, credit to low-income resellers is risky and capital-hungry, and customer-service complaints are likely in a model with deliveries and instalments (a search summary mentioned a consumer-complaints page; not read).

milestones.value: A R$8.5 million pre-seed led by Maya Capital funds the first product and team.
Vendah is registered in São Paulo by Luis Felipe Franco and Marcelo Canovas, before it has launched, to build an app for resellers selling through social media.
Vendah goes through Y Combinator (Winter 2023), which later co-invests in its seed.
Vendah announces a R$12 million seed, a catalogue of more than 700 home, kitchen and baby items, more than 30,000 resellers served, and plans to expand to Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte.

description.value: Web-based motion design tool that lets designers turn static designs into animations and videos, with AI to generate effects and batch variations, for creative and product teams.

long_description.value: Jitter is a web-based motion design tool, pitched as Figma for motion: a designer who can lay out a screen, a brand asset or a social post should be able to animate it without learning a timeline-heavy program such as After Effects. Users import designs (most often from Figma through its plugin, and since October 2025 from Figma Buzz, plus images and vector shapes), animate layers with presets, curved paths, morphing shapes, gradients and blur on an infinite canvas, collaborate with product and marketing teammates in a shared workspace, and export to video (up to 4K, .mov, .mp4, .webm), GIF and Lottie for apps and websites. Its site says more than 20,000 creative teams use it, with customer stories from Perplexity, Deliveroo and the design studio 27b. The recent product focus is AI and production at scale. Users can describe an effect in words and get an editable animation; Jitter AI generates variations, turns still images into video, and, since July 2026, 'Superagents' built into the editor can remix templates, animate complex scenes from scratch and turn one asset into a campaign of many sizes, formats and languages, with batch export. A Brand Kit (beta, November 2026) stores a brand's colours, text styles and easings, and the product can be driven by an AI assistant through an MCP connection. It sells subscriptions per editor per month (a free plan with 3 files, 720p export and a limited AI allowance; paid plans called Max and Ultra, whose prices were not readable). It was started in 2020 in Paris by Etienne Albert and Sébastien Robaszkiewicz and went through Y Combinator's Winter 2020 batch, with a team of seven at that time. Directory sites list Norte Ventures among its early backers, but no readable source describes the round, so the amounts and Norte's participation remain unverified. In mid-2026 Figma announced its own integrated motion tool at Config; Jitter's co-founder welcomed it as proof that motion has become part of the design process, while presenting Jitter as built for the production stage (ten versions, five formats, three languages, all on brand).
