investment_thesis.value: Problem: motion has become part of brand and product (app interactions, ads, social posts, launch videos), but most designers cannot animate: the professional tools (After Effects) are slow to learn and sit outside the design process, so the work is handed off or skipped. Teams also need many versions of one asset for different formats and languages. Logic: a collaborative, browser-based tool that imports from Figma, uses presets and AI, and exports to video and Lottie lets the designer do the job, and per-editor subscriptions grow with team size. Why now: Figma made design collaborative on the web, AI can now draft animations and variations from a prompt, and short video is the default format for marketing. Market (our estimate): Figma crossed US$1.056 billion of revenue in 2025 growing 41% (diginomica, read), showing the scale of web design software. Jitter says over 20,000 creative teams use it (company claim, free and paid). If paying teams averaged 5 editors at US$15 to US$25 per editor per month (our assumption; the plan prices were not readable), 5,000 paying teams would give about US$4.5 million to US$7.5 million a year, and 20,000 paying teams about US$18 million to US$30 million. A strong outcome, motion reaching a tenth of Figma's revenue, would be around US$100 million. What is different: it is a pure motion product built around the designer's workflow (Figma import, templates, brand kits, AI agents) rather than a general video editor, and it has an early lead among motion tools on the web (our assessment). Fit with Norte: aggregator pages list Norte among early backers, but no readable source confirms it, so we cannot say how Norte got involved (a French, YC-backed team, outside Norte's Brazilian base); the Manifesto's bet on obsessed founders and top funds on the cap table is consistent with a YC company, but this is our reading only. Risks: Figma launched its own integrated motion tool in June 2026 (Jitter's blog reacts to the announcement; the alternativeto summary was not read), and Adobe is the incumbent; AI video generators can bypass hand-made animation; and growth figures are the company's own.

milestones.value: Jitter starts in Paris and joins Y Combinator (Winter 2020) with a team of seven, to build a motion design tool as simple as a design tool.
Jitter adds a Figma Buzz plugin so marketing and social designs made in Figma Buzz can be imported and animated in one click.
Jitter launches Superagents, AI agents inside the editor that remix templates, animate scenes from scratch and produce campaigns in many sizes, formats and languages.
Jitter releases Brand Kits (colours, text styles and easings shared across a workspace) and 4K, GIF and Lottie export, for teams that make motion at volume.

description.value: Brazilian AI platform for tax intelligence that cross-checks a company's tax documents against Brazilian tax rules to flag savings and risks, and helps reconcile the new IBS/CBS tax assessment.

long_description.value: Norma is a São Paulo startup that applies AI to Brazilian tax compliance, which its founders describe as the most complex tax regulation in the world. It says it is neither a law firm nor 'one more software': it was founded by engineers and tax specialists to turn tax rules into decision infrastructure for companies. It has two products. Malha Fiscal reads all of a company's tax documents against Brazilian tax regulation and quantifies, in reais, both opportunities to cut the tax burden and tax risks, leaving the company to decide what to do. Conciliação da Apuração Assistida rebuilds in near real time the company's IBS/CBS assessment (the new consumption taxes from the tax reform) from its tax documents and events and points out differences with the figures of the tax authority, before they become a cost or a fine. The platform also updates product registers in minutes instead of days, validates invoices in one click, reads XML and SPED files, handles unlimited company registrations (CNPJs) and multiple simultaneous users, connects to ERPs such as TOTVS, Oracle and SAP without migration, and offers custom integrations and expert support. It offers a free diagnostic report in seven days. We read no pricing; revenue most likely comes from software and service contracts (our reading). The founders, CEO Renato Sanabria (ex-ITA), CFO André Corrêa (ex-USP) and CTO Bruno Assis (ex-USP), saw repeatedly the same pattern in companies: outdated product registers, constant tax changes, a flood of invoices, and teams spending hours putting out fires. Work started in 2023 and the company was registered in April 2024. Its site says it has invested R$10 million in technology, monitors about 5,000 companies and has identified R$455 million of risk and R$684 million of opportunities (all unaudited company figures). Its LinkedIn page showed about 10 employees in November 2026. Customers named on the site are mid-sized Brazilian distributors and food companies; in November 2026 the company said that, with its AI, one of the main supermarket chains of Espírito Santo recovered about R$500,000 a month in tax credits that would otherwise have been lost from January, and it was featured in the ABRAS retail magazine SuperHiper and in Portal Contábeis' guide on assisted assessment. The CBS starts in January 2027, which is the commercial window it is working toward. No funding round has been found.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: Brazil's tax system is among the most complex in the world, and companies handle it with spreadsheets and legacy systems while the tax authority has built a sophisticated cross-checking system (the 'malha fiscal'). The site claims tax litigation equals about 75% of GDP against 0.3% in the OECD, a figure we could not verify. Product registers go stale, rules change all the time, and teams spend hours fixing errors that become overpaid tax or fines. The logic: an AI that reads every invoice against the rules can find credits the company did not claim and risks it did not see, and can show the value in reais, so the sale is easy to justify (a free diagnostic in seven days, then a share of the value found, as we read the model). Why now: the tax reform replaces several taxes with the IBS and CBS from 2027 (the CBS starts in January 2027 and the government has refused to postpone it, as Norma's own November 2026 post reports), which forces every company to review its registers, rebuild its assessment and compare it with the tax authority's, and creates a large wave of work for 2026 and 2027. Market: no published size was read. Our estimate: if 30,000 to 60,000 Brazilian companies large enough to need automated tax review (our assumption) each pay R$30,000 to R$150,000 a year, the revenue pool is about R$0.9 to R$9 billion a year; Norma says it monitors 5,000 companies today, which would be about 8 to 17% of that count if all paid, though most are likely free diagnostics. What could make it special: tax-specific AI trained for Brazilian rules rather than a general tool, the reconciliation with the authority's figures, and integrations with the ERPs companies already use; competitors are the large tax-software vendors, big accounting firms and tax-tech startups, not named in the sources read. Fit with Norte (our reading): a team of technical founders attacking a deep, regulated problem at a moment of forced change, in an area where a connector can bring clients and hiring; but no source places Norte in Norma, no round was found, and the company has about 10 staff, so this is an early, unproven thesis. Risks: the tax reform could be simplified or delayed, large competitors (including the tax authority's own calculator and ERP vendors) could give away what Norma sells, AI errors in tax advice carry legal liability, and a sale cycle built around one regulatory deadline may leave revenue lumpy after 2027.

milestones.value: A major supermarket chain in Espírito Santo is reported (by Norma) to have recovered about R$500,000 a month in tax credits with its AI, and Norma appears in the ABRAS magazine SuperHiper ahead of the CBS start in January 2027
Publishes, with Portal Contábeis, a guide on the most common errors in the assisted CBS assessment, and tracks the Receita's planned batch-adjustment module

description.value: Brazilian accounting and financial platform for doctors working as PJ: company opening, invoices, taxes, accounting and a PJ account in one app, with an AI assistant on WhatsApp.

long_description.value: Caveo is a financial and accounting platform for doctors who work as legal entities (PJ). Since 2015, when hospitals were allowed to hire physicians as PJ, a large share of doctors have had to open a company, issue invoices for each hospital shift, pay taxes and keep books, a bureaucratic job that newly graduated doctors, living off on-call shifts, handle badly. Caveo handles it in an app and on WhatsApp: it opens the company, issues invoices, debits taxes automatically, keeps the accounts, receives payments by Pix in a PJ account and suggests how much to transfer to the doctor's personal account. It added tools specific to doctors, such as a shift calendar, a wallet with useful information and a tax simulator, plus an AI assistant on WhatsApp, and it runs community activities (networking between new graduates and experienced doctors, learning tracks and help to win the first shifts). Revenue came almost entirely from subscriptions: R$147, R$247 or R$397 a month depending on the doctor's billing (average ticket about R$250 a month in 2025). The company is moving customers from the software service to its own bank account and plans to add investments, credit cards, insurance and pension products; a first financial product, 'guaranteed receipt' (an advance on the 30 to 90 days that hospitals take to pay doctors), was planned for the second quarter of 2026. Its go-to-market goes through medical schools: it says it operates in 93% of Brazil's medical schools, reached an estimated 8% of the 2023 graduates, 18% in 2024 and about 40% in 2025, and gets 95% of its sales by referral with an NPS close to 90 (company figures). After building 'almost a new company' in the second half of 2025 to serve experienced doctors with more complex taxes (Lucro Presumido instead of Simples, office doctors and surgeons), those now make up 30% of new customers. The company was founded in São Paulo by Wilgo Cavalcante (CEO), who saw the demand while doing accounting consulting for a client and moved to São Paulo and to the Link School of Business, where he met co-founder Lorenço Boettcher; the sources date the start to 2021 (registry, Baguete) or 2022 (Brazil Journal, NeoFeed). It raised R$6.5 million from a pool of doctors, then in June 2024 a round of about US$1 million with R$2 million from Afya's venture arm and angels such as iFood co-founder Guilherme Bonifácio and Alan Chusid of Spin Pay, which gave it access to Afya's 32 medical schools and its White Book app used by about 45% of Brazilian doctors. In February 2025 it raised R$20 million led by Kortex Ventures (whose investors include Fleury, Sabin and Bradesco Seguros) with ONEVC, Zenda and Norte Ventures, and in December 2025 closed the Series A at R$54 million in total with a R$34 million tranche led by Zenda that brought in Enseada, the family office of SulAmérica's founders. Traction: about 10,000 doctors in February 2025 and more than 20,000 by December, growth of 400% in 2024, annualised recurring revenue of about R$25 million in November 2025 and a projection of R$50 million in January 2026. Its closest comparable in the sector is Contabilizei, the market leader in online accounting with a PJ account.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: since 2015 hospitals can hire doctors as PJ, so most Brazilian doctors, who start on on-call shifts, must open a company, issue invoices and pay taxes, and more than 70% say they feel insecure about accounting and tax issues (Caveo survey, Startups.com.br). Generic accountants do not know shift work, and hospitals pay 30 to 90 days late. Logic: a specialised subscription (R$147 to R$397 a month) wins loyal, high-income users, and the PJ account that holds their receipts creates a base for financial products (receivables advance, cards, insurance, pensions). Distribution through medical schools and Afya's ecosystem gives low-cost acquisition (95% of sales by referral, per the company). Why now: Pix, open finance and AI make accounting automatable, and the number of doctors is growing fast. Market (our estimate): Brazil has about 650,000 doctors and is expected to pass one million by 2032 to 2035 (CEO figures in Brazil Journal; Startups.com.br cites Demografia Médica 2025: over 1 million in 2035). At the company's own pricing of about R$250 a month (R$3,000 a year), 650,000 doctors are a R$1.95 billion a year software market, and 1 million would be R$3 billion; with the bank, credit and insurance revenue per doctor, the total could be a multiple of that. Caveo already says it has more than 20,000 doctors (about 3% of today's total) and annualised revenue of R$25 million, which agrees with 20,000 x R$250 x 12 = R$60 million at full billing (so some customers are on lower plans or recent). A realistic strong outcome is 15% to 25% of doctors, or R$300 million to R$750 million of subscription revenue at today's prices, before financial products. What is different: it sells only to doctors, with shift tools, medical-school distribution and a strategic investor (Afya) and CVCs with health distribution (Kortex with Fleury, Sabin and Bradesco Seguros). Fit with Norte: it joined the pre-Series A and the Series A extension, after strong funds, which fits its pattern of connecting top funds and angels to a company already finding traction (our reading of the Manifesto; the founder's interviews and the round do not state why Norte invested). Risks: Contabilizei, the leader in online accounting with PJ accounts, can serve doctors too; doctors may leave once they become established and need bespoke accountants; credit products (receivables advance) bring risk; and the numbers are company-reported and the growth is concentrated in one segment of newly graduated doctors.

sub_sector.value: Accounting and financial platform for doctors

milestones.value: Wilgo Cavalcante and Lorenço Boettcher start Caveo in São Paulo, after Cavalcante saw that doctors hired as PJ since 2015 had strong, poorly served demand for accounting.

Afya, the medical-education group, invests R$2 million through its venture arm in a round of about US$1 million, giving Caveo access to its 32 medical schools and the White Book app; Caveo then served clients in 17 states.
Caveo raises R$20 million with Kortex Ventures and has almost 10,000 doctors; it starts moving customers from SaaS to its bank, aiming for 20,000 to 30,000 doctors by year end.

Caveo closes a R$54 million Series A (R$34 million in December led by Zenda), serves more than 20,000 doctors, reports annualised revenue of about R$25 million and starts targeting experienced doctors, who are 30% of new clients.
Caveo plans its first financial product, guaranteed receipt (advance of hospital receivables), for the second quarter, and says it expects annualised revenue of R$50 million in January.

description.value: Brazilian healthcare AI company that reads clinical data and reports and turns them into actions with measurable financial return for hospitals, health insurers, clinics and diagnostic networks (formerly NeuralMed).

long_description.value: Level (levelai.com.br; the company was called NeuralMed until April 2026) sells an intelligence layer for hospitals, health insurers, clinics and diagnostic networks. It reads clinical data from the systems they already run (electronic records such as Tasy and MV, imaging systems RIS and PACS, reports and prescriptions), joins it with operational and financial data, and turns it into actions with a measurable financial return. The site gives examples: AI that reads radiology reports and finds critical findings that were never acted on (for instance a nodule noticed in an exam done for another reason), a risk score by disease, exams, drugs and history, the 2% of patients who concentrate 80% of costs found before admission, more than 120 clinical triggers that start traceable actions, and a path from exam to finding to protocol to procedure to revenue that can be audited. A WhatsApp assistant contacts patients to schedule visits or warn them of a needed test, and the platform covers oncology, asthma, diabetes and hypertension. Customers include hospitals Moinhos de Vento and Mãe de Deus and Santa Casa, in Porto Alegre. The business model changed in 2025. Software had been sold as separate algorithms with six-month to one-year deployments; the offer is now two software-as-a-service packages (Light and Full), implemented in 4 to 8 weeks with about 90% of the work done by Level's team, and the company promises it will not charge if agreed targets are not met in the agreed time, which cut the sales cycle from more than 180 days to 30 to 60 days. A new customer type is the pharmaceutical industry, which benefits from early diagnosis of cancer; the first contracts were with Adium (Uruguay) and an unnamed European company. It was started in 2018 as NeuralMed by Anthony Eigier (CEO; founder of the startup accelerator Tree Labs and co-founder of the mobile-games company Fanatee) and radiologist André Castilla (CMO), to apply artificial intelligence to medical images and texts. Its first products were TrIA, for triage in hospitals and laboratories, and Atlas, launched in 2022, for monitoring chronic and oncology patients and for pharma. It raised R$3.2 million in March 2021 from Alexia Ventures, Norte Ventures, MG Tech and the IDB, then R$10 million in August 2021 led by the health insurer Grupo NotreDame Intermédica (which took 9.29%), and in 2022 a round led by Good Karma Ventures, its third in 18 months, with 5 million lives in its customers' bases; NeoFeed counts US$7.7 million raised in total from NotreDame Intermédica, the IDB, Kortex Ventures and GK Ventures. By June 2025 the company had reached its lowest point, with monthly recurring revenue under R$100,000 and only eight clients. After a nine-month reset with Mariana Gaspers (a former finance and revenue executive at Twilio, Hilab and Ascential, who joined in September 2024 and became founding partner), it relaunched in April 2026 as Level, with 36 clients, annual recurring revenue up from under R$1.2 million to R$5 million, and a further R$10 million contracted, with the aim of growing it by the end of 2026 (company figures to NeoFeed). Its algorithms, it says, run 350 times faster than a human reviewer and are close to 500 times.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilian hospitals, insurers and labs hold large amounts of clinical data (reports, exams, records) that nobody reads at scale, so critical findings are missed, high-cost patients are identified late and revenue and prevention opportunities go unseen, while insurers' medical costs keep rising (operators' operating profit fell 10% to R$5.6 billion in the first half of 2026, Folha de Pernambuco). Logic: an AI layer that connects to existing systems (Tasy, MV, RIS, PACS), finds the few patients who drive cost or revenue and triggers an action can be paid for by the financial result it shows; the offer 'no result, no fee' lowers the buyer's risk. Why now: language models and vision models make reading reports and records cheap, and payers need to cut medical-loss ratios. Market (our estimate): Brazil has 53.1 million private health-plan beneficiaries and 698 medical operators (ANS, via O Liberal, September 2026), plus thousands of hospitals, clinics and labs. If 300 institutions (operators, hospitals and diagnostic networks, our assumption) paid R$0.5 million to R$2 million a year (our assumption; Level's ARR is R$5 million for 36 clients, about R$140,000 each, so the assumption is a reach for much larger deals), the market would be R$150 million to R$600 million a year in Brazil; pharma contracts for early diagnosis and Latin America add upside. Level's present R$5 million ARR is therefore a small share, and the case rests on enlarging the average contract. What is different: it sells results, not algorithms, integrates without replacing systems, and combines clinical and financial data; its radiologist co-founder and a customer base of Porto Alegre hospitals give clinical credibility. Fit with Norte: Norte was in the 2021 pre-seed and followed on in the August 2021 round, and the sources do not show whether it continued after (our reading of the Manifesto: a follower at the earliest stages that connects the company to funds and talent). Risks: the company almost failed in mid-2025 (eight clients, MRR under R$100,000), so the recovery is recent and based on company figures; success-based pricing shifts risk to Level and can slow revenue recognition; sales to hospitals are slow and depend on integrations; and in-house AI by large hospital groups and electronic-record vendors may compete.

sub_sector.value: Healthcare data intelligence for hospitals and insurers

milestones.value: Anthony Eigier and radiologist André Castilla start NeuralMed to use AI to detect findings in medical images and texts and help clinical decisions.
NeuralMed raises R$3.2 million from Alexia Ventures, Norte Ventures, MG Tech and the IDB, planning to serve more than 20 hospitals that year.
Grupo NotreDame Intermédica, a health insurer with 7.2 million beneficiaries, takes 9.29% in a R$10 million round and keeps using the technology as a customer.

NeuralMed closes its third round in 18 months, led by Good Karma Ventures, and launches Atlas to monitor chronic, oncology and pharma patients next to its original triage product TrIA, with a base of 5 million lives.
NeuralMed reaches its lowest point, with monthly recurring revenue under R$100,000 and eight clients, and starts a nine-month reset with a business-led offer.

NeuralMed relaunches as Level, with Mariana Gaspers as founding partner, two software packages, results-based terms, a first pharma contract and 36 clients; annual recurring revenue rises from under R$1.2 million to R$5 million.

description.value: Brazilian legal-tech platform that gives lawyers one subscription with calculators, asset searches, case management, an AI assistant (JusGPT) and payments for their daily work.

long_description.value: Jusfy is a Brazilian legal-tech platform that sells lawyers a single subscription with dozens of tools, and describes itself as the operating system of the Brazilian lawyer. It started with calculators for the everyday numbers of legal practice (alimony, bank-financing and abusive-interest reviews, FGTS, rent debts, labour and civil calculations), then added searches by CPF, CNPJ or licence plate to find a debtor's assets, a jurisprudence search across Brazilian courts, a bank of petition templates, electronic signature and, from 2025, JusProcessos (case workflow management, sold as an add-on) and JusGPT, an AI assistant that drafts petitions, summarises cases, reviews documents and transcribes WhatsApp audio. The company also sells website building and marketing tools for lawyers, a lawyer-client matching feature and, in 2026, Jusfy Pay, a payments and billing product that is the first step of a financial-services line for lawyers. The business is a subscription: in 2022 plans cost R$59 to R$97 a month depending on the number of searches, and today there are three plans (One, Ultimate, Black) with a 7-day free trial, plus customised packages for law firms, legal departments and municipalities, and partnerships with state bars (OABs). The company was founded by Rafael Saccol Bagolin, a lawyer from Rio Grande do Sul who had practised since 2010, with software engineer Juliano Lima and lawyer Cristian Bastianello; the registry shows the company opening on 26 January 2021. Bagolin has said the company was bootstrapped, had cash and was already at breakeven before its outside rounds. Traction: about 4,500 subscribers and R$300 thousand of monthly revenue in November 2022; 14 thousand clients at the start of 2024 and 28 thousand at its end, with R$25 million of revenue in 2024; 30 thousand clients in March 2025, 47 thousand and a team of 72 in August 2025; more than R$50 million of annual revenue in 2025 (up about 118%) and more than 60 thousand active professionals in 2026, with the state bars of Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and others among its clients. Backers: a R$7 million seed in December 2022 led by SaaSholic with Norte Ventures; a pre-Series A in March 2025 at about US$30 million valuation with MAYA Capital, SaaSholic, Norte, FJ Labs and The Legal Tech Fund; and a US$15 million Series A in July 2026 led by Quona Capital, the first Brazilian investment of Thomson Reuters Ventures. The money goes to financial services for lawyers (Jusfy Pay, credit), new AI products and a version for law students.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil has about 1.5 million registered lawyers (OAB register, November 2026, via Advbox), 72% of them self-employed (OAB and FGV's Perfil ADV study), and the CEO says about 87% work alone or in small firms. These professionals spend hours on low-value work, such as calculating alimony, reviewing financing contracts, searching for debtors' assets, drafting standard petitions and chasing clients for fees, with a patchwork of tools and no finance department; banks also treat lawyers as difficult customers (irregular income, they sue banks). The courts received 40.9 million new cases in 2025 (a record), so the workload keeps growing. Logic and why now: a cheap, all-in-one subscription removes the need to buy many point tools, calculators are a proven entry point because they save money immediately, and generative AI lets the same subscriber draft and review work that used to need a junior associate (Bagolin's stated view is that AI makes the solo lawyer 'superpowered'). The data and daily use of the platform give the company what banks lack to price credit to lawyers, which is the fintech step (Jusfy Pay, receivables advance). Market and reachable share: our own bottom-up estimate, not a sourced market size. Brazil has 1.5 million lawyers, of whom roughly 1.1 million are autonomous. Jusfy's 60 thousand active professionals are about 4% of all lawyers. If a strong outcome reaches 10% to 25% of lawyers (150 to 375 thousand) at R$1,000 to R$2,000 a year (its 2025 revenue of more than R$50 million over about 50 thousand clients is roughly R$1,000 per client, an assumption), the subscription market is about R$150 million to R$750 million a year in Brazil alone, and payments and credit could add revenue per user (Quona cites Toast and Shopify as the pattern). What is different: Jusfy started from calculators and searches and now bundles AI, workflow, payments and credit for the solo and small-firm lawyer, a segment large vendors tend to ignore; it grew from R$300 thousand a month in late 2022 to above R$4 million a month in 2025 while reportedly at breakeven. The sources read do not name competitors; Clio is the best-known comparable abroad (legal software plus payments), but no page with its figures could be read, so no figure is used. Fit with Norte: our reading is that a founder who is a practising lawyer, paired with an engineer, a bootstrapped business with revenue from early on, and a need for strong funds and operators on the cap table (SaaSholic, MAYA, FJ Labs, Quona, Thomson Reuters) fit Norte's stated model of backing obsessed founders and bringing top funds and talent; Norte was in the seed and the pre-Series A. Risks: regulation of the legal profession (a Startups.com.br headline says OAB-RJ allows AI but restricts legal-tech intermediation models), generative AI that large vendors or model providers can bundle, and a credit business that needs capital and risk control; the fintech launch slipped from September 2025 to 2026.

milestones.value: Jusfy opens as a company in Rio Grande do Sul (registry date 2021-01-26); lawyer Rafael Bagolin, engineer Juliano Lima and lawyer Cristian Bastianello start with calculators for lawyers.
Jusfy has about 4,500 subscribers, R$300 thousand of monthly revenue and plans of R$59 to R$97 a month, and sets the goal of becoming the lawyer's operating system in five years.
Revenue reaches R$2 million a month and R$25 million in the year while the client base doubles from 14 thousand to 28 thousand, mostly small law firms plus companies and city halls.

Renato Sacramento (ex-Hotmart) joins as chief product and technology officer and Emanuela Araujo (ex-Sami Saúde) as CFO; the team grows from 40 to 72 and clients from 27 thousand to 47 thousand by August.

Jusfy launches JusProcessos (case workflow, bought as an add-on by 10% of its 30 thousand subscribers) and JusGPT (a free AI assistant used by 15 thousand people a day), the two bets its pre-Series A funds.
Jusfy launches Jusfy Pay, its payments and billing product, which Quona says already earns far more revenue per user among adopters; it is the start of its financial services for lawyers.
Jusfy ends 2025 with more than R$50 million of revenue, up about 118%, and signs partnerships with the OABs of Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro that could reach up to 400 thousand lawyers.
Jusfy passes 60 thousand active lawyers and closes a US$15 million Series A led by Quona with Thomson Reuters Ventures, the corporation's first investment in Brazil.

description.value: Argentine company that acquires and partners with e-commerce brands in Latin America and offers pymes regional expansion, multichannel software, logistics, working capital and sourcing in China.

long_description.value: Elevva is an Argentine company that buys and partners with e-commerce brands in Latin America and helps small and mid-sized sellers scale them. It was started in 2021 by three Argentine e-commerce operators, Félix Elizalde, Maximiliano Chab and Aníbal de Frankenberg, who had run brands sold on the region's marketplaces, in categories such as home and garden, apparel, computing and electronics. The original idea was the 'e-commerce aggregator': Elevva would acquire or partner with leading sellers and put in its team, its technology and its capital, while the sellers brought their product knowledge, building a portfolio of brands that share logistics, sourcing and software across countries. From day one it also developed its own brands in categories where it saw no partners and set up its own operation in China. Its site today describes a wider menu for pymes: selling a brand to Elevva's portfolio; regionalisation (entering new countries with its infrastructure, logistics and regulatory know-how); a SaaS to run multichannel sales, inventory and shipping from one place together with a logistics operator; working-capital financing, which it launched as a lending unit in 2022; and product development and sourcing in China for private labels. The company says it moved from only acquiring brands to being a strategic partner for small businesses. The sources read do not say how it earns from each line, nor give revenue, headcount or the brands it owns. Timeline: it announced its Colombian launch in December 2021, seeking about 50 partner companies there; in December 2021 it made an offer for the Chilean fitness-equipment brand BodyTrainer, a deal that closed in April 2022; and in May 2022 it announced a US$30 million seed round with Asymmetric Capital, MatterScale Ventures, Canary, Redwood Ventures, Latitud, BluStone, Primo Ventures, Norte, Stanford GSB's 23Fund, Bolt Ventures and angels such as Pierpaolo Barbieri (Ualá), Ariel Lambrecht (99) and Matt Robinson (GoCardless), to keep adding brands, invest in technology and start the lending unit. The BodyTrainer purchase later became a dispute: the sellers say Elevva paid only the first half of the price (about UF 197,881, roughly 6 billion Chilean pesos) and sold inventory below cost, and in late 2025 they filed a criminal complaint for fraud in Chile after a Santiago arbitration court ordered Elevva to pay the balance with interest; Elevva denies any fraud, says the sellers hid information and has appealed the arbitral award. The matter is unresolved in the sources read. It matters for anyone assessing the company's acquisition model.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: in Latin America small and mid-sized businesses that sell online lack three things at once: regional scale (each country has its own marketplaces, logistics and rules), working capital, and operating know-how in logistics, inventory and marketing. Many founders also have no exit for a good brand. The founders' own reading in 2022 was that the opportunity in Latin America is large and different from other regions because e-commerce penetration is low and small firms have little access to capital. Logic and why now: a consolidator that buys or partners with brands, then shares software, logistics and sourcing from China across countries, can raise margins and growth on brands that are too small for big retailers; adding a lending unit and a SaaS turns the same expertise into services to non-acquired sellers. The 2020-2021 e-commerce boom gave sellers brands worth buying and gave investors an appetite for 'aggregators'. Market and share: no independent regional market size was read. As a size indicator, Argentina's e-commerce chamber (CACE) reported that Argentine online retail sold 645 million units in 2025, with sales of about 35.3 trillion pesos, up 60% nominally against 31% inflation (preliminary results, Revista Mercado); converting that figure to dollars needs an exchange rate we did not read, so we give no US figure. A strong outcome would be a portfolio and services platform across Argentina, Chile, Colombia and Mexico, but the sources do not disclose Elevva's revenue, so we cannot estimate its share. What is different: it combines acquisition with services and, according to its founders, with an operation in China and its own software; most Latin American peers are marketplaces or software vendors. Comparables abroad are cautionary: Thrasio, the leading Amazon aggregator, filed for Chapter 11 in February 2024 with about US$495 million of debt cut, after the roll-up craze faded with slowing e-commerce growth (CNBC). Fit with Norte: our reading is that a seed of US$30 million with global and regional funds, led by three operators with direct e-commerce experience, matches Norte's stated interest in obsessed founders and in bringing top funds onto the cap table; Norte joined as one of many investors in the seed, a follower role. Risks: the aggregator model depends on paying fair prices and integrating brands, and the BodyTrainer dispute (arbitral award against Elevva, criminal complaint, reputation) is direct evidence of the main risk; thin transparency (no revenue, no brand list, no news of a later round); macro volatility in Argentina; and competition from Chinese platforms such as Temu and Shein in categories like apparel (Forbes Argentina headline, not read).

milestones.value: Elevva starts operations in Colombia, aiming to become the partner of at least 50 e-commerce companies, as the founders put their record running regional marketplace brands to work.
Elevva closes the purchase of BodyTrainer, a Chilean seller of fitness equipment, after making its offer in December 2021; the price is to be paid in three instalments.
Elevva announces a US$30 million seed round and launches a lending unit that offers working capital to small sellers, to keep adding brands and invest in technology.

BodyTrainer's founders file a criminal fraud complaint in Chile after a Santiago arbitration court ordered Elevva to pay the unpaid balance; Elevva denies fraud and appeals the award, a public dispute over its acquisition practice.

description.value: Brazilian software company, from Campinas, whose platform runs, monitors and governs Python automations and AI-generated scripts inside companies, after starting as a developer-first RPA tool.

long_description.value: BotCity is a Brazilian software company, based in Campinas, that began as a code-first RPA (robotic process automation) tool and is now positioning itself as the governance and orchestration layer for Python automations and AI-generated scripts inside companies. It was started in 2020 by Lorhan Caproni (CEO, previously founder of the social-impact edtech Phomenta) and Gabriel Archanjo (CTO). Their bet went against the market: instead of drag-and-drop flowcharts for business users, as UiPath or Automation Anywhere sell, BotCity let developers write automations directly in Python, using computer vision to operate any screen, including desktop and legacy systems with no API, and added a platform to schedule, monitor and audit the robots. Early customers were technology-intensive Brazilian startups that used it, for example, to automate supplier approval (a task of up to ten days done by hand) or to integrate their products with customers' ERPs. Products today, on its English-language site, are an Orchestrator (scheduling, CI/CD, versioned and isolated runtimes, workload distribution, retries and logs for business-critical Python) and a tool, announced as Sentinel in 2025 and shown on the site as Sprav, that discovers code created by employees and their AI agents on endpoints, applies company policy and decides before execution what may run. The pitch is that once ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot return Python for any request to 'automate this', every employee can create code that runs outside IT's control (shadow AI), with risks of leaked sensitive data, flawed code and dependence on one person. BotCity says its customers include Bayer, LG, XP, QuintoAndar, Stone, Raia Drogasil and Sicredi (Startups.com.br, 2025), and it runs a distributed, remote team. It does not disclose customer count or revenue. Funding: a R$15 million seed in December 2021 co-led by Astella and the SoftBank Latin America Fund with Alexia Ventures, Norte Ventures and angels; admission to Y Combinator's Winter 2022 batch; and a R$65 million Series A announced on 25 September 2025 led by Four Rivers, with Y Combinator, Astella and Upload. The money is to fund global expansion (offices in the US and UK are targeted) and research on new products such as Sentinel.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: companies automate more and more of their operations with scripts, and since generative AI began returning working Python for any request (the CEO dates the turn to 2023-24), people outside IT create automations that run on company machines with no audit, access policy or owner. The IT Forum interview cites IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report, saying 87% of Brazilian companies still have no formal AI-governance policy, and surveys that 40% to 65% of employees at large companies use AI tools their IT area has not approved (figures as quoted by the article, we did not read the IBM report). Logic and why now: BotCity has been building the infrastructure to run, version, schedule and monitor Python automations since before the AI wave, so it is positioned to sell governance when the volume of scripts explodes. UiPath's CEO makes the same argument in 2026: when software gets cheaper to build, more gets built and the value shifts to the platforms that govern and orchestrate it (diginomica, March 2026; a vendor's view). Market and reachable share: no independent size for 'Python governance' exists, since the category is new. As rough anchors: the RPA market is projected at US$7.64 billion by 2028 (StartupHub, a secondary source quoting a forecast, treat as an order of magnitude), and UiPath, the listed leader, ended its fiscal year in January 2026 with US$1.853 billion of annual recurring revenue and US$1.611 billion of revenue (diginomica). A strong outcome for BotCity would be a niche but global enterprise-software business: for example 500 enterprise customers paying US$50 to US$150 thousand a year (our assumption) is US$25 to US$75 million of recurring revenue, about 1.5% to 4% of UiPath's ARR. What is different: it is built by developers for developers and started in code, while the large RPA vendors started from low-code for business users; it pairs governance with execution (Orchestrator) rather than only scanning for risks, it has a team already distributed and, per its CEO, a global structure from the start, and it is backed by Astella, SoftBank, Four Rivers and Y Combinator. Competitors named by the sources: UiPath and Automation Anywhere (RPA), plus the new AI governance vendors that the articles do not name. Fit with Norte: our reading is that two technical founders who built a global-first company out of Campinas, whose product needs distribution and top funds and operators on the cap table, match Norte's stated model of backing obsessed founders and bringing top funds to the cap table; Norte joined the seed alongside Astella and SoftBank. Risks: the repositioning from RPA to governance is recent and unproven in revenue (not disclosed); big RPA, cloud and security vendors can bundle governance; the Series A press does not list Norte, so follow-on is unconfirmed; the product name changed (Sentinel, Sprav) which may signal an unfinished product line.

milestones.value: Lorhan Caproni and Gabriel Archanjo start BotCity in Campinas to give developers a code-first alternative to drag-and-drop RPA, using computer vision to operate any application.
BotCity announces a R$15 million seed with Astella, SoftBank Latin America Fund, Alexia Ventures and Norte Ventures, and sets a goal of 5,000 developers worldwide within 18 months.
BotCity goes through Y Combinator (Winter 2022 batch) .
The spread of ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot, which return Python code for any request, turns BotCity's Python-first approach into a governance problem, in the CEO's account.

BotCity announces a R$65 million Series A led by Four Rivers at its first AI & Automation Summit, with more than 400 leaders, and unveils BotCity Sentinel to find automations running outside IT control.
BotCity targets commercial offices in the United States and the United Kingdom and promotes its governance platform at the Gartner CIO & IT Executive conference in São Paulo in September.

description.value: Silicon Valley startup, founded by Brazilians, that built foundation models for banks to predict credit risk and customer behaviour from their own data; acquired by Nubank in June 2024.

long_description.value: Hyperplane was a data-intelligence startup that built foundation models for banks: a platform on which a financial institution could train, evaluate and deploy self-supervised deep-learning models on its own customer and transaction data, to predict credit risk, collections, churn, income or the next product a customer would buy. Instead of the regressions and gradient-boosted trees most banks use, Hyperplane's neural networks were trained on sequences of unstructured behaviour, such as click streams, transactions and text, and a bank could train hundreds of bespoke models from one hub. It was founded in Silicon Valley in 2022 (one article says 2021) by two Brazilians, Felipe Lamounier (CEO, who had worked at TOTVS and was part of the founding team of StartSe) and Felipe Meneses (the first Brazilian to win a Thiel Fellowship, who was studying at Stanford), by Daniel Silva (previously in AI at Google, described as a head at Google Brain) and by Rohan Ramanath (from LinkedIn's AI division). They chose Brazil as the first market because Brazilian banks adopt financial technology fast, and worked in stealth with three banks as design partners, which grew to about a dozen Brazilian institutions by launch; one neobank raised its credit-limit transaction volume by 46% with better income prediction. In December 2023 Hyperplane came out of stealth with a US$6 million seed (about R$30 million) led by Lachy Groom with SV Angel, Clocktower Technology Ventures, Liquid2 Ventures, Soma Capital, Latitud, Atman Capital, Crestone VC and Norte, and said it would expand to the United States. Seven months later, on 26 June 2024, Nubank announced it had acquired the company, a transaction Startups.com.br's sources say was done by share swap and whose price was not disclosed. Nubank's CEO David Vélez called the deal small for the bank but extremely strategic, saying tests showed Hyperplane's models beat Nubank's own credit-decision algorithms on the area-under-the-curve metric. The founders said they chose to bet on the bank most ready to use the technology rather than sell to many institutions. The team now works inside Nubank, and in 2025 Nubank reported training and deploying billion-parameter foundation models across several predictive use cases after eight months of work with the Hyperplane engineers.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: banks sit on large first-party datasets (transactions, app behaviour, customer service text) but most of their predictive models still rely on tabular features and linear or tree-based models, so a large share of the signal in unstructured and sequential data is unused. Nubank's CEO says about 70% of banks' global profit pool is in credit, so gains of 5% to 15% in credit decisions are very large for a bank (his statement, Brazil Journal). Logic and why now: the 2022-2023 progress in large sequence models made it plausible to train a foundation model on a bank's own data, and the founders, from Google Brain, LinkedIn and the Brazilian ecosystem, had the technical and sales profile to deliver it. Brazil's open-finance and Pix environment (Lamounier's argument) made Brazilian banks eager, early customers. Market and share: no independent market size was found. Our own estimate, with assumptions: if about 1,000 mid-sized and large banks and lenders worldwide could pay US$200 to US$500 thousand a year for a model platform, the revenue pool is US$200 to US$500 million; a leading vendor reaching 10% to 20% of it would have US$20 to US$100 million of recurring revenue. The actual outcome was an acquisition by Nubank, a customer with more than 100 million customers and quarterly revenue above US$2.7 billion (Yahoo/TechCrunch). The price is undisclosed, so we cannot say the return. What is different: it was one of the first companies to sell foundation models trained on a bank's own data, and Nubank's tests, according to its CEO, showed an improvement over its internal models; a dozen Brazilian bank customers before launch is strong traction for a seed company. No competitors were named in the sources read. Fit with Norte: our reading is that a technical founding team from Google Brain and LinkedIn, aimed at Brazil, with a US lead investor (Lachy Groom) and Latin American funds such as Latitud, fits Norte's model of backing obsessed founders and bringing top funds to the cap table; Norte took part in the seed, which ended seven months later in an acquisition by Nubank. Norte's own return is not known. Risks: a narrow product that a large customer can build in-house (the reason Nubank bought it); concentration in a few Brazilian banks; and the uncertain price. This company is an exit, so the main risk for a reader is that the outcome was small and the return undisclosed.

milestones.value: Felipe Lamounier, Daniel Silva, Rohan Ramanath and Felipe Meneses start Hyperplane in Silicon Valley and work in stealth with three banks as design partners, starting with Brazil.
Hyperplane comes out of stealth with a US$6 million seed led by Lachy Groom, already serving about a dozen Brazilian banks; one neobank reports a 46% rise in credit-limit transaction volume.
Nubank announces the acquisition of Hyperplane, seven months after its seed; Nubank's CEO says tests showed its models beat the bank's own credit algorithms.

Nubank says it has deployed billion-parameter foundation models in several predictive use cases in the first eight months after the acquisition, with the Hyperplane founders still supporting the work.

description.value: Brazilian startup, born in the UK, that runs a trade-in platform for used smartphones: stores scan and value the old phone, and Doji sells it to registered buyers for a commission.

long_description.value: Doji is a trade-in platform for used smartphones. Retailers, including Claro and TIM franchises, use its software to offer customers a discount or credit for the old phone as part payment; a customer or store clerk scans the device, an AI model inspects it from photos and about 300 possible defects (an earlier description says more than 70 checks), discounts only the cost of repairing each fault and checks first that the phone is not reported lost, stolen or still financed. Doji then offers the phone, in a stock-exchange-like order book, to registered buyers such as resellers, repair shops and insurers, who have said in advance how much they will pay for each model, and picks the phone up from the store. It is asset-light, charges stores no monthly fee and earns a commission of 10% to 20% on each sale; it is also launching advance-payment and financing products for buyers. Doji was founded by Fernando Montera Filho (CEO), Satyen Fakey and Bilal Khan, who met during a master's programme at Oxford. Montera, a Brazilian serial entrepreneur who sold Becommerce to Mercado Livre in 2017 and worked there until 2021 (and sold another venture, Hubsters, to CloudKitchens in 2023), was under a non-compete in Latin America, so the team started in the United Kingdom in 2021 with a consumer marketplace that priced phones like commodities, so that every iPhone in a given condition sells at one price. The idea came when he was disappointed with the dealer's offer for his car and found that used goods pass through many intermediaries. The UK business raised a US$3 million seed in November 2021 led by Canary with Norte Ventures, 1289 Capital and angels (US$800 thousand before, US$3.8 million in total), grew to about R$1.7 million of monthly revenue in the fourth quarter of 2023, but could not raise a Series A: marketplaces had high customer-acquisition cost and the UK market already had a clear winner, Back Market. After about 18 months, Doji opened in Brazil in August 2023 (RBS Ventures invested in October 2023); it closed the UK operation in January 2024, rebuilt the product as trade-in as a service in a few weeks and had its first Brazilian contracts and revenue by May 2024. In 2025 it raised about R$10 million (reported as US$2 million) in June with Positive Ventures, Niu Ventures, Seedstars, Canary, Mago Capital, Exit North Ventures and, per PEGN, Raio Capital and Norte, plus R$3 million from Indicator Capital in November. By then it served 350 stores, moved R$3.5 million of goods a month, had processed more than 50 thousand phones, had 25 people and said it grew 35% a month, aiming for breakeven and a Series A within a year.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilians keep a large stock of phones in drawers (the CEO says about R$1 trillion, and that 80% of people never sell an old phone), phones lose about 30% of value a year, and the current ways to sell are either consumer-to-consumer (photos, descriptions, scams) or trade-in programmes at low prices run by intermediaries that force buyers to take whole lots. Logic and why now: trade-in lets the retailer sell more new phones, the consumer gets a fair price, and buyers pay a higher unit price for just the models they want, so the platform earns a commission without holding stock. Smartphone prices are high in Brazil, the official market sold 31.8 million units and R$47.7 billion in 2025 (Abinee/IDC via Tecnoblog), and the largest trade-in player, Trocafone, recently entered extrajudicial recovery (Brazil Journal, November 2025), leaving the segment without a clear leader. Market and share: our bottom-up estimate. If trade-ins and resales of used phones in Brazil reach 20% to 40% of the 31.8 million units sold new (6 to 13 million phones a year, assumption) at an average of R$600 to R$1,200 (assumption), the flow is about R$4 billion to R$15 billion; at a 10% to 20% commission the revenue pool is R$0.4 billion to R$3 billion. Doji's current R$3.5 million a month of goods is about R$42 million a year, under 1% of the low end; a 5% to 10% share of the pool would mean R$20 million to R$300 million of revenue. The CEO's R$1 trillion figure is a claim, not a market size. What is different: it is agnostic and sits in the store, working with operators and franchises, instead of buying phones itself like Trocafone, and its order-book model pays more per phone to buyers who want specific models; the founders have already built and sold two companies. Competitors named: Trocafone, Allied's Trocafy and Assurant (which buys phones from Vivo's trade-in), and Back Market in Europe. Fit with Norte: our reading is that a repeat founder who found a market and changed course quickly when the first thesis failed matches Norte's stated interest in obsessed founders, and Norte stayed with the company from the 2021 seed to the 2025 round (named in the 2021 articles and by PEGN in 2025), a follower role alongside Canary. Risks: the 2021-2023 marketplace did not scale and the company had to start again; the business depends on retail and operator partners; margin pressure if buyers or retailers integrate the same technology; and thin disclosure (no audited revenue).

milestones.value: Fernando Montera Filho and two Oxford classmates start Doji in the United Kingdom, a marketplace that prices each used phone model and condition like a commodity.
Doji announces a US$3 million seed led by Canary after ending its beta weeks earlier with 1,000 registered users, 100 transactions and 25 employees across the UK, Brazil and India.
After the seed Doji launches in the UK with a team in London and Birmingham.
Doji opens in Brazil after 18 months in the UK, and RBS Ventures invests in October, mainly in media, to build the brand in Rio Grande do Sul.

Unable to raise a Series A in the UK (revenue was R$1.7 million a month at the end of 2023), Doji closes its UK operation and rebuilds as trade-in as a service in Brazil, with its first revenue by May.
Doji raises about R$10 million (US$2 million) after its pivot and begins to offer advance-payment and financing products; it has 25 people and grows about 35% a month, in its own account.
With a R$3 million extension from Indicator Capital Doji serves 350 stores, including Claro and TIM franchises, and moves R$3.5 million of goods a month.

description.value: Brazilian B2B auto-parts marketplace that lets mechanic workshops find, compare and order the right part for a car by licence plate, with fast delivery from many suppliers.

long_description.value: Mecanizou is a Brazilian B2B marketplace for auto parts that connects independent mechanic workshops with parts suppliers. The workshop enters the car's licence plate and the part it needs, by app, website or WhatsApp; the company's proprietary part-identification technology, backed by a team of specialists, finds the right part among hundreds of thousands of items from many suppliers and returns, in under a minute, options with prices, brands and delivery times, and logistics partners deliver it to the workshop within hours. The workshop pays nothing to use the platform and Mecanizou earns a commission on the parts it sells; it also sets the selling price, helped by machine learning, from the prices suppliers suggest. The site also invites suppliers to join, and says that car owners can compare parts and buy with a guarantee of origin; its customers say they appreciate multi-plate carts, weekly coupons and credit terms. The company was started in 2021 by Ian Faria (CEO), who had been an executive at Kavak in Brazil, and André Simões (CTO). They visited workshops to understand their pains, noticed that the only technology mechanics used was WhatsApp, and began, in a rented house in the north of São Paulo, with a spreadsheet that produced a PDF and a test with 40 workshops and seven people. Growth in the first year was around 70% a month. In January 2022 it raised a US$4 million seed (press says led by Monashees, Alexia and H2O Capital, while LAVCA says Alexia led it). In March 2023 it raised a US$14.5 million Series A (R$76 million) led by Monashees with Alexia Ventures, FJ Labs and Dalus Capital, to expand beyond the north zone to the rest of the city, the ABC region and Guarulhos and to invest in data and part-identification technology. At that point it had more than 1,000 registered workshops, more than 200 suppliers and over 600 thousand items; by February 2024 it reported 1,200 workshops, 300 suppliers, 700 thousand parts and a waiting list of 2,000 workshops, still serving only the city of São Paulo. In 2024 it launched AIrton, its first AI assistant, to serve workshops faster on WhatsApp, and hired a former Creditas data director as head of technology and data. The company puts the national opportunity at 121 thousand workshops, 48 thousand parts stores and distributors and a potential US$22 billion of sales (its own estimate). The sources read do not give revenue, profit or news after mid-2024.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: in Brazil, mechanics decide which parts are bought for most repairs, yet they have no digital tool to find the right part for a given car. The supply chain (automaker, parts factory, distributor, retailer) is fragmented and asymmetric, one part fits several models, and workshops depend on phone calls and WhatsApp to get quotes, so repairs take longer and wrong parts are common (Convergência Digital, 2024). Logic and why now: a marketplace that solves the identification problem (which part fits this plate) and then offers price comparison and fast delivery attracts workshops, and the workshops' demand brings suppliers. The company charges the supplier side a commission, so workshops use it free. Smartphone and WhatsApp habits and cheap last-mile delivery in São Paulo made this possible, and AI helps catalogue and match parts. Market and share: Mecanizou's own figures are 121 thousand workshops, 48 thousand parts stores and a US$22 billion potential (a company claim, not independent). Our check, with assumptions: if a workshop buys R$10 thousand to R$20 thousand of parts a month, 121 thousand workshops buy R$14 billion to R$29 billion a year; a commission of 8% to 15% (assumption) gives a revenue pool of about R$1 billion to R$4 billion; a strong outcome of 5% to 10% of workshop purchases would be R$0.7 billion to R$2.9 billion of volume and roughly R$60 million to R$430 million of commission revenue. This is order of magnitude only. What is different: it focuses on the mechanic, not the car owner, and invests in proprietary part-identification (plate to part) and a specialist team; it claimed 70% monthly growth in its first year. No competitors are named in the sources read. Fit with Norte: our reading is that two operating founders (an ex-Kavak executive and a CTO) building a data-heavy marketplace in a traditional offline sector, with Alexia, Monashees and FJ Labs on the cap table, fits Norte's stated way of backing obsessed founders and bringing top funds to the table; Norte's participation, however, could not be confirmed in any page we read. Risks: marketplaces have thin margins and heavy logistics; the sources show growth only in São Paulo city until at least 2024; last public news is from mid-2024, so current traction is unknown; and incumbents (distributors, large retailers) can build their own ordering tools.

sub_sector.value: B2B auto parts marketplace for workshops

milestones.value: Ian Faria and André Simões, after visiting workshops, start Mecanizou in a rented house in the north of São Paulo, testing the idea with a spreadsheet and 40 workshops.
Mecanizou raises a US$4 million seed and expands within the north zone of São Paulo, growing about 70% a month in its first year.
A US$14.5 million Series A led by Monashees funds expansion to the rest of São Paulo, ABC and Guarulhos; the platform has more than 1,000 workshops and 200 suppliers and 600 thousand items.
Mecanizou serves 1,200 workshops with 300 suppliers and 700 thousand parts, with 2,000 more on a waiting list, using machine learning to match parts to cars and deliver in hours.
Mecanizou launches AIrton, an AI assistant that serves workshops on WhatsApp, and hires Vinícius Coimbra, ex-Creditas data director, as head of technology and data.

description.value: Argentine healthtech that sells a SaaS platform and APIs to health insurers, funds and providers to run digital care: appointments, video consultation, e-prescription, billing and patient follow-up.

long_description.value: Osana Salud (Osana) is an Argentine healthtech that builds technology infrastructure for the health industry: instead of selling to patients, it sells to the organisations that finance and deliver care, such as health insurers, social-security funds, hospitals and pharma. Its SaaS platform, called Osana Open Health Platform, is omnichannel and meant to be integrated quickly through simple APIs with a provider's or insurer's own management systems, and it covers the whole patient journey: digital membership card, provider directory, appointment booking, video consultation, payments and billing, continuous follow-up of patients with chronic conditions, treatment adherence, e-prescription, electronic health record and digital pharmacy. The company's argument is that insurers and providers can launch new services faster and with lower development cost by plugging into a common layer instead of building and integrating many separate systems. Osana started in 2019, a few months before the pandemic, with the founder's own money, and was built by Andrés Lawson (CEO), a co-founder of the fashion e-commerce company Dafiti who left it in 2014 and also founded and chairs the Argentine Health and Technology Chamber, and Jorge López (co-founder and COO). The first step was to build alliances with providers and insurers and iterate the product, and within a few months, according to Lawson, hundreds of thousands of people were using services through its technology. In August 2021 Osana announced a US$20 million Series A led by General Catalyst, with Quiet Capital, Preface Ventures, FJ Labs, AforeVC, K50 Ventures and Addition, which with an earlier unannounced seed brought its 2021 funding to about US$26 million, billed as the largest Series A for a Latin American healthtech. At that time it said its software reached more than 6 million patients, with contracts with providers and insurers including Sanatorio Güemes and PAMI (a fund with about 5 million members), and it planned to triple its team with remote hires and open offices in São Paulo and Mexico City. By August 2022 it had more than 100 staff and commercial operations in Argentina, Brazil and Mexico, said it wanted 60% of its revenue to come from Brazil and Mexico by 2023, and named further clients such as Hospital Austral and Hominis. It was listed by CB Insights among the 150 most promising healthtechs in the world and by HolonIQ among the top 50 in Latin America, and won the Sadosky innovation award of the Argentine software chamber (CESSI) in late 2022. The company's site was republished in February 2026, so it is still operating, but the sources read give no revenue or any financing after 2021. Press-release claims about the World Economic Forum (Technology Pioneer, Edison Alliance, HEAL) appeared only in search results and are not used here.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Latin American health systems are fragmented between insurers, social-security funds and providers that run on old management systems; around half of people in the region lack access to quality care, according to the founder, and each insurer or hospital that wants digital services (appointments, video consultation, e-prescription, follow-up of chronic patients) has to build and integrate them from scratch, which is slow and costly. Logic and why now: the pandemic made video consultation and e-prescription standard practice in a few months, so payers and providers needed to deploy them quickly. A platform with APIs and ready modules reduces time to market and development cost for each client, and the same technology serves many customers. Market and share: no independent market size was found. Our own estimate, with all inputs as assumptions: if 1,000 insurers, funds and large provider networks in Argentina, Brazil and Mexico could pay US$100 to US$300 thousand a year for such a platform, the pool is US$100 to US$300 million; a leading vendor with 10% to 20% share would have US$10 to US$60 million of annual revenue. The company says its software reached more than 6 million people in 2021, and its largest known customer, PAMI, alone serves about 5 million members (LAVCA/TechCrunch). What is different: Osana sells infrastructure to payers and providers rather than competing with them, is developer-friendly and API-based, and had unusually strong early backing for a Latin American healthtech (General Catalyst, a health-focused investor, and Addition). Competitors are not named in the sources read. Fit with Norte: our reading is that a repeat founder (Lawson co-founded Dafiti) with a regional infrastructure thesis fits Norte's stated interest in obsessed founders; Norte appears in an aggregator list of seed investors (Dealroom) but is not named in any page we read, so its role, and whether it was a follower, is unconfirmed. Risks: enterprise health customers buy slowly and often pay late, the company needs scale in Brazil and Mexico to reach its plan, there is no public financing after 2021 and no revenue disclosure, and large Argentine, Brazilian and global health-IT vendors can offer overlapping modules.

sub_sector.value: Health infrastructure platform for insurers and providers

milestones.value: Andrés Lawson, co-founder of Dafiti, and Jorge López start Osana with their own money and build the first version of a health infrastructure platform just before the pandemic.

Osana announces a US$20 million Series A led by General Catalyst, serving more than 6 million patients through contracts such as Sanatorio Güemes and PAMI, and plans to triple its team and open offices in São Paulo and Mexico City.
Osana has more than 100 employees and commercial operations in Argentina, Brazil and Mexico, and is named by CB Insights among the world's 150 most promising healthtechs.
Osana wins the Sadosky Innovation award of the Argentine software chamber for its Osana Open Health Platform, an omnichannel SaaS for payers, providers and pharma.

description.value: Brazilian health-data company that helps brokers, employers, operators and hospitals audit and manage corporate health plans, using independent claims analysis and clinical review to negotiate price adjustments.

long_description.value: Suridata is a Brazilian health-data company that helps the buyers of corporate health plans negotiate and manage them. Its customers are insurance brokers (corretoras), employers, health plan operators (including self-managed schemes and cooperatives) and hospitals. The company collects the fragmented claims data that operators send, cleans and reorganises it, audits medical bills, and returns independent reports and clinical analysis made by physicians and nurses trained in population health, so that a broker or HR team can face the operator's own numbers with its own. The pitch is that the operator always arrives at a price-adjustment negotiation with its data, and Suridata gives the buyer a counter-argument. There are three core products, offered in levels of depth: Suri Alerta (monthly monitoring of each policy's loss ratio, with alerts on usage spikes, at-risk chronic patients and high-cost cases, plus a broker dashboard and ANS benchmarking), Suri Controle (adds audit of medical bills, a clinical commentary from Suridata's physicians and negotiation-ready indicators) and Suri Gestão (the full service, which lets a broker offer active health management without a medical team of its own, with action plans, absence management, a map of the whole population, pharmacy data, annual diagnoses and monthly forecasts of hospitalisation costs). Complementary tools include a white-label portal with the broker's branding, English reports for multinational headquarters, benchmark reports, occupational-health cross-checks and in-person health assessments. Its own cases, which are anonymised and are the company's claims, include a request for a 68.7% price adjustment reduced to 14% after an analysis of each active hospital authorisation, a 39.13% request reduced to the medical-inflation index, a loss ratio of 124.93% corrected to 104.93% after finding an undue tax in the calculation, a refund after a fraud with 282 reimbursed consultations (R$55 thousand), and R$4 million saved over two years from a preventive-exam campaign. The company's site and the registry say it started in 2018 (the legal company opened on 5 November 2018, in São Paulo); it runs as a 100% remote team and blogs and speaks at industry events such as the UNIDAS and CONAU congresses and AI Brasil Experience in 2026. No press article about its funding was readable: an aggregator lists Norte Ventures and the insurance group Alper's technology arm as investors in a 2023 round, but this is not confirmed by any page we could read.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: in Brazil, corporate health plans are bought through brokers and negotiated each year with the operator, which has the claims data and proposes the price adjustment. In 2025 collective plans had an average adjustment of 11.15% (ANS data reported by Jornal de Brasília and Monitor Mercantil), 14.81% for contracts with up to 29 lives, and the buyer usually has no independent way to check whether the operator's loss ratio is right. Logic: a third party that cleans and audits the data, finds billing errors and cost drivers and issues clinical analysis gives the broker a concrete argument, and its own cases show reductions of about 14 to 55 percentage points in a requested adjustment. The product is sold in levels, so a broker can start cheap with monitoring and move up. Why now: persistent medical inflation (11% in 2025, per a Suridata blog post title) raises the value of cost control, and AI and data tools make data cleaning cheaper. Market and share: no independent size could be established. Our reasoning, with no figures sourced for the number of brokers or buyers: the product serves Brazil's collective health plans, which in 2025 average a double-digit annual price increase, so even a small percentage saved on a large premium base is valuable, but we could not read the number of beneficiaries, premium volume or brokers. A reasonable path is a niche software-plus-services business, not a mass-market platform. What is different: the mix of data engineering with physicians and nurses, independent reports aimed at brokers (distribution through them) and white-label portals. Competitors named by aggregators include Blue AI; other healthtechs (Axenya, HealthBit) compete for the employer's health-cost budget. Fit with Norte: our reading, which is not confirmed, is that a technical data company inside the health insurance chain, in the stage and domain Norte backs, could have been a small, network-driven investment (an aggregator lists Norte in 2023), but no readable page names Norte, so we do not rely on it. Risks: dependence on the operators' data formats and goodwill, services-heavy delivery that limits software margins, a low-visibility company with no public financing or customer count, and large brokers building their own analytics.

sub_sector.value: Health plan data analytics and auditing

milestones.value: Suridata Tecnologia opens in São Paulo to turn health-plan data into decisions for buyers of corporate plans.

Suridata stays visible in the supplementary-health sector, writing on and attending the UNIDAS congress, CONAU (cooperatives) and AI Brasil Experience, and offering three product tiers (Suri Alerta, Suri Controle, Suri Gestão).

description.value: Brazilian software that lets restaurants and delivery businesses take and grow orders on their own WhatsApp channel, with an AI attendant, digital menu, loyalty and marketing tools, without marketplace commissions.

long_description.value: Brendi is a Brazilian software company that helps restaurants and delivery businesses sell through their own channel, mainly WhatsApp, instead of paying commissions to delivery marketplaces such as iFood. Its virtual attendant, Brenda, is an AI that answers customers at any hour, takes text and voice orders, suggests extras and sends the Pix payment link; around her the platform bundles a branded digital menu, order management and printing, WhatsApp broadcasts, a customer-recovery tool, a cashback loyalty programme, coupons, profit reports and a live view of the delivery. The website now describes a team of eleven AI agents (service, paid traffic, social media, deliveries, finance, menu and others), a 15-day free trial and plans priced by the restaurant's monthly revenue, with paid traffic sold separately; the company says it charges 0% commission per order. The story, as told on the company's own page: Daniel Frageri, now CEO, left his engineering course at ITA to help his family's bakery, saw that every delivery owner had the same problem and started Brendi as a marketing agency (paid traffic and social media) for delivery businesses. Customers arrived but manual, slow service could not keep up, the operation collapsed and the agency failed. The founders restarted from that pain and built Brenda, then grew into a full platform, and the company says active clients grew 20 times. A 2022 city-hall article says it was created by three ITA graduates in São José dos Campos, was in the Startup São José programme, had 45 delivery clients and 20 employees, had received R$650 thousand with Locaweb among its investors, and aimed at 300 clients by the end of that year. By the 2026 seed round it had 7,100 restaurants (85% in smaller cities, where delivery apps are less present), had grown processed orders from 140 thousand to 420 thousand a week in a year, reported annual recurring revenue of nearly US$5 million and a gross margin above 40%, and planned to reach 10,000 to 15,000 restaurants by year end; part of the round bought back shares from early angels. In November 2026 the company says it serves more than 9,500 restaurants, more than 70 million WhatsApp conversations and more than R$2 billion in restaurant sales, and it opened a key-accounts area for restaurant chains and franchises, with royalty and marketing-fee collection on the platform.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil's food-service sector had revenue of R$495 billion in 2025 (Abrasel; R$540 billion projected for 2026) and more than 1.5 million establishments, most of them small. Delivery apps already take 58% of delivery sales (99Food/Abrasel survey) and charge commissions that the 2022 city-hall article puts at up to 30%, so a small owner gives away margin and does not own the customer relationship. Logic: the Brazilian customer already orders by WhatsApp, and an AI that answers instantly, takes the order and closes the payment turns the owner's own channel into a sales channel with no commission, while the loyalty, broadcast and recovery tools bring the customer back. Why now: cheap language models made 24-hour conversational ordering viable (the company's own story shows the earlier manual agency broke on service volume), and Pix removed the payment friction. Market and share: no independent figure for software spend exists in the pages read. Our bottom-up estimate: the company reports almost US$5 million of ARR over 7,100 restaurants, about US$700 a year (about R$330 a month) per client; if 1.5 million establishments are the ceiling, a realistic reachable base is a fraction of those that do delivery, say 100,000 to 200,000 restaurants over several years (our assumption, about 7 to 13% of establishments), which at today's price is roughly US$70 to 140 million of ARR, and more if the platform adds payments, credit and marketing spend. This is a range for Brazil only, not a forecast. Different: it sells to the smallest restaurants in smaller cities, where 85% of clients are, with an AI-first product that evolved from a failed agency, so the founders learned the service bottleneck first-hand. Competitors named in search results: OlaClick, Saipos, Delivery Direto and Kuppi; we did not compare features. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders and helps with connections, funds on the cap table and hiring; Brendi's founder is a young ITA engineer who rebuilt after a failure, and the 2026 round brought Propel Ventures, a US fund, and angels from iFood and Hyperplane, which fits Norte's follower and connector role (our reading, not Norte's statement). Risks: low switching cost and many rivals in restaurant software; dependence on WhatsApp (Meta) pricing and rules; small customers churn; the iFood and 99Food apps may cut commissions or add direct-sales tools.

sub_sector.value: AI order-taking and CRM for restaurant delivery

milestones.value: Brendi starts in São José dos Campos as a marketing agency for delivery businesses, selling paid traffic and social media, founded by three ITA graduates including Daniel Frageri.

With R$650 thousand raised in recent months and Locaweb among its investors, Brendi serves 45 delivery businesses with 20 employees and aims at 300 clients by year end, helped by the Startup São José programme.
Brendi announces a US$6.6 million seed led by Propel Ventures, with 7,100 restaurants and 420 thousand weekly orders, to reach 10,000 to 15,000 restaurants and buy back early angels' shares.
Brendi hires Juliana Cicereli as head of key accounts, a new area for restaurant chains and franchises, and says it now serves more than 9,500 restaurants.

description.value: Brazilian AI lab with a foundation model that reads a company's relational database and predicts outcomes such as default, churn and fraud, sold to banks, telecoms and marketplaces by API and batch.

long_description.value: Avra is a Brazilian AI lab that builds a foundation model for relational data, the tables of customers, accounts, transactions and events that sit in a company's database, and sells predictions on top of it. Instead of flattening those tables into one row per customer, as traditional models do, its model (called Avra RFM on the website) reads the database as it is, as a graph that changes over time, and predicts outcomes such as churn, default, fraud or conversion without building a new model for each question. It is delivered by API for live decisions, in batch written to the client's data warehouse, as relational embeddings that the client's own models can use as features, and through a visual workflow tool called Studio; every model is backtested on the client's history and run in shadow beside the current one before it decides anything, and each client's data and model are isolated. Revenue comes from enterprise contracts with banks, telecoms and marketplaces, supported by what the company calls forward-deployed engineers who work inside the customer.
