Origin: the company was started in early 2024 (registry opening 2024-02-06) by Viviane Meister, CEO, and Bruno Alano, a former OpenAI researcher, and began as an AI service for small and medium businesses, using a graph model of the Brazilian business ecosystem to score credit risk and predict customer value; it gained visibility when Nubank bought Hyperplane, the closest competitor in audience segmentation. In July 2024 it announced a US$2 million round led by MAYA Capital with Norte Ventures and Sequoia Scout, serving two large companies and testing with six more. Since then its pitch has widened from SMEs to any relational enterprise data. Its published case says a leading Brazilian bank added Avra's prediction to its SME credit-card policy and flagged 70% of future defaulters before approval while keeping 95% approval, lifting its in-house model by 4 KS points, with the bank's own risk team running the backtest; the bank is now testing it for new approvals and for recovering rejected applicants. The company publishes research notes (a three-part series on its graph foundation models, the last in August 2026), lists nine open roles in São Paulo and remote, and in November 2026 appears at the Bloomberg Línea Summit.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: banks, telecoms and marketplaces decide on credit, fraud, churn and pricing with models trained on flat tables, although the information that matters is in who is connected to whom: a supplier that pays late, a partner's other firm entering recovery. In Brazil this is sharpest for small companies, which Sebrae counts at almost 24 million active small businesses in the last quarter of 2025, most with little history at any bank. Logic: a graph model pre-trained on the Brazilian business network can score a company from its CNPJ alone, including ones the lender has never served; the published case reports 70% of future defaulters flagged with 95% approval kept and a 4 KS-point lift over the bank's own rating (the company's own account, backtested by the bank). It sits beside the incumbent model, so the buyer takes little risk. Why now: graph neural networks and foundation-model techniques are mature, open finance and data-sharing rules enlarge the data lenders can use, and Nubank's purchase of Hyperplane showed that AI-for-credit data teams are worth buying. Market and share: no independent size for relational-AI software was found. Our estimate, labelled as an assumption: Brazil has perhaps 50 to 150 large banks, fintechs, telecoms and marketplaces that decide credit or churn at scale; at an assumed contract of US$300 thousand to US$1 million a year, winning 20 to 40 of them is roughly US$6 to 40 million of annual revenue in Brazil, with more upside in Latin America. Different: schema-agnostic pre-training on relational data, a Brazil-specific company graph, and research-grade publishing, while most rivals sell one use case. Comparables: Fundamental raised US$255 million in 2026 for a tabular foundation model (TechCrunch headline in search results, not read), which shows investor appetite for the category, and Hyperplane sold to Nubank. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than Norte; Avra's founders include a former OpenAI researcher, and Norte's network of operators can open banks, which is where enterprise sales are decided (our reading, not Norte's statement). Risks: long enterprise sales cycles and concentration in a few clients; data-access and privacy rules (LGPD) over company data; strong rivals, including the banks' own teams and global labs; the pivot from SMEs to a general platform may stretch a small team.

sub_sector.value: Relational foundation models for risk and prediction

milestones.value: Avra opens as a company in Brazil (registry opening 2024-02-06), started in January by Viviane Meister and Bruno Alano as an AI platform for credit risk and sales prediction for small and medium businesses.

Avra announces a US$2 million round led by MAYA Capital, with Norte Ventures and Sequoia Scout, serving two large companies and testing with six others, after Nubank's purchase of Hyperplane raised its visibility.
Avra publishes the third part of its series on graph foundation models in production, reporting that relational embeddings were the largest driver of improvement in a live client deployment.
Avra appears at the Bloomberg Línea Summit on 23 November and has nine open roles in research, engineering and enterprise sales.

description.value: Brazilian waste-management company that runs collection, transport and final destination for businesses through one digital platform and contract, using an asset-light network of audited partners.

long_description.value: Musa is a Brazilian waste-management company that runs the whole chain, from collection to final destination, for businesses, through one digital platform and one contract. It started as an asset-light marketplace that connects waste generators (bars, restaurants, supermarkets, offices, industries), haulers and recyclers, with no trucks or landfills of its own: it supplies the bags and bins, trains the staff, separates waste into organic, recyclable and other, schedules daily pickups and shows the process in an app. The pitch is that 100% of the waste becomes a product or service: organics go to partners that turn them into fertiliser and, with fly larvae, into animal-feed protein, and recyclables go back to industry. Today the site presents Musa as the infrastructure that unifies the links of Brazil's waste chain: collection, transport and final destination of hazardous, non-hazardous and recyclable waste for units anywhere in the country, a network of audited partners, automatic issue and closing of the mandatory transport and final-destination documents (MTR, CDF, DMR), carbon and performance indicators, a dashboard of cost per unit, and a 30-day start (map flows, design the strategy, mobilise the partners, release the Portal Musa and train the team); the customer gets one invoice for many sites and Musa takes the margin from a better price in its network. Where it came from: Fabrício Guimarães, formerly of Philips marketing, and Martin Junck, a Frenchman, saw in a trip to Switzerland that restaurants served food on reused tableware, found that waste reuse was an undigitised sector with social impact, went through Singularity University's acceleration in Silicon Valley and started Musa in 2020 (registry opening 2020-11-13) with their own capital; later investors named in the press include Kaszek and the German fund JFC, and Lower Carbon Capital lists Musa in its portfolio. Traction told by the company: in May 2022 it launched a zero-landfill, CO2-neutralised service with Alelo for the card issuer's merchants; in December 2022 it had 130 employees, had collected more than 15,000 tonnes in Greater São Paulo and was close to operational break-even; a company profile of June 2023 gives more than 550 clients, more than 18,000 tonnes reused and more than 15,000 tonnes of CO2 avoided. In 2024 Anderson Taniguchi, formerly of Rappi operations, joined as COO and a registry administrator.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil produces about 80 to 89 million tonnes of urban waste a year but recycles between 4% and 8% of it (ImpactAlpha, 2025, and InfoMoney, 2022, quoting the founder, differ on the exact rate), the sector is fragmented and informal, and a company with several sites handles many haulers, invoices and legal documents. The law requires waste to be tracked and sent to licensed destinations, so a business that buys waste services on price risks fines and bad reputation. Logic: an asset-light platform that signs one contract with the generator and uses audited partners in every region gets the efficiency of a vertically integrated operator without the capital of trucks and landfills; the digital record produces the documents and the ESG numbers the customer needs. Why now: tighter regulation (reverse logistics, landfill closure) and ESG reporting make traceability a purchase criterion, and large chains want one supplier for all units. Market and share: Lower Carbon Capital, an investor in Musa, puts Brazil's waste sector at about US$35 billion (an investor claim, not independent). Our reasoning: if Musa's margin as an intermediary were 10 to 20% of the spend it handles, each 1% of that market handled equals US$350 million of waste spend and US$35 to 70 million of gross profit; a realistic outcome in the next years is a fraction of 1%, so this is a mid-sized business whose upside depends on becoming the default provider to multi-site chains. The margin is our assumption, not a reported figure. Different: asset-light, one contract and one portal for many sites, with data on cost and recycling per unit; known rivals in the search results (Vertown for industrial traceability, Solos for catadores, large operators) cover parts of this. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders and connects them to top funds and angels; Musa's investors reported by the press are Kaszek and JFC, and Norte appears only in aggregators, so any fit is our reading. Risks: thin gross margin and operational complexity in a physical business; dependence on partners' quality and licences; slow enterprise sales; the rate of 100% reuse is a company claim; no readable round information, so funding runway is unknown.

milestones.value: Musa is opened as a company in São Paulo by Martin Junck and Fabrício Guimarães, after they saw reused tableware in Switzerland and decided to digitise waste management; they began with their own capital after Singularity University's acceleration.

Musa and the card issuer Alelo launch a zero-landfill, CO2-neutralised waste service for Alelo's merchant clients, with daily pickups and tracking in an app; supermarket groups Super Local and San Sato are early users.
Musa has 130 employees, has collected more than 15,000 tonnes of waste in Greater São Paulo and says it is close to operational break-even, with Kaszek and JFC among its investors.
A company profile reports more than 550 clients, more than 18,000 tonnes of waste reused and more than 15,000 tonnes of CO2 avoided.
Anderson Taniguchi, previously head of courier strategy operations at Rappi, becomes an administrator of the company, which the team profile lists as COO.

description.value: Mobile games company that acquires, partners with and runs mature free-to-play games, rebuilding monetisation, user acquisition and live operations; formerly Super Company.

long_description.value: Attach Media Partners (AMP) buys, partners with and runs mature mobile games. It looks for free-to-play titles that already have loyal players, downloads and revenue and have been published for more than 12 months, and takes them to a next stage: it rebuilds games from the core with sharper monetisation, user acquisition and live operations, and offers developers a simple, quick process with little effort so they can move on to future projects. Its site's three verbs are amplify (bigger audiences for games that earned them), revamp (proven games rebuilt from the core) and champion (games with more life left in them). The portfolio, per its LinkedIn page read through Linked API on 2026-11-24, spans more than 30 titles, from action and racing to rhythm and casual games, including Kill Shot Bravo, Guitar Band, Drag Racing, Hollywood Story and Hidden Escape; together they have been downloaded more than 100 million times, with more than 10 partnerships, and the page shows about 45 employees. The company was formerly called Super Company (Supercompany, domain supercompany.io), a name it used from 2021 to 2026 according to the same LinkedIn page, and the old site described it as taking care of the app-store and Google Play games of developers, focusing on casual and mid-core titles. Its co-founders on LinkedIn are Bruno (CEO) and Douglas Souza, and a VP of corporate development sits in São Paulo. No press article about the company, its owners, its acquisitions or its funding could be read, so the story is thin: this text is built from the company's own pages only.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: thousands of mobile games that once earned money are no longer actively run by their studios, which have moved to new projects and lack the user-acquisition and live-operations skills to extract value from an older title. Logic: a buyer that purchases or partners on those games cheaply and operates many of them with shared monetisation, marketing and operations tooling can earn more from the same installed audience, a portfolio logic similar to other game consolidators. Why now: the company's own claim is that games with downloads and revenue after 12 months are available from developers who want a simple exit. Market and share: no sourced market size was read; the only quantities are the company's own (more than 30 titles, more than 100 million downloads, about 45 staff), so no revenue or share estimate is made. Different: a Brazilian-led team with product backgrounds (the CEO's profile shows roles at iFood, MovilePay and Zoop, read through Linked API) that works with developers across several countries. Fit with Norte: aggregators list Norte as a seed investor in 2022 (not a readable Source here); the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders and brings the right funds and people to the cap table, which would fit a founder-led acquisition vehicle that needs capital partners (our reading). Risks: portfolio revenue depends on old titles whose audiences decay; user acquisition costs rise; competition for acquisitions from larger consolidators; thin public information on performance and financing. Confidence low because no market figure or press source was read.

sub_sector.value: Mature mobile game acquisition and live operations

milestones.value: Super Company changes its name to Attach Media Partners (AMP) and presents itself as an acquirer and operator of proven mobile games, with more than 30 titles and more than 100 million downloads.

description.value: Brazilian software company whose AI assistant prepares meetings, records conversations in the CRM and drafts follow-ups for investment-advisory firms; it began as a WhatsApp assistant for self-employed professionals.

long_description.value: Assis is a Brazilian software company that began as a WhatsApp virtual assistant for self-employed professionals and now sells an AI assistant to investment-advisory firms. In its current form the product, called Assis for investment advisory, works behind the scenes of an advisor's day: before a meeting it gathers the client's history from the CRM, calendar, e-mail and WhatsApp into a short briefing and agenda; after the conversation it organises the summary, the agreements and the next steps and writes them into the CRM for the advisor to review; between meetings it prepares follow-up messages, monthly report summaries (with the original PDF from the authorised source), notices to groups of clients and referral follow-ups. Every message passes through the advisor before it is sent, and investment decisions stay with the firm. It connects to Gmail, Outlook, Google Calendar, Microsoft Teams, WhatsApp, HubSpot, RD Station and Salesforce, Google Meet is marked as coming soon, and the sales route is a diagnostic call that tailors flows to each firm. The earlier product: in April 2023 Assis announced its first round of R$27.5 million, before launching, to build a ChatGPT-based assistant for solo entrepreneurs that handled first contact, reminders, quotes, availability and charges, in a model that would earn from payment capture and a SaaS subscription; in tests, 23% of users reported higher sales. It was founded by Raphael Machioni (CEO), co-founder and former CEO of the benefits company Vee, sold to Swile in 2020; João Bergamo (CPO), former Vee CFO; and Vagner Dutra (CTO), a founding member of PicPay's technology team. When the company changed from self-employed workers to advisory firms is not stated on the pages read; the 2026 site cites a July 2025 InfoMoney report on the use of CRMs by XP advisors.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: in Brazil an investment advisor is an independent professional who sells and follows up investments for a broker, and the value of the job is the client relationship. Advisors spend part of every day on preparing meetings, writing notes into the CRM and chasing follow-ups, and the site cites a figure from XP's head of CRM that advisors who use a CRM raise 2.5 times more, which only helps if the CRM is actually filled. Logic: an assistant that reads the calendar, mail and WhatsApp, drafts the briefing and the post-meeting record and leaves the human to approve gives the advisor hours back (the site's own simulation: 10 meetings a week x 30 minutes = 5 hours a week per advisor) and makes the CRM complete without typing. Why now: language models can summarise and draft well enough, and the advisor channel has grown: Ancord counted 27,425 accredited advisors in April 2026, with 20,087 linked to institutions, and 1,072 new ones in four months. Market and share: our bottom-up estimate: 20,000 linked advisors times an assumed subscription of R$300 to R$600 a month (assumption, no price on the page) is R$72 to R$144 million a year, or about US$13 to 26 million at R$5.6 per dollar; a strong outcome of 20 to 30% of advisors would be roughly US$3 to 8 million of annual revenue in this niche, so the thesis needs expansion to other relationship-driven professions, as the original self-employed product tried to do. Different: workflows tailored to each firm with human approval, which suits a regulated business, and a team that raised R$27.5 million before launch with prior exits from Vee and PicPay. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than Norte does and brings top funds onto the cap table; the 2023 round had Costanoa, MAYA, Canaan, Latitud, FJ Labs and others beside Norte (our reading of the fit, not Norte's statement). Risks: the niche is small; the company has changed its target customer once; incumbents (CRM vendors, brokers' own tools and large AI assistants) can add the same features; advisors depend on the broker's systems and compliance rules; no public traction numbers for the new product.

sub_sector.value: AI assistant and CRM for investment advisors

milestones.value: Assis is opened as a company in São Paulo by Raphael Machioni and João Bergamo, formerly CEO and CFO of the benefits company Vee, with Vagner Dutra, an early member of PicPay's technology team.

Assis announces a R$27.5 million first round, before launch, from Costanoa, MAYA, Canaan, Norte Ventures, Latitud, FJ Labs, K50, 1616, BFF and angels, to build a ChatGPT-based assistant for self-employed professionals; testers reported 23% higher sales.

Assis presents itself as an AI assistant for investment-advisory firms, with briefings, CRM records and follow-ups for the advisor to approve, connected to e-mail, calendar, WhatsApp and CRMs such as HubSpot and Salesforce.

description.value: Brazilian company, formerly Comp, that co-builds companies' HR functions with HR experts, AI engineers and custom software, covering 11 HR areas from recruiting to offboarding.

long_description.value: Zivo, until November 2026 called Comp, is a Brazilian company that builds a company's human-resources function with it, mixing HR specialists, AI engineers and software. Its site describes it as an AI-native HR partner: it co-builds the whole function end to end, from recruiting to offboarding (11 HR areas), with custom tools running on a layer it calls People.OS that holds all the client's people data; clients start with one or more areas and pay a monthly fee based on size and complexity, and decisions to hire, promote or dismiss stay with people. The model, which the founders call a superpowered HR teammate, places experts inside the client's routine as a right hand of the head of HR (forward-deployed). Examples on the site and in the press: Nubank uses a custom tool to prepare more than 90% of its job offers, QuintoAndar's manager satisfaction with performance reviews rose from 25% to 96%, PicPay's HR business partners build salary offers with market data inside policy, Creditas moved variable pay and long-term incentives out of spreadsheets, Dock runs a PeopleHub on People.OS and Hapvida, with more than 75,000 employees, puts its people data in one place; the site lists more than 150 clients such as Vivo, iFood, Sem Parar, Ascenty and RecargaPay. Origin: the company was founded in July 2022 in Brazil by Christophe Gerlach, an American, and Pedro Bobrow, a Brazilian, who met at Cornell, where they had built a food-delivery company that was acquired in their last year; Gerlach then worked at General Atlantic and Bobrow at Lyft, and after two years studying HR they moved to São Paulo. They began with a free salary-benchmark platform and compensation surveys, with more than 350 users and data on 70,000 employees at the time of the 2023 round, and planned to charge for salary tables and competitor analysis; later it moved into full HR services. A R$14 million first round in March 2023 was led by Kaszek with Canary, Norte and 1616 and 40 angels; in February 2026 a R$100 million Series A was led by Khosla Ventures, its first investment in Brazil, with Keith Rabois joining the board. On 17 November 2026 the company changed its name to Zivo, said AI for HR passed US$10 million in annual recurring revenue (five times in 12 months, about 85% of revenue, about 100 clients), and announced plans to enter the United States in the first quarter of 2027 with hires in New York and Miami.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: large employers in Brazil take decisions on pay, performance and hiring with spreadsheets, old survey data and processes designed for risk avoidance, and the HR function is rarely treated as a product with users; the founders say it would have a very low NPS among leaders and employees. Logic: pairing senior HR specialists with engineers who build custom software on the client's own rules and data produces tools (offer letters, variable pay, budgeting, manager workflows) that generic HR suites do not, and every tool built adds to a reusable data layer. Why now: AI lets a small team build and run HR workflows that used to need large systems or outsourced firms, and big Brazilian companies (Nubank, Vivo, iFood) are open to bespoke work. Market and share: no independent figure for Brazilian spend on HR consulting and software was read. Our estimate, with assumptions labelled: US$10 million of ARR over about 100 clients is roughly US$100 thousand a year per client (our arithmetic; about US$85 thousand if only the AI-for-HR share is counted). If Brazil has 1,000 to 3,000 employers large enough to buy this (assumption, no source) and 10 to 30% of them became clients at that price, revenue would be roughly US$10 to 90 million a year, and the US entry would widen it but is untested; this is a range for Brazil only. Different: services and software together, custom for each client, with the 2023 salary-data asset as a start, and a founder team with prior exit and investment-bank experience. Competitors: HR suites, compensation-data firms and consultancies (named generally; we did not read competitor pages). Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders it believes know more than Norte does and connects them to top funds; Norte was in the first round alongside Kaszek and Canary, and the Series A brought Khosla (our reading, not Norte's statement). Risks: a services-heavy model may limit margins and scale; large clients concentrate revenue; customers can build in-house with AI; the US entry is new; the rebrand and growth numbers are the company's own.

milestones.value: Christophe Gerlach and Pedro Bobrow, who had built and sold a food-delivery company at Cornell, found Comp in Brazil after two years studying HR, starting with a salary-benchmark platform.

Comp closes a R$14 million first round led by Kaszek with Canary, Norte, 1616 and 40 angels, with more than 350 users and data on 70,000 employees, to expand its salary data and charge for salary tables.

Comp raises a R$100 million Series A led by Khosla Ventures, its first investment in Brazil, and moves from compensation data to full HR services with experts and AI engineers inside client teams, serving more than 150 clients.

Comp becomes Zivo, reports more than US$10 million of annual recurring revenue (five times in 12 months) and about 100 AI-for-HR clients, and plans to open in the United States in the first quarter of 2027.

description.value: Brazilian AI platform that forecasts demand and manages ordering and stock of fresh fruit, vegetables and greens for supermarkets and distributors, to cut waste and stock-outs.

long_description.value: Aravita is a Brazilian software company that uses artificial intelligence to help supermarkets and food distributors buy and manage fresh fruit, vegetables and greens (FLV in Portuguese), the products with the shortest shelf life and the most volatile demand. Its pitch is that a generic replenishment tool fails on fresh food every day, because the system's stock rarely matches what is on the shelf, so Aravita is built only for perishables. The platform corrects the FLV stock every day before ordering, forecasts demand for each store from weather, seasonality, shelf life, promotions and events, forecasts stock-outs from sales rather than from recorded stock, takes minimum display into account, supports centralised purchasing (forecast of the aggregate and distribution-centre stock), gives store managers an ordering app with alerts on likely spoilage and stock-outs, and a control panel called Farol that ranks actions for the teams (losses, stock-outs, fill rate). It describes the product as ordering as a service. The company was started in 2022 by Marco Perlman (CEO), who had founded the photo-printing company Digipix in 2004 and moved to its board in September 2022; Aline Azevedo (CPO), formerly a product manager at Loft and an IT manager at Ambev; and Bruno Schrappe (CTO), founder of SapienX. They began a pilot in early 2023 with a chain of dozens of stores around São Paulo, then raised a R$12 million seed in March 2023 led by Qualcomm Ventures and 17Sigma, with Bridge, DGF, Alexia Ventures, Big Bets and Norte, plus angels from ClearSale and ex-Locaweb and Submarino, and HiPartners, a retail-focused fund, added an undisclosed amount in July 2023. In the first year it had 30 connected stores; by July 2026 it had more than 100, a contract of two years with the São Paulo chain St. Marche and two other chains not named, a fivefold revenue increase in 2025 and a reported tripling in the first half of 2026, but it had not reached break-even and, per AgFeed, had raised only that one round. Next steps named in 2023 were other perishable departments such as bakery, deli, fish and meat counters and computer vision.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: fresh produce is the hardest category in a supermarket. Embrapa estimates that over 40% of fruit, vegetables and greens in Brazil are wasted (AgFeed 2026), shelf life is short, and demand moves with weather and price, so buyers either empty the shelf, losing sales, or over-order and lose margin. Logic: an AI that forecasts per store and corrects the real stock daily, delivered as ordering as a service, cuts both errors; the company says the problem is the daily mismatch between recorded and real stock, which it corrects before ordering. Why now: deep-learning forecasting is feasible at store level, the founder said five years earlier it could not be done, and supermarkets have digital sales data. Market and share: Brazil's supermarket sector had sales of R$1.067 trillion in 2024 (Abras) and R$1.14 trillion in 2025 (search summary; not read). Fresh produce share and software price were not found. Our estimate, labelled as assumption: if fresh produce is 5 to 8% of sales (assumption) that is R$55 to 90 billion a year in Brazil; a vendor that charges 0.2 to 0.5% of the fresh sales of the stores it serves (assumption) earns R$110 to 450 million a year if it served all of them, so serving 10 to 20% would be about R$11 to 90 million (US$2 to 16 million) a year; adding other perishable departments and other countries widens it. This is a rough range. Different: single focus on FLV against general replenishment tools, daily stock correction, and a large-chain strategy because chains hold the best data. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders and brings top funds onto the cap table; here Qualcomm Ventures and 17Sigma led and Norte took part in the seed, with a founder who built and ran Digipix for 18 years (our reading, not Norte's statement). Risks: slow sales cycles with big chains and few customers, so concentration; no break-even yet; the large replenishment vendors can add fresh-produce modules; results depend on store data quality; only one round raised, so runway may be tight.

sub_sector.value: AI demand forecasting for fresh produce retail

milestones.value: Aravita starts a pilot in a supermarket chain with dozens of stores in the São Paulo region, focused first on fresh fruit, vegetables and greens.
Aravita announces a R$12 million seed led by Qualcomm Ventures and 17Sigma, with Norte among the investors, to expand its AI forecasting for fresh produce.
HiPartners, a fund focused on Brazilian retail tech, adds an undisclosed amount to the seed and offers to connect Aravita to large supermarket chains.
Aravita passes 100 connected stores (30 in its first year), says 2025 revenue grew fivefold, and works with St. Marche and two other chains, though it has not yet reached break-even.

description.value: Latin American payments company that offers cross-border payments and 24/7 FX through stablecoin rails and a single API, with Mexican peso rails and market making for non-USD stablecoins.

long_description.value: Capa is a financial-infrastructure company, with a Mexican legal entity, that moves money between Latin America and the rest of the world using stablecoins underneath and one API on top. Its site calls it a 24/7 FX and payment platform: it receives local currency (for example Mexican pesos through SPEI), converts fiat to stablecoins and back around the clock, and settles to local bank accounts, so fintechs, payment companies, financial institutions and corporations can send and receive first- and third-party cross-border payments, hold treasury and fund local entities, all through an API, SDK or dashboard, with clients able to start transacting within 24 hours. A market-making arm provides liquidity from OTC markets, exchanges, DeFi protocols and DEXs, with a focus on keeping non-USD stablecoins, such as a digital Brazilian real and a Mexican-peso stablecoin, close to their fiat value. Customers pay through FX spreads and fees (our reading: the pages read do not state pricing). A customer quote on the site says payouts fell from 48 hours to 10 minutes and FX costs dropped by more than 60%. The company began as a crypto on-ramp and off-ramp for buying and selling crypto with Mexican pesos, founded by CEO Juan Diego Oliva (who had worked at Tools for Humanity and the Arbitrum Foundation) and CTO Juan David Torres Velasco (previously at Microsoft and co-founder and CTO of the Mexican start-up Alcancia), with a CFO and a CMO named in the press, and it announced a US$2.5 million pre-seed round in early 2025 (including a US$1 million extension) and said it operated in Mexico and the Dominican Republic and would expand to similar markets; in April 2025 it joined the Borderless.xyz stablecoin payment network to provide Mexican local rails, and in May 2025 it integrated Ondo's yield-bearing USDY so Mexican users could deposit pesos and receive dollar-denominated Treasury exposure on Solana. Its LinkedIn page lists San Francisco as its headquarters and about 41 employees, while its legal entity and CEO are in Mexico City. It has since moved to an enterprise payments and stablecoin FX positioning, partnered with Brale on on-chain rates for non-USD stablecoins and with BRL1 and Polygon Labs on the digital real, and in June 2026 chose DFNS as its core infrastructure for accounts, transactions, treasury and governance, supporting MXN, USD, EUR, USDC, USDT, BRL1, MXNB and more.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: moving money between Latin America and the world still means slow settlement, high FX costs and a separate banking relationship in every country. Mexico alone received US$61.8 billion in remittances in 2025 (Banxico, down 4.6% from the 2024 record of US$64.7 billion), and more than 95% comes from the United States, so the corridor is large, and companies that pay suppliers, contractors or users across the region face similar friction. Logic: stablecoins settle in minutes at any hour, and a company that holds local rails and liquidity can quote competitive FX and let clients integrate once through one API; Capa says clients cut payout times from 48 hours to 10 minutes and FX costs by more than 60% (a customer testimonial on its own site). Why now: dollar and local-currency stablecoins are mainstream enough that regulated partners such as Borderless.xyz, Ondo and DFNS build on them, and a digital Brazilian real and Mexican-peso stablecoin now exist. Market and share: the 2025 remittance flow to Mexico alone is US$61.8 billion; a provider keeping 0.3 to 1% of the volume it handles (assumption, no price read) would earn US$0.2 to 0.6 million per US$100 million moved; if Capa reached 1 to 3% of the Mexican inbound flow (US$0.6 to 1.9 billion a year, our assumption) that is roughly US$2 to 19 million of annual revenue in that corridor alone, before B2B flows to other countries. Different: local rails and liquidity in Mexico, focus on non-USD stablecoins, and an API for enterprise rather than only consumer on-ramps. Fit with Norte: aggregators list Norte as an investor, but no readable source names it, so we only say that the Manifesto describes Norte as bringing the right funds and people to cap tables, which suits a crypto-infrastructure team backed by Alter, Reverie and crypto angels, led by a CEO from the Arbitrum Foundation and Tools for Humanity ecosystems and a CTO who worked at Microsoft and co-founded an earlier start-up (our reading, from their LinkedIn profiles). Risks: regulation of stablecoins and crypto in Mexico, Brazil and the United States; thin spreads and competition from Borderless.xyz-type networks, banks, Wise-style players and other stablecoin start-ups; remittance volumes fell in 2025; reliance on partners for custody and rails; the company changed positioning from consumer on-ramp to enterprise FX.

sub_sector.value: Stablecoin FX and cross-border payments for Latin America

milestones.value: Capa announces a US$2.5 million pre-seed round (including a US$1 million extension) backed by Alter, Reverie and angels from Coinbase, Ripple and others, to strengthen its crypto on/off-ramp in Mexico and expand to nearby markets.
Capa joins the Borderless.xyz stablecoin payment network, bringing its Mexican local payment rails, liquidity and FX rates to the network's clients.

Capa integrates Ondo Finance's USDY so users in Mexico can deposit pesos through local bank accounts and receive a dollar-denominated, Treasury-backed token on Solana, exiting back to pesos at any time.

Capa chooses DFNS as the core infrastructure for accounts, transactions, treasury and governance behind its cross-border payments and stablecoin FX platform, supporting MXN, USD, EUR, USDC, USDT, BRL1 and MXNB.

co_investors: angel investors from Coinbase, Ripple, Polygon Labs and Ondo

description.value: Rio de Janeiro holding that takes restaurant brands (Tapí, Amélie, Juliette, Nema) into franchising and offers its own franchise-management software (Nola, Supfy) to franchisors and franchisees.

long_description.value: Arcca (Grupo Arcca) describes itself as a digital holding for franchising: it takes promising food brands, turns them into franchise networks and runs them with its own technology. The group says it was created in January 2021 and traces its history to 2009, when it started Vezpa Pizzas in Rio de Janeiro, its first brand, later expanded to São Paulo and Brasília. In 2022 two more brands joined: Nema, a naturally fermented bakery, and Tapí Tapioca e Açaí, a Brazilian-ingredients snack shop that began as a food truck in Rio. In March 2026 Tapí had 12 units in Rio and São Paulo, launched a 12 m² kiosk format for malls and airports (the first at Vogue Square, Barra da Tijuca, developed with Grupo Arcca) and planned 10 more stores in 2026, aiming above R$17 million of revenue. In 2024 Amélie Crêperie (a Paris-style crêperie about ten years old) and Juliette Bistrô (an Art Déco French bistro) joined. The second leg is software: the group says it opened its own technology to the market in 2023 through Nola, a management system for franchise networks, with Supfy for purchasing; both automate management and purchasing and give franchisors data on each unit. Revenue comes, in our reading, from franchise fees and royalties on its own brands and from software subscriptions; the site gives no prices or customer numbers. The sources give no funding round, headcount or revenue for the group itself. Its market is large and growing: ABF counted R$301.7 billion of franchise revenue in 2025 across 202,444 units.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil has 3,297 franchise networks and 202,444 units, but many are run on spreadsheets and the franchisor's own know-how; good local food brands often fail to scale because they lack standard processes, purchasing and data. Logic: Arcca takes promising brands, professionalises them and puts one software layer (Nola, Supfy) under all of them, so each new brand reuses the same playbook and purchasing power; selling the software to outside franchisors would add a recurring line. Market: ABF measured R$301.7 billion of franchise revenue in 2025; if franchise software and management fees took 0.1% to 0.3% of system revenue (our assumption) the pool would be roughly R$300 million to R$900 million a year, and brands the group owns earn royalties on their own systems (Tapí alone aims above R$17 million of revenue in 2026). What is different: it combines brand ownership with its own technology, where most franchise software vendors have no brands and most brand groups have no software. Fit with Norte: our reading is that a small, operator-led team using technology to scale a fragmented offline sector matches Norte's stated focus on obsessed founders and on connecting them with the right people; nothing in the sources says why Norte backed it. Risks: concentration in Rio restaurants, franchise units failing, and no public evidence of paying outside software customers or of the group's revenue.

sub_sector.value: Franchising holding and franchise management software

milestones.value: Vezpa Pizzas, the group's first brand, is created in Rio de Janeiro; it later expands to São Paulo and Brasília.
Grupo Arcca is born as a holding that consolidates about a decade of learning in franchising.
Nema (a naturally fermented bakery) and Tapí Tapioca e Açaí join the group, which then runs three brands.
Arcca opens its own management technology to the market through Nola, so other franchise networks can use it.
Amélie Crêperie and Juliette Bistrô join the group, both born in Rio de Janeiro.
Tapí launches a 12 m² kiosk franchise model for malls and airports, developed with Grupo Arcca; it has 12 units and plans 10 openings in 2026.

description.value: Global crypto asset manager that packages the crypto market into regulated index funds and ETFs (Brazil, United States and others), built on the Nasdaq Crypto Index it co-developed with Nasdaq.

long_description.value: Hashdex is a crypto asset manager that lets professional and retail investors hold crypto through regulated index funds and ETFs instead of buying coins directly. It was founded in 2018 by Marcelo Sampaio, a Silicon Valley veteran of Microsoft and Oracle who had been investing in crypto since 2011 and could not find a product good enough, and Bruno Caratori, a former head of risk at Gávea with a Stanford MBA; InfoMoney's account says a third founder, the Harvard-trained mathematician Thiago Costa, was part of the trio. They started in the United States but, because Brazil's regulation was friendlier, began operating there. The core idea was an index, because nobody could know which coin would win: first its own (Hashdex Digital Assets Index), replaced in 2021 by the Nasdaq Crypto Index (NCI) built with Nasdaq. In February 2021 Hashdex listed on the Bermuda Stock Exchange what it calls the world's first crypto index ETF; in April 2021 it launched HASH11 on Brazil's B3, the first crypto ETF there, which raised over R$600 million in its offering and passed R$1 billion in net assets in a week; it also has ETFs for Bitcoin (BITH11) and Ethereum (ETHE11) and mutual funds sold on platforms such as XP, BTG and Guide, with 150,000 holders in May 2021. Revenue is mainly a management fee of 1.3% to 1.5% a year (Brazil Journal, 2021); one fund charges a performance fee. In May 2021 it raised a Series A led by Valor Capital to widen the product range and go international, with the plan to triple headcount. In 2023 Brian Brooks, former Coinbase chief legal officer and acting US Comptroller of the Currency, joined the board for Valor. In March 2026 the company named Caratori global CEO, Sampaio executive chairman and Mick McLaughlin US CEO, a formalisation of a shared management model, with offices in New York, Rio de Janeiro and London. Its own site says it manages over R$6 billion in index products in eight countries as of 30 September 2026, including what it calls the first multi-asset crypto ETF in the US.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: most investors want crypto exposure but cannot pick winners, custody coins safely or handle the tax and legal burden; institutions and advisers often cannot hold coins at all. Logic: a regulated index product (fund or ETF) wraps the whole asset class in a familiar format that brokers can sell, and an index co-built with Nasdaq gives it credibility; once the product exists, assets compound with a management fee. Why now: Brazil's CVM allowed crypto funds, B3 listed HASH11 in 2021, and US spot crypto ETFs followed. Market: Brazilian declared crypto volume was R$506 billion in 2025 (Receita Federal data compiled by Fintrender), mostly stablecoin flows rather than holdings, so it is a trading figure, not an asset base; the company itself reports R$6 billion under management in index products. A realistic strong outcome is a few tens of billions of reais of assets, which at the 1.3% to 1.5% fee Brazil Journal reported (the US ETF fee is likely lower, our assumption) would be roughly R$200 million to R$500 million of revenue a year. What is different: first-mover regulated index ETFs in Brazil, the Nasdaq partnership and a presence in the US, Europe and Latin America, against competitors such as Bitwise and larger asset managers. Fit with Norte: our reading is that Norte joined a Series A led by Valor Capital as a follower, which fits its stated role of bringing in the right people and funds; the founders are the kind of obsessed, technical operators it says it backs. Risks: revenue depends on crypto prices and flows; fee compression as BlackRock and others compete in the US; regulation; and the 2026 reduction in Europe (a lead from a search summary, not verified).

milestones.value: Marcelo Sampaio and Bruno Caratori found Hashdex to give investors regulated, diversified access to crypto through index products; it starts in the US and builds its operation in Brazil.
Hashdex lists the Hashdex Nasdaq Crypto Index ETF on the Bermuda Stock Exchange, which it calls the first crypto index ETF in the world, tracking an index co-developed with Nasdaq.
HASH11, the first digital-asset ETF on Brazil's B3, goes live after a R$600 million-plus offering and passes R$1 billion in net assets within a week, among the three largest ETFs on the exchange.
Hashdex raises a R$135 million Series A, announcing R$3.5 billion under management and more than 150,000 investors, to expand its products and go international.
Brian Brooks, former Coinbase chief legal officer and acting US Comptroller of the Currency, joins the board as Valor Capital's representative, to advise on global regulation.
Co-founder Bruno Caratori becomes global CEO, Marcelo Sampaio executive chairman and Mick McLaughlin (ex-Bitwise, who joined in 2024) US CEO, to push the US ETF platform and global expansion.
The company reports more than R$6 billion in index products across eight countries, including the first multi-asset crypto ETF in the US.

description.value: Brazilian identity verification, risk management and digital onboarding platform, using biometrics, document validation and background checks to help companies prevent fraud.

long_description.value: idwall was a Brazilian regtech that helped companies know who they were dealing with and stop identity fraud. Its platform covered document validation, facial biometrics, background and compliance checks on people and companies (it says it had processed data on nearly all Brazilians and on 18 million companies), and configurable digital-onboarding flows; it also had a consumer identity app, MeuID, which an investor from GGV described in 2021 as potentially the first true super-app in Latin America. It sold mainly to businesses and earned from usage-based and subscription fees (our reading; the sources do not state its pricing). Lincoln Ando (CEO) and Raphael Melo founded it in São Paulo in mid-2016. It backed early momentum with a 500 Startups investment, a Series A led by Monashees and Canary in 2018, a US$10 million Series B led by Qualcomm Ventures in 2019 (with ONEVC, GGV, Globo's Ithaca and others), and a R$210 million Series C in June 2021 led by Endurance with GGV, Península, Monashees, Canary, Qualcomm, ONEVC, Ithaca and Norte; the 2021 round came when it had more than 300 customers including 15 banks (two of the three largest) and seven financial unicorns such as Cielo, Ebanx, iFood, Loggi and Quinto Andar, and a strategic partnership with Mastercard. By 2026 it had more than 400 customers, among them Bradesco Saúde, SulAmérica, Shopee, QuintoAndar, Globoplay and Claro, had raised about R$260 million in its first ten years, and said it had helped avoid more than R$8 billion in fraud and had received more than 700 million queries. It competed with Unico, a Brazilian unicorn in the same field, and CERTTA (formerly CAF). In May 2026 Serasa Experian, Brazil's largest datatech, agreed to buy it, to strengthen its authentication and anti-fraud range after buying ClearSale in 2024 for R$2 billion; terms were not disclosed, press sources put the price at R$400 million (Valor's Pipeline) or R$450 million (Startups.com.br), and a venture investor told Bloomberg Línea such a figure suggests some investors may have got back about what they put in. CADE cleared the deal without restrictions and Serasa Experian completed it on 1 July 2026; idwall stays in Serasa's identity, biometrics and onboarding offering.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: digital services (fintechs, marketplaces, delivery apps) need to open accounts and sign up customers in minutes, but Brazil has a large amount of identity fraud, documents are easy to fake, and checking people means querying many public and private databases. Doing it in-house is slow, costly and a compliance risk. The logic: an API that unites document and biometric validation with background checks, plus the data to decide, lets a company onboard a real person quickly and prove it to a regulator; each client's queries improve the models, and the customer base compounds (more than 700 million queries, which the company ties to more than R$8 billion in fraud avoided). Why now: Pix and digital banks created an onboarding rush in 2018-2021, regulators required know-your-customer controls, and AI increased the sophistication of fraud, which Serasa cites as a reason for its purchase in 2026. Market: no independent figure was read. Our estimate is bottom-up: Brazil has several thousand regulated financial institutions and fintechs, large marketplaces and insurers that onboard at scale; if 3,000 to 10,000 companies (our assumption) each spend R$100,000 to R$1 million a year on identity verification and fraud prevention, the pool is about R$0.3 to R$10 billion a year. The market evidence we did read is an outcome: Serasa bought idwall for a reported R$400 to R$450 million after ClearSale for R$2 billion, showing a strategic buyer values the category, and that idwall's own result was modest. What was different: a wide offering (document, biometrics, background and onboarding in one), a strong list of financial clients, and well-known backers (Qualcomm, GGV, Endurance, Monashees, Canary); competitors Unico (unicorn) and CERTTA/CAF were larger or better funded in some segments. Fit with Norte (our reading): founders who built a regulated, data-heavy product in a segment that fintechs needed, and a follow-on role in the large 2021 round alongside Endurance and GGV, where Norte's network connects funds to the cap table; this is consistent with the Manifesto's 'follower and connector' stance, not Norte's statement. Risks that materialised or remain: strong competition (Unico, CAF) and price pressure on a commoditising check; clients who can build in-house; and, as a venture outcome, a sale at about R$400 to R$450 million against R$260 million raised, which is below what the 2021 round implied, so late investors may not have earned a multiple.

Serasa Experian completed the acquisition

description.value: Brazilian "hospital at home" company (formerly ISA Lab, home lab tests and vaccines) that sends a network of nurses and clinicians to patients' homes for exams, urgent care, rehabilitation, infusions and palliative care, paid mainly by health insurers.

long_description.value: Isa Saúde (ISA) takes hospital-level care to the patient's home in Brazil. It began as ISA Lab, which sent independent nurses to collect blood and apply vaccines at home, with salaried "biocondutores" carrying the samples to a lab; the brothers Fernando Pares (an economist, CEO) and David Pares (a doctor, chief medical officer), serial founders who had sold the electronic-records startup AvalDoc, started it in 2017 (the date they give; other outlets say 2018 or 2019). Their father had founded the LEGO lab chain, bought by Fleury in 2008. The model works like a decentralised network: autonomous nurses and professionals, trained for several weeks (38 days of onboarding, according to the CEO), rated by patients in the app, paid more when they score well and removed when they do not. In 2021 ISA Lab raised its first round and entered seven more states; in 2022 it raised a Series A, then bought Saúde C (home care, founded in 2020), and renamed itself Isa Saúde as it moved to more complex care: urgent home care, de-hospitalisation, rehabilitation, infusions, chronic-disease monitoring and palliative care, all under what it calls a hospital at home (it compares itself to a hospital with 700 beds across Brazil). Customers are mainly health insurers (more than 25 operators in 2025; earlier Sami, GNDI, SulAmérica, Bradesco and Amil), who pay per service; the company says its costs are 40% to 70% of traditional home care or hospital stays, readmissions are under 2% against 11% in traditional home care, and it grew revenue at 98% a year over three years without disclosing revenue. By October 2025 it had more than 4,000 professionals, over 1,500 visits a day in more than 60 cities in São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Bahia and the Federal District. That month it closed a R$160 million (US$30 million) Series B led by IFC, with IDB Lab, Dalus and Endeavor Catalyst, to grow organically and buy traditional home-care companies.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilian insurers pay hospitals per procedure, claims keep rising and many patients (elderly, chronic, post-surgery) occupy beds that home care could serve more cheaply and safely; traditional home care is local, slow and prone to fraud. Logic: a decentralised network of nurses and clinicians, coordinated by one app, gives insurers a per-case price lower than a bed (the CEO says 40% to 70% of hospital or traditional home-care cost) and gives professionals extra income; tech tracks every visit so quality and billing can be audited. Why now: insurers' margins were squeezed (claims ratio about 82% in 2025 after years above 85%), so cost-reducing partners get paid attention. Market: the health insurance sector took in R$391.6 billion in 2025 (ANS); if 2% to 5% of that went to home-based care (our assumption, since no source splits it), the pool is R$8 billion to R$20 billion a year; the company, with R$160 million just raised, would need 5% to 10% of that to reach R$1 billion of revenue, its stated five-year goal from 2022. What is different: a nurse-network model that started in lab collection (cheap, high frequency) and climbed to complex care, versus traditional home-care providers with salaried teams; comparables are Beep Saúde (home exams) and traditional operators. Fit with Norte: our reading is that Norte joined the first institutional round of founders who are serial operators with a networked health-industry background (the family's lab chain) and brought in follow-on capital through its network; the later rounds list Norte nowhere, so we cannot say it followed on. Risks: dependence on a few insurers, clinical quality and liability in the home, price pressure when insurers renegotiate, and integration of acquisitions.

milestones.value: Brothers Fernando and David Pares, who had sold AvalDoc two years earlier, found ISA to take lab exams and vaccines to patients' homes through autonomous nurses.
ISA Lab raises its first round (R$13 million) to enter seven more states and invest in technology; it relies on hundreds of autonomous nurses and "biocondutores" that carry samples to the lab.

A R$60 million Series A, with VOX Capital, FIR Capital, Endeavor Scale-up, Kortex (Fleury, Sabin and Bradesco Saúde) and Yaya Capital, funds ISA Care, home treatments such as infusions, and a goal of R$1 billion in revenue in five years.

ISA buys Saúde C, a home-care startup founded in 2020, in its first acquisition, and takes the name Isa Saúde to offer home hospitalisation, rehabilitation, palliative care and a 24-hour nursing line.

Isa Saúde announces a R$160 million (US$30 million) Series B led by IFC, the largest of the year for a Latin American health startup, serving 25+ insurers with 4,000+ professionals and 1,500+ visits a day.

description.value: Brazilian legal AI company whose virtual specialists (Laura for legal work, Lia for client contact on WhatsApp) draft petitions and contracts, research case law and run client service for law firms.

long_description.value: Lexter (Lexter.ai) is a São Paulo legal-technology company that sells AI assistants to law firms. It started in 2020 with a product for M&A due diligence that read and analysed legal documents, used by large firms such as Demarest, BMA, Cescon Barrieu, TozziniFreire and Lobo de Rizzo, and took part in Mattos Filho's Attix programme. CEO and co-founder Pedro Jahara, a serial founder (BelugaDB, R2U.io, RevMob, Bain), led the company through Y Combinator's Winter 2022 batch, which it describes as Brazil's first legal-LLM company. In 2023 it soft-launched the Assistente Lexter (the 'Assistente Contencioso'): the lawyer describes a case, the system checks it against current Brazilian law, suggests a strategy and writes a first draft of the petition or defence. Jahara stressed that the tool is an assistant that does not replace the lawyer and was built to avoid invented case law; in November 2023 a waiting list of 1,000 firms was reported, and about 180 firms used it by April 2024. In April 2024 it raised R$16 million (about US$3 million) led by Alexia Ventures, to reach small and mid-sized firms through a freemium model, to strengthen security, and to expand the Instituto Lexter, a research and education arm on AI in law. The current site presents a platform with two virtual specialists: Laura, which drafts pieces, contracts, case-law searches and summaries, and Lia, which handles external client contact by email and WhatsApp (via Meta's official API), qualifies leads and answers case-status questions; some features (routing to humans, automatic contracts) are marked as coming soon. Revenue comes from software subscriptions with a free entry tier; the sources give no prices or revenue.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil has more than 1.5 million registered lawyers, 72% of them self-employed, and about 72,000 offices (Advbox's estimate), most with 3 to 5 people, doing repetitive drafting, case tracking and client updates by hand while the courts process a large volume of new cases. Logic: large language models can write a first draft of petitions and contracts, and a model grounded in Brazilian law and with the lawyer in the loop is safer than a generic chatbot; legal work is high-priced time, so even small savings justify a subscription. Why now: 77% of lawyers surveyed by OAB-SP in 2026 said they use AI frequently, up from 55% a year earlier, so adoption is moving from experiment to habit. Market: with roughly 72,000 firms and 172,000 self-employed lawyers in Advbox's addressable base, an annual subscription of R$2,000 to R$6,000 per firm (our assumption, between a typical software seat and a premium tool) gives about R$150 million to R$430 million a year; adding the larger firms and in-house departments could double it, and a strong outcome would be a leading share of that pool. What is different: it started with large firms and security (no invented case law) and now adds client-facing automation (Lia on WhatsApp), competing with Jusbrasil, Jurídico.AI, Looplex and global tools. Fit with Norte: our reading is that a network of operators and a repeat founder building an AI product with a Y Combinator pedigree match Norte's stated profile; the only source for Norte's participation is an aggregator we could not confirm. Risks: foundation-model vendors and global legal AI moving into Brazil, low switching cost, price pressure and dependence on a few model providers (the 2024 articles cite GPT-4).

milestones.value: Pedro Jahara and partners start Lexter.ai in São Paulo with a document-analysis product for M&A due diligence, sold to large law firms.
Lexter goes through Y Combinator (Winter 2022) and raises a pre-seed with Grão.VC and Canary, becoming known as Brazil's first legal-LLM company.
Lexter soft-launches the Assistente Lexter, a generative-AI tool that drafts initial petitions and defences from the case description; about 180 firms adopt it by early 2024.
Jahara tells an Itaú Cubo event that 1,000 law firms are on the waiting list for the litigation assistant, still in tests with a select group to avoid hallucinated case law.
Lexter raises R$16 million led by Alexia Ventures to take its AI beyond large firms to small and mid-sized ones and to expand its Instituto Lexter.
The current product is a platform of two virtual specialists, Laura (legal drafting and research) and Lia (WhatsApp and email client service), offered through self-service signup.

description.value: Brazilian-born AI platform that reads billions of public videos (YouTube, TikTok, Instagram and others) to show large brands what audiences care about, with a "Share of Attention" metric and an AI copilot, sold as a subscription.

long_description.value: Winnin is a cultural-intelligence software company. It analyses public video consumption on YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and Twitch (about 2 million videos a day, according to InfoMoney in 2024) to tell brands, agencies and media companies which topics, formats, creators and communities are rising, so marketing and creative teams start from evidence. It began in 2014 inside Coca-Cola's Founders startup programme: Gian Martinez, then a creative director at Coca-Cola, started it with Carlos Camolese (COO) and Erich Oliveira (CTO), after finding that even Coca-Cola could not answer what people actually want to watch. Coca-Cola financed a seed round; ZX Ventures (AB InBev's venture arm) and the founders of the Rio fund Dynamo, as individuals, came in a later round; by mid-2020 Martinez said he had raised US$8 million. Building the platform took about five years, and revenue tripled in 2020 as Winnin Insights moved to a software-as-a-service model sold to the whole advertising industry. Customers include Google, Coca-Cola, Netflix, Meta, AB InBev, Nubank, Unilever, Nestlé, Danone and agencies; in 2024 it had 76 clients and 35% to 40% of revenue came from outside Brazil. Clients mostly pay an annual subscription. In July 2024 Winnin announced an undisclosed Series A led by Alexia Ventures and Kaszek (Coca-Cola and AB InBev left the cap table), to open a US office with a US head, strengthen leadership and push internationally; it also joined the AWS Generative AI Accelerator (US$200,000 in credits) that year. The 2025 product has three parts: Share of Attention, a metric of the share of consumer attention a brand captures within its category and country, rebuilt in 2025 to count positive attention only; ZAI, a cultural-intelligence copilot; and sentiment analysis; the 2026 site adds creative and creator briefs and territory analysis. In March 2026 it hired Guilherme Arruda, formerly of Google and General Motors South America, as VP of growth and strategic partnerships.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: global brands spend more than US$1 trillion a year on advertising (dentsu forecasts US$1.06 trillion in 2026) but decide creative and media with surveys, agency intuition and platform dashboards that show their own performance, not what audiences care about before it shows up in sales. Logic: people leave a large public trail in video (views, comments, creators, topics), and AI can group it into communities and territories, giving marketers a leading indicator; a subscription metric such as Share of Attention can become an industry reference and sit in the CMO's weekly routine. Why now: video and social dominate spend and generative AI makes it cheaper to read and write about video at scale. Market: our estimate, bottom-up, is that if the 2,000 largest advertisers in the world each spent US$100,000 to US$500,000 a year on cultural-intelligence software and research (our assumption, from enterprise insight-software pricing), the pool is US$200 million to US$1 billion a year; on 76 clients in 2024 the company is at a few percent of that. What is different: Brazilian-built but with global enterprise clients (Google, Coca-Cola, Netflix, Meta, Unilever); proprietary attention metric rather than raw social listening; it competes with social-listening and trend-analytics vendors (names not researched here). Fit with Norte: no readable article names Norte (only an aggregator does), so our reading of the fit is generic: a repeat-operator founding team with global ambition, where Norte's stated role of connecting founders to the right people and funds (it would have helped reach brands and Series A funds) would apply. Risks: dependence on the data access rules of YouTube, TikTok and Meta, competition from platform-owned analytics and large social-listening vendors, concentration among a few large clients, and a long enterprise sales cycle.

sub_sector.value: Cultural intelligence and video analytics for marketing

milestones.value: Gian Martinez, Carlos Camolese and Erich Oliveira start Winnin, inside Coca-Cola's Founders programme, to answer what people really want to watch online; Coca-Cola becomes a shareholder and funds a seed round.
Winnin tripled its revenue and took Winnin Insights to a software-as-a-service model for the whole advertising industry, with Nestlé, Danone, Africa and GUT among its clients.
Winnin is selected for the AWS Global Generative AI Accelerator and receives US$200,000 in cloud credits to build and test AI solutions.
Winnin announces a Series A led by Alexia Ventures and Kaszek, adds their partners to the board and plans a US office led by Rodrigo Maroni and a growth VP from Pinterest.

Winnin rebuilds Share of Attention to count positive attention only and launches ZAI, its AI copilot for cultural intelligence, and a sentiment tool that separates real engagement from crisis attention.
Guilherme Arruda, a 12-year Google leader who was also a Winnin client at General Motors South America, becomes VP of growth and strategic partnerships to expand globally.

description.value: Brazilian software platform that lets real estate agencies and independent brokers run rentals digitally: tenant and owner credit checks, rental management and payouts, e-signature, insurance issuing and lead capture, sold by subscription.

long_description.value: Alude is a software platform for Brazilian real estate agencies and brokers who want to work digitally, with a focus on rentals. It was launched in 2019 by three friends, Jota Junior, Alef Miranda and Alexandre Dubugras (the CEO), and went through Y Combinator's Winter 2020 batch. In its first version the platform was free for traditional agencies and automated the paperwork of a rental: background and credit checks of the tenant, document collection and validation, online signature and the purchase of insurance, which let a contract close in a day; the company earned its revenue from financial and household products sold on top, above all residential insurance and rental guarantees, and said it wanted to become Latin America's largest provider of home insurance and rental guarantee. In September 2020 it closed a US$3.3 million seed co-led by Ribbit Capital, Y Combinator, Global Founders Capital and Maya Capital with angels such as Hugo Barra and founders of Stone, VivaReal, Wildlife, Brex, Gympass, Ingresse and Plaid; at that time 150 invited agencies used it for all their rentals, with 150 on a waiting list, and the goal was 20,000 rentals in 2021. The platform also gave brokers a database of about 332,000 property owners to prospect. Today the site presents a broader operating system for agencies: more complete tenant and owner file analysis (by CPF or CNPJ in one click), rental management that automates billing, payouts and reports, e-signature with legal validity without a digital certificate, insurance issuing and a robot that scans the web for owner-posted listings so brokers can call and win the listing. It is sold by plan, with a free trial, and the company says more than 20,000 agencies use it. No later round or acquisition was found.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: renting a home in Brazil means weeks of paperwork, credit checks, guarantees (a guarantor or deposit) and manual collection, handled by agencies that rarely invest in software; Brazil has about 650,000 active brokers (Cofeci/DataZAP, 2025) and only 19% of real estate firms use AI against 85% in the US, so tools are behind. Logic: give agencies the workflow for free or cheap, own the tenant file, and earn on insurance and financial products or on subscription; a broker with a digital rental file closes faster and keeps clients. Market: a bottom-up estimate is that if 100,000 agencies and independent brokers (our assumption of the addressable base from 650,000 brokers, 71% self-employed) paid R$100 to R$300 a month, the software pool is R$120 million to R$360 million a year, with insurance and payment margins on top; the company says it already has 20,000 agencies, which at R$100 to R$300 a month would be R$24 million to R$72 million a year if all paid (an upper bound, since the count is its own claim). What is different: Y Combinator and Ribbit backing, a product built around the full rental flow and a robot for listing capture; competitors are rental-guarantee fintechs and the large property portals' tools (names not researched here). Fit with Norte: our reading is that Norte joined an early round of repeat operators in a fragmented market where a network of fintech and proptech operators helps distribution; no readable article names Norte for Alude, so the fit is inferred from its Portfolio listing alone. Risks: low willingness to pay among small agencies, dependence on insurer margins, competition from portals and guarantee fintechs, and no public funding news since 2020 (cash runway unknown).

sub_sector.value: Software for real estate agencies and rentals

milestones.value: Jota Junior, Alef Miranda and Alexandre Dubugras launch Alude in Brazil to digitise rentals for brokers; it joins Y Combinator in early 2020.
Alude closes a US$3.3 million seed with Ribbit Capital, Y Combinator, Global Founders Capital and Maya Capital and notable angels, with 150 agencies using the product and 150 on a waiting list.
The platform is now a broader agency system (file analysis, rental and payout management, e-signature, insurance issuing, listing capture) sold by subscription, with a claimed 20,000 agencies.

co_investors: founders of Stone, VivaReal, Wildlife Studios, Brex, Gympass, Ingresse and Plaid

description.value: Mexican platform that runs bus transport without owning buses, partnering with local operators. It started with intercity routes for passengers and now also sells employee transport to companies.

long_description.value: Kolors is a Mexican mobility company that runs bus transport without owning a single bus. It partners with small, medium and large operators who own and drive the vehicles, while Kolors does the rest through its technology: route and schedule planning, pricing, tracking, customer service, marketing and sales. The CEO compares the model to Uber's. It started with intercity passenger routes in Mexico, which it called a 'smart-bus platform' or an airline on wheels: virtual stops in malls and hotels, on-board attendants, Wi-Fi and snack sales, and a rewards programme; it carried more than 7 million passengers in 2023, over 70% of them millennials and Gen Z, and ran a pilot between Los Angeles and Las Vegas. More recently it has moved to employee transport, selling recurring contracts to companies that need to move workers to the same place at the same time every day (industrial parks, production lines, remote plants); by October 2026 it operated in more than 50 Mexican cities, adding new ones every month, and says it can open a city in a week or less. It uses AI for several years in routing, vehicle-size choice and scheduling, and in one example it solved a client's office parking jam by finding pick-up bays about 500 metres from the building. It earned from bookings and onboard sales on the intercity routes and now from corporate contracts (our reading of the sources). The company was founded in 2020 by Rodrigo Martínez, a third-generation bus operator, and Anca Gardea, during the pandemic. It raised a seed (Alumni Ventures and Expa) and, in June 2022, a US$20 million Series A led by UP.Partners with Maniv Mobility, Toyota Ventures, K5 Global and Mazapil, plus existing investors including Tuesday Capital, Expa, Lowercase, Moving Capital, MGV, Brainstorm Ventures, Bling Capital and Amplifica, for US$26 million in total, to expand in Mexico, Latin America and cross-border US travel and to push toward electric fleets. In 2026 the CEO is weighing expansion outside Mexico, starting with industrial peripheries, but no countries or dates are given. We found no verifiable funding or revenue figures after 2022, and the date of the shift from intercity to staff transport is not stated.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: in Mexico and much of Latin America, intercity and staff bus transport runs on small, individually owned operators with manual planning and uneven service, while factories and offices must bring workers in daily around the clock, and tens of thousands of kilometres of corridors lack a good option. The logic: separate the vehicle from the platform. Operators keep the capital and the driving; Kolors sells planning, data, customer experience and trust, so it can scale without buying fleets, and employee-transport contracts are recurring, predictable and tied to a daily need. Why now: the pandemic-era launch grew fast (millions of passengers in a short time, said Maniv's principal), mobility investors backed the asset-light model, and a nearshoring-driven rise in Mexican industry gives staff transport a bigger base of customers. Market: no independent size was found for Mexican staff transport. The only figure read is a global ride-hailing value of US$4.17 billion in 2026 (Mordor Intelligence, relayed by Ecosistema Startup), which is a different market, and an IDB statement that Latin American transport needs could double by 2050. Our rough estimate: if 1 to 2 million Mexican workers use employer-provided transport (our assumption) at US$40 to US$100 a month per rider (our assumption), the spend is about US$0.5 to US$2.4 billion a year; a platform taking a 10 to 20% margin on a 10% share would earn about US$5 to US$50 million. This is a niche that can be profitable, not a huge one, unless the model moves to more countries. What is different: the asset-light model, the AI routing and the speed of opening cities (a week), plus a founder from a bus-operating family and a history of intercity data; competitors are local staff-transport firms and the operators themselves, not named in the sources. Fit with Norte (our reading): a founder with deep sector roots and an operator's pragmatism, in a region where a connector can help with funds and corporate clients; however, no source places Norte in either round and the Manifesto's stage and size focus is only loosely matched, so this fit is weak. Risks: thin margins and dependence on operators' service quality (the experience is shared between two companies), concentration on a few corporate clients, little public information on profitability or funding since 2022, and the pivot away from the intercity thesis the investors backed.

milestones.value: Closes a US$26 million funding package including a US$20 million Series A, and plans to expand its intercity network in Mexico, other Latin American markets and cross-border US travel
Carried more than 7 million passengers
Pilots a Los Angeles to Las Vegas route outside Mexico and launches the Kolors Rewards programme, while carrying more than 7 million passengers in the year
Operating employee transport in more than 50 Mexican cities and weighing expansion outside Mexico

description.value: Brazilian healthtech that started as a medical-cannabis marketplace (teleconsultation, prescription, Anvisa import approval, delivery and follow-up) and now also runs a digital pharmacy for chronic-disease medicines after buying Pill in 2026.

long_description.value: Cannect is a patient-centred healthtech for chronic conditions, built first around medical cannabis in Brazil. It was created in 2021 by Allan Paiotti, who had just left the executive directorship of Hospital Alemão Oswaldo Cruz and became CEO, and Fernando Domingues, co-founder of the telehealth company Conexa Saúde, who had the idea and became chairman, with early backing from the founders of Adventures, Thiago Maluf of Igah Ventures and two physicians. The first version, launched in August 2021 with about 200 products from a mapped portfolio of 350, solved the path that drives doctors away: the patient finds a doctor (via Conexa's teleconsultation if needed), receives a prescription, Cannect gets Anvisa's import approval (up to 10 working days; delivery averaged 25 days), buys through sellers that cannot sell directly, and delivers at home, earning a percentage of each sale; subscriptions were planned for a second stage. The startup raised more than R$1.5 million from angels, then a seed of a little over R$10 million in late 2021 and early 2022, and in 2023 a round of undisclosed size led by Supera Capital and BluStone with YaaX Capital and family offices, bringing the total to R$40 million. It bought the content portal Cannalize and the course platform Dr. Cannabis. In 2023 it passed R$50 million in transactions; by May 2024 more than 50,000 people had been treated, about 3,000 doctors were registered (of about 5,000 allowed to prescribe), about 800 curated products were listed, and a R$5 million media-for-equity deal with 4Equity was meant to fund educational media. In August 2026 the group, which says it has 100,000 patients, bought the digital pharmacy Pill (150,000 subscription customers, 17,000 medicines) to extend from cannabis to any chronic disease, with automatic refills, and it projects revenue above R$200 million by the end of 2028. It operates a licensed pharmacy for national and imported medicines and a physician network with courses and technical support.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: millions of Brazilians with chronic pain, epilepsy, anxiety and other conditions can benefit from cannabis-based medicines, but only about 5,000 doctors are authorised to prescribe, imported products need Anvisa approval, prices are high and delivery was slow, so many patients and doctors give up. Logic: an end-to-end marketplace removes the friction (consultation, prescription, approval, purchase, delivery, follow-up) and keeps the patient on a monthly treatment, which is recurring revenue; it aggregates demand rather than making its own products. Why now: Anvisa rules allowed controlled import and sale, and acceptance is growing: Kaya Mind counted R$971 million of medical-cannabis sales in 2025 and about 873,000 patients in Brazil. Market: R$971 million in 2025 (Kaya Mind via Exame) is the market's current size; if patients double within three years and spend the same, it would be about R$2 billion; a platform taking a 10% to 15% commission and a share of 15% to 25% of that would see roughly R$30 million to R$75 million of net revenue (our assumptions), which is why the Pill acquisition, which extends the model to all chronic medicines, matters for scale. What is different: aggregator of many brands (about 800 curated products) and integrated telehealth, versus competitors with their own products; scale (100,000 patients, 3,000 doctors). Fit with Norte: our reading is that a network of health and capital-markets operators (Conexa, Afya, Igah, Adventures angels) around a regulated, taboo-heavy category is the kind of opening where Norte's connecting role fits; no readable article names Norte for any round. Risks: regulatory change (Anvisa, medical councils), marketing limits in a restricted category, concentration on a few import suppliers, price sensitivity, and integration of the Pill acquisition.

sub_sector.value: Medical cannabis marketplace and digital pharmacy

milestones.value: Cannect launches officially as a medical-cannabis marketplace, with 200 products, Conexa teleconsultation for prescriptions and a service that handles Anvisa approval, purchase and home delivery.
A seed round of a little over R$10 million, with angels from Afya, Advent and Go4it, funds the growth of the platform (first investment already above R$1.5 million).
Transactions through the platform pass R$50 million for the year.
