Cannect announces its first institutional round, led by Supera Capital and BluStone, taking total funds raised to R$40 million, to build an app and invest in marketing and in its content and education arms (Cannalize and Dr. Cannabis).

A R$5 million media-for-equity deal with 4Equity gives Cannect TV, outdoor and influencer media to educate the public on medical cannabis; by then more than 50,000 people had been treated and about 3,000 doctors were registered.
Cannect buys the digital pharmacy Pill (150,000 subscription clients) to go beyond cannabis into all chronic diseases, and projects revenue above R$200 million by 2028.

description.value: Brazilian private security network: smart street-facing cameras ("Camaleões") installed on condominiums, homes and shops, linked to a 24-hour intelligence center and to the police, reading licence plates and sending real-time alerts for stolen vehicles.

long_description.value: Gabriel is a Brazilian security company that builds a private network of smart cameras for public safety. It was founded in 2020 in Rio de Janeiro by Erick Coser (CEO), Otávio Miranda and Sérgio Andrade, after the idea of a software layer over existing city cameras failed because many were non-working "scarecrows"; they then designed their own hardware, the Camaleão, a pair of high-resolution cameras with a 180-degree view of the street. The cameras are installed on the facades of condominiums, houses and shops, always pointed at public space, and are lent to the subscriber (hardware as a service) under a four-year contract; the more buildings join, the denser and smarter the network gets, which gives neighbours a free-rider benefit and drives word-of-mouth sales. Footage and licence-plate readings go to a 24-hour intelligence centre, which validates alerts and calls the police (the data is passed to the military police for free), and which also supports investigations after crimes. In 2021 the plans started at R$199 a month; in 2026 the average ticket was about R$800 a month, from R$400 to R$20,000 for club-style condominiums. The company started in Leblon and Ipanema, raised a R$66 million Series A led by SoftBank in October 2021, entered São Paulo in December 2021 (Pinheiros and Jardins) and in January 2024 raised a R$35 million extension co-led by Astella and Qualcomm Ventures to densify São Paulo. In 2026 the company reported operating break-even after three months of positive EBITDA, growth from 4 to 45 cities in the year, about 22,000 cameras in about 8,000 buildings in Rio, São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo, 4 million plate readings a day, revenue up 100% in the last year and 200% the year before; in November 2026 it counted 8,500 clients, 24,000 cameras and 75 cities in five states, and took R$20 million of subsidised credit from Desenvolve SP to build a third-generation camera with two sensors and a Qualcomm chip, to describe street events in natural language and act preventively. The company reports that over three years its images helped arrest 830 people and locate 17 missing persons.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilian households and businesses spend heavily on private security (electronic security alone billed R$16 billion in 2025, up 73% since 2021, according to Abese via InvestNews) but each building's cameras are isolated, mostly cheap and rarely used by the police, so streets do not become safer. Logic: a network of street-facing cameras is worth more than the sum of its parts (plate reading and alerts across a district), so each new building lowers the cost of safety for its neighbours and drives word-of-mouth growth; owning the hardware, router and software keeps costs low (the CEO says it operates at about 1% of the cost of Smart Sampa for half the capacity) and recurring four-year contracts make revenue predictable. Market: with 8,500 clients at about R$800 a month (company figures) the run-rate is about R$80 million a year; the CEO's target of 10% of São Paulo's condominiums would be about 2,000 buildings (Brazil Journal), which implies about 20,000 condominiums in the city (our arithmetic); a full penetration of São Paulo condominiums at R$800 a month would be about R$190 million a year, and with Rio, other capitals, houses and shops the realistic pool is some R$1 billion to R$2 billion a year (our estimate, 5 to 10 times the São Paulo figure), against an electronic-security market of R$16 billion. What is different: its own hardware plus a licence-plate network connected to the police at no cost to the state; competitors include portaria remota providers, tótem camera networks such as Yellowcam, and public systems such as Smart Sampa. Fit with Norte: our reading is that Norte joined the Series A beside SoftBank, Globo Ventures and Canary, consistent with its role of bringing top funds onto the cap table of obsessed founders; Norte is named in two articles for 2021. Risks: legal and privacy debate about private surveillance of public space, hardware capex and the lock-in of four-year contracts, dependence on a single Chinese supplier, and the new product's cost.

sub_sector.value: Private smart-camera network for public safety

milestones.value: Erick Coser, Otávio Miranda and Sérgio Andrade found Gabriel in Rio de Janeiro; after dropping the idea of integrating existing city cameras, they build their own Camaleão camera and start in Leblon and Ipanema.
Gabriel raises a R$66 million Series A led by SoftBank, with more than 1,500 cameras in Rio's Zona Sul (five times the state government's network in the city) and an arrest count of 18 that year.
Gabriel enters São Paulo, in Pinheiros and Jardins, with 300+ cameras, after demand from residents, to prove it can replicate its Rio network.

A R$35 million extension of the Series A, co-led by Astella and Qualcomm Ventures, funds the densification of São Paulo; by then it served 600 condominiums there and had helped in 3,200 cases and 250 arrests.
The company takes R$25 million of working-capital debt from Itaú Asset Management, its first debt financing.
Gabriel reaches operating break-even after three consecutive months of positive EBITDA and expands from 4 to 45 cities in the year, with a claimed 100% revenue growth in the last year.

Desenvolve SP lends R$20 million to build the third-generation camera, with two sensors and a Qualcomm chip, able to describe street events and act preventively; the company has 8,500 clients and 24,000 cameras in 75 cities.

description.value: Argentine infrastructure company that lets banks, retailers, consumer-goods firms and fintechs with a network of merchants offer their own white-label payment acceptance and financial services through SmartPOS terminals with an app store.

long_description.value: Menta is a Buenos Aires company that sells payment-acceptance infrastructure as a white label. The idea is that a company which already has a network of small merchants (a bank, a large consumer-goods maker, a regional retailer, a delivery or e-commerce platform, a fintech or super-app) can offer those merchants its own card-acceptance and financial services without building a payments company: Menta supplies the SmartPOS terminals under the client's brand, a store of apps that runs on them, the processing and back office, a modular payments platform and the local integrations in each country. The terminal can carry more than payments, such as bill payment, credit, investments, crypto cash-in, loyalty programmes or even table and stock management, and clients or third parties can add their own apps. It earns a fee on each approved transaction and shares revenue with the client, so it only earns when the client does; integration is plug-and-play in about a month with no installation cost, or custom for larger clients. Its first clients were large networks in Argentina, then Mexico and Colombia, and the company says merchants adopted it easily and that it yielded nearly six times more than the solution they used before. The company was started in 2021 by three people from payments: Virginia Folgueiro (CEO, an early Google employee in Latin America who led merchant solutions at Naranja X and had to build a similar product there, which gave her the idea), Alejandro Quirno Lavalle (originally CMO, later CFO; ex-U.S. Bank, with an earlier car-leasing fintech) and Santiago Lorenzo (CTO, 20 years in payments technology, ex-Prisma and Visa). They met over a beer and cofounded Menta in December 2021, after a pre-seed of US$1.7 million led by Pear VC with Matterscale and Gilgamesh, and joined Pear's W22 cohort. In October 2022 it announced a US$6 million seed led by Base10 Partners, with Pear, Matterscale and Gilgamesh, at a reported valuation of about US$33 million, and said it would use the money to consolidate Argentina, Mexico and Colombia and to hire. By April 2024 Forbes Argentina, which named it a Promesa Forbes, reported US$23 million in billing, about 40 people, clients among banks, large retailers and big-tech firms (e-commerce, last-mile, fintechs, super-apps) and plans for Peru, Chile and Brazil; Linked API shows 54 employees on its LinkedIn page in November 2026. The company works remotely and describes itself today as the technology infrastructure that lets any company give its own payment and financial services.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: in Latin America a large share of small merchants still lack a good way to accept cards (the CEO says two in three have no access to payment solutions, a company claim), while the companies that already serve them (banks, distributors, consumer-goods makers, retailers, marketplaces) would like a payments product but building one in-house takes more than two years, an army of developers and long regulatory processes. The logic: Menta turns that into a product they can launch in weeks under their own brand, with a terminal that becomes a platform for other services; the timing is that debit and digital payments are overtaking cash (the FIS Global Payments Report 2022, quoted by Forbes and Bloomberg Línea, projected debit cards to be the most used in-store method in 2025 with a 25.2% share). Market size, our own estimate with labelled assumptions: assume 30 large enterprise clients across Argentina, Mexico, Colombia and the next markets by a strong outcome, each deploying 50,000 terminals, with an average of US$3,000 a month per terminal and a net take of 0.3% to Menta; that is about US$9 per terminal per month, US$450,000 a month per client, US$5.4 million a year per client and roughly US$160 million a year for 30 clients. The company said US$23 million in billing in 2024 with about 40 people, so it would be at about 15% of that scenario already; a figure that mixes volume and revenue should be read with care. What is different: white label plus an app store on the terminal, multi-country with one integration, revenue share instead of up-front cost, and a team that includes people who built a merchant solution at Naranja X and ran payments technology at Prisma and Visa. Comparable companies in the region (Pomelo for card issuing, which is also in Norte's portfolio) show the infrastructure-for-fintechs thesis works at scale. Fit with Norte, our reading of the Manifesto: experienced operators who know the sector better than any investor, a round led by Silicon Valley funds (Base10, Pear) where a Latin American fund can connect customers and local operators, and early revenue. We could not confirm that Norte took part in a given round, so this fit is a reading, not a fact. Risks: the model depends on a few large clients (concentration), competition from acquirers and super-apps that give their own terminals, regulation of payment processing and, in Argentina, currency and macro volatility; and only 2022 and 2024 press exists, so the current figures are unknown.

sub_sector.value: White-label payment acceptance for B2B networks

milestones.value: Virginia Folgueiro, Alejandro Quirno Lavalle and Santiago Lorenzo cofound Menta to give any B2B company its own payment and financial solution, starting from Folgueiro's experience of how hard it was to build one at Naranja X.
Joins Pear's W22 cohort, whose Silicon Valley backing helped it raise its seed that year.
Opens an office in Mexico, its second market after Argentina, with the white-label terminal model.
Announces its launch in Colombia, aiming to be the leading embedded-finance solution for B2B companies there by 2023, and at the same time a US$6 million seed.
Has about 30 employees working remotely, with the main operation in Argentina and presence in Mexico and Colombia.

Reports US$23 million in billing, a team of about 40, clients among consumer-goods firms, banks, large regional retailers and big-tech companies, and plans for Peru, Chile and Brazil; Forbes names it a Promesa Forbes.

description.value: Brazilian fintech that automates accounts receivable for companies that sell on credit: a multichannel collection ruler (e-mail, WhatsApp, SMS), ERP and bank integrations and an AI agent that negotiates with debtors on WhatsApp.

long_description.value: Neofin is a São Paulo fintech that automates accounts receivable and collections for medium and large companies that sell on credit. Its core product is an automated collection ruler (a schedule of messages and actions) that starts before an invoice falls due and keeps going after it does, by e-mail, WhatsApp and SMS, with a different tone and next step for each debtor profile: a customer who always pays on time gets a friendly reminder, a repeat late payer gets a firmer track that can end in credit-bureau listing and protest. Around the ruler it sells a collections CRM with effectiveness reports, a WhatsApp inbox, automatic negativation and protest, extrajudicial notification, a debtor renegotiation portal and, since 2025-2026, an AI collections agent that talks to debtors on WhatsApp 24 hours a day, answers questions, sends payment slips and closes settlements. The platform plugs into the customer's ERP and bank files through an open API and a long list of integrations (TOTVS, SAP, Sankhya, Omie, Nomus and the main Brazilian banks), and has a partnership with Serasa for credit analysis and negativation. Customers are in education, distribution, accounting, industry, occupational health, telecom and securitisation funds; named cases include Unifecaf, Contabilidade Pinheiro, Bebidas Nude, BHub (which recovered 4.9 times more value after due date within two months, by the case page) and the Loja do Mecânico. It sells software on subscription plus usage, to companies, so it is B2B. Neofin was founded in January 2023 by Laura Camargo (CEO, ex-Pátria and General Atlantic; Latamfintech adds Gympass and Inventa), Arthur Cunha (CFO, ex-Credit Suisse and iFood/Movile) and Leandro Sarmento (ex-IBM and Empiricus), who each saw finance teams chase late payments by hand, in spreadsheets, over more than 14 years of combined work in finance; the first people to back it were angels Cesar Carvalho (Wellhub, formerly Gympass) and Patrick Sigrist (iFood and Nomad). In February 2025 it announced a R$35 million seed round led by Quona Capital and Upload Ventures with 17Sigma, 1616 Ventures, Far Out, BFF, Norte and Canaan, described as one of the largest seed rounds for a Brazilian fintech founded by a woman; at that time it had about 300 clients, processed about 80,000 collections a month and had 53 employees, and planned to quadruple its client base within 2025. The money was for a fully automatic renegotiation portal, an advanced collections CRM and the WhatsApp AI agent, plus hiring in data, machine learning and AI. By April 2026 the company said more than 55% of interactions were solved without a human and that clients recovered over 50% more credit, and its site now claims more than 1,000 companies.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: Brazilian companies that sell on credit (invoices, boletos, tuition, subscriptions) still chase late payers with spreadsheets, a few generic e-mails and a person on the phone, which is costly, embarrassing for both sides and slow, while default is high: Serasa figures quoted in the trade press put overdue debt in Brazil at R$382 billion and about 30% of companies as listed as defaulters. Founders who lived this as finance leaders (Laura Camargo as a finance director) built the product. The logic: collection is a repetitive, rule-based, multi-channel conversation that fits software and now language models well. Brazil has the data rails (ERP and bank-file integrations, boletos, Pix) and the channel (WhatsApp is where debtors answer), so an AI agent that reads the open invoices, offers terms and closes an agreement cuts cost per collection and lifts recovery; Neofin reports over 50% more recovery and more than half of interactions solved without a human (company claims). Market size, our own bottom-up estimate with labelled assumptions: assume about 300,000 Brazilian medium and large companies that sell on credit and could buy a collections platform, at an average of R$1,500 to R$3,000 a month (R$18,000 to R$36,000 a year) gives roughly R$5 to R$11 billion a year in software spend; a strong outcome of 3% to 5% of that is about R$150 to R$550 million of annual revenue. The company counts 300 clients in early 2025 and 1,000 or more on its site, so it is still near 0.3% of that count. Credit-recovery fees or usage on top would enlarge it. What is different: it focuses on the pre-due and post-due ruler with deep ERP/bank integration instead of being a debt-buying collector, it combines Serasa data with the AI agent, and it sells to mid-market companies that are too big for spreadsheets and too small for a call-centre vendor; partners such as Nomus (an ERP that already had a basic ruler and chose to plug Neofin in) show the integration route. Why it fits Norte, our reading of the Manifesto: highly intelligent, obsessed founders with direct finance experience, a round led by top funds (Quona, Upload) where Norte is a follower and can add its network of operators and angels (the angels Cesar Carvalho and Patrick Sigrist are from the same Gympass/iFood circle), and revenue from early on. Risks: ERPs and banks can add their own collection modules (the Nomus case shows ERPs already ship basic rulers), WhatsApp policy and cost changes affect the main channel, regulation of collection practices, and the market for software seats among mid-sized companies is fragmented, so growth depends on partner channels; the press reports are mostly the company's own numbers.

milestones.value: The first outside backers are angels Cesar Carvalho (founder of Gympass, now Wellhub) and Patrick Sigrist (iFood and Nomad), who bet on the idea before the institutional seed.
Neofin is founded by Laura Camargo, Arthur Cunha and Leandro Sarmento to replace the manual, embarrassing way companies chase late payments with an automated, personalised collection ruler.
Nomus, an industrial ERP, announces a partnership so that any receivable it creates flows into Neofin's ruler through a custom API integration, a template for selling through ERP partners.
Reaches about 300 clients, 80,000 collections a month and 53 employees and announces a R$35 million seed to build an automatic renegotiation portal, a collections CRM and a WhatsApp AI agent.
Publishes the BHub case: the accounting and finance platform replaced manual collection with Neofin's ruler and recovered 4.9 times more value after due date within two months.
Presents its AI collections agent on WhatsApp, reporting more than 55% of interactions solved without a human, over 50% more credit recovered and up to 95% lower out-of-hours service cost.

description.value: Brazilian wealth-advisory company that combines a proprietary investing AI with human advisors, using Open Finance to consolidate a client's assets and monitor them around the clock.

long_description.value: Decade is a São Paulo wealth-advisory company that pairs a proprietary investing AI with human advisors, aimed first at wealthy Brazilians who have built assets but get no private-bank-style advice. The client connects bank and brokerage accounts through Open Finance (or uploads statements and describes assets that do not show up, such as property or investments abroad), and Decade consolidates everything into one view by asset class, geography and risk, with the fees and the inner composition of each fund. It then diagnoses the portfolio (concentration, expensive products, tax inefficiency, mismatch with the client's goals), watches the market and the client's spending around the clock and raises alerts, lets the client chat with the AI to run simulations and compare investment theses, and gives each client a dedicated advisor on WhatsApp or video. The pitch is the service that multi-family offices and private banks give to the ultra-rich, without the commissions and product-pushing that the founders say distort Brazilian advice (it calls the category a 'Inteligência Patrimonial'). It makes money from a subscription of R$200 a month for the platform, the AI and advisor support, plus a by-invitation fee-based product for clients with R$5 million or more onshore and offshore, which competes with multi-family offices; it has integrations with BTG Pactual, XP, Genial and C6, and operates under a CVM investment-advisory licence while its asset-management arm (Decade Asset Management) is in the process of CVM accreditation, which would allow managed portfolios and, later, executing orders. The company was founded in September 2025 by Vitor Olivier (CEO), one of Nubank's first engineers, who built the NuConta, ran the business in Brazil and then operations and became CTO before leaving in August or September 2025, and Felipe Meneses (head of AI), the first Brazilian Thiel Fellow and cofounder of Hyperplane, the credit-AI company Nubank bought in August 2024; they met at Nubank after that deal and began talking about using AI in finance. The startup was first named Frontier Technologies. Its seed round of US$85 million, closed at the end of 2025 and announced on 2026-08-04, is the largest seed round in Latin America on record, ahead of Pax's US$40 million: it was backed by Benchmark, Greenoaks and Diffusion, with Brazilian funds Atlantico and Norte Ventures (which had been in Hyperplane). With a team of 26 engineers and financial advisors, it spent about 11 months in stealth, ran an internal beta for about six months with a few clients (following, by its own account, a few billion reais of wealth) and opened a waitlist on the day of the announcement, letting people in gradually and prioritising product quality over volume.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: only about a third of Brazilians hold any investment and Olivier says just 7% could retire on their own resources, while advice is either unavailable or conflicted: advisors paid on commissions have reasons to sell the product with the highest fee, and a country where public bonds pay above 14% a year makes the cost of bad advice large. Decade's logic: language models plus Open Finance make it cheap to read a client's whole financial picture, run simulations and monitor it continuously, so a small team of human advisors can serve many more clients, and the 'service of the ultra-rich' can reach the upper-middle class. Why now: Open Finance, the Pix generation's digital habits and, above all, capable AI, which is the 'new technology wave' that Olivier says matched Nubank's smartphones-and-cloud moment. Market size, our estimate with labelled assumptions: Anbima counts R$8.5 trillion held by Brazilian individuals in 2025, of which R$2.63 trillion in private banking and R$3.13 trillion in high-income retail, so about R$5.8 trillion sits with clients that can pay for advice; UBS counts about 386,000 dollar millionaires and about 43,000 adults with US$5 to 100 million. The R$200 monthly subscription alone is small: 40,000 subscribers would bring about R$96 million a year (assumption), so the economics rest on fees from managed portfolios and fee-based advisory. If Decade reached 1% of that R$5.8 trillion (about R$58 billion, assumption) at a 0.5% to 1% fee, revenue would be about R$290 to R$580 million a year, in Brazil only, and Olivier says the ambition is global. What is different: founders who built the largest Brazilian digital bank's core and an AI-for-credit company sold to it, backing from Benchmark and Greenoaks, no commissions, and a human-plus-AI model, versus robo-advisors and private banks. Fit with Norte, our reading of the Manifesto: Norte backed Meneses earlier at Hyperplane, which suits its focus on repeat, obsessed founders and on bringing top funds onto the cap table; the round is led by funds far larger than Norte, so Norte's role is a connector and follower. Risks: no track record or proven product yet (The Next Web notes it launched on a waitlist with nothing shipped), a regulatory path still open (the asset-manager accreditation is pending), the history of personal-finance apps failing to win the public (Startups.com.br recalls Nubank's own discontinued Olivia), competition from banks, XP and BTG with huge distribution, and a very large round that sets a high bar. Estimated with low confidence because the market arithmetic is ours.

milestones.value: Nubank acquires Hyperplane, the AI-for-credit company cofounded by Felipe Meneses; he and Vitor Olivier meet at Nubank and begin discussing AI in finance.
Vitor Olivier, who left Nubank in August or September 2025 after nearly 12 years, founds the company with Felipe Meneses; it is first called Frontier Technologies.
Runs an internal beta for about six months with a restricted group of clients whose wealth, by the company's account, totals a few billion reais, while building the platform and a 26-person team.

Obtains integrations with BTG Pactual, XP, Genial and C6 for viewing positions and, later, executing orders through the platform; operates under a CVM advisory licence and files for an asset-manager licence to offer managed portfolios.
Leaves stealth, announces a US$85 million seed, the largest in Latin America, opens a waitlist and launches a R$200-a-month subscription with a human advisor on WhatsApp.

description.value: Brazilian marketplace for credit backed by property (home equity), real-estate financing and vehicle-backed loans, comparing offers from more than a dozen banks and credit funds for consumers and companies.

long_description.value: Flow, which trades as FlowCredi, is a São Paulo marketplace for credit backed by property (home equity), plus real-estate financing and credit backed by a vehicle. The customer enters the type of property and the amount, and FlowCredi's specialists compare offers from a network of banks and credit funds (the site says more than 20 institutions, the CEO said 14 players were integrated in November 2026) and guide the person through the process; rates quoted on the site start at 1.09% a month for home equity (up to 240 months and up to 60% of the property value), 11% a year for real-estate financing (up to 420 months and 80% of the value) and 1.79% a month for vehicle-backed credit. It serves consumers directly and also companies, and it has been building white-label channels with partners in education (medical schools, so that families can pay tuition with a property-backed loan), health (loans to clinics for equipment and to patients for procedures) and architecture (renovations), testing about 12 channels in which home equity is not normally sold. FlowCredi is paid on the credit it places, funded mainly by credit-rights funds (FIDCs) and real-estate funds. The team behind it ran Credihome, a real-estate credit marketplace founded in 2017 by Bruno Gama, Caio Alfano and Deivid Bastos and acquired by Loft in 2021; Alfano and Bastos started FlowCredi in 2024, with former Credihome executives Rodrigo Gordinho and Mayle Vaz in the leadership, and Bruno Gama took over as CEO in late 2025 (Startupi calls all four of Bastos, Gordinho, Vaz and Alfano founders, while Startups.com.br and LatamList name Alfano and Bastos). The thesis is that home equity, which they put at about R$10 billion in 2024 and R$11 billion in 2025, can grow ten times or more as the Legal Framework for Guarantees (2023, which allows the same property to back more than one loan) matures, much as real-estate credit went from R$5 billion to more than R$230 billion a year. In December 2025 it announced a R$3.5 million pre-seed co-led by Verve Capital and Norte Ventures with angels Patrick Sigrist, Rafael Duton, Leandro Abreu and Gabriel Lacombe, having approved more than R$500 million of home-equity credit in 2025 with a team of 31. In April 2026 it hired a CFO (Rafael Rodrigues Lopes) and a head of new channels (Denis Senhorini); in the first half of 2026 business owners were 32.1% of home-equity contracts, up from 14.9% a half-year earlier; and by November 2026 it said it had passed R$100 million in home-equity operations in 2026 and received more than 10,000 leads a month. The CEO also warns that costs can reach 25% to 30% a year with indexers and insurance, so the product suits people who can settle fast, not people reorganising debt.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: Brazilians pay some of the world's highest rates on cheque especial, cards and personal loans while many own a paid-off property that could secure credit at 1.5% to 1.8% a month with terms up to 20 years; most borrowers have never heard of home equity, the product is complex and each lender asks for different documents. The logic: a marketplace that compares lenders and handles the process makes the cheaper product easy to buy, and partnerships in education and health put the offer at the moment of need (tuition, surgery, renovation). Why now: a high Selic that widens the gap versus unsecured credit, the 2023 Legal Framework for Guarantees (the same property can back more than one loan), and funding from FIDCs and real-estate funds. Market size: the press quotes about R$10 billion of home equity originated in 2024 and R$11 billion in 2025, with a sector projection of up to R$500 billion (a company-quoted figure, not independent), against more than R$230 billion a year of real-estate credit. Our estimate with labelled assumptions: if home equity reaches R$50 billion a year in Brazil within five to seven years (an assumption that is far below the R$500 billion projection), a marketplace that places 5% of it originates R$2.5 billion a year and, at a 2% to 3% placement commission (assumption, not sourced), earns R$50 to R$75 million of revenue; at the company's R$500 million approved in 2025 the same commission gives R$10 to R$15 million. What is different: founders who already built and sold a credit marketplace (Credihome to Loft), a distribution strategy based on partners outside the traditional channel and a white-label offer, and a broker model that does not carry credit risk on its balance sheet. Fit with Norte, our reading of the Manifesto: repeat founders with a track record in the sector, an early round co-led with Verve where a connector adds angels and top funds, and revenue already flowing; Norte co-led the pre-seed, which is an earlier stage than most of its follow-on positions. Risks: as a broker it depends on lenders' appetite and on FIDC funding, competition from Creditas, Bcredi and bank channels (the team's own résumés list Bcredi and Pontte as competitors), take-rate pressure as lenders go direct, and the consumer risk that the CEO himself highlights (total costs up to 25% to 30% a year, danger when used to reorganise debt), which could bring regulatory scrutiny. Confidence low because the market size is a company-quoted projection plus assumptions.

milestones.value: FlowCredi is created by Caio Alfano and Deivid Bastos with former Credihome executives, to bring home equity to a wider public after they sold their earlier real-estate credit marketplace Credihome to Loft in 2021.
Approves more than R$500 million of home-equity credit in the year, becoming a visible marketplace for people replacing expensive debt with property-backed loans.
Bruno Gama, a Credihome cofounder, takes the CEO post as the company, with 31 employees, starts testing about 12 new sales channels, among them partnerships with medical schools and health providers.
Business owners reach 32.1% of home-equity contracts in the first half, up from 14.9% in the second half of 2025, as financially better-informed entrepreneurs use the product for working capital.
Hires Rafael Rodrigues Lopes as CFO and Denis Senhorini to lead a new-channels area, strengthening finance and commercial expansion after the pre-seed.
Passes R$100 million in home-equity operations in 2026, receives more than 10,000 leads a month, has 14 lenders integrated and prepares a health channel for doctors, clinics and patients.

description.value: Brazilian fintech with an AI agent that guides people, mainly in income classes C and D, through credit: it finds the offers they can really get from partner lenders and follows the loan to the end. It is paid by lenders, not by users.

long_description.value: Aro is a Brazilian fintech that puts an AI agent between consumers and lenders. Instead of listing twenty offers on a marketplace, the agent talks to the user (in the app or on WhatsApp), reads their situation through open banking and behavioural data, finds out which lenders would really approve them, and follows the loan through to the end: it collects documents, checks employment from official sources, does biometrics and, if the person is in debt, shows what is blocking credit. The product covers payroll-deducted loans (consignado CLT), personal loans, loans backed by the phone as collateral and credit for people with a negative record, and it is aimed mainly at income classes C and D, who need the most guidance. The user pays nothing. Aro earns from the lender side, with three sources: a distribution fee, payment for data, and other technology services sold to lenders, including correspondent banks that were outside the big marketplaces and now get an approval pipeline of about four hours. It was created in August 2024 by Pedro Milanez, Nubank's first employee and co-founder of the proptech Lastro, and Yuri Mannes, a former vice-president of innovation at BR Media Group. The MVP went live between November and December 2025 (the press gives both months), the company left stealth on 13 April 2026 with a US$2.5M pre-seed led by ONEVC and 17Sigma with Norte Ventures, Gilgamesh and Grão VC, and by then it had passed 100 thousand users and had lent more than R$2 million from its own cash (tickets of up to R$200, using Celcoin's banking licence). By late August 2026 it reported 600 thousand registered users, about 40 integrated lenders, 200 thousand people arriving each month with growth entirely organic, annualised revenue of US$1 million (target US$3M to 4M by year end) and originations that had gone from R$100 thousand a month in December 2025 to a goal of R$10M to 15M a month by December 2026. The company dismantled its own lending book in a carve-out because it conflicted with its role as a neutral agent. Next come three embedded-finance contracts with third-party platforms (one with a benefits company), a possible new round abroad in early 2027, and, in 2027, insurance, accounts, payments, card management and agentic payments.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: Brazil has 84.2 million adults with overdue bills (51.1% of adults, R$597.4 billion in debt in September 2026, Serasa), and in the same month finance companies passed utilities as the second-largest source of overdue debt. These people, mostly in classes C and D, face a crowded and confusing supply of loans, are often refused, and have no equivalent of the private banker or advisor that exists in investing; the founders call credit the main pain in the financial relationship. Today they are served by marketplaces that show many offers few of which are approved, by bank correspondents, or by nobody. The logic: an agent that works for the user, reads open-banking data, knows each lender's rules and carries the person through contracting can lift approval and cut the friction that lenders pay to remove. Lenders pay for qualified, pre-verified demand, so the user pays nothing, which avoids the problem that earlier personal-finance apps (Guiabolso is the example the co-founder gives) had in charging users. Why now: cheap language models make a conversational advisor possible at class C and D scale, open banking supplies the data, and Pix lets money reach the user at once. Market size and reachable share (our estimate): in Brazil, 84.2 million people have overdue debts and many more borrow. If 5% of that group contracted one loan a year (4.2 million loans) at an average ticket of R$3,000 (our assumption), the annual flow would be about R$12.6 billion; a distribution fee of 3% to 5% (our assumption, in line with commission practice) would be R$380 to 630 million a year of revenue pool for distributors in that segment alone, before data and software fees and before insurance and payments. The company's own goal of R$10M to 15M a month by December 2026 would be under 1.5% of that flow; a strong outcome of 5% to 10% share is plausible only if lender coverage grows well beyond 40. What is different: it sits on the user's side but is paid by lenders, it integrates correspondent banks that marketplaces skip, it keeps the user to the end of the contract, and it sells technology services to lenders. Growth has been fully organic, reaching 600 thousand registered users in about eight months. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders who know more than it does, builds on a network and adds value by connecting the right people and bringing funds to the cap table. Aro's founder said he chose the pre-seed investors because the business will need funding, and wants credit-specialist funds next; connecting a first-time-fund-raiser to credit funds and to lenders is where a network helps. Risks: dependence on a few lender partners and on their approval rules; credit quality in the C and D segments and the reputational risk of showing rates up to 22% a month (the site discloses them); regulation of correspondents and of data use; incumbents (large marketplaces, banks' own apps) copying the agent; and the unproven claim that AI guidance improves repayment, which the Let's Money piece also flags.

sub_sector.value: AI credit assistant and lender distribution

milestones.value: Pedro Milanez and Yuri Mannes create Aro to give people an AI guide through credit, starting from the idea that the layer of service and advice that exists in investing was missing in lending.
The MVP goes live as an agent that compares and brokers loans from partner lenders; NeoFeed dates the launch in November 2025 and Startups.com.br says operation began in December.
Aro leaves stealth and announces a US$2.5M pre-seed with more than 100 thousand users and over R$2 million lent from its own cash, in small tickets of up to R$200.

Reports 600 thousand registered users, about 40 integrated lenders and US$1 million in annualised revenue, with originations that grew from R$100 thousand a month in December 2025 and a goal of R$10M to 15M a month by December 2026.

Winds down its own lending operation in a carve-out so that the agent stays neutral between lenders, and starts closing three embedded-finance contracts, one with a benefits company, to put its agent inside other platforms.

description.value: AI-native media company that creates synthetic influencers and characters as global, multilingual intellectual properties, run across platforms by a small team and monetised through brands, licensing and communities.

long_description.value: Fly Media (written FlyMedia in the press) is an AI-native media company that creates synthetic influencers and characters and treats each one as an intellectual property (IP) that can be scaled globally, in the way Disney treats its characters. The characters are built with AI from their personality to the content they publish, are multilingual from birth, and are meant to run across platforms with a small team: the CEO says that one AI influencer lets the company make 100 creatives for a brand in a day, against about 10 for a human creator. The company says it does not sell hours of video or custom avatars to brands, because that would put a ceiling on the business; its main customer is the audience (B2C), with brand partnerships, licensing (notebook covers, the education sector) and communities as the way the IPs make money. Its site presents an internal production platform, Fly Studio, that takes a character from script to storyboard to finished video and feeds each piece's performance back into the character's profile; Fly Hub, a Discord community where AI creators take classes on virality and compete in paid championships; and a counter of cumulative views across its IPs (the site says more than one billion views and more than ten original IPs; these are company figures that change in real time). The founder is Victor Trindade, known as Eagle, who co-founded the Neagle and FOCO channels (23 million followers and over 5 billion views by his account), the influencer agency FANSTAR in 2021 and the Gen Z fintech NG.CASH, where he worked with Mario Augusto Sá, who is a co-founder of FlyMedia. In April 2026 he said the company had been an influencer agency for about ten years and an incubator of human creators, which he found unreliable because he could not control creators' motivation; the lesson led to the AI IP model. FlyMedia launched on 11 December 2025 with a R$20 million (about US$3.7 million) seed led by ONEVC with Big Bets, Alter Global, the a16z Scout Fund, Norte, Hypersphere, Verve, FJ Labs and individual investors including Fersen Lambranho. By April 2026 its first two characters had traction in under two months: Zuka, a talking football that reached 500 thousand followers in 40 days with no paid media and whose world also became a map in Fortnite, and Foka, an animal character who explains the conversations of X, launched a week after Big Brother Brasil 26 began and reached 60 thousand followers on Instagram. The money is meant to develop the first AI influencers, narrative universes and digital brands for several markets.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: creator-led media is hard to scale and hard to control. A human creator tires, changes goals, carries reputational risk and can leave; the founder's own agency and incubator, which spent about ten years and a lot of energy training creators, found that stability and delivery could not be guaranteed. Brands, on the other side, want large volumes of creative at low production cost. The logic: generative video, image and voice models make it possible to build a character with a defined personality and produce its content in volume, in several languages, and to own the resulting IP instead of renting a person's attention. Why now: model quality has crossed the threshold at which synthetic characters can hold an audience (Zuka reached 500 thousand followers in 40 days according to Forbes), and short video is a cheap funnel to long-form watch time, which the CEO says is the metric he optimises. Market size and reachable share: the Forbes pieces quote a Grand View Research figure of about US$50 billion for synthetic influencers by 2030 and a projected creator economy of US$480 billion by 2027; both are second-hand figures from reports not read, so they are leads. A bottom-up sketch, with every input our assumption: if ten IPs each reached 5 million followers and earned US$0.50 per follower per year from licensing, brand deals and products, revenue would be about US$25 million a year; a breakout IP of the kind that Disney-style franchises produce is worth far more, but it is a power-law outcome, not a base case. A realistic strong outcome is a global brand portfolio in the tens of millions of dollars of annual revenue, not a share of the whole creator economy. What is different: it is a studio for owned AI IPs rather than a tool or an agency, it comes from a founder who has already built audience (Neagle, FOCO), an agency and a fintech with seven million users, and it has an internal production pipeline (Fly Studio) and a creator community (Fly Hub). Comparables are Lu do Magalu, a virtual influencer with over 20 million followers (Forbes), and Disney as the model of IP monetisation. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders who know more than it does, and creates value by connecting people and bringing top funds and angels to the cap table. This round combines ONEVC as lead, a16z Scout, FJ Labs and Alter, and angels who are NG.CASH alumni; Norte's role is the kind of follower in a syndicate of founder-friendly funds that the Manifesto describes. The founder is a repeat entrepreneur with a distribution advantage. Risks: the company is a few months old and its traction is two characters; audience attention on synthetic characters may be fickle, and platforms may limit AI-generated content or label it; IP monetisation outside advertising is unproven; model providers and copyright rules for AI-generated works are open; and the business needs hits, so outcomes are dispersed.

milestones.value: FlyMedia is announced with a R$20 million seed led by ONEVC, to build AI influencers as global IPs; it comes from Victor Trindade, co-founder of NG.CASH and of the Neagle and FOCO channels.

Reports that Zuka, a talking football, reached 500 thousand followers in 40 days with no paid media and extended its world into a Fortnite map, evidence for the AI IP model after under two months of operation.

description.value: Brazilian AI platform that gives professionals and companies access to more than 50 AI models in one subscription, and, through Squad.com, a team of autonomous AI agents for small businesses.

long_description.value: Inner AI is a São Paulo company that sells a platform where professionals and companies use many AI models in one place. The first product, launched in April 2024 after months in beta, centralises more than 50 models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others) with templates by area of work, image, video and presentation generation, meeting transcription, ten courses on applying AI by segment and a base of case law, at a lower price than buying each tool; the company runs about twenty models on its own servers, has SOC 2 security certification and keeps customer data out of the model providers' training. The site shows a bundle of its Inner 4.0 platform with Agent mode and Mago, a personal assistant on WhatsApp, at R$79.90 a month. The company was created in 2023 by Pedro Salles (CEO), who built the interface and calibrated the models, and Eduardo Mitelman (CRO). In April 2024, with a team of nine, it announced a R$12 million pre-seed led by Canary after less than a year in operation, with customers such as Claro, Embraer, Mercado Livre and Bayer; the aim was to be a Brazilian Canva and later a global product. The first sector served was human resources (onboarding and training material). In April 2026 it raised a R$30 million seed co-led by Canary and ONEVC with Norte, Crivo and the UK's Phenomen VC, at a valuation of R$500 million and R$42 million raised in total, claiming more than one million users and customers such as Embraer and Vivo. The same month it launched Squad.com, a second product aimed at small businesses: a team of autonomous agents that work 24 hours a day, starting with sales on WhatsApp, finance and marketing, and now also legal management, recruiting and operations (agents named Maky, Waz, Fin, Júri, Pipo and Opy). It opened an AI store on Avenida Paulista in April 2026, described as the first in Brazil, where entrepreneurs configure their agent team in person. In October 2026 Vivo Ventures, the corporate venture arm of Vivo, invested an undisclosed amount in Squad.com as an extension of the seed, and the two plan a 2027 tour along the BR-116 highway to bring the agents to entrepreneurs at Vivo stores, starting with three cities in the Southeast.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: professionals and small companies in Brazil want the productivity of generative AI but face dozens of tools with separate subscriptions, English interfaces, no templates for their work and security doubts. Small businesses, in the CEO's words, are 99% of companies in Brazil, and most cannot hire people to build agents. The logic: a single subscription that bundles the best models, localised in Portuguese, with sector templates, local legal data and security certification, solves the first problem; agents that run sales, finance and marketing tasks on WhatsApp solve the second, because WhatsApp is where Brazilian small businesses already work. Why now: model prices are falling, agents can now complete tasks, and a telecom distributor (Vivo) is willing to carry the product to its small-business customers. Market size and reachable share: Sebrae counts almost 24 million small businesses in operation in the last quarter of 2025 (as summarised in search results; the Sebrae release read here reports 3.93 million new ones opened from January to August 2026). If 1% of the 24 million paid R$80 a month (our assumption, the price of today's combo), annual revenue would be about R$230 million; 5% would be about R$1.15 billion. For professional users the base is larger still (the Brazilian labour force), but we have no sourced number. The company claims one million users already, but paying users and revenue are not disclosed. What is different: Brazilian localisation, own infrastructure with SOC 2, large enterprise references (Embraer, Vivo, Sabesp, Bayer), a physical store and a telecom distribution partner, and a founder pair that moved from a wrapper to an agent product within two years. Comparables: Canva (the stated analogy, valued at US$26 billion in the 2024 article) and the global model aggregators; the main competitors are the model makers' own apps. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders and adds value by connecting the right people and bringing top funds and corporate partners to the cap table. Inner AI's path from a Canary-led pre-seed to a seed co-led with ONEVC and then a Vivo strategic extension is the kind of syndicate building the Manifesto describes; Norte's role as a follower in a seed with strong leads fits that. Risks: the model aggregation layer is exposed to price cuts and to OpenAI, Anthropic and Google selling directly in Portuguese; the shift to Squad.com is a second product with a different customer and a distribution partner whose results are not yet known; user numbers are not paying users; and a valuation of R$500 million sets a high bar for the next round.

sub_sector.value: AI productivity platform and agents for SMEs

milestones.value: Pedro Salles and Eduardo Mitelman create Inner AI in São Paulo and spend the first year testing the product with enterprise partners.

Launches the platform officially after months in beta with a R$12M pre-seed led by Canary, a team of nine and customers such as Claro, Embraer, Mercado Livre and Bayer, aiming to be a Brazilian Canva.
Raises a R$30M seed at a R$500M valuation, reports more than one million users and launches Squad.com, a team of AI agents that work around the clock for small businesses.
Opens a physical Squad.com store on Avenida Paulista, described as the first AI store in Brazil, where entrepreneurs set up their agent team with help.
Vivo Ventures invests in Squad.com as an extension of the seed, and the two plan a 2027 tour along the BR-116 highway to take the agents to entrepreneurs at Vivo stores.

description.value: Brazilian AI accounting startup. It began as a full-service accounting firm for mid-sized companies and now offers to run the operations of existing accounting offices, with software doing routine work and accountants reviewing.

long_description.value: BOND is a São Paulo startup that uses AI to run the operations of accounting. It began, in the April 2026 press, as a full-service accounting firm for small and mid-sized companies with annual revenue between R$3.6 million and R$50 million: for the complex, high-touch cases a human accountant serves the client, with about ten times more reach thanks to AI tools, and for routine work (payroll, tax slips, a dismissal simulation that takes a traditional firm days and BOND minutes, instalment of an overdue Simples slip) everything is automated. Its current site presents a second shape: a partnership for accounting offices, in which BOND takes over the operation (team, systems and office space) of an existing firm while the firm keeps its clients, brand and advisory work. BOND says the software closes the month in about one hour, answers employees' payslip questions by voice or text with a human review before it is sent, checks each client's tax position at the Receita through Serpro and the client's certificate, and converts data from the main accounting ERPs (Domínio, Questor, Contmatic, SCI, Alterdata). The offer is for firms with monthly recurring revenue from R$40 thousand and promises to keep the firm's margin, with BOND earning from scale; the press says it was also considering buying client portfolios from traditional firms. The date of the shift from direct service to the partner model is not public. The founders are Matheus Oliveira, an early Loft employee who then worked at the family office FitPart and founded his own manager, FW Capital, in 2022, and Gabriel Jordão, who spent 14 years at Jusbrasil as a programmer and then product director. They say the sector is highly fragmented (more than 100 thousand offices), uses ERPs from the 2000s and has ageing owners with no succession plan, and that startups such as Contabilizei and Agilize serve micro-businesses but not mid-sized ones. The company was created in about December 2025 (it was four months old in April 2026), opened its Brazilian entity in February 2026, and announced on 15 April 2026 a round of R$10 million (about US$2 million), led by Propel with Kiara, Norte Ventures, Hypersphere and the iFood co-founder Patrick Sigrist. At that point it served ten beta clients and was about to start selling.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: Brazil has more than 100 thousand accounting offices (101,880 registered organisations, with a 40% increase between 2020 and 2025, according to a benchmark reported by Sitecontabil), and 79% of them have no structured sales area. Most are small, run by ageing owners with no succession plan, work on old ERPs and spend very little on technology; their clients, especially companies with R$3.6M to R$50M of revenue, get slow service and often pay more tax than necessary. The logic: accounting, payroll and tax compliance are rules-driven, document-heavy and repetitive, a good fit for software plus human review. By operating the back office of many offices on one stack, BOND can lower unit cost and keep the office owner's margin while giving the client faster service. The new partner model also solves its own distribution problem: instead of winning thousands of SME clients one by one, it takes over books of business through offices that already have them, and offers owners a succession route. Why now: language models read documents and talk to employees reliably enough to automate most tickets, and the tax reform adds complexity that offices struggle to handle. Market size and reachable share (our estimate): Sebrae reports 3.93 million new small businesses opened from January to August 2026 (Agência Sebrae). Take the roughly 100 thousand offices as the channel. If a typical office has R$40 thousand to R$150 thousand of monthly revenue (the company's minimum is R$40 thousand; the upper figure is our assumption), the sector's yearly billing is on the order of R$50 to 180 billion; our share assumption is that BOND operating 1% to 3% of offices at an average R$80 thousand a month would be R$0.96 to 2.9 billion a year in managed revenue, of which BOND keeps the part that is not paid back to the offices (its fee is not public). This is a rough order of magnitude, not a market report. What is different: it is a service business built on its own software rather than a tool sold to accountants, it positions AI as a way to make fewer errors rather than to cut cost, and the founders combine product (Jusbrasil) with finance and real-estate operations (Loft, FW Capital). Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders and adds value by connecting the right people and bringing top funds and angels onto the cap table. A first round led by Propel, with Hypersphere, Kiara and an iFood co-founder alongside Norte, matches that pattern; a service roll-up needs funding, introductions to office owners and hiring help, areas where a network helps. Risks: service quality and liability when AI makes a tax error; the transition of clients between offices is operationally heavy; unit economics are unknown and the company has few clients (ten at announcement); acquiring portfolios needs capital; the pivot between two models in months shows the model is still being found; and incumbents (Contabilizei, Agilize, ERP vendors) may add AI.

sub_sector.value: AI-run accounting operations for firms and SMEs

milestones.value: Matheus Oliveira and Gabriel Jordão start BOND to automate accounting for small and mid-sized companies with AI and human accountants.
Announces a R$10M round led by Propel with ten beta clients, to build more automation and grow organically and by buying client portfolios from accounting firms.

description.value: Brazilian startup that gives pharmacy counter staff an AI copilot integrated into the pharmacy system, which suggests product use, care and complementary items in real time.

long_description.value: Maggu AI is a Brazilian startup that gives pharmacy counter staff an AI copilot. Most attendants are not pharmacists and, after interviews with more than 100 of them, the founders found that they could not answer more than two questions about most products; the Maggu system plugs into the pharmacy's management software and, in real time and inside the normal sales flow, tells the attendant how a product is used, what care it needs (for example, avoiding the sun after an acid anti-wrinkle treatment), which complementary items fit and what to explain, which supports pharmaceutical attention and raises basket size and customer satisfaction. Its knowledge base holds technical data, package inserts and information on more than 1.6 million products sold in Brazilian pharmacies. The offer is plug and play: the pharmacy keeps its systems and adds the layer on top. The company was created in 2023 by Felipe Trevisan and Luiz Andrade, with co-founders Pedro Magela, Reslley Gabriel and Rérica Lins; Magela and Gabriel had created and sold parts of startups before (SnackIn, an autonomous-market company whose operation was partly bought by Shopper), another partner sold a company to Infracommerce, and Lins comes from pharmacy retail. It raised an undisclosed pre-seed in 2024 from Latitud and Airborne Ventures. In 2025 it grew its customer base about twenty times, mainly among small and mid-sized independent pharmacies, which adopt new technology faster. On 9 March 2026 it announced a R$22 million seed led by DGF Investimentos with Norte Ventures and IC Ventures as new investors and follow-on from Latitud and Airborne, at a R$138 million valuation and more than R$28 million raised in total. It was connected, through system integrations, to about 17.5 thousand pharmacies, of which 2.2 thousand were actively using the platform and the rest were in technical activation. The plan stated then: about 500 pharmacies added a month, rising to about 2 thousand a month by year end; close the first large chain contract within 30 to 60 days; near 30 thousand pharmacies actively using the platform by the end of 2027 (about 30% of Brazilian pharmacy retail, by the founder's account); a Series A in 2026; and a possible first pilot in Mexico at the end of 2027, since Latin America has close to 270 to 300 thousand pharmacies.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: pharmacy is Brazil's first point of contact with the health system, but the counter is staffed by high-turnover attendants who cannot know thousands of products; management systems are mostly transactional. Independent pharmacies are the majority by count and the company's first customers. The logic: a language-model copilot fed with product and clinical content and integrated into the existing system gives each attendant the knowledge of a pharmacist at no hardware cost, and the pharmacy pays because basket size, cross-sell and customer experience improve. Why now: model quality, plus 2026 changes in the sector (a March 2026 law allows pharmacies inside supermarkets and pharmacy clinical services are growing) raise the value of good counter service. Market size and reachable share: the Medicina S/A page reads about 93 thousand pharmacies and drugstores in Brazil in November 2026 (net margin of the large listed chains between 1% and 3%), and Abrafarma ranks the largest chains at R$118.5 billion of revenue in 2025 with 11,688 stores across associated chains (Mercado & Consumo). Our estimate of the independent pool is therefore on the order of 80 thousand stores. If a store paid R$300 to R$500 a month for the copilot (our assumption, not disclosed), 30 thousand stores would be R$108 to 180 million a year in Brazil; a large-chain contract would be worth more per customer. A realistic strong outcome is 20% to 30% of Brazilian pharmacies, which is what the company's own target implies. Latin America would add up to about three times the store count. What is different: it is a vertical copilot at the point of sale, integrated into the management system rather than a chatbot app; it already has 17.5 thousand integrations, the team has operated retail and pharmacy before, and nine of ten owners reportedly close at the first conversation (company claim). Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders and adds value by connecting people and bringing top funds to the cap table. A seed led by DGF (a software specialist) with Latitud and Airborne already on the table, and a founder team made of repeat entrepreneurs, is the sort of syndicate in which a follower role is natural. Risks: only about 2.2 thousand of 17.5 thousand connected stores use the product, so conversion and retention are the main unknown; pharmacy margins are thin and independents are under pressure; chains may build their own AI or buy from system vendors; the pricing is not disclosed; and the quality and liability of health advice from AI require review and regulatory attention.

sub_sector.value: AI copilot for pharmacy counter staff

milestones.value: Felipe Trevisan and Luiz Andrade found Maggu with three co-founders to put an AI copilot at the pharmacy counter.
Raises an undisclosed pre-seed from Latitud and Airborne Ventures to build the product and its integrations with pharmacy management systems.
Multiplies its customer base about twenty times, mainly among small and mid-sized independent pharmacies.

Announces a R$22M seed led by DGF at a R$138M valuation, with 17.5 thousand pharmacies connected and 2.2 thousand actively using the platform, and a goal of near 30 thousand active stores by end of 2027.

description.value: Brazilian antifraud platform that uses machine learning to block fraudulent e-commerce purchases while approving legitimate ones, reducing chargebacks.

long_description.value: Legiti was a Brazilian antifraud startup for online merchants. It connected to a client's site or app through an API, collected data on how each user behaved, and scored every transaction with a predictive model built on thousands of features (more than 3,000 in 2020 and more than 4,000 by 2022), refined every day: how many purchases in the last 24 hours, how long a user spent on each page, how far the delivery address was from the buyer's IP location. The aim was to block real fraud, which produces chargebacks, without blocking legitimate buyers, the 'false positives' that Brazil Journal said made up about two thirds of the R$9 billion a year that Latin American banks and retailers lost to e-commerce fraud. Clients paid a monthly fee for each transaction analysed; the first were mostly delivery and pet-product companies (Zee.Now, Shipp, then ZeeDog, Americanas Delivery, Petz, Daki and Rei do Pitaco). For Zee.Now, the pet-products e-commerce, it cut chargebacks by 64% and lifted sales conversion by 1.34 percentage points. The founders, Pedro Sanzovo (Brazilian) and Pearson Henri (American), met on their first day at Stanford, both worked for about three years at Palantir, and set up Legiti in São Paulo in June 2019, first thinking of working as freelancers until they saw how many scams hit Brazilian platforms, which usually paid the bill themselves. It raised a US$2.5 million seed in 2020 led by Kaszek Ventures with Global Founders Capital, Iporanga Ventures and Norte Ventures, and a R$42 million round in January 2022 led by Kaszek with GFC, Iporanga and Picus Capital. In January 2022 it had 13 customers, had prevented more than R$53 million of fraud, had 40 staff and planned 65, at least 50 customers and R$3 million of annual revenue for 2022. In March 2023 the US fraud-protection company Signifyd announced it was adding Legiti's engineers, data scientists and customer-success experts, including both founders, to its team and opening a São Paulo R&D hub; the announcement is a team hire, not a stated acquisition of the company, and we found no later activity or product from Legiti itself.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: in Brazil, e-commerce platforms usually absorb the cost of card fraud and of the filters meant to stop it. Brazil Journal (2020) reported that fraud attempts happen every 16 seconds in Latin American e-commerce and cost banks and retailers about R$9 billion a year, of which an estimated two thirds is false positives (good customers blocked) and only one third is real chargebacks, so classic rules-based filters lose money in both directions. The logic: a model that learns each user's normal behaviour from many signals, and adapts daily as fraudsters change tactics ('an infinite game of chess', as the founder said), can approve more good orders and block more bad ones; the first clients (delivery apps with high fraud and thin margins) would feel the gain in conversion and chargebacks at once. Why now: the pandemic moved sales online (Canaltech), Brazilian instant payment and card fraud grew, and machine-learning tooling made it possible for two Palantir alumni to build a data product with a small team. Market: Brazil Journal's R$9 billion a year of losses is the size of the problem; our estimate of the vendor revenue is that if fraud and false-positive losses are the pool and a vendor can capture 2 to 5% of the losses it removes as fees (our assumption), the revenue pool is about R$180 to R$450 million a year across Latin America; Brazil alone is a share of that. The company's 2022 target of R$3 million of revenue and 50 customers shows the early stage. What was different: Palantir-style data engineering, behavioural features rather than rules, and fees per transaction aligned to the merchant's volume; the competitors were far larger (the sources do not name them; Signifyd, which hired the team, is a leading example). Fit with Norte (our reading): two technical founders with a clear thesis who got Kaszek, GFC and Iporanga around them, and a seed stage where a connector adds investors, which fits the Manifesto's 'follower' role; Norte is named in the 2020 seed (Brazil Journal). Outcome and risks: antifraud is a scale and data game dominated by global vendors, and Legiti's team joined Signifyd in March 2023 within about three years of its seed, with no later activity found, so the venture outcome appears limited; the lesson is that data advantage needs volume that a young company in a niche may not reach before a larger player buys its talent.

milestones.value: Founded by Pedro Sanzovo and Pearson Henri

Announces a US$2.5 million seed led by Kaszek Ventures, with Global Founders Capital, Iporanga and Norte Ventures; its early clients are delivery companies, and one pet-products delivery customer sees chargebacks fall 64%
Reached 13 customers, including Petz, Daki and Americanas Delivery
Raises R$42 million, reports it has prevented more than R$53 million of fraud, and plans to grow from 40 to 65 staff and from 13 to at least 50 customers during the year
Signifyd announced it was hiring Legiti's fraud experts and both founders and opening a São Paulo R&D hub

description.value: Brazilian company that builds AI-driven credit operations for software companies, marketplaces and other businesses: risk models, pricing, collections and funding access, delivered through banking-as-a-service providers.

long_description.value: Core AI is a São Paulo company that lets software companies, marketplaces and other businesses offer credit to their own customers without building a lending operation. It positions itself as the intermediate layer between the end client and banking-as-a-service providers such as Celcoin, QI Tech and Stark Bank: those providers supply the ability to lend, but not the expertise to analyse data and build the best credit model, so the company builds the whole credit pipeline for the client using AI and the behavioural and transactional data the client already holds (a real-estate software firm, for example, has years of rental payment data). The site lists four building blocks: receivables anticipation embedded in the client's product, a white-label credit platform ready to operate, a connection to the credit market for funding, and AI models that estimate default, set limits, rates and conditions for each customer, detect fraud and run collections with a multi-agent system by voice, WhatsApp and email. Clients connect by API or use the white-label product; the models are tuned on the client's own data. The company says it can set up a credit pipeline in under a month, and it earns a mix of a fixed take rate and a share of results. It was founded in 2025 by Enrico Francesco Damiani and Fernando Martins, who have worked together for more than eight years: they met at university, when Martins founded an HR-tech, Preparo, that helped companies hire interns, and Damiani was its first employee; after selling it they led data science, analytics and machine learning at Stone. NeoFeed also names Carolina da Costa Carvalho as a founder, with an MBA from Columbia. They started from the shared pain that credit was hard to get in Brazil. In July 2025 it announced a pre-seed led by Big Bets (US$1 million, according to NeoFeed; Brazil Journal later says a US$400 thousand round came right after its creation) with angels including Daniel Silva of Hyperplane, Fersen Lambranho of GP and Lívia Kuga, ex-Stone. It was already working in real estate and health, with rent anticipation for landlords and receivables anticipation for doctors, with more than 40 thousand active users, 70% of the base pre-approved, default below 1% and credit released in seconds (company figures), funded by family offices and angels. On 19 March 2026 it raised a US$4.1 million seed led by 14B (one of the managers that came out of the split of Upload Ventures) with Big Bets, Norte Ventures, Nameless and the New York manager BFF and the Stone founders André Street and Eduardo Pontes as angels. At that time it had five clients (one is Alude, a management system for real-estate agencies that uses it for a rent-anticipation product) and expected more than US$3 million in revenue in 2026. The money is for the team and the platform.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: more and more software companies, marketplaces and platforms want to lend to their customers because credit turns into a growth tool, but running credit is expensive and complex: risk modelling, data, legal flows, monitoring, collections and funding. Banking-as-a-service providers supply the rails, not the know-how, and standard bureau-based rules ignore the richer data these companies hold, so approval is low and default high. The logic: a specialist decision layer that uses the platform's own data to approve more at the right price, and agents to automate documents and collections, makes a credit product a feature that a software company can switch on in weeks. Why now: the Central Bank's BaaS and Pix rules have matured, AI agents cut the operational cost of credit, and more platforms see credit as revenue. Market size and reachable share: the Central Bank reports a total credit stock of R$7.444 trillion in September 2026 (55.5% of GDP; household credit +9.9% in twelve months, corporate +6.5%). The company's niche is embedded credit through software platforms, for which no independent size was found. Our bottom-up sketch: if 2,000 software and marketplace clients each originated R$20 million a year (our assumption), the flow would be R$40 billion; at a 1.5% take rate plus profit share (our assumption, the real take is not public) revenue would be about R$600 million a year; the company targets about US$3 million of revenue in 2026 with five clients. A strong outcome is therefore a few percent of embedded-lending originations in Brazil, with Latin America as a later option. What is different: it does not compete with the BaaS providers, it sits on top of them and shares risk results with the client; the two founders led data science at Stone and have an eight-year working relationship; early cases (rent and doctors' receivables) show low default, if the company figures hold. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders and brings top funds and angels to the cap table. Core AI added Stone's founders, Big Bets and 14B in a year, and credit infrastructure needs funding partners and sector introductions that a network can supply; Norte entered at the seed. Risks: concentration (five clients); the product depends on BaaS providers and on funding from family offices and angels, not yet from institutional credit funds; default rates may rise outside the first two segments or in a worse credit cycle; regulation of credit and data use; and competition from the BaaS providers' own decision tools and from the clients' own data teams.

sub_sector.value: AI credit decisioning layer for embedded lending

milestones.value: Enrico Damiani, Fernando Martins and Carolina da Costa Carvalho found Core AI to turn any software company into a credit platform; the first clients are in real estate and health.

Announces a pre-seed led by Big Bets with Hyperplane's Daniel Silva, Fersen Lambranho and Lívia Kuga as angels, already serving rent and doctors' receivables anticipation for more than 40 thousand active users.

Raises a US$4.1M seed led by 14B with five clients, Alude among them, and a target of over US$3M in 2026 revenue; it presents itself as the last mile of credit on top of banking-as-a-service providers.

description.value: Brazilian deep-tech company with an AI platform that gives industrial operators a single view of each critical asset and recommends auditable maintenance, parts and logistics decisions.

long_description.value: Datamint is a Rio de Janeiro company that builds an AI platform to manage physical assets in critical industrial operations such as oil and gas, energy, sanitation, heavy industry and, as targets, pharmaceuticals, steel and cement. Its Asset 360 Platform pulls data from ERPs (such as SAP), maintenance systems (EAM and CMMS), SCADA, sensors, documents and images into one semantic model of each asset (its function, position, criticality, dependencies, history, parts and logistics) and puts specialised agents to work on it: Asset Ledger (the data layer), Asset Inventory Studio (critical parts and stock) and SmartRoute Agent (logistics), with more agents planned. The system ranks maintenance by consequence for the operation instead of queue order, decides maintenance, parts and logistics together, and records each intervention as traceable evidence for audits and regulators. A key difference is what it calls auditable AI: it combines AI models with deterministic systems, operational rules and mathematical optimisation so that every recommendation can be traced, explained and verified, which matters in regulated sectors where generative models alone are not enough. It runs on top of existing systems without replacing them, and uses partners' technology such as Google and Nvidia and databases such as Neo4j and Redis. In practice the platform produces many small suggestions that add up: for a solar-power client it found accumulated dirt on a row of panels and, from the plant's security cameras, tall vegetation shading the panels. The company was founded in 2021 within the PUC-Rio orbit by Hélio Lopes, a computer-engineering researcher and long-time PUC-Rio professor (the press gives his career as 34 years in Baguete and more than 40 years of teaching in Brazil Journal), with some of his postgraduate students, and began as a bootstrapped consultancy for oil, gas, energy and sanitation clients. About two years before June 2026 it decided to move from consulting to a product platform, after finding that managing physical assets was the main pain. Túlio Ribeiro, for two decades a venture-capital manager at Lanx Capital who had known Lopes since the early 2000s, joined as partner and CEO in April 2026 to lead sales. On 12 to 17 June 2026 it announced a seed round of US$5 million (about R$25 million) led by Headline, with Opus Investimentos, Valutia, Kittyhawk and others, to expand the platform, strengthen engineering and accelerate sales in Brazil and abroad, and to enter pharmaceuticals, steel and cement.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: asset-intensive operators (oil and gas, energy, sanitation, heavy industry) own thousands of assets but their data sits in separate systems: the ERP knows the cost, the maintenance system the work order, SCADA the state, and nothing knows the whole asset. People connect the pieces by hand, interventions are queued rather than prioritised by consequence, and procedures live in the heads of long-tenured staff, so capital is lost and decisions come late. The logic: a shared semantic model of each asset, with auditable AI on top, can turn existing data into ranked, traceable recommendations, and because it overlays existing systems it avoids a costly replacement. Why now: operators are trying AI, but most enterprise AI is in isolated projects or personal productivity; regulated plants need traceability, which gives a hybrid (AI plus rules plus optimisation) an edge over pure generative tools. Market size and reachable share: no independent size for Brazilian industrial asset management was readable; market-research pages quote global estimates for predictive maintenance (about US$10.4 to 10.6 billion in 2024) and enterprise asset management (about US$5.5 to 7.5 billion in 2026) that differ widely and were seen only in search summaries, so they are leads, not Sources.
