Our bottom-up sketch, with every input an assumption: if 1,500 large industrial sites in Brazil and 10,000 worldwide could pay US$200 thousand a year for a platform contract, Brazil would be about US$300 million a year and the world about US$2 billion; a realistic strong outcome is a few dozen to a hundred customers, which is US$5 to 20 million of recurring revenue. What is different: it started as a consultancy with real field knowledge and academic depth, the platform is built around the asset rather than the sensor or the work order, and it stresses auditability. Comparables in Norte's own portfolio and on the market are predictive-maintenance companies such as Tractian (sensors first) and enterprise vendors (SAP, IBM and others), against which Datamint positions as a decision layer on top. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs obsessed, highly intelligent founders and adds value by connecting the right people at the right time and bringing top funds onto the cap table. Datamint is a deep-technology company with a professor-founder and an experienced venture-capital manager turned CEO, and it needs enterprise introductions and later-stage funds; none of the readable articles names Norte, so Norte's participation is not confirmed. Risks: long enterprise sales cycles and the shift from consulting to product; large incumbents (SAP, EAM vendors) and sensor-led competitors moving up; integration effort for each client; revenue and customer numbers are not disclosed; and the founder-CEO split is recent (CEO since April 2026).

milestones.value: Hélio Lopes and some of his postgraduate students found Datamint as a bootstrapped consultancy in data and AI for oil and gas, energy and sanitation companies.
Túlio Ribeiro, a former venture-capital manager at Lanx Capital, joins as partner and CEO to lead the move from consultancy to a scalable platform.
Announces a US$5M seed led by Headline to scale the Asset 360 Platform in Brazil and abroad and to enter pharmaceuticals, steel and cement.

description.value: Colombian fintech building an AI-native bank for real estate in Latin America: it collects and disburses rent for real estate agencies, offers landlords rent guarantees and advances, and runs AI agents for property management.

long_description.value: Palomma, based in Medellín, Colombia, says it is building the 'AI-native bank for real estate' in Latin America, starting with rent. It works through real estate agencies in a B2B2C model: AI agents that automate the agency's leasing, sales and collections conversations; a payment gateway specialised in rent that collects from tenants and pays out to landlords and agencies (treasury and disbursement included); Palomma Plus, a rewards programme for tenants; rent guarantees; and Palomma Advance, which gives landlords up to 12 months of rent in advance. Money comes from owning the rent flow and then monetising it with credit, guarantees and insurance (the Y Combinator profile describes this plan; fees are our reading). By November 2026 it served more than 500 agencies and 200,000 tenants, processed about US$130 million of rent a month (about US$1.5 billion a year), and had grown annual recurring revenue from about US$100,000 to about US$3 million in roughly 18 months. The company began as something else. Cipriano Echavarría, a Duke economist from Medellín who sat at David Vélez's old desk at Morgan Stanley, wrote to the Nubank founder, joined Nubank's team in Colombia and learned how to scale consumer banking; with two MIT engineers, Felipe Monsalve (Meta, Bloomberg) and Nicolás Gómez del Campo (J.P. Morgan trading systems), he started a payment method that let people pay online businesses directly from their bank account in Colombia, which was weeks from launch in March 2023 when Y Combinator admitted it to its Winter 2023 batch (US$500,000 from YC, with Latitud and Nido Ventures also backing it). After a pivot, it found its niche in digitising and financing rent (the date is not stated in the Forbes article; a secondary profile says 2024). It closed a US$14 million round in November 2026 led by Cometa (Mexico) with Volpe Capital, Clocktower, Tekton, Simma and Yango Ventures, and returning backers Y Combinator, Nido, Norte Ventures and 17Sigma; US$10 million is recorded as the Series A and the rest as an earlier pre-Series A without date or investors. The funds are to consolidate Colombia, strengthen guarantees and prepare international expansion.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: renting is the largest recurring financial flow in Latin American real estate, yet it is run by agencies on manual processes, bank transfers and thin technology, and banks have not designed anything for it. In Colombia, 41% of households live in rented homes (DANE, via Forbes Colombia), the highest share in the region and fourth in the world, which means about 8 million households paying rent and an annual flow above US$30 billion. Landlords wait for payment and want cash early, tenants have little access to credit, and agencies lose time on collections. The logic: whoever owns the rent flow sees the best data on both sides and can sell credit, guarantees, advances and insurance on top, which is why Palomma starts with the agency's software and AI (to win the customer) and with payments (to own the flow), then monetises through financial products. Why now: language models can run the agencies' leasing and collections conversations, bank-to-bank rails (and Pix-like systems) make collection cheap, and the Colombian rental guarantee market is only partly served. Market: the company's figures, relayed by Forbes Colombia, put real estate financial flows in Latin America at US$565 billion a year with rent the biggest and most recurring at about US$205 billion (the YC profile says US$235 billion; the two differ). Our estimate of the revenue pool: its present US$3 million of ARR on about US$1.5 billion of annual rent processed implies a take of only about 0.2%; if financial products raise the blended yield to 0.5% to 1.5% of the rent flow (our assumption), then capturing 5 to 10% of Colombia's roughly US$30 billion would be about US$7 million to US$45 million a year, and 5 to 10% of the region's US$205 billion would be about US$50 million to US$300 million a year. What is different: a focus on one vertical where it owns agencies, payments and credit, a team with Nubank and big-bank experience, and the sector pioneers backing it; competitors named by the source are traditional banking groups such as Grupo Aval and Grupo Bolívar, and rent-guarantee players like CredAluga in Brazil are comparables abroad (from our other research). Fit with Norte (our reading): founders who showed they could pivot, a regional thesis that matches other Norte-backed rental-guarantee companies and a connector role at the early stage; Forbes lists Norte among returning investors, so it backed an earlier round, but no source describes that round. Risks: ARR is small against the US$130 million monthly flow, so margins on payments are thin; credit and advances can bring losses; Colombia is one market and cross-border rent rules vary; and the company has already pivoted once.

sub_sector.value: Real estate rent payments and AI

milestones.value: Admitted to Y Combinator's Winter 2023 batch
Weeks from launching its bank-to-bank online payment method in Colombia, with deals already signed with several e-commerce platforms, and backed by Latitud and Nido Ventures alongside Y Combinator

Reaches more than 500 agencies, 200,000 tenants and about US$130 million of rent processed a month, with ARR up from about US$100,000 to about US$3 million in roughly 18 months, and raises US$14 million led by Cometa

description.value: New York software company that sells a shared workspace where people and AI agents work as teammates, with shared memory, roles, permissions, approvals and budgets.

long_description.value: Oasis (Oasis HQ, at joinoasis.com) is a New York software company that sells a shared workspace where people and AI teammates work together. Its argument, set out on its About page, is that AI agents arrive like rookies with talent but no chemistry: they do not know a team's norms, so they create drag, overspend and lose context when the team switches models or tools. Oasis is the place where they can learn from the work itself. The product combines rooms (group chats where people and agents share context and co-edit documents, sheets or code), a shared memory that carries what the team has learned across any model or harness, roles and permissions per agent (View, Use, Edit or Admin), approval rules for actions such as sending an email, recurring scheduled work, reusable instructions and skills, per-agent budgets that connect spend to projects, tasks and outcomes, and a choice of models from those the organisation approves. Teammates log into the tools the team already uses (for example Salesforce) with their own computer and browser, and the company says its agreements with model providers prohibit training on customer data and that a DPA covers each customer. Example agents on the site do sales prospecting, follow-up of commitments made in calls, and campaign suggestions. The company is led by ex-Palantir forward-deployed engineers, who say they have deployed agent systems in the real world: Stefano Fantini Delmanto is the CEO and Naveen Sharma, with a background in AI, robotics and applied mathematics, is a founder; blog posts are signed by Stefano, Naveen and Jayson. It is listed in a16z's speedrun accelerator and the first dated blog post is from 28 April 2026. The company has no public funding round, press coverage or customer list that could be read, so this profile rests on its own pages.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: companies are starting to give AI agents real work but agents live in individual chat windows, terminals or scripts; each person rebuilds context, there is no shared memory, permission model or budget, and when the team changes models or tools the learning is lost. Less technical teams cannot assemble multi-agent teams at all, as the founders say on their accelerator page. The logic: if the workspace owns the memory, roles, permissions and cost accounting, then models and agents become interchangeable parts, and the team's accumulated context becomes the asset. This is the same logic that made collaboration suites sticky: the system of record for how a team works. Why now: agents are capable enough to act in business tools, and enterprises need governance (approvals, budgets, data terms) before they let them. Market size and reachable share: no independent market-size source was read. Our bottom-up sketch, with all inputs our assumptions: if 100 thousand mid-sized and large organisations worldwide paid US$30 thousand a year for an agent workspace, the pool would be US$3 billion a year; a strong outcome of 3% to 5% of that would be US$90 to 150 million of annual revenue. This is an order of magnitude only, since the category does not yet exist as a budget line. What is different: it treats agents as teammates with roles, shared memory and limits instead of as tools, it is model- and harness-agnostic, and it is built by engineers who deployed agents at Palantir, which supports credibility with large customers. Competition is broad: the model providers' own enterprise workspaces and agent platforms, collaboration suites adding agents and automation platforms; none of them was read for this profile. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders who know more than it does, and creates value by connecting the right people and bringing top funds onto the cap table. A young team of technical founders in New York, inside a leading accelerator, is the type of early bet where Norte's network of operators and funds may help with first customers and follow-on investors; the size and date of Norte's investment are not public. Risks: the category is crowded and moving quickly, and large model and software vendors can bundle similar features; the product's value depends on companies trusting agents with tools and data; the company is months old with no public customers or revenue; and, as a team in the US with a Brazilian investor, it depends on fundraising there.

sub_sector.value: Workspace for human and AI agent teams

milestones.value: Publishes its first dated blog post, "Why Oasis exists", on why powerful agents are only useful when they can coordinate, share context and keep people in control.

description.value: Latin American company building AI superintelligence platforms (its product is SERAPH) for security, intelligence and defense institutions.

long_description.value: Akash builds what it calls superintelligence platforms for security, intelligence and defense institutions in Latin America. Its product, SERAPH, is an intelligence platform that brings institutional data, open sources and geospatial intelligence into one context, uses AI agents and specialised models to test hypotheses and trace evidence, and produces assessments that evolve as new information arrives, with human judgment at the centre. According to its site the company was founded by Latin American talent returning to the region (it mentions Olympiad medallists, researchers and engineers, with experience at the technological frontier) to help the region's institutions solve their most important problems, and it presents itself as a company with regional conviction and hemispheric ambition. The site, available in Spanish and English at akash.earth and akash.si, names no customers, funding or launch date, and no press coverage or registry data was found, so little else can be stated. The legal name in the footer is Akash Research, Inc., and the company's LinkedIn page, which lists about five people, places it in Mexico City, in line with the site's Latin American focus. Its co-founders are Máximo Nájera, CEO, a researcher who was a Huawei tech fellow and led research at the robotics and AI laboratory of Mexico City's Ibero university, and Efrain Quintero, chief technology officer; the CEO's role dates from December 2025. The domains were registered in September 2025 (akash.earth, 2025-09-24) and September 2026 (akash.si, 2026-09-23), according to the public domain registry (RDAP), which suggests how recent the company is.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: security, intelligence and defense institutions in Latin America face a flood of institutional records, open-source information and satellite or geospatial data that analysts must connect by hand, with little local tooling built for the region's languages and realities. The logic: AI agents that can gather evidence, test hypotheses and keep assessments up to date can multiply the output of scarce analysts, and a regional builder with local talent has a trust and context edge over foreign vendors when the buyer is a government institution. Why now: general-purpose models have made this kind of analysis possible, and governments are looking for sovereign or regional options. Market size and reachable share: no source was read. Our sketch with assumptions only: if 200 institutions across Latin America (national intelligence, police, armed forces, border and customs agencies) paid US$500 thousand a year, the pool would be US$100 million a year; capturing a quarter would be about US$25 million. This is an order of magnitude only. What is different: it is regional and mission-driven, claims world-class technical talent (Olympiad medallists), and builds one platform that fuses institutional, open-source and geospatial data. Comparables abroad are defense-intelligence AI companies that have raised large rounds; none was researched for this profile. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders who know more than it does, and builds on a network that opens doors; a founder team that the site describes as top technical talent selling to institutions needs introductions to buyers and later-stage funds, which a network can supply. No source documents Norte's investment. Risks: long and political public-sector sales cycles; reputational and ethical scrutiny of surveillance and defense tools, which the site's 'human judgment' language reflects; export and data-sovereignty rules; and the absence of any public evidence of customers or funding; the team is small (about five people on LinkedIn), the CEO is a researcher and the other listed co-founder's background was not read.

sub_sector.value: AI intelligence platform for security and defense

description.value: AI lab that trains, deploys and keeps improving custom models for the work that a company's AI agents do, using the customer's own data, traces and feedback.

long_description.value: Asteras presents itself as a frontier AI lab that trains, deploys and keeps improving models for the work a company's AI agents do. Its argument is that a better prompt, more tools or a rebuilt harness only take an agent so far, and when the model itself is the bottleneck the same failures keep returning while the cost of getting the work done grows; the alternative is to train a model on the work. The site describes a loop in which the customer's harness, agent traces and institutional knowledge become the environments and datasets used to train a model; Asteras then evaluates quality, response time and cost against what the agent does today, deploys a model that meets the performance targets in the Asteras cloud or the customer's own cloud, and feeds real usage and user feedback into new rounds of evaluation and training. The customer's team builds the agent and Asteras works on the model, across both training and inference, so that results are judged in the customer's application at production cost and scale; it also promises to evaluate new architectures and training methods against the customer's needs. The site's description tag and privacy page use a broader wording (an applied AI lab building domain-specific models, agentic systems and production AI workflows for teams with specialised knowledge), so the offer may include services as well as the model platform. The site (in English and Spanish, with a GitHub organisation that has no public repositories) names no customers, price or funding and no press coverage or registry data was found, so little else can be stated. Its contact section gives Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and its LinkedIn page, which lists about seven people, describes it in the same words as the site; the CEO and co-founder is Thiago Tergolino, based in Rio de Janeiro, joined by co-founders Matheus Secco, chief of research (a quantitative researcher who worked at Goldman Sachs and several Brazilian funds), and Bruno Lerner (a data scientist who led credit-limit models at Nubank and was CTO of Meetal); both started at Asteras in June 2026, which dates the company to 2026. The same site is served at asteras.ai.

investment_thesis.value: The problem: companies that build AI agents on general models hit a ceiling; prompts and tooling stop improving results, and inference costs rise as the agent does more. The logic: a model trained on the company's own traces and data can do a narrow job better and at a lower unit cost than a large general model, and the company can keep improving it from usage. A lab that does the training and the serving removes the need for the customer to build a research team. Why now: open-weight models, cheaper training methods and agent traces make fine-tuning and reinforcement-style training on company workflows practical. Market size and reachable share: no source was read. Our sketch with assumptions only: if 5,000 companies worldwide with production agents each paid US$300 thousand a year for custom model training and serving, the pool would be US$1.5 billion a year; a strong outcome of 2% to 4% would be US$30 to 60 million. The category is new and the number is an order of magnitude only. What is different: it positions as a lab, not a consultancy, and sells improvement of the model itself instead of better prompting; the full loop (environments from the customer's traces, evaluation, deployment, continuous retraining) is the claimed differentiator. Competitors include the large model labs' own fine-tuning and reinforcement-learning services, open-source tuning tools and other custom-model startups; none was researched. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders who know more than it does and adds value through connections to people and funds. A technical team in a fast-moving frontier niche benefits from introductions to early customers and later funds. No source documents Norte's investment. Risks: model labs can offer the same service and move down-market; customers' data and traces are sensitive; the value depends on proving cost and quality gains in production; and there is little public evidence of customers or funding (the team is three co-founders, one with a quantitative-finance background and one from Nubank's data science, plus a handful of colleagues on LinkedIn).

sub_sector.value: Custom AI model training for company agents

description.value: Shopping assistant that lives in Instagram direct messages: the user shares a post, reel or story and it identifies the products in it and shows where to buy them, with prices from several stores. It is free to use and links to the retailer.

long_description.value: Cartsy is a consumer shopping assistant for people who 'shop with their eyes'. The user follows the account @cartsyapp on Instagram and sends it any post, reel or story, as they would to a friend; photos, screenshots and plain text also work. Cartsy reads the video or image, spots each item and searches real stores across the web, then replies with the matching products and prices and a link straight to the retailer, where the user buys at the store's price. The same account works in a web app at cartsy.com and in an iOS app, with one history, one collection of saved finds and one cart shared across Instagram and the web: products, posts and uploads are kept and searchable, users can bookmark products, build collections (gift ideas, outfits) and compare offers from several stores. It answers in English, Portuguese and Spanish. The service is free: users pay only for what they buy at the store, and the privacy policy says that a Cartsy-managed checkout may be offered (with a payment processor holding the card data), so revenue probably comes from retailer commissions or checkout, though the site does not say. The product belongs to CR AI Labs, Inc. and the landing page shows 'Backed by' the logo of Speedrun; a16z speedrun's own company page confirms that Cartsy is in its seventh residency cohort (SR007), is based in New York and has a team of three. That page, written by the company, describes it as the agentic-commerce layer for social media, aimed at what it calls the US$120 billion social-commerce market (the company's own figure), turning content into something shoppable in seconds with multimodal language models and a product-matching engine of its own, either as a creator's link-in-bio storefront or as an AI shopping agent that people use inside Instagram or TikTok. The founders are Alain Michel, CEO, a Brazilian entrepreneur with a Duke economics degree who founded the pet-products company Mundo Pet (sold to Cobasi, according to his speedrun profile), co-founded Lastro and was COO of BR Media Group; and Raul Dagir, founder and chief product officer, a Stanford graduate and hardware engineer who worked at Two Sigma and co-founded drachma before this. Their LinkedIn profiles, read through Linked API, show them in a stealth company from September 2025 and January 2026. The site still collects a waitlist for early access, and no press, funding round, user numbers or launch date were found.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: shoppers see products they want in videos and posts on social platforms, but finding where to buy the exact item means screenshots, guessing and many tabs. Logic: vision and language models can now recognise items in a video, match them to catalogues and rank real offers in seconds, and a chat inside Instagram removes the need to install anything; distribution rides on a channel where the users already are. Why now: models that read video cheaply, and conversational interfaces becoming the default way to ask for things. Market: no market figure was read for this company; the relevant pools are retail affiliate and checkout commissions on social-driven purchases in Brazil and Latin America, and we do not have an independent number. A rough way to size it, as an assumption, is users x purchases x basket x commission: 1 million monthly users buying twice a year at US$60 with a 5% commission would give about US$6M a year; this is our own arithmetic on assumed inputs. What is different: it works where the discovery happens (the direct message) and handles any format, with one account across Instagram and the web. Fit with Norte (our reading): a consumer AI product at the earliest stage, in an a16z speedrun cohort, run by two repeat founders (one with a pet-products company sold to a listed retailer and a Brazilian media and ad-tech operating role, one a Stanford engineer who built and left an earlier start-up); the Manifesto's emphasis on backing obsessed founders and connecting them to top funds and angels fits, though no readable source says whether or when Norte invested, so this remains our reading. Risks: dependence on Instagram's platform rules and messaging access (Meta may change or block automation); strong incumbents and affiliate players; free product with an unproven revenue model; no traction figures; a small team of three. Confidence is low because the market and traction evidence is only the company's own pages and an accelerator profile.

description.value: Pre-launch Brazilian platform with a waitlist that lets people take a position on future events through contracts offered by the broker Genial; Hedix is a technology company and says it is not itself authorised by the central bank or the securities regulator.

long_description.value: Hedix is a very young Brazilian company whose site, in mid-November 2026, is a single page with a waitlist. Its tagline is 'Negocie o amanhã, hoje' (trade tomorrow, today) and its call is to turn a view of the future into a position. The legal notice is the clearest description of the model: HEDIX Tecnologia e Marketing Ltda. presents itself as a technology company that is not an institution authorised by the Banco Central or the CVM, does not intermediate, distribute or advise on investments and is not a counterparty. The offer, distribution and intermediation of the contracts on the platform are done exclusively by Genial Institucional Corretora de Câmbio, Títulos e Valores Mobiliários S.A., and the operations are registered at the CSD, a central depository. The notice warns that the contracts carry risks, including total loss. The structure (a front-end company, a licensed broker and a registered contract) is the one that Brazilian players in event contracts are using while the rules for prediction markets are still being written, and it suggests Hedix belongs to that category, but the site does not say so and no press coverage of Hedix was found. The registry shows the company opened on 2025-10-03 in São Paulo with two administrators, João Marcelo da Cunha Pinheiro Naves Gomes and Matheus Brandão Salomão, and a US limited-liability company (HEDIX LLC) joined as a partner on 2025-12-29, which often marks a first institutional round, but no round was found. Nothing is public about customers, volume, launch date or funding.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilians already bet and trade on outcomes (elections, the central bank, football, reality shows) through offshore sites or bookmakers, while Brazil has no consolidated, authorised domestic player in prediction markets, according to Finsiders Brasil in March 2026. Logic: if the product is an event contract, the question is who can offer it legally. Hedix's structure (a technology front-end, with distribution by a licensed broker and registration at a central depository) is a way to offer it inside the financial-market perimeter rather than as a bet, which is the route regulators in the US (derivatives) and Brazil (the CVM and B3, which announced an authorised predictive market for professional investors) are leaning towards. Why now: 2026 is an election and World Cup year, and prediction markets reached record volumes abroad (Polymarket's volume reached US$2.4 billion in a week at the start of March 2026, per Finsiders). Market size: no Brazilian figure was read; as an assumption, if 1 million Brazilians traded US$300 a year with a 2% take for the platform the revenue pool would be about US$6M a year, and 5 million traders would make about US$30M, with the broker taking part of it; this is arithmetic on assumed inputs, not data. Differentiation: partnership with an established broker (Genial) from day one. Fit with Norte (our reading): a pair of young founders at the earliest stage in a regulated niche where connections to funds, a broker and regulators matter more than product at first; Norte took part in no round that we could verify. Risks: regulation can shut or restrict the category (a Brazilian article places platforms in limbo since April 2026 for entertainment, political and sports events, a lead not read here); the site shows no product, team page or traction; the broker owns the licence and the customer; competitors include Prévias (CVM crowdfunding route), B3 and XP with Kalshi. Confidence is low because the product type, the market and the founders' backgrounds are inferred.

founders.value: João Marcelo da Cunha Pinheiro Naves Gomes

description.value: Platform that lets any developer or AI agent add the official WhatsApp Business API to a product, through an API, SDKs, a CLI and a visual workflow builder. It earns from usage and, since July 2026, as a Meta Business Solution Provider that handles billing.

long_description.value: Kapso is a developer platform for WhatsApp. Companies that want to sell, support or run workflows over WhatsApp normally have to deal with Meta's official Business API directly: registering numbers, approving message templates, managing webhooks and, above all, billing. Kapso wraps all of that. A developer can connect a number in minutes and then use a typed API and TypeScript SDKs, a command-line tool, an MCP server and agent skills for coding assistants (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex), a shared inbox with human handoff, a visual workflow builder with AI-agent nodes, broadcasts, serverless functions and logs of every request. The pitch is 'the fastest way to add official WhatsApp to your product': a customer of a Kapso user can link their own WhatsApp Business number through a generated onboarding link, and the user's app then sends messages and runs automations on that number. The free tier gives 2,000 messages a month and some credits. The founder is Andrés Matte, a former partner at the Chilean pre-seed fund Platanus Ventures, who built the product largely alone. In his own telling, twelve months before the seed round it was unclear whether Kapso would be a useful product: he worked long days for a handful of early users, saw small absolute numbers but steady weekly growth, and changed nothing. Growth then came from developers telling other developers, with no sales team or paid ads: 5,000 developers in January 2026, 10,000 in March (doubled in ten weeks, helped by a post about giving an AI agent a WhatsApp number in two commands that the company says reached 700 thousand views) and more than 28,000 by August 2026, when the platform was processing more messages in one hour than in the whole of August 2025 (company figures). Users named by the company run dental clinics in Latin America, a store operated entirely over WhatsApp in Korea and customer-support agents in Europe. In mid-2026 Kapso became a Meta Solutions Partner and a Business Solution Provider, which let it launch Kapso-managed billing at Meta's rates with no markup, so that end customers no longer add a payment method inside Meta. On 2026-08-23 it announced a US$1.4M seed round backed by Norte Ventures, Latitud, Newtopia, Platanus, Hypersphere, Semilla Ventures and Chile Ventures, plus more than ten angels including the Auth0 co-founders and the Cornershop co-founder; Matte says several investors were users first and the round closed without a pitch deck. Origin and team: Matte's LinkedIn profile dates his Founder role at Kapso to April 2024, after almost four years (2020 to September 2023) as co-founder and general partner of Platanus Ventures, the Chilean pre-seed fund, and earlier work as a software engineer; he also taught a start-ups course at the Universidad de Chile. Kapso's LinkedIn page lists three employees and 2024 as the founding year. The company's legal entity is Kapso, Inc., a Delaware corporation (its terms and privacy policy give a Wilmington address); the privacy policy says Kapso is based in the United States and works with an affiliated team in Chile, Kapso SpA, which handles engineering, operations and customer service, and Matte's profile places him in Santiago. The owner's reading of LinkedIn is that all three are Chilean, work without a public office and have been trying for a long time to hire a fourth person; we could not verify the hiring posts, and the company page shows no open jobs. Agents and AI users: Kapso's MCP server and agent skills let an assistant such as Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or Codex read and act on a user's WhatsApp account, and a plugin lets a personal agent be messaged from a phone; Kapso released an official Chat SDK adapter on 2026-06-02 (Vercel listed it on 2026-06-23). A third-party guide of 2026-11-09 repeats a company figure of more than 40,000 developers. Meta's terms, in force since 2026-01-15 according to that guide, stop AI companies from distributing general-purpose chatbots over the Business API, so business-scoped bots are allowed but a public 'ask me anything' assistant is not. The stated direction is to be the communications infrastructure layer that developers and AI agents build on, rather than to ship end-user apps.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: WhatsApp is the default channel for talking to businesses in Latin America, India, Brazil and much of Europe, but the official Business API is painful to adopt: number registration, template approval, webhooks and Meta billing slow every team that wants to build on it, and the older hacks on unofficial APIs are unreliable. Logic: Kapso sells the missing developer layer (an API, SDKs, CLI, MCP and a workflow builder) and, since it became a Meta BSP in 2026, also the billing. Two tailwinds make it timely: AI agents are conversational by default and need an interface people already use, and Meta now charges for all messages, so every customer needs billing from day one, which Kapso removes. Market (rough, assumption-based, no independent size was read): the company says WhatsApp has 3 billion users and that it has 28,000 developers. If 1,000 teams paid US$200 to US$500 a month that is US$2.4M to US$6M a year; 10,000 such teams would be US$24M to US$60M, before any share of message volume if it resells Meta messages. A strong outcome is a leading independent WhatsApp developer platform in Latin America with a global long tail; the figure is our own arithmetic and is labelled as an assumption. Second audience: Kapso's MCP server works with ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor and Codex and it has a plugin for personal agents, so tech-savvy individuals running agents could become a long tail beyond B2B teams; Meta's rule since 2026-01-15 against general-purpose chatbots on the Business API limits this to business-scoped use (third-party guide, 2026-11-09), so we treat it as upside, not as the base case. Differentiation: developer-first distribution (the company says growth came with no sales team or ads), agent-friendly tooling, official-API compliance and a founder who built the product largely alone and knows the Platanus network. Fit with Norte (our reading): a small round for a technical founder whose first users became investors matches the 'obsessed founder' profile; Norte's network of operators and funds in Brazil, the largest WhatsApp market for businesses, is where connections could help, and Norte joined a round of many specialised funds. The team is three people on LinkedIn (all Chilean and, per the owner, trying for a long time to hire a fourth), which is a concrete place where Norte's help with recruiting and its network could matter (our reading, hiring unverified). Risks: a three-person team and key-person dependence on the founder; Meta controls pricing and partner rules and could narrow BSP margins or build the tools itself; competitors such as Twilio and other BSPs are larger; revenue was 'not great' a year before the round; the traction figures are company claims.

milestones.value: Andrés Matte starts Kapso as its founder, after leaving Platanus Ventures, the Chilean pre-seed fund he co-founded, in September 2023; he builds the product largely alone.
Kapso reaches 5,000 developers, growing organically with no sales team or paid ads.

Kapso ships Playbooks (pre-built prompts for its in-product agent), GPT-5.2 support in the agent and finer control of workflows: pause and resume, wait timeouts, jumping to a node and scheduled broadcasts.

Kapso crosses 10,000 developers, doubling in ten weeks after a post about giving an AI agent a WhatsApp number in two commands (700 thousand views, per the company) brought thousands of sign-ups in days.

Kapso releases an official WhatsApp adapter for Vercel's Chat SDK, so a developer can write a chat agent once in TypeScript and run it on WhatsApp through Kapso; Vercel lists it as a vendor-official adapter on 2026-06-23.
Kapso becomes a Meta Business Solution Provider and launches Kapso-managed billing, so developers can own the whole billing experience of their WhatsApp product at Meta's rates with no markup.
Kapso announces a US$1.4M seed round and reports more than 28,000 developers and more messages processed in one hour than in the whole of August 2025.
A third-party guide describes Kapso's MCP server working inside Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and Codex, and repeats the company's figure of more than 40,000 developers, up from 28,000 in August.

description.value: Brazilian AI company that automates the operational work of sales teams at manufacturers, distributors and wholesalers: turning WhatsApp lists and PDF or Excel orders into quotes and entered orders, and telling each salesperson what to do at each point of sale.

long_description.value: Kayro sells artificial intelligence for the commercial operation of manufacturers (consumer-goods industries), distributors and wholesalers in Brazil. Its premise is that sales teams in these companies spend their time on operational tasks, act as order takers and receive confusing guidance, while WhatsApp has become one of the main sales channels with no visibility for the company. The product has several parts. For the field salesperson it crosses the company's own data and gives hyper-personalised direction on what to do at each point of sale, with the argument behind the recommendation, and organises the day (what to do, in which order, at which stores). For order intake, the list that arrives by WhatsApp comes back as a quote with the items identified and the company's commercial conditions applied, and orders in PDF, Excel and other formats enter the sales-force system without retyping. It also matches the point of sale's sell-out with the manufacturer's sell-in to warn when a product is about to run out at the customer, sends commercial offers only to the right customers, and turns salesperson-customer conversations into indicators (service level, what is won and lost). A separate product, the Sales Copilot (Copiloto de Vendas), puts an assistant inside the team's WhatsApp so salespeople ask questions in natural language, managers receive reports and alerts about drops in performance, upsell and churn, with integration to ERPs, CRMs and spreadsheets. The company supports two teams in one operation, street sellers and telesales, and says telesellers become ten times more efficient. Data is captured by API, direct database connection, data lake or file export; each customer's data is separated at database level, is not used to train Kayro's own models and is handled under the LGPD; each customer has an engineering and business team and a customised deployment. Kayro is based in Jardim Europa, São Paulo, and has three co-founders, all early in their careers. Antonio Matarazzo Affonso Ferreira is the CEO; before Kayro he founded and sold WebHorse, a marketplace for show-jumping horses that, by his own account, connected R$3.5 million of horse sales in two years, and he was a member of FGV's entrepreneurship league (2023 to 2024). His profile describes Kayro as helping industries, distributors and wholesalers sell more volume and a better mix with AI built into WhatsApp. Paulo Chade worked on AI deployment and then product at Enter (2025 to April 2026) and did internships at Ant Group (credit-scoring models, 2024) and BTG Pactual (blockchain, 2022). João Henrique Santos was a software engineer at Segura (2024 to July 2026) and, from 2023 to 2025, a course assistant at Harvard University (CS50, Math 1A and Math 21b). Their profiles date the Kayro roles to April 2026 (Antonio and Paulo) and August 2026 (João). The business runs through a Brazilian company, Datacado Ltda, opened in September 2025 with Antonio and Paulo as administrators; a US company called Kayro, LLC became one of its partners on 2026-08-07. Harvard may be what connects the founders, but only João's profile shows a Harvard role, so this is a lead and not a finding. The site names no customers, revenue or funding, and no press coverage of Kayro was found, so the story after the founding is unknown.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: in Brazilian consumer-goods distribution the salesperson is the main interface with tens of thousands of small points of sale, but the work is manual (retyping PDF and Excel orders, quoting a long WhatsApp list line by line) and guidance is generic. Size of the sector: the ABAD and NielsenIQ ranking reports that wholesale-distributors earned R$616.6 billion in 2025 (up 11% in real terms), that the 768 respondent companies cover 49% of it and 1.18 million points of sale, that physical stores account for 38% of sector revenue, sales representatives 27% and salaried salespeople 22%, so most revenue still depends on human selling (Mercado & Consumo, 2026-05-12). Logic: large language models can read free-form WhatsApp messages and messy order files and match them to a product catalogue, which was not feasible a few years ago, and the data to power recommendations (sell-in, sell-out, history) already exists inside these companies; selling to the commercial team of a manufacturer is a high-ticket B2B sale. Market (assumption, not data): if 500 to 1,500 manufacturers and distributors in Brazil have commercial teams large enough to buy, at R$200 thousand to R$600 thousand a year each, the pool is R$100M to R$900M a year; a strong outcome would be a leading position in Brazilian CPG and food distribution, with a later move across Latin America. What is different: it covers both the order desk and the field visit with customer-specific integration, and it gives instructions rather than dashboards. Comparables in the same lane: Sharpi (US$4M seed in August 2026 led by NXTP and ONEVC, 20 active customers, per Startups.com.br), which shows investor appetite and competition. Fit with Norte (our reading): a vertical-AI company selling to Brazilian industry, where Norte's operator network in distribution and retail can open doors, at the earliest stage. Founders (from their own LinkedIn profiles, read 2026-11-25): Antonio Matarazzo Affonso Ferreira (CEO, founded and sold a horse marketplace), Paulo Chade (AI deployment and product at Enter, internships at Ant Group and BTG) and João Henrique Santos (software engineer, Harvard course assistant): a young, technical team, which fits Norte's wish for obsessed founders it can help with hiring, customers and follow-on funds. Risks: Sharpi and others already have traction, customers are ERP-bound with long integration cycles, the company's reach claims are not verified and the team is very young (the Kayro roles date from April and August 2026) and the profiles show one earlier venture, a marketplace, and no earlier enterprise-software company. Confidence is low: the market figure rests on assumed inputs and the founders are known only from their own profiles.

sub_sector.value: AI sales copilot for industry and distribution

milestones.value: Antonio Matarazzo Affonso Ferreira (CEO) and Paulo Chade start Kayro as co-founders, according to their LinkedIn profiles; Paulo left his product role at Enter the same month, so Kayro became his full-time job.
João Henrique Santos, a software engineer at Segura until July 2026 and a former Harvard course assistant, takes the third co-founder seat, completing the founding team.

description.value: Brazilian AI platform that follows tax laws and court and administrative decisions every day and shows each company where its operation has tax risk or money on the table, including a comparison with the tax reform; sold to companies, accounting firms, law firms and individuals.

long_description.value: Manor presents itself as an AI layer of tax intelligence for Brazilian companies. Its starting point is that following Brazilian tax rules alongside a company's operation is humanly impossible: the site cites IBPT for the number of new tax laws published every day, plus dozens of decisions, and the tax reform runs until 2033 (2026 is a test year with CBS at 0.9% and IBS at 0.1%; PIS, COFINS and IPI are phased out and ICMS and ISS fall to 90%, 80%, 70% and 60% of today's rates while IBS rises). Manor reads laws and decisions daily from federal, state and municipal sources and from STF, STJ, TRFs, state courts, CARF and the Receita Federal, summarises them with filters by source, tax and theme, connects them to each customer's operation, flags risks (a divergent tax classification, for instance) before they become problems, keeps the customer's tax matrix up to date with the official source beside each change, and organises the grounds to decide whether to keep, adjust or contest. It also compares current law with the reform. It sells in four ways: a corporate plan for the tax and finance teams that answer for taxes; a partnership for accounting firms, so they can offer clients new, higher-value services; a partnership for law firms, with research on official sources and changes affecting each client; and an individual subscription, a basic tax-research copilot with official sources, with 30% off under approval and partnerships with the OAB (the site's wording). The founder is Rodrigo Salvador, a repeat entrepreneur from Rio de Janeiro. He started the student network Passei Direto in 2012, at 22, with a co-founder (Brazil Journal names André Simões), and ran it as CEO; in March 2021 UOL Edtech bought 100% of it, mostly in cash, an exit for all its funds (Redpoint eventures, Valor Capital, Península, Crescera, Endeavor Catalyst and Chegg), and Salvador and his partner stayed on as UOL Edtech executives. His profile shows CEO of Passei Direto until January 2022 and then VP of Strategy, M&A and the B2B business unit at UOL. MIT Technology Review named him one of its Innovators Under 35 Latin America in 2022, and his profile also cites Forbes 30 Under 30 and Endeavor. Since October 2025 his profile lists him as co-founder of a 'Stealth Startup' under the headline 'Helping to build the future of tax'; it does not name Manor, so the link to Manor is our inference from the headline and from the registry, where he is the sole administrator of Manor Desenvolvimento de Software Ltda., opened on 2025-09-01 in Campinas with R$1.54 million of capital and a US company, Manor Tax LLC, as a partner from the first day. The owner's own reading of his profile suggests that other co-founders exist, but no readable page names them. The site names no team, customers, revenue or funding, and no press on Manor was found, so traction and funding are unknown.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazilian companies pay for one of the most complex tax systems in the world and are about to live through the biggest change in decades, the 2026 to 2033 transition to CBS and IBS with the old taxes running in parallel. Tax teams and accounting firms cannot read every new law and ruling, so they miss credits and take avoidable risks. Logic: language models can read and summarise legal text at low marginal cost, and a product that ties each change to a specific company's operation (not a generic news feed) turns tax into a daily, auditable routine; the reform gives a dated reason to buy now. Market (assumption, not data): Brazil has 101,880 registered accounting organisations (Escola Exchange benchmark, via Sitecontabil), and 79% of them have no structured commercial department, which says many are small and under pressure to find new services. If 2% of them (about 2,000) paid R$1,000 to R$3,000 a month, that is R$24M to R$72M a year from accountants alone; a corporate plan for mid-sized and large companies could be larger per customer, and law firms and individuals add a long tail. A strong outcome is the default tax-monitoring layer for Brazilian accounting firms and mid-market tax teams. What is different: daily monitoring that is linked to the customer's own operation and to the reform, an OAB partnership channel for lawyers and a partner channel through accountants who already own the customer relationship; and a founder who has already built and sold a Brazilian internet company. Fit with Norte (our reading): Rodrigo Salvador built Passei Direto from age 22 to a sale to UOL Edtech in 2021 and then worked inside a large group on strategy, M&A and B2B, so he is the kind of obsessed, proven founder the Manifesto describes; a vertical AI company that sells through accounting firms and enterprise tax teams is a place where a network of operators helps with introductions, hiring and first revenue. The owner reads many Norte connections in his profile; that is an observation we could not verify from a page. Norte's participation is not documented in any Source. Risks: established tax-content and compliance vendors and ERPs add similar AI features; wrong tax answers carry liability; the depth of the product and its customer base are not verifiable; the company is months old, and only one of its founders is known. Confidence is low.

milestones.value: Rodrigo Salvador, who had sold Passei Direto to UOL Edtech and then led strategy, M&A and B2B at UOL, begins working full time on a new tax-technology company; his profile calls it a stealth startup and does not name Manor, so this is our inference.

description.value: Brazilian fiduciary administrator for structured funds (FIPs, and later FIDCs, FICs and FIFs), combining proprietary software and an experienced regulatory team so fund managers can focus on investing.

long_description.value: Nash is a Brazilian fiduciary administrator (administrador fiduciário) built for structured funds. In Brazil every investment fund needs an administrator that handles registration of investors, quota accounting, regulatory filings, custody relationships and the reports sent to investors; for private equity and venture funds (FIPs) and receivables funds (FIDCs) this work has long been done with spreadsheets, e-mail and paper. Nash says its proprietary technology and a team with decades of experience in banks and administrators absorb the operational and regulatory machinery of the fund so the manager can concentrate on investing. The platform has two sides. The manager portal gives a dashboard with net assets, quota value and returns, real-time digital registration of investors, automated offers and capital calls, and a named person responsible for each manager. The investor portal offers automated onboarding with real-time KYC, a consolidated view of the investor's funds, capital calls and income statements, and a document room. The software is integrated with the main settlement banks, certifiers and registrars. Nash earns fees for administering funds; the site does not publish prices. The company was started by Francisco Aguiar, a technology and financial-services executive of more than 15 years and a former partner of Softpar (sold to Sinqia), and José Joaquim Neto, a lawyer and former VP at Hudson Advisors (Lone Star Funds) with more than 10 years structuring funds. Ernane Alves, a former director of fiduciary administration at Apex Group and Vórtx, joined as founding partner and runs fiduciary administration, with a legal and regulatory head from Lefosse, Stocche Forbes and White & Case and a compliance head who was Apex Group's LATAM head. In September 2025 Nash announced an institutional round of R$15 million from Maya Capital, Big Bets and Norte. It asked the central bank for a securities distributor (DTVM) licence in November 2025 and began administering FIPs in April 2026 after CVM and ANBIMA approved it. Its next step, subject to regulatory approval, is the DTVM authorisation, which would let it also provide custody and bookkeeping and administer FIDCs, FICs and FIFs. No press coverage was found; every fact above comes from the company's own site and the company registry.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Brazil's structured-fund industry has grown fast but the back office has not. FIPs and FIDCs are run by managers who depend on administrators that handle investor registration, capital calls, quota accounting and filings through e-mail and spreadsheets, and the investors (including new retail and qualified ones) expect the experience of a digital bank. Logic: since CVM Resolution 175 and the rise of private credit, thousands of fund classes need an administrator, and a software-first administrator can serve each one at lower cost and with better data than a bank-owned one; it also earns a recurring fee on assets that tend to stay in closed funds for years. Market: ANBIMA reports that FIDCs held R$741 billion in net assets in November 2025, with about 3,800 fund classes and 426 managers, and that FIPs and FIDCs raised R$60.1 billion and R$57.6 billion net in 2025, the largest inflows after fixed income. Our rough estimate of the revenue pool: administration plus custody and bookkeeping fees of perhaps 0.05% to 0.15% of assets (our assumption, not a sourced figure) on FIDC assets alone gives R$0.4 billion to R$1.1 billion a year; adding FIPs, FICs and FIFs makes the pool meaningfully larger. If Nash won 3% to 5% of fund assets in a decade, that is on the order of R$10 million to R$50 million of annual revenue; this is a range from our arithmetic, not a forecast. Different: the founders come from fund administration (Apex, Vórtx), fund law and fund software (Softpar), and the company is building its own regulated entity rather than selling software to incumbents, which is harder but gives control of the experience. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders, does not meddle with operations and adds value by connecting people and bringing top funds to cap tables; a regulated administrator needs exactly that, since its customers are fund managers, many of them in Norte's network of 400+ operators and investors. This is our reading, not a statement by Norte. Risks: the licence path is long and partly pending (the DTVM licence was not granted when the site was read); incumbents (Vórtx, Apex, Oliveira Trust, BTG and Itaú units) compete on price and trust; and administration revenue is small per fund, so the business needs scale and a clean regulatory record. The company is also very young, with no public customer or asset figures.

sub_sector.value: Private credit infrastructure and fund administration

milestones.value: Nash closes an institutional round of R$15 million with Maya Capital, Big Bets and Norte, which funds the technology and the regulatory process to become an administrator.
Nash files its request for a securities distributor (DTVM) licence with the Brazilian central bank, the step that would allow custody, bookkeeping and the administration of FIDCs, FICs and FIFs.
CVM and ANBIMA approve Nash as an administrator of FIPs and it begins fiduciary administration of private equity and venture funds, its first operating product.

description.value: Pediatric guidance and teleconsultation service that runs entirely inside WhatsApp: a free AI assistant (Dra. Med) answers parents at any hour and hands the case to a registered pediatrician, by text or video, when needed.

long_description.value: Sempre+ is a Brazilian pediatric service that lives entirely inside WhatsApp. A parent sends a message, with no app to download and no sign-up, and the first reply comes from Dra. Med, a health assistant trained by the company's medical team that listens to the case, explains first care, what signs to watch and when to seek a doctor or the emergency room. That conversation is free and unlimited, any hour of the day. When a case needs a diagnosis, prescription or treatment, Dra. Med hands it to a pediatrician registered with the CRM, who continues in the same chat by text or by video. Each consultation is paid on its own, with no subscription or lock-in: the company's machine-readable page lists R$27 for a text consultation and R$43 for video. Prescriptions and certificates are issued during the consultation when needed. The medical team is published with name, CRM number and training hospital (Sírio-Libanês, Albert Einstein, HC-FMUSP and São Paulo's public health system), the technical responsible is Dra. Nicole Micheloni, and the service says it follows Brazil's telemedicine rules (CFM Resolution 2,314/2022) and the LGPD. It serves children and adolescents from 0 to 18, always with a legal guardian starting the conversation, and is explicit that it is not an emergency service. The idea, as the company tells it, is that almost every parent's doubt about a child's health arises outside office hours, when the choice is between waiting in fear and a night in the emergency room. The founders are two operators who worked together at the Belo Horizonte edtech Trybe. Bruna Keiserman, founder and CEO, started on Sempre+ in October 2025; her profile shows ex-Amazon and ex-BCG in the headline, then Chief of Staff to the CEO (2021) and COO (2022 to March 2024) of Trybe, running a 200-person operations team, an Entrepreneur-in-Residence stint at the venture firm Atlântico in 2024 to develop her next venture, COO of BrandLovrs from November 2024 to February 2025, and an earlier food-delivery startup, Mimic, which she founded in 2019. Gabriela Migliorini, co-founder and chief product and technology officer, joined in January 2026 after being Head of Product for Jus IA at Jusbrasil in 2025; before that she was one of Trybe's first employees (number 20), as Head of Data from 2019 and then Head of Product, and she studied computer engineering with research and data roles in France and at Michelin. The venture firm Valutia lists Sempre+ in its portfolio as an early-stage health company bringing primary care to millions of Brazilians through WhatsApp, with a claim of 150 million-plus Brazilians without health insurance (Valutia's figure, not checked); the page gives no founding year, amount, date or round type, so no Round is recorded. The legal entity is dPed Serviços de Saúde Ltda, opened in March 2026 in São Paulo; the registry lists the two founders as administrators and a foreign partner, dPed Holding LLC, that entered in June 2026, which suggests a US holding structure around the company's first outside funding. The homepage claims more than 9,000 consultations and a 9.8 customer rating, both the company's own, undated figures. No press coverage was found, so traction beyond what the site shows, other investors and plans are unknown.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: parents of young children have urgent but usually minor questions at night and on weekends, and the usual answers are an emergency room, an unreliable internet search or a wait for an appointment. Logic: WhatsApp is the channel Brazilians already use for everything, telemedicine has been legal since 2022 (CFM Resolution 2,314/2022, per the company's own pages), and language models make a free first-line assistant cheap enough that only cases needing a doctor cost money. A free triage that converts to pay-per-consult at R$27 to R$43 is also an easy trial for a family without health insurance. Market: Brazil's population under 18 is on the order of 50 million (our approximation of IBGE Census data, not verified from a page we read), in perhaps 25 million households (our assumption). If 5% of those households became regular users who pay for three consultations a year at about R$35, the pool is about 1.25 million families x 3 x R$35, roughly R$130 million a year; a range of R$50 million to R$400 million covers 2% to 8% adoption and two to four consultations. A share of 5% to 10% of that pool would be R$7 million to R$40 million of yearly revenue, before any subscription, employer or insurer channel. Different: it is WhatsApp-native with no app, starts free with an assistant, and publishes its doctors' CRM numbers; other WhatsApp pediatric services exist (a search turned up Usawa Care in Portugal), so the idea itself is not unique and the edge has to come from execution. Fit with Norte (our reading): the founders come from Trybe, a company in Norte's own portfolio, where Bruna Keiserman was COO and Gabriela Migliorini an early employee and Head of Product, so they are operators a Norte network already knows; the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders at an early stage, does not meddle with operations and adds value by connecting people, hiring and revenue from day zero, which fits a consumer health start-up that needs doctors, health-plan buyers and consumer-growth operators. The venture firm Valutia, whose portfolio page also lists Caveo, Nomo, Datamint and Refer, all in Norte's portfolio, backs the company; whether Norte took part is unknown, and no Round is recorded. Risks: quality and liability in remote pediatric care, regulatory limits on AI and telemedicine (the company's own terms cite a 2026 CFM resolution), high acquisition costs for a pay-per-use consumer product, and no evidence yet of repeat use or margins. The company opened in March 2026, so almost everything is untested.

milestones.value: Bruna Keiserman, a former Trybe COO who had spent 2024 as an Entrepreneur-in-Residence at the venture firm Atlântico looking for her next venture, starts full time as founder and CEO of Sempre+, the start of work on a pediatric service inside WhatsApp.

Gabriela Migliorini, Head of Product for the Jus IA legal assistant at Jusbrasil in 2025 and an early Trybe employee, joins as co-founder and chief product and technology officer, giving the company its technical lead for the Dra. Med assistant.

description.value: Enterprise AI infrastructure startup that connects and organises a large company's scattered data (ERPs, CRMs, data lakes, spreadsheets, documents) into a governed context layer, a 'company brain', that AI models and agents can use at lower token cost.

long_description.value: Strattum is a Brazilian startup that builds the layer between a large company's scattered data and its artificial-intelligence tools. Most big firms keep information in ERPs, CRMs, data lakes, spreadsheets and documents; when they connect a CRM directly to a language model, the answers are poor and the token bill is high. Strattum does not build agents or models of its own. It connects those sources once, organises and relates the information, and keeps it in a governed 'context layer', which it calls the company brain, so that different models and agents can reuse the same context with fewer tokens and cheaper models. It stresses four benefits for large enterprises: faster AI projects, lower operating cost, data sovereignty (the technology runs in the customer's own environment) and information governance with access controls. It sells across industries (retail, finance, technology and the real economy) with a first focus on financial services and on Brazil. Revenue comes from a hybrid model: a fixed platform subscription that includes a token allowance, plus a transactional fee above it; dedicated forward-deployed engineers help each customer start, though the company says it does not aim to profit from that service. The company was founded in early 2026 by Carlos Eduardo 'Kadu' Monguilhott, CEO, who spent 11 years at Neoway, including as CEO, and took part in its sale to B3 in 2021 (R$1.8 billion, per Mixvale), and Rafael Viana, CTO, co-founder of the identity-verification company Certta, where they met. In June 2026 it announced a US$3.2 million pre-seed co-led by Maya Capital and ONEVC with Norte Ventures and three angels, among them Andrew Prozes (former CEO of LexisNexis) and Jim Peck (former CEO of TransUnion, now at NielsenIQ). It said it already had initial customers with high tickets for the stage and planned 35 hires by the end of 2026, including people from QuintoAndar, Red Hat and Neoway. By late July it had begun testing the platform abroad and was weighing a new round for international expansion, with an ambition to become a Brazilian big tech. On 2026-09-09 it acquired Tropicalia, a Silicon Valley context-engineering start-up founded in 2025, in an acqui-hire: Tropicalia ceased operating and its founders Arthur Guttilla (head of product marketing and partnerships) and Leonardo Miranda (application team) joined Strattum. Next steps named: connecting the company brain to more enterprise customers, advancing governance and putting more use cases in production on cheaper models.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: large companies want to put AI into production but their data sits in ERPs, CRMs, data lakes and documents that were never organised for it, so projects stall or burn tokens on unstructured context. The company cites a statistic from the press that only 6% of large companies have structured data good enough to feed AI models (a claim relayed by Mixvale, not independently checked). Logic: the models are becoming a commodity and cheaper, so the lasting value moves to whoever owns the governed context layer; a platform that connects the data once, runs inside the client's environment and lets the client switch to cheaper models has a clear return (lower token cost) and a clear buyer (the CIO or head of data). Market: no independent market-size page was read. Bottom-up estimate: Brazil has on the order of 10,000 companies with 500 or more employees (our assumption, not a verified count); if a platform subscription plus usage is worth R$300,000 to R$1.5 million a year to such a customer (our assumption), the total addressable pool is R$3 billion to R$15 billion a year, and with 10% to 20% adopting enterprise AI context platforms in the next five years, R$0.3 billion to R$3 billion. A 5% to 10% share of that would be R$15 million to R$300 million a year in Brazil, before any foreign expansion, which the company says it is testing. Different: the founders have sold complex data products to large Brazilian firms (Neoway, which B3 bought for R$1.8 billion per Mixvale, and Certta), have angels who ran LexisNexis and TransUnion, and focus on the context layer rather than agents; comparables abroad in data and context infrastructure raise much larger rounds, but we did not read their pages. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed, highly capable founders and adds value by bringing top funds and angels to the cap table and connecting the right people; Strattum's round came with two leading seed funds and senior angels, and its enterprise sale benefits from introductions to corporate buyers. This is our reading, not a Norte statement. Risks: crowded space (data platforms, cloud vendors and model labs add context features), long enterprise sales cycles, services-heavy deployments (forward-deployed engineers) that can hurt margin, and the company is only months old with traction figures that are its own.

sub_sector.value: Data and context platform for AI agents

milestones.value: Strattum announces a US$3.2 million pre-seed co-led by Maya Capital and ONEVC with Norte Ventures, to validate its platform and build engineering, a large first cheque for a Brazilian pre-seed.
Strattum starts testing its platform in foreign markets and says it is considering a new raise to expand internationally, stating the ambition to become a Brazilian big tech.

Strattum acquires Tropicalia, a context-engineering start-up founded in Silicon Valley in 2025, in an acqui-hire that brings its two founders into the executive and application teams and adds an application layer to the company brain.

description.value: Rio de Janeiro company that builds and runs AI agents for businesses, plugged into the email, calendar, CRM and databases a team already uses and driven by natural-language conversation, deployed in days.

long_description.value: Taicor describes itself as 'the AI company of Rio' and sells AI agents that it says work in days rather than months. The agents are offered as a service: they connect to the tools a team already uses, such as e-mail, calendar, CRMs and databases (the terms name Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 integrations through OAuth), and carry out tasks that users ask for in natural language. The agents read data on demand and, according to the terms, Taicor does not store, copy or sell the data they reach. The site's call to action is for a prospect to tell the company where its team loses time, and Taicor 'shows what is possible' with an answer in one business day and a demo; it also advertises that it is hiring people who are exceptional at applied AI. The page states it is powered by Claude. The two founders come from finance rather than from software companies. João Henrique Lisboa, a programmer and engineer by training, was for more than ten years a technology investor as partner and co-portfolio manager at IP Capital Partners (2014 to 2025 on his profile); his profile dates his Taicor co-founder role to January 2026, and he is a Claude Community Ambassador with Anthropic who hosts the Claude community events in Rio. Luiz Guilherme Gama, co-founder from April 2026 on his profile, was founding partner and CEO of the investment firm Vista Capital from 2015 to 2024, after Vinci Partners, and sits on the board of a medical centre. The registry lists Gama as administrator since the company opened on 2025-05-13 and Lisboa since 2026-04-16. The Mapa IA Brasil directory lists Taicor among Brazilian AI-agent start-ups, in 'Agents and automation', Rio de Janeiro, with both founders. The founders' public activity is the visible traction. On 2026-03-23 Lisboa hosted the second Rio edition of Claude Code for Everyone, an event sponsored by Anthropic, and on 2026-06-30 the Claude Meetup Rio, with VTEX and Taicor as local sponsors. Behind the brand is Taicor Tecnologia Ltda, opened in Rio with a capital of R$2 million, and a foreign partner, Taicor LLC, joined on 2026-10-08, which points to a US holding set up after outside money. The terms of use are dated 19 March 2026 and the privacy notice November 2026. Despite searches by company name, domain and the founders' names, no customer, case study, pricing, revenue or funding announcement was found, so what Taicor has built for clients is unknown.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: companies know AI agents could remove repetitive work from their teams (inboxes, calendars, CRM updates, reporting), but few have the engineering time to build agents that work reliably with their own tools and data. Logic: models are now good enough to act through e-mail, calendar and CRM connectors, so a firm that packages agents, integrations and deployment as a service can go live in days and learn from many customers. Market: no market-size page was read. Our rough estimate: Brazil has on the order of 100,000 firms with enough staff to buy an agent service (our assumption); at R$60,000 to R$300,000 a year each (our assumption) the pool is R$6 billion to R$30 billion, and a realistic 1% to 3% reached in five years would be R$60 million to R$900 million, a very wide range because we know neither the customer segment nor the price. Different: nothing in the product is visible yet beyond speed to deploy and a Rio base; agent-as-a-service is crowded (model labs, automation vendors and many Brazilian start-ups listed in directories such as Mapa IA Brasil). What is distinctive is the team and its position: two former investors, one a programmer by training, who sit at the centre of the Claude community in Rio (a Claude Community Ambassador host and sponsors of local events), which is a channel to the first customers and to talent. Fit with Norte (our reading): the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders and helps with hiring, revenue from day zero and bringing funds onto cap tables; founders with ten years of investing behind them know the cap-table side already, and an applied-AI services company needs customers and talent more than capital, which is where a connector is useful. This is our reading only; Norte's participation is not documented. Risks: commoditisation by model providers, services-like margins, dependence on a single model vendor (the site says it is powered by Claude), and almost no public evidence of customers or traction, so the case rests on the founders; both come from finance and neither has run a software company that we could verify.

sub_sector.value: Applied AI agents for business teams

milestones.value: João Lisboa, a technology investor for ten years at IP Capital Partners, starts as co-founder of Taicor, bringing an investor's network and a programmer's training to the new agent company.
Lisboa hosts the second Rio edition of Claude Code for Everyone, an Anthropic-sponsored community event on building with AI agents, the first public sign of Taicor's place in Rio's Claude community.

Luiz Gama, founder of the investment firm Vista Capital until 2024, joins Taicor as co-founder on his profile, completing the two-founder team (he has been the registry's administrator since the company opened in 2025).
Taicor and VTEX are the local sponsors of the Claude Meetup Rio, hosted by Lisboa, which shows the company paying to be present in the community that supplies its early customers and hires.
Mapa IA Brasil's October 2026 edition lists Taicor among Brazil's AI-agent start-ups, with both founders named.

description.value: Early-stage security company that says it protects businesses against AI-powered attacks, calling itself an 'Iron Dome' and the first and final line of defence; services are sold by enquiry.

long_description.value: Backline Inc. presents itself as 'the Iron Dome against AI-powered attacks' and 'the first and final line of defence to stop AI-powered attacks'. Its public footprint is a single landing page: a headline, an address for business enquiries about its services, an address for people who want to join, and a 'backed by' line with the logos of Village Global, Behring Founders and Norte. The site does not describe any product, price, customer, founder or place; the page was registered as a domain in November 2025 and carries a 2026 copyright, which suggests a company in its first months, probably in stealth. It should not be confused with Backline AI (backline.ai), an Israeli start-up that fixes software vulnerabilities with AI agents and raised a US$9 million seed in January 2025; that company's investors do not include the three named on this site, and it is a different business. The owner supplied the legal name Backline Tecnologia Ltda (CNPJ 66.810.297/0001-69), a software company opened in São Paulo on 2026-04-29 with one administrator, Leandro Silva Duarte, and a US partner, Backline Holdings, Inc., that entered on 2026-10-21; that link to this site rests on the owner's word, the name and the 'Inc.', and no page states it. Nothing more can be said until the company publishes more.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: attackers are using AI to find and exploit weaknesses faster and with more convincing phishing and impersonation, while most companies' defences were built for human-paced threats. Logic: a security company built from the start around AI-driven offence could be positioned for the next wave of corporate security spending, and the site is deliberately minimal, which fits a stealth start. Market: no page was read on market size, so we give none beyond the direction: cybersecurity is a large and growing line in corporate budgets, but any figure here would be our guess. What is different: we cannot say; the site names no product, founders or customers. Fit with Norte: the site shows Norte as one of three backers with Village Global and Behring Founders, which is consistent with Norte's Manifesto of backing obsessed founders and bringing in other funds; the founders are not identified in any source we read, so we cannot judge the founder fit. This is our reading only. Risks: the company may be in stealth with no product yet, security is crowded and well funded, and there is a namesake (Backline AI) that can confuse customers and investors. The thesis is deliberately short because the evidence is almost nil.

description.value: Brazilian platform for building and running AI agents across customer service, sales and retention in large companies, made by Namastex Labs, a generative-AI research lab from Uberlândia.

long_description.value: KHAL is a Brazilian platform for building and running AI agents in the customer-service, sales and retention operations of large companies. It is made by Namastex Labs (legal name Namastex Labs Serviços em Tecnologia Ltda, trade name KHAL), a generative-AI research lab from Uberlândia, Minas Gerais. The pitch is that CX teams are 'held hostage by their own software': KHAL takes a company's knowledge base, rules and past conversations, maps conflicts and duplicates between them, and puts agents in production across chat, voice and WhatsApp, with the service, sales and retention context kept in one place so that the customer never retells the story. The company says the first agent is live in two weeks and sells through forward-deployed engineers who work inside each client in squads (the careers page lists senior and mid-level FDEs, a knowledge-base ETL owner and customer-success and enterprise-sales leads). It also runs AI CX Brasil, a media and research arm with a news radar, guides, columns and studies, and a free 'IAzômetro' diagnostic of how mature a company's use of AI in service is.Namastex Labs was founded in 2022 (the company says in the second half of the year, three months before ChatGPT; the registry opens it on 2022-04-26) as a research lab in Uberlândia with Felipe Rosa as the administrator since day one.
