In 2023 and 2024 it contributed to the open-source Langflow project and released its own tools, among them Genie, with thousands of weekly downloads, and its first enterprise work came from outside Brazil. In 2025 a merger with an AI-native edtech gave it product vision and knowledge of the CX market, and KHAL took shape as an agentic platform for enterprise CX. Antonio Gouveia, who the company calls KHAL's founder and who has been an administrator of the legal entity since April 2026. Customers named are Hapvida, Callink and Movecta. For Hapvida, a large Brazilian health-insurance group, KHAL built Eugênia, a sales agent that went live 13 days after the decision to start (17 April 2026), is connected to 16 legacy systems, talks by text, voice and image, and in six months served more than 400,000 people, of whom more than 13,000 bought a plan (27,000 lives); the company says leads that passed through it convert three times more. For Movecta it reads support tickets, fills more than ten Salesforce fields and routes the case with about 90% accuracy and almost no human validation. All of these figures are the company's. In September 2026 KHAL ran a stand at CONAREC and collected 1,035 survey answers from 478 companies; in October 2026 it hired Tarcísio Gotto (15 years at Zup, the last as CTO) to lead technology and Riemann Cesar (more than 25 years in Contax, AlmaViva and Algar) to lead revenue. In August 2026 a US entity, Namastex Labs LLC, became a partner of the Brazilian company, and the company says it is expanding go-to-market outside Brazil. No funding round was found in readable sources.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: large Brazilian consumer-facing companies (health insurers, banks, telecoms, retailers) run service and sales contact centres with thousands of agents, fragmented legacy systems and strict regulation, and their chatbots were rule-based and failed at anything not scripted; each unresolved contact costs money and each missed lead is lost revenue. Logic: language models now make it possible for an agent to read policies and past conversations, query internal systems and finish a task, so the contact centre can be partly replaced and, more importantly, can start selling and retaining; the company's Hapvida case (live in 13 days, 400,000 people served in six months, 13,000 plans sold, three times the conversion of leads that did not pass through the agent, all company figures) is the kind of proof large buyers need to repeat the project in other journeys, and KHAL's model of engineers embedded in each client turns one project into expansion. Why now: LLM agents became reliable enough in 2025 and 2026, and Brazilian service is heavily outsourced and labour-based. Market: the only independent size read is the consultancy E-Consulting's estimate that Brazil's contact-center market, outsourced and in-house, billed R$54.1 billion in 2019 (R$51.3 billion in 2018; TI Inside), which is old, so we treat it as an order of magnitude of about R$50 to 70 billion a year today (our assumption, not a source). If AI agents captured 10% to 20% of that spend, the pool is R$5 to 14 billion a year (about US$1 to 2.5 billion at roughly R$5.5 a dollar); a vendor that took 5% to 10% of that pool would bill about R$250 million to R$1.4 billion (US$50 to 250 million). Latin America and other countries are an upside the company states as its plan, not evidence. What is different: it starts from a research lab with open-source credibility (Langflow, Genie), sells outcomes to enterprises rather than a self-serve tool, ships fast, and has hired leaders from Zup and the outsourcing industry who know its buyers. Competitors are global agent platforms (Sierra, Decagon and Netomi were named as raising money in CX funding roundups in the search results; those pages were not read), Brazilian conversational vendors and the BPOs themselves, which will also sell AI. Fit with Norte: our reading, not Norte's statement. Norte says it backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders, builds on its network of operators and does not meddle in operations; KHAL's team came out of research and sells to large companies, where an operator network can open doors and help hire senior go-to-market talent, as the October 2026 hires suggest the company needs. Risks: crowded category where foundation-model providers and global platforms can undercut; enterprise concentration (Hapvida is the reference); long sales cycles; the services-heavy, FDE-based delivery limits margins and speed; and little public information (no round, price or revenue found). Confidence is low: the market size is old and every traction number is the company's.

milestones.value: Namastex Labs is founded in Uberlândia as a generative-AI research lab, a few months before ChatGPT, with the team working full time on the technology before the market had validated it.

The team contributes to the open-source Langflow project and releases its own tools, including Genie, with thousands of weekly downloads; its first enterprise projects are with universities and companies outside Brazil.

A merger with an AI-native edtech gives the team product vision and knowledge of the customer-experience market, and KHAL begins to take shape as an agentic CX platform on top of Namastex's technology.

The Eugênia sales agent built with KHAL goes live at Hapvida on 17 April, 13 days after the decision to start; connected to 16 legacy systems, it later serves more than 400,000 people and sells more than 13,000 plans.

KHAL has a stand at CONAREC in São Paulo (23-24 September) and runs its AI-maturity survey, collecting 1,035 answers from 478 companies; Hapvida's marketing VP and Antonio Gouveia present the Eugênia case.

KHAL hires Tarcísio Gotto, 15 years at Zup and its CTO, to lead technology, and Riemann Cesar, with 25 years at Contax, AlmaViva and Algar, to lead revenue, building a senior team to sell to large service operations.

description.value: Venezuelan cloud administrative system for small and medium businesses (sales, inventory, accounts, reports in bolivars and dollars), with Fina Presta, a loan for the businesses that use it.

long_description.value: Fina is a Venezuelan software company that sells a cloud administrative system to small and medium businesses and is now adding credit on top of it. The product replaces the notebook, the Excel file and the phone notes with one platform for sales, inventory, accounts receivable and payable, bank accounts, customers and profit reports, working in bolivars and dollars at the same time: it takes the Central Bank of Venezuela's rate, computes the exchange difference and lets the same invoice be issued in bolivars, dollars or euros. It is built for poor connectivity and power cuts, and runs from a phone. Customers are bodegas, hardware and auto-parts shops, clothing and tech stores, restaurants, barbershops and distributors. The subscription starts at about US$35 a month (Bloomberg Línea, at the official rate) and includes invoicing, inventory and a basic CRM; the company says its customers asked, before Fina, for nothing more than Excel or a notebook (about 90% according to a co-founder), so the real competitor is having no system at all, and that foreign tools such as QuickBooks do not handle several currencies in one account. The company also ships AI features: stock is loaded from a photo of the supplier invoice, and Nina, an agent trained on the business's own sales, costs and cash flow, answers questions such as what to restock. The founders are four Venezuelans: Enrique Rivas (CEO), Diego Aponte, Alejandro Fariña (CTO) and Sebastián Sánchez. Rivas and Aponte had started, in their teens, Caracas Ron, a liquor delivery business, and an imported-goods shop; the cash that did not match, the inventory that vanished and three administrative systems that did not fit Venezuelan trade led them to build their own. Fina reached the market at the end of 2023. Its second line is Fina Presta, a loan for businesses that have used Fina for at least 60 days: US$100 to US$3,000, no collateral or paperwork, requested inside the platform, paid out in bolivars in under 30 minutes and repaid in fortnightly instalments, with a line that grows as the business pays on time; the pilot users spent 85% of the money on stock. The lender uses the sales and inventory history Fina already holds as its credit data. In August 2026 Fina announced a US$1 million seed round co-led by SquareOne Capital and Tomorrow Capital, with Norte Ventures, Platanus and Neer Venture Partners and Latin American SaaS and fintech angels (Omie, Bold, Conta Simples, Colektia, Hackmetrix). It followed two smaller earlier rounds of US$100,000 and US$350,000 (Startup Researcher, undated). The company reports more than 5,000 active businesses, close to US$2 million in annual recurring revenue and about 50 new customers a day, and says Fina Presta grows 2x month over month. The money is for financial products and AI tools over six months, digital invoicing, automatic financial statements that could become an auditable credit history, and, longer term, expansion across Latin America with a goal of US$10 to 20 million ARR.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: Venezuelan small businesses (bodegas, hardware stores, parts shops, restaurants) run on notebooks, Excel and chat messages, price in two currencies on the same day, lose stock without noticing and cannot show a lender any history; ERP and accounting tools built for stable economies assume one currency, stable internet and an accountant. Logic: a very low-cost subscription (about US$35 a month) wins the daily record of sales, stock and cash; that record is then the only credit data the business has, so lending to the same customers is cheaper to underwrite and safer than any outside lender can manage. Why now: electronic invoicing rules from the tax authority (SENIAT) make a system an obligation, and since January 2026 the country moved from excluded to a market foreign investors are looking at (LatAm Fintech), with the UNDP projecting 2026 growth of 7.4% and inflation near 272%, so many businesses need tools to see their numbers before investing. Market: no recent official count of Venezuelan SMEs was readable. The only figure read is a Fedecámaras president's 2018 statement of about 280,000 companies, down from more than 490,000 twenty years earlier (Panamá América, EFE), which is old and probably lower today; our assumption is 150,000 to 250,000 formal businesses that could use such a system. Bottom-up: 5,000 customers at US$35 a month is US$2.1 million a year, which matches the US$2 million ARR the company reports; 100,000 customers (the CTO's multi-year ambition) would be about US$42 million a year in subscriptions; at the assumed 150,000 to 250,000 businesses, the whole subscription market is roughly US$60 to 100 million a year at this price, so a strong outcome is a 30% to 50% share, around US$20 to 50 million, and lending revenue (loans of US$100 to US$3,000 repeated through the year) can add as much again if credit losses are controlled. Beyond Venezuela the company says it wants to reach other emerging markets, which is a stated aim, not evidence. What is different: it is designed for dollarised, two-currency commerce and low connectivity, sells to the business that has no system at all rather than displacing a rival, and has a lending product that uses its own data. Comparables named in the sources and read: Omie (Brazil) and Bold (Colombia), whose founders invested as angels, built administrative or payments platforms for small businesses in unstable economies; Cashea (Venezuela, US$100 million raised in 2026 per Bloomberg Línea) shows investor appetite for Venezuelan fintech. Fit with Norte: our reading, not Norte's statement. Norte says it backs obsessed founders who know more than it does, adds value by connecting people and bringing top funds and angels to cap tables, and does not meddle in operations. Fina's founders ran two businesses of their own before building the product, the round brought funds from four countries and Brazilian SaaS operators who have solved the same problem (Omie's CEO), and it is a small, early cheque in a market where a Brazilian network can open doors. Risks: country risk (sanctions rules, inflation near 270%, currency controls and a possible policy reversal); concentration of a lending book in one economy where defaults and funding for loans are unproven (the pilot's results are the company's own); a small market in dollars per customer; and key-founder dependence. Confidence is low to medium: the market size rests on an old count and our assumptions, and almost all traction figures come from the company.

sub_sector.value: SME management software and credit for emerging markets

milestones.value: Fina reaches the market in Venezuela with a simple administrative system for small businesses, built after its founders ran a delivery liquor shop and an imported-goods store on Excel and found no system made for Venezuelan trade (bolivars and dollars the same day).

Fina launches Fina Presta, a no-collateral loan of US$100 to US$3,000 for businesses that have used Fina for 60 days, paid out in under 30 minutes in bolivars. It turns the sales and inventory history into credit data and, by August, was growing 2x month over month according to the company.

Fina announces a US$1 million seed round and says it serves more than 5,000 active businesses, with nearly US$2 million in annual recurring revenue, with funds from the United Kingdom, the United States, Chile and Brazil.

Fina presents its AI layer: inventory loaded from a photo of the supplier invoice, and Nina, an agent trained on the business's sales, costs and cash flow that answers questions such as what to restock. It also announces digital invoicing and automatic financial statements as the next launches.

description.value: Technology group for Brazilian grocery retail formed in 2026 by joining the supermarket-software companies Bluesoft and VR Software, which aims to apply AI and agents to stock, pricing and store operations.

long_description.value: Quantum is a technology group for grocery retail that began operating in Brazil in September 2026 by joining two established supermarket-software companies, Bluesoft and VR Software, and presents itself as building the next generation of software infrastructure for food retail, with vertical software, cloud platforms, data and AI. Bluesoft sells to medium and large regional chains and VR Software to local and regional supermarkets; both keep their brands for now, so the first step is consolidation: shared products and customers, lower costs and one data base on which to run AI. Together the companies have more than 500 people and, according to the announcement, are set to reach more than 10,000 food-retail customers soon, with about US$25 billion in gross merchandise volume going through their systems. Quantum was created by a group of entrepreneurs led by the American Jake Lovelady, its CEO. André Faria, Bluesoft's CEO, and Vinicius Borgo and Renato Domingos, the founders of VR Software, became partners of Quantum and part of its technology leadership. The investors named are André Street (co-founder of Stone), Augusto Lins and the funds Axa, BNP Paribas, LTS, Canary, Atmos, Maya and Positive; the list is partial and does not state the amount, the stage or whether Norte took part. The plan is to invest more than R$1 billion in technology for the sector in the first 12 months, applying AI and agent-based technology to stock, pricing, purchasing and store operation, with the stated aim that efficiency gains should reach food prices. Its LinkedIn page, read through Linked API on 2026-11-24, describes a technology group for grocery retail 'globally', with São Paulo as its location. No public product page of its own was found: the qntco.com.br site did not answer.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: supermarkets run on thin margins (gains of half to one percent of sales matter), and their software is fragmented: several ERPs, point-of-sale and supplier integrations and support teams that do not share data, so stock-outs, idle stock (Scanntech's August 2026 radar, quoted by Descomplica: 4.7% of items out of stock, 11.4% of items in the store that do not sell) and poor pricing and purchasing remain. Logic: Quantum buys the systems that already run inside thousands of stores (Bluesoft, VR Software), so it owns the data and the daily workflow, and can then add forecasting, pricing and purchasing agents on one data base; consolidation also lowers support and development cost per client. Why now: language-model agents make it practical to automate purchasing and pricing decisions, and the founders of both acquired companies stay as partners. Market: the Ranking ABRAS 2026 reports R$1.14 trillion of food-retail revenue in 2025, with self-service stores at R$563.6 billion, 439,728 stores and 9 million jobs (Central do Varejo, 2026-04-30). The software spend on top is not published in a page we read; our assumption is 0.3% to 0.6% of self-service sales, or R$1.7 to 3.4 billion a year (about US$300 to 600 million at R$5.6 a dollar), which is only an order of magnitude. If the group reached 10,000 clients and a 10% to 20% share of that spend, revenue would be R$170 to 680 million a year (US$30 to 120 million). The R$1 billion investment plan and the target of 10,000 customers are the company's, not evidence. What is different: it starts with scale and installed base, not a pilot; it is led by operators and investors with a track record (the co-founder of Stone is an investor); and its brands stay close to two customer segments. Competitors are the other established retail-software vendors and global suites; none was read for this entry, so none is named. Fit with Norte: our reading, not Norte's statement. Norte says it brings top funds and angels onto cap tables, helps generate revenue from day zero and does not meddle in operations; a roll-up led by a seasoned CEO, with Maya and other Brazilian funds, is a case where a connector can help with funding partners and hiring. Norte's role in this round was not found in any readable source. Risks: integration risk of merging two software companies (customers and engineers leaving), a consolidation thesis that depends on funding and on the quality of data, long sales cycles in a fragmented client base, and the possibility that the R$1 billion plan is not met. Confidence is low: the software-spend share is our assumption, and there is no round size, valuation or Norte confirmation.

milestones.value: Quantum starts operating in Brazil by integrating Bluesoft and VR Software, with more than 500 professionals, a target of more than 10,000 food-retail customers and about US$25 billion of merchandise going through their systems; it announces more than R$1 billion of technology investment in its first 12 months, with AI and agents at the centre.

description.value: Stealth-stage Brazilian startup building 'The Finance Agentic Layer': AI agents for the finance and accounting back office. Its site is an under-construction page.

long_description.value: Glue is a stealth-stage Brazilian startup that describes itself as 'The Finance Agentic Layer'. Its site, useglue.ai, is a single 'under construction' page with that tagline and two contact addresses, so the product is not public. What is known comes from its two co-founders' LinkedIn pages, read through Linked API on 2026-11-24: Mateus Parra Sgarbosa, a former head of finance at the insurtech Azos (which he saw grow from seed to a Series B with more than 200 employees and about US$50 million raised), says that closing the books took 25 days or more and that errors were frequent, and that he is building a company to reinvent accounting and the back office in Latin America with AI and local knowledge; his experience entry, from May 2025, says the company is in the ideation phase of an AI startup that uses agents to automate reconciliation, accounting entries and tax workflows. Vitor Pajaro, the second co-founder, is a former chief of staff and head of revenue operations at Rocket.Chat and D1 and a venture investor at Astella from July 2022 to September 2025; he lists a co-founder role at a stealth company in São Paulo from November 2025. The two profiles do not name Glue, so the identification of the company with these founders comes from the owner's context note and is not confirmed by a public page. The domain useglue.ai was registered on 2025-09-15. Nothing public states a customer, a launch, a round or a business model; the company should be read as an AI-for-finance-and-accounting product still being built.

investment_thesis.value: Problem: finance teams and accountants in Brazil spend days closing the books, reconcile bank and ERP records by hand and track a complex tax system; one of the co-founders describes closings of 25 days or more and frequent errors at a fast-growing insurtech. Logic: language-model agents can read statements, invoices and ledgers, propose reconciliations and journal entries and prepare tax steps for a human to approve, so accounting becomes software and not hours; the layer sits on top of existing ERPs, which lowers the cost of adoption. Why now: reliable LLM agents arrived in 2025 and 2026. Market: Brazil has 101,880 registered accounting organisations, up 40% from 2020 to 2025, with almost 540,000 professionals working (Escola Exchange benchmark reported by Sitecontabil, read). The rest is our assumption, not data: if a finance agent layer were sold at R$20,000 to R$60,000 a year to 3% to 8% of the offices (about 3,000 to 8,000 clients), revenue would be R$60 to 480 million a year (US$11 to 86 million at R$5.6 a dollar); adding in-house finance teams of mid-size companies could multiply this, but no count was read. What is different: the founders combine first-hand finance operations (a head of finance who lived the problem) with a venture investor who has seen many companies' stacks; it is too early to say what the product does differently. Competitors in AI accounting exist in Brazil (for example Bond, in this portfolio, and others); none was studied here. Fit with Norte: our reading, not Norte's statement. Norte says it backs obsessed, intelligent founders who know more than Norte does and adds value by connecting the right people and bringing top funds and angels; a pre-product team with strong operating and investing backgrounds is the kind of stage where such a network matters. Risks: no product, customers or round are public; crowded category with well-funded rivals and the ERPs themselves; trust and liability in accounting; and the founders' identification with Glue is unverified. Confidence is low.
